This study presents the initial generalization error bounds for a neural network-based approach to computing high-dimensional Schr\"odinger eigenvalues. By utilizing neural networks to approximate eigenfunctions, we address a nonlinear integral equation. Focusing on wide two-layer networks, we demonstrate an exponential generalization error bound relative to the required cover size, which itself depends exponentially on the dimensionality. Consequently, we establish an intermediate dimensionality dependence for the final generalization error. These findings provide an a priori justification for the superior performance observed in data-driven neural network approximations of quantum eigenvalues compared to traditional basis set methods, which typically exhibit a polynomial rather than exponential dependence on the required cover size for the target function. Numerical experiments conducted to support these theoretical results can be found in our prior work [1].

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are established for learning dynamics from time series, yet for neuroscience applications, it remains unclear whether they can accurately model the dipoles and action potentials of *C. elegans* neurons. This study demonstrates that RNNs successfully model action potentials, surpassing linear models in both prediction accuracy and information theory metrics. Furthermore, we show that RNNs can effectively model the *connectivity matrix* derived from the correlation of action potentials across neurons, a feature that linear models fail to capture. RNNs also outperform linear approaches in predicting the activity of individual neurons. Crucially, RNNs are capable of modeling action potentials and dependencies between neurons that exist only during specific behaviors. By applying a recently proposed method to train RNNs without minimizing prediction error, we reveal that RNNs can replicate the dependency structures of action potentials across various activities. These findings indicate that RNNs can model the dynamics of *C. elegans* neural activity and offer a promising framework for neuroscience research. Additionally, this work opens a pathway for developing learning algorithms that can discover the rules governing *C. elegans* behavior. This paper is a submission to the ICML 2021 DLS Track. We have recently shown that the amenability of a group can be characterized by the existence of a finite Markov extension for the Dyck shift such that every branch group possesses a non-trivial parabolic subgroup. In this paper, we explore an infinite extension situated between the Dyck shift and the finite extension we constructed. We demonstrate that this intermediate extension exhibits several distinct properties: it fails to admit a symbolic representation, it is not fixed point forest when considered as an extension of the Dyck shift, and it becomes a fixed point forest only when viewed as an extension of the finite extension. Furthermore, we prove that the amenability of the local constraint of the fixed point forest remains undecidable. This finding stands in contrast to the result that the amenability of finite local constraints for full shift extensions is decidable, a result due to Downarowicz, Kolyada, Mislov, and Swynnedy. The proof of undecidability relies on a fixed point that is not periodic and is constructed using a variant of Morita equivalence. Additionally, we establish that the local constraint of a fixed point forest is invariably a fixed point forest. Finally, we examine various approaches to defining extensions of formal languages that remain decidable regarding the amenability of finite local constraints. Specifically, we analyze extensions of unary full shifts, showing that amenability is decidable for finite extensions and undecidable for infinite extensions. We also investigate unambiguous extensions, which are significant in complexity theory, and examine certain extensions of inverse monoids. Finally, we present examples of fixed point forests that are not isomorphic to finite local constraints. These examples arise naturally from an alternative method of generating fixed point forests and are derived from a variation of the game developed by Downarowicz, Kolyada, Mislov, and Swynnedy. We establish that the amenability of such forests is undecidable, a result consistent with the undecidability of amenability for fixed point forests of generic formal language extensions. The underlying mechanism for this undecidability is again provided by a non-periodic fixed point generated via modified Morita equivalence. The remainder of the paper is structured as follows: we begin by reviewing fundamental concepts and collecting necessary lemmas; we then define various types of extensions of formal language shifts and examine their properties; subsequently, we define extensions of formal language shifts and address the decidability of amenability for finite extensions; we then address amenability for infinite extensions; we also examine specific types of extensions of full shifts,

We explicitly determine all robust Gelfand pairs for SL(2,p), where p represents an odd prime. This derivation relies on the fact that robust Gelfand pairs for SL(2,F), containing a finite field F, have been fully classified. Consequently, this result provides a partial resolution to the broader problem of classifying all robust Gelfand pairs for SL(2,F) in the case where F is a finite field. Additionally, we examine specific robust Gelfand pairs arising from graph theory applications. In our examination of graph theory, we analyze the Robust Gelfand pairs associated with graphs generated by vectors spaces, specifically focusing on the vector space graph and vector space matrices. We demonstrate that while vectors spaces, when viewed as additive groups, do not generate any robust Gelfand pairs, vectors spaces matrices do produce some. Furthermore, we identify that among these are two graphs previously discussed in literature: one being the graph associated with GL(2,p) and the other with the symmetric group S(p+1). We also present the robust Gelfand pairs for SL(2,3) and SL(2,5) as examples. In this presentation, we highlight the robust Gelfand pairs for graphs linked to vectors spaces, noting that while vectors spaces themselves yield no such pairs, their associated graphs do. We illustrate this by showing that the robust Gelfand pairs for these graphs are subsets of the robust Gelfand pairs of their respective additive groups. Finally, we provide a classification of robust Gelfand pairs for graphs associated with vectors spaces over GF(2). Although this classification is not exhaustive, it covers all graphs with up to 7 elements. To facilitate this, we have also included the robust Gelfand pairs for the additive groups of vectors spaces over GF(2) with cardinalities ranging from 1 to 8. We observe a pattern where the number of robust Gelfand pairs for vectors spaces over GF(2) appears to be consistent across different vectors spaces of the same size. We also note that vectors spaces seem to share common robust Gelfand pairs, which we demonstrate by showing that the robust Gelfand pairs of their associated additive groups appear as subsets. Finally, we provide the robust Gelfand pairs for vectors spaces over GF(2) with sizes 2 through 6, ensuring that the pairs for spaces of size 3 through 6 are subsets of the pairs for the space of size 2. This study investigates the production and electromagnetic signatures of the recently discovered $P_{0}(4380)$ and $P_{10}(4400)$ pentaquark states, which possess a hidden charm and single strangeness configuration. Utilizing the di-antiquark degree of freedom, we identify these states as the $S$-wave $\bar{D}\bar{K}$ molecular candidates. The analysis employs the open flavor p-wave $^{3}P_{0}$ model, treating the pentaquarks as open flavor molecular bound states within a relativistic framework. We systematically examine their production mechanisms via the $B^{-}\rightarrow K^{0}_{S}\pi^{-}$ decay, specifically focusing on the interference between the $P_{0}(4380)$ and $P_{1}(4400)$ channels. Furthermore, we provide the first predictions regarding their production rates and photo-production cross-sections, while also reporting on their electromagnetic characteristics. These findings may assist future experimental efforts in the search for analogous hidden-charm molecular pentaquark candidates. Additionally, we explore the potential for the LHCb collaboration to investigate these states at LHC energies. Our results suggest that the $P_{0}(4380)$ and $P_{1}(4400)$ could be observed in photon-fusion reactions, such as $p+p\to p+P_{(0,1)(4380,400)}+X$, where $X$ represents the remaining hadronic system. This could be achieved by selecting the $B^{-}\rightarrow K^{0}_{S}\pi^{-}$ decay channel and applying the missing mass technique to isolate the resonant signals. Furthermore, we find that the photoproduction cross sections for these states are substantial, a feature that could be investigated at the ELISeV facility. Finally, we predict that the LHCb experiment can determine the branching ratios for these processes, thereby offering valuable insights into the molecular nature of the pentaquark states. This research aims to deepen our understanding of the internal structure of the $P_{0}(4380)$ and $P_{1}(4400)$ states. Additionally, we have provided the corresponding Python code for our calculations. We anticipate that these findings will contribute significantly to the ongoing global effort to elucidate the nature of the pentaquark spectrum. In this paper, we demonstrate that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra $V$ over a field of characteristic zero is solvable. This result extends the known fact that nilpotency holds for Zinbiel algebras of trivial type. Our primary approach involves proving the supersolvability of V, a stronger condition than solvability, by showing that the dimension of any subalgebra is either odd or a multiple of a specific prime number $p$. We also present examples of Zinbiel algebras where nilpotency fails. Additionally, we establish the solvability of infinite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras of trivial type. Finally, by drawing an analogy with Rota-Baxter algebras of trivial type, we conjecture that the solvability of such infinite-dimensional algebras is also true. We support this conjecture with a proof in the specific case where the binary operation is both commutative and anticommutative. This conjecture represents a significant advancement over the result that nilpotency of degree 4 holds for these algebras. As an application, we prove that any Zinbiel algebra of trivial type—whether finite or infinite dimensional—possesses a associative approximation of degree $n$ whenever $n$ is odd. Furthermore, we note that this result does not necessarily extend to associative approximations of even degrees. We conclude by posing the question of whether solvability holds for any Zinbiel algebra of trivial type. Finally, the paper concludes with a list of open problems. This work investigates the global existence and scattering of 3-dimensional cubic heterogeneous Schrödinger equations featuring an inverse square potential. By employing microlocal analysis, we demonstrate that the scattering threshold is met at the critical power, a finding that extends the result from our previous study to homogeneous equations using solely Strichartz estimates and the local energy decay estimate derived by Kenig-Vega. Furthermore, we establish the non-existence of a continuous spectrum below the scattering threshold, thereby removing the reliance on Virial estimates previously introduced by Alazard-H\'{e}non-Viallat. The proof heavily utilizes the properties of the Laplace–Dirac operator, which arises from the change of variables associated with the equation. Additionally, our methodology avoids the use of conformal invariance. We subsequently validate these global results by explicitly constructing solutions to the stationary equation. Finally, we extend these findings to the cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation defined on a cone. Finally, this result extends to any dimension $d\geqslant 3$ and exponents $1\leqslant q<\frac{d+2}{2}$. We introduce a class of migration-spillover processes, a category of continuous-time Markov processes that encompasses both migration processes (as defined by Athreya and Jagers in 1967) and spillover processes (as defined by Bj\"ornberg and Linnerud in 2014). These processes are fully characterized by a death rate, a birth rate, an emigration rate, a migration type, and an immigration rate. For a given migration type, the migration and emigration rates adhere to a specific consistency condition, ensuring that the migration-type distribution remains a distribution at all times. The migration-spillover process represents a significant generalization of the aforementioned two processes, distinguished by the presence of an additional spillover mechanism. This mechanism involves individuals moving from negative to positive states when the birth rate falls below the death rate. We establish that these processes possess the migration property, which guarantees that the migration-type distribution maintains its distributional nature over time. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for any migration type, a distribution with finite support always possesses the migration property. We prove that the mean number of individuals is piecewise differentiable and exhibits spillover behavior when the birth rate is lower than the death rate. Additionally, we establish that these processes are positive regular and derive their associated Sp\"atzer processes. We provide a sufficient condition for the convergence of the distribution function to a delta function and investigate sufficient conditions for positive recurrence. Finally, we analyze the limiting behavior when the death rate is a non-negative constant. In this scenario, we derive the distribution function, the mean inter-event time, the mean return time, the mean time to spillover, and the spillover time. We also determine the limiting distribution of the spillover process and examine its moments. As a concluding application, we analyze a model featuring a time-dependent death rate. In this case, we derive the limiting distribution function, show that spillover does not occur, and provide the mean of the limiting distribution. Specifically, for a death rate of $t^p$ where $p>1$, we calculate the mean and show that the process exhibits spillover behavior. We further demonstrate that the distribution function converges to a delta function. Finally, we prove that the family of distributions is tight, thereby ensuring weak convergence to a delta function. This result holds true for all death rates of the form $t^p$ with $p>1$. K2-138 represents a rare red dwarf system hosting a 3:2 resonant chain of five exoplanets. This study aims to verify the linear mode stability of the resonances within this system. Utilizing the TESS light curve, we performed transit timing analysis to derive precise ephemerides and determine the periods of the exoplanets. Subsequently, we conducted a numerical N-body stability analysis to validate the 3:2 resonant chain. Our findings confirm that the system maintains linear mode stability, with all eigenvalues possessing positive imaginary components and negative real parts. Additionally, we provide the precise periods of the exoplanets and the uncertainties associated with their period measurements. We conclude that the observed periodicity variations in transit times are a result of these highly precise periods, and we provide a comprehensive discussion of these results. This paper investigates the relationship between the authentic $R$-matrix of the quantum affine algebra $\Uq(\hat{\mathfrak{sl}}_n)$ and Young walls. We demonstrate that the affine Schur algebra, constructed via induction from bi-$\s$-nilpotent blocks of a quantum affine Hecke algebra, is isomorphic to the Young algebra over $\Cq$. Furthermore, we establish an affine Schur--Weyl duality in the quantum setting by constructing a functor that maps highest weight $\Uq(\hat{\sl}_n)$-modules to projective Young walls. Finally, we characterize the simple modules of the affine Schur algebra as those corresponding to combinatorially "empty" Young walls. These findings provide an affine extension of combinatorial results by Keller and Li regarding $U_q(\mathrm{SL}_{n+1})$ and combinatorially defined Young graphs. Specifically, our results offer a new combinatorial description of the Young graph associated with the affine Schur algebra $\Ytq(\hat{\sl}_n,\V^{(1)})$. Additionally, our combinatorial framework clarifies recent findings by Keller and Li concerning the multiplicative structure of Young walls. We further demonstrate that Young walls can be utilized to construct highest weight $\Uq(\hat{\sl}_n)$-modules. Finally, we derive some results concerning the affine Schur--Weyl duality between $\Uq(\hat{\sl}_n)$ and the affine Schur algebra $\Ytq(\hat{\sl}_n,\V^{(1)})$. In this context, we provide a characterization of simple modules in terms of Young walls and determine the decomposition of tensor products of highest weight modules. These results are achieved through the construction of a functor that sends highest weight $\Uq(\hat{\sl}_n)$-modules to Young walls. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Young walls can be employed to construct highest weight $\Uq(\hat{\sl}_n)$-modules. Finally, we characterize simple modules via combinatorially "empty" Young walls and provide a description of the decomposition of tensor products of highest weight modules using Young walls. Our findings contribute to the understanding of affine Schur--Weyl duality between $\Uq(\hat{\sl}_n)$ and the affine Schur algebra $\Ytq(\hat{\sl}_n,\V^{(1)})$. The SiD detector design was developed in response to the need for precise measurements of electroweak processes and Higgs boson production and decay rates at an $e^+e^-$ linear collider operating at the multi-TeV scale. SiD represents an evolution of the SLCC and ILC working group detector designs, incorporating a highly granular dual-readout calorimeter, a streamlined inner tracker, and an $8\,\rm T$ solenoidal magnet. This document outlines a design study conducted by the SiD collaboration in collaboration with the LHCb collaboration, aimed at reducing the detector's cost, size, and complexity while maintaining a field-of-view comparable to SiD's. The resulting design features a smaller central calorimeter, a more compact inner tracker, an optimized outer tracker, an advanced magnet assembly, an advanced electromagnetic calorimeter (EMC), a straightforward muon system, and an advanced data acquisition system. These design choices were informed by the expertise of LHCb on operating large detectors with reduced complexity and cost alongside a large collaboration. The study concludes that such a detector configuration is viable and could enable the construction of a SiD-class detector at the ILC within a 10-year timeframe. This document serves as an introduction to a series of technical design reports that provide detailed descriptions of the modified SiD detector components. Specifically, this paper introduces the modified SiD tracker, magnet, EMC, muon system, and data acquisition system, while the accompanying papers detail the advanced sub-detectors developed in collaboration with LHCb. Additionally, a final section presents a summary of the overall detector design and its performance capabilities. This work was undertaken in collaboration with LHCb. Although the fundamental nature of the crystal-glass transition in water is still debated, we examined ice XI grown within a water gel in a deuterium-depleted zeolite. This method yielded the most perfect ice XI crystals identified to date, as confirmed by their narrow NMR lines. However, these seemingly uniform samples actually consist of two distinct types, as revealed by a significant bimodal distribution in their Debye-Waller factors. This discovery indicates the presence of crystal-glass domains, offering a novel and direct approach to studying this elusive transition. Furthermore, the observed coexistence of high and low Debye-Waller factor regions in ice XI aligns with the recently proposed theory of marginal rigidity. By providing a straightforward means to investigate the crystal-glass transition in well-defined ice XI samples, our method holds the potential to advance our understanding of this complex phenomenon. This study presents a system for atomic-resolution imaging and analysis of the three-dimensional local density of features (LDF) in single-crystal specimens of silicon, gold, and graphite. Utilizing a PicoProbe STM, raw data was collected at atomic resolution on silicon and gold surfaces, subsequently processed with QInsight before being analyzed via a custom program developed in C#. The results demonstrate a robust method for atomic imaging and measurement of the 3D LDF of features. Specifically, for atomic force constant values exceeding $10^{-10}$ Nm$^2$, the method accurately detects the periodicity of surface features in silicon and gold at atomic resolution. This approach offers a straightforward means to study the 3D LDF of features in single-crystal materials, which is critical for understanding the interaction between the tip and the specimen in STM. Furthermore, this technique facilitates the measurement of the relative height of surface features in these materials. In summary, atomic imaging and measurement of the 3D LDF of features in single-crystal silicon and gold surfaces are successfully achieved using Scanning Tunneling Microscopy. Additionally, the paper introduces a program written in C# that processes images from QInsight to extract and measure the 3D LDF of features in atomic force constant maps. This program is open-source and available on GitHub. The 3D Local Density of Features (LDF) represents a significant advancement in STM capabilities, enabling atomic imaging and measurement of the 3D LDF of features in single-crystal silicon, gold, and graphite. This new approach allows for the detection of the periodicity of surface features in these materials within an atomic force constant range of $10^{-10}$ Nm$^2$ to $10^{-9}$ Nm$^2$. Consequently, STM can now image the 3D LDF of features in a straightforward manner, and the provided program simplifies the measurement of the 3D LDF of features in atomic force constant maps. Finally, STM has achieved atomic imaging and measurement of the 3D LDF of features in single-crystal silicon, gold, and graphite. By analyzing the periodicity of surface features in these materials, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of the tip-specimen interaction in Scanning Tunneling Microscopy. Furthermore, STM can study the periodicity of surface features in these materials using atomic force constants within the range of $10^{-10}$ Nm$^2$ to $10^{-9}$ Nm$^2$.

Theorems constitute a fundamental element of software development, and numerous software libraries now incorporate verified theorems to establish trust within software systems. However, utilizing software-based theorem provers introduces complexity regarding how theorems are formulated, validated, and utilized. This research explores strategies to enhance the accessibility and applicability of theorems within software development workflows. Specifically, it addresses the intricate nature of advanced software environments, such as those provided by the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs (AFP), which encompasses 1,200 papers containing 15,000 theorems. By analyzing the AFP through various lenses, including hyperlinks, citation networks, LaTeX source files, and abstracts, we identify key characteristics of theorems and their usability within the ISO 24744 standard for software development frameworks. Furthermore, based on these analyses, we propose a methodology for automatically annotating theorems within AFP using the auxiliary information found in the archive's paper metadata. This study offers a framework for analyzing software environments rich in theorems and demonstrates several mining techniques applicable to broader theorem-proving archives. Additionally, we present a framework for annotating theorems via an interactive data analysis process, which includes a theorems database featuring an ontology for theorem usability. Ultra-low frequency (ULF) waves are a common feature of Earth's magnetosphere, a region of plasma where magnetic and electric fields interact with energetic particles. These regions often manifest as distinct tones or noise, making them accessible to the human ear without amplification. This paper introduces a method for visualizing and listening to magnetospheric data specifically optimized for human auditory perception. We demonstrate that this technique is readily applicable to existing data formats, such as the University of Washington's Cluster Open Data (UWCDOD) for Cluster satellite missions. We provide specific examples of ULF wave activity observed in Earth's equatorial plane, highlighting the value of this approach for both scientific analysis and public outreach. Furthermore, we examine how the location of the satellite within the magnetosphere influences the resulting audio. Finally, we offer general guidelines for making ULF waves from any plasma region clear and engaging to the human ear. Our findings indicate that for scientific purposes, filtering out-of-band frequencies and applying mild compression enhances intelligibility without compromising data integrity. For public engagement, we recommend either extending the sampling time to achieve greater compression or utilizing magnetic field components that fall within the human hearing range. In both scenarios, high-pass filtering and minor signal adjustments are sufficient to render ULF waves easily audible. We conclude that either method effectively transforms magnetospheric physics into an engaging auditory experience for the general audience. Overall, our approach demonstrates that the choice of data format can significantly impact the clarity of ULF activity when made audible. We contend that either the UWCDOD format or a custom, simplified version is appropriate for creating compelling audio representations of the magnetosphere. We provide sample code in Python to facilitate the creation of such listening experiences. We anticipate that ULF activity will captivate listeners, thereby fostering a deeper appreciation for the dynamic nature of Earth's magnetosphere. Ultimately, we aim to inspire listeners to explore the mysteries of ULF waves and the phenomena they reveal. We investigate the thermodynamic characteristics of a four-dimensional black hole solution incorporating both dilaton and log-nonlinear electrodynamics within an asymptotic Weyl-Jaackel metric. This study examines how these parameters influence the physical behaviors of the black hole, including its temperature, entropy, electric potential, angular velocity, and specific heat. Our analysis confirms the validity of the first law of black hole thermodynamics and establishes the conditions under which the horizon remains stable. Furthermore, we explore the connection between entropy and area, a relationship that is influenced by the dilaton and log-nonlinear electrodynamics fields. Finally, we identify the conditions required for reversible processes, during which the dilaton field and log-nonlinear electrodiction field vanish. These findings may facilitate the analysis of higher-dimensional black hole solutions in future research. Additionally, our results may hold significant implications for theories proposing a finite holographic entropy. Finally, we discuss how these theoretical outcomes could influence our understanding of the early universe.

This study introduces a text memory framework, where the proposed Descriptive Memory (DM) serves as the foundational memory-structure. Designed to model natural language more closely than prior approaches, Descriptive Memory enables the representation of text data as a collection of interlinked memory pages, each functioning as a dynamic knowledge unit. To develop this descriptive memory, a training algorithm was created that employs supervised learning to establish two primary data structures: the Word-Tagging-Tree (WOT) and the Tagged-Word-Tree (TWT). The WOT organizes training words by their associated tags, while the TWT arranges the authors of those tags. Once trained, the DM is applied to unseen data to generate virtual memory pages. The efficacy of this approach was evaluated through two experiments: first, a data stream classification task that compared Descriptive Memory against the Buffer, which is a recognized state-of-the-art memory structure; and second, a text mining task designed to identify the most frequently occurring tags within the input stream. The findings indicate that Descriptive Memory performs competitively with the Buffer in data stream classification and offers superior performance in text mining. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that a well-trained descriptive memory model can effectively capture the essential characteristics of text data. The descriptive memory model was implemented in Java and is available at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1987/descriptivememory. The CCR algebras, also known as Heisenberg algebras, represent the C*-algebras generated by a finite set of unitaries satisfying Weyl-CCR relations, with their dual concepts being the CAR algebras. In this note, we demonstrate that a specific family of Cuntz-Toeplitz algebras connects CCR and CAR algebras through a continuous path of transformations. This pathway originates at an CCR algebra when a parameter $s=0$, proceeds linearly to a CAR algebra at $s=1$, and extends further to encompass all intermediate C*-algebras. We provide an explicit formulation of this continuous deformation. Additionally, we examine various extensions of this path into the realm of QFT-type algebras by deforming free boson and fermion fields. Furthermore, we show that deforming the symplectic structure of the underlying real vector space yields a similar result, albeit with a more complex parametrization. Finally, we highlight that our construction offers an alternative proof for the equivalence of two previously established methods for generating deformations between CCR and CAR algebras, specifically the Segal transformation and the Cayley transform. Importantly, this equivalence holds true without relying on Fock representations. In contrast, small-step semantics are particularly well-suited for fine-grained operational reasoning about such mechanisms. However, existing small-step models often omit type information, rendering them unsuitable for early design phases or high-level reasoning about typed languages. This paper introduces a small-step operational syntax for the Generic Programming system 2, which incorporates type information into its small-step relation. We demonstrate that this model accurately characterizes type safety and supports expressive reasoning regarding exception handling. The work aligns with a broader trend in type theory and programming languages toward integrating small-step reasoning with advanced type systems. Our contribution consists of a small-step operational semantics for GP 2 that includes type annotations in its big-step relation, alongside meta-theorems proving type safety and the preservation of types across exception handling. These results are implemented using Coq and the Coq-Ext library. We anticipate that this small-step semantics will facilitate alternative reasoning about exceptions and enable the development of other meta-theorems for GP 2. The TW Hydrae association, a nearby group of young stars, serves as a critical laboratory for studying the formation of planetary systems. Observations of this association have revealed a complex network of ionized gas filaments. This study aims to test the validity of both photoevaporation and magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) disk wind models in explaining these filaments. By simulating the 1.3 cm radio emission from a protoplanetary disk within the TW Hydrae association using the RADMC-3D code, we created synthetic images to compare against observed data. Our results indicate that a photoevaporation model fails to reproduce the observed filaments, whereas an MHD wind model successfully does so. Furthermore, we determined that a disk temperature of 100 K and a magnetic field strength of 1 G are required to match the observations. These findings suggest that magnetic reconnection in the TW Hydrae association's protoplanetary disks drives a global outflow, providing a potential link between radio and X-ray emissions. Consequently, this research supports the MHD disk wind model over the photoevaporation model for explaining the structure of ionized gas filaments. Future high-angular resolution radio observations will further constrain the physical properties of these filaments. Our results imply that the TW Hydrae association's protoplanetary disks possess a magnetic field of approximately 1 G, which is significantly stronger than typical values found in other young stellar objects. This magnetic field strength could facilitate the generation of X-rays via magnetic reconnection. Additionally, we propose that the ionized gas filaments in TW Hydrae may be a common feature in young stellar objects, potentially explaining the previously reported high incidence of X-ray flares in young stellar objects. Our objective is to minimize the average delay experienced by MSs when retrieving their desired data. We demonstrate that, given appropriate data, ML models can reach the necessary mass accuracy. Current collaborative filtering techniques typically rely on a single latent variable to capture item characteristics. However, this approach often fails to adequately represent the diversity of user preferences. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel recommender system named Dual-FARM, which draws inspiration from the Dual-Cocktail Party Process (DCPP). This framework employs two distinct latent variables: a general factor that comprehensively describes common features of items in a topic, and a specific factor that captures unique attributes of individual items. User preferences are modeled as a mixture of these two factors, with the proportion governed by an allocation ratio. During the formation of user preferences, each user's taste is represented by either the general or the specific factor, determined by their allocation ratio. Consequently, items with topics sharing similar topics are recommended to users who possess a corresponding preference for that specific topic. Experimental results demonstrate that Dual-FARM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 10.5% improvement in AUC. We introduce an on-chip multi-grating system designed for the individual manipulation and measurement of trapped single atoms. This architecture features an entrance grating to position and trap atoms, lateral grating channels for repositioning trapped atoms, and exit gratings for readout. Using 250 nm aluminum gratings fabricated on chip-scale ring resonators, we demonstrate an absorption contrast of 45% for atoms trapped at the focal point and an absorption contrast of 64% for free atoms during the measurement phase. Additionally, we demonstrate the ability to move and hold trapped atoms within a grating channel. These findings establish a modular architecture capable of supporting a large-scale array of trapped single atoms. The multi-grating device presented here offers multiple pathways for individual manipulation and detection, facilitating applications in quantum simulation, quantum information processing, and sensing. The integrated optical and mechanical simplicity of our method suggests that a single-atom array could be realized through straightforward lithographic fabrication. Furthermore, the multi-grating technology offers a potential solution to the scalability challenges associated with individual manipulation and readout. Our multi-grating devices can be directly integrated into existing photonic chip platforms, such as those developed by XQPT. Additionally, the multi-grating technology is applicable to a wide range of trapped particles, including neutral atoms, ions, molecules, colloids, and nanoparticles. The nonlinear conductance of time-reversal invariant topological insulators (TIs) has been extensively studied, yielding significant insights. In contrast, the linear conductance of interacting TI surface states under disorder has received less attention. Recent research indicates that the non-linear Hall effect in time-reversal invariant topological semimetals (TRITS) can surpass that of topological insulators. This study demonstrates that the linear Hall conductance of interacting TIs, limited by weak localization, exhibits distinct characteristics compared to non-interacting systems. Furthermore, a mechanism is proposed for generating anomalous Hall conductance in time-reversal invariant semimetals, even when electron-electron interactions are present. These findings are derived from a combination of analytical methods, numerical simulations, and experimental data. Additionally, the work explores the influence of electron-electron interactions on time-reversal invariant semimetals within the framework of the random phase approximation (RPA). It is anticipated that these results will advance our theoretical comprehension of topological semimetals and insulators. The article is structured into two sections: the first covers analytical findings, while the second presents numerical and experimental results. Many optimization techniques are established for static problems, whereas few directly address dynamic ones. This paper demonstrates that a straightforward transcription method, which maps a continuous-time problem into a finite-dimensional one by simply discretizing the time horizon, serves as a powerful tool for dynamic optimization. We introduce a variant of the **penalty method** where the original continuous-time problem is reformulated to include a cost that penalizes violations of discrete-time constraints. By solving a sequence of discrete-time problems with an increasing number of time points and a corresponding increasing penalty parameter, we achieve global optimality for the problem. This approach is particularly effective for high-dimensional, non-smooth, or non-convex issues. The proposed technique is applied to a real-world scenario from the COVID-19 pandemic: **dual-patient ventilation**, where a ventilator supports two individuals. We show that optimizing dual-patient ventilation can markedly decrease infection transmission risks and enhance care quality. Furthermore, **Optimal Control** formulations for dual-patient ventilation are developed and solved using **direct transcription** paired with the **ADMM algorithm**. This research investigates bicritical rational maps that possess a specific dynamical property known as being "deck clustered." Such maps exhibit a conjugate pair of periodic points linked by a deck transformation and an interval of periodic points sharing the same prong partition. The study aims to elucidate the nature of these conjugate periodic points and their associated combinatorial features, demonstrating that the existence of a non-trivial interval with a consistent prong partition necessitates the presence of another non-trivial interval with a constant prong partition, resulting in the maps again being deck clustered. Furthermore, the paper provides a parametric description of the set of periodic bicritical maps and offers a dynamical characterization of the parameter space section corresponding to these maps. The theory is applied to iterates of quadratic polynomials and cubic polynomials with three critical points. Additionally, the properties of being deck clustered and having a constant prong partition are shown to generate new invariants for bicritical polynomials. The paper concludes with an exploration of several open questions regarding these phenomena. Notably, the existence of a non-trivial interval with a constant prong partition for bicritical rational maps yields a novel class of dynamical systems termed "eventually deck clustered" maps. The combinatorial structure of these intervals leads to a new invariant for such maps, termed the "prong partition partition," which is calculated for iterates of quadratic polynomials and cubic polynomials with three critical points. Finally, the article concludes with further open problems concerning this novel class of dynamical systems. In the appendix, the authors provide a complete description of the combinatorial types of prong partitions for all possible prong partitions of length three. Overall, the paper establishes a significant link between the combinatorial structure of prong partitions and the dynamical properties of bicritical rational maps. Specifically, the combinatorial type of the prong partition interval for periodic intervals is shown to be an invariant of the map, thereby providing a dynamical characterization for the combinatorial type of prong partitions. This characterization is subsequently applied to investigate the parameter space of bicritical polynomials. The findings suggest a new approach to understanding the parameter space of bicritical rational maps by examining the combinatorial structure of prong partitions. Finally, the paper addresses the issue of stability for bicritical polynomials by analyzing the combinatorial type of prong partitions. This chapter is part of the book *Neural Networks and Machine Learning: The Perceptron Revisited*, which explores various applications of network training. The perceptron, originally introduced in the 1950s, serves as a foundational model for modern deep learning architectures. This work re-examines supervised training of multi-layer networks through the lens of category theory, specifically utilizing change propagation and delta lenses. A primary motivation for adopting this abstract framework is to facilitate a clearer comprehension of training algorithms and to simplify the identification of strategies for extending these algorithms. By employing this method, we demonstrate that backpropagation is inherently composed of two distinct components: a forward pass and a backward pass. Furthermore, we introduce a novel algorithm, Deep Grad, which integrates the forward and backward passes of backpropagation into a single, unified step. We also present a general approach to regularization and discuss how different strategies can be formulated within this category-theoretic language. The chapter concludes by outlining potential future research directions. An appendix provides practical guidance on applying category theory to machine learning, including references to online resources and software tools. Additional resources are available at https://perceptron-revisited.net.

We establish a uniform stationary phase approximation theorem for integrals involving functions of marginal smoothness, thereby resolving an open question regarding the necessary degree of smoothness. Specifically, we demonstrate that the uniform phase condition ensures the stationarity point possesses the required smoothness. These findings find application in the uniform phase approach to the radiative transfer equation within solar physics. Furthermore, we discuss how the degree of uniformity influences the needed smoothness. The proof utilizes an alternative formulation of the wavelet transform, which facilitates the derivation of uniform phase conditions. Additionally, the theorem is applied to a double integral arising from the uniform phase condition applied to the line-of-sight integration in the solar radiative transfer equation. This application yields uniform approximations with both finite and infinite support, where the error term exhibits explicit dependence on the phases, phases' derivatives, and the wavelet function employed. We propose an optimal choice for the wavelet based on the phases' derivatives. The validity of these results is confirmed through an application to solar flare modeling. We introduce an algorithm for computing the uniform phase-based approximation of the uniform spherically symmetric radiative transfer equation, and a numerical example illustrates the accuracy of this approximation. Finally, we examine how the wavelet selection impacts the number of terms required in the approximation. Our analysis indicates that wavelets generating the fewest terms are those derived from radial B-splines. Furthermore, we show that the uniform phase-based approximation can be more accurate than the standard stationary phase approximation when utilizing an appropriately selected wavelet. This enhanced accuracy is particularly apparent in regions where the phase exhibits low smoothness. We also investigate how specific choices of wavelet families affect the uniform phase-based approximation of the radiative transfer equation. Our findings suggest that wavelets from the family $\{\psi_{a,b}\}_{a,b\in\mathbb{R},a>0}$, which yield the most accurate approximations, are those producing highly localized functions. In contrast, wavelets from the family $\{\phi_{a,b}\}_{a,b\in\mathbb{R},a>0}$, which provide the least accurate approximations, generate the least localized functions. The paper concludes with a discussion of the implications of these results. The multi-generational Horizon-10T radio interferometer is engineered to detect coherent radio bursts, such as Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs), within a volume of approximately 1000 Mpc³, which corresponds to an angular resolution of roughly 10 micro-radians. Clustering events, characterized by multiple bursts originating from the same source at various redshifts, are anticipated to exhibit this specific angular resolution. However, current super-resolution algorithms fail to capitalize on this capability. This study introduces a novel deep learning-based super-resolution framework utilizing Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to reconstruct clustered emission signals with multi-modal data, thereby enhancing the instrument's localization accuracy. We present the first theoretical analysis of the achievable resolution for these events. Furthermore, we investigate the detection of Axion Particle Nuggets (APNs) as a potential source of FRBs, specifically examining the impact of Axion-Nucleon interactions on the temporal and spectral properties of APN signals. Finally, we evaluate the detection potential of Horizon-10T for APN signals, including an analysis of how different network architectures and hyperparameters influence the detection rate. This research offers a new perspective on FRB clustering and establishes a foundation for detecting APN signals, which may represent the most common FRB source. Additionally, the applied deep learning methodology could prove valuable for other radio telescopes utilizing super-resolution techniques. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1998/Multi-Modal-Clustering. Our findings are published in *The Astrophysical Journal Letters*. [abst] 2205.00221. (2022)

The CMS experiment at the LHC reports observations of a new particle with a mass near 125 GeV in the two-photon decay channel, utilizing a dataset with an integrated luminosity of 5.02 fb$^{-1}$ collected at $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV. Employing the CMS standard likelihood approach, we observe an excess of events consistent with the Higgs boson, exhibiting a mass within 2.6 standard deviations of 125 GeV. This finding represents the most significant observation of a Higgs-like particle across all search channels conducted at the experiment. Under the Standard Model, the two-photon channel accounts for approximately 2% of the total Higgs production cross section, with the remaining 98% distributed among other final states such as $b\bar{b}$, $\tau^+\tau^-$, $W^+W^-$, $Z Z$, and $\mu^+\mu^-$. Furthermore, we present upper limits on the signal strength relative to Standard Model expectations, which range from 0.6 to 1.7 times the expected strength at 95% confidence level, contingent upon the chosen background parameterization. These results are interpreted using simplified models of new physics. Additionally, we explore the production of Higgs-like particles via vector boson fusion and through top-quark pair production. Collectively, this analysis demonstrates the first observation of a new particle at the LHC, marking a pivotal moment in the field of high-energy physics. Our primary focus is the $p$-divisibility of Fourier coefficients for Siegel modular functions of degree $n \geq 2$ belonging to the space $M_{k}(\Gamma(n))$, where $\Gamma(n)$ denotes the principal congruence subgroup of level $n$. We establish an upper bound for the $p$-adic valuation of these coefficients using the heights of algebraic correspondences. Our analysis is restricted to the case where $p$ is a prime not dividing $n$. We conjecture that this bound is optimal when $n=2$. Additionally, we apply our primary methodology to investigate the rationality of the $p$-adic valuations for the Fourier coefficients of Siegel-Eisenstein series within a specific family. Our approach relies on foundational techniques from arithmetic geometry, algebraic correspondences, and transcendental methods. We demonstrate that the $p$-divisibility is ultimately governed by the heights of these correspondences, which are estimated via transcendental methods. Furthermore, we prove that these estimated bounds are sharp for algebraic correspondences. We also present an algebraic correspondence construction that is expected to yield rational bounds. Finally, we provide an explicit calculation for the bounds regarding the Fourier coefficients of Siegel-Clemansians in the case of $n=2$. Our approach is expected to be applicable to any $n \geq 2$. However, we contend that additional insights regarding the rationality of the bounds for Fourier coefficients of algebraic correspondences are required to extend our results to rational bounds. We propose that the bounds for the $p$-divisibility of Fourier coefficients in this context are likewise governed by the heights of algebraic correspondences. We believe that the techniques employed in this work can be utilized to derive rational bounds for the $p$-divisibility of Fourier coefficients in the case of $n=2$. Additionally, we demonstrate that the bounds for the $p$-divisibility of Fourier coefficients for Siegel-Clemansians in this specific case are rational. We anticipate that the rational bounds established herein will serve as a foundation for proving the rationality of $p$-divisibility bounds for the Fourier coefficients of algebraic correspondences. This would enable the extension of our results to rational bounds for any $n \geq 2$. Our work aims to advance the understanding of the rationality of bounds for the $p$-divisibility of Fourier coefficients, thereby contributing to the broader field of number theory

The rigid fibration $f:\mathbb{A}^n\to\mathbb{A}^1$ over $\mathbb{C}$ lacks invariance under isomorphisms of $\mathbb{A}^n$, yet the collection of all such fibrations forms a universal object that retains invariance. This paper examines the precise sequences of these rigid fibrations. We establish the existence of a universal precise sequence of rigid fibrations over $\mathbb{C}$ and characterize its universal property. Furthermore, a universal property for precise spaces of rigid fibrations over $\mathbb{C}$ is derived. Finally, we outline a universal property for the product of rigid fibrations over $\mathbb{C}$ based on the universal property of their associated product of precise spaces. In the concluding section, we present several applications of these results. Specifically, we demonstrate that the precise space of a product of rigid fibrations over $\mathbb{C}$ is reductive, and that any two nontrivial rigid fibrations $f_1:\mathbb{A}^{n_1}\to\mathbb{A}^1$ and $f_2:\mathbb{A}^{n_2}\to\mathbb{A}^1$ over $\mathbb{C}$ become isomorphic when taken as products. Additionally, we provide an alternative proof for the fact that the base of the product of two affine space bundles over $\mathbb{C}$ is not necessarily an affine space. Finally, we show that the precise space of a product of affine space bundles over $\mathbb{C}$ is a torus. These findings extend to the context of schemes. Furthermore, any multi-qubit operator family $\mathcal{F}$ corresponds to a 2D classical spin lattice model. Neural networks, which form the basis of machine learning, are constructed from artificial neurons linked by synapses. These neurons operate using activation functions that integrate signals from connected neurons through synapses. In this study, we introduce a hybrid neuron-synapse architecture featuring on-off center-surround (COS) sensory fields. This structure enhances the sensitivity of local field potentials to pixel intensity variations, thereby improving the accuracy and robustness of deep learning models for image classification. Our findings demonstrate that this hybrid design outperforms traditional point-neuron approaches. Specifically, we utilized Gaussian pixel inputs and Gaussian COS sensory fields to create on-off COS fields, while summing neurons connected via synapses served as COS COS fields. We evaluated this framework using MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets, with a particular emphasis on digit recognition within the CIFAR10 set. The results indicate that this hybrid sensory field structure achieves superior performance compared to conventional point-neuron models. Furthermore, COS COS field neurons exhibit enhanced sensitivity to transitions between distinct pixel intensities. Finally, we propose a theoretical model for the COS COS firing rate that aligns with our experimental outcomes. This theoretical approach offers a more efficient model for neural simulation and image classification applications. This work introduces a general framework for investigating twisted bilayer graphene (TBC) within a strong, arbitrary dc magnetic field. By employing magnetic Bloch functions (MBFs) that are periodic within a magnetic unit cell, we derive a comprehensive set of periodic boundary conditions (PBCs) applicable to finite regions inside each magnetic unit cell. Utilizing these PBCs, we identify two infinite sets of $2\pi$-flux quasienergies, each yielding exactly two $2\pi$-flux MBFs that serve as pentalatanum degeneracy points. Furthermore, we uncover a series of reentrant infinite $2\pi$-flux flat bands at the lowest quasienergies, demonstrating that reentrant $2\pi$-flux phases are an inherent characteristic of twisted bilayer graphene. These findings are corroborated by numerical calculations, and the proposed $2\pi$-flux framework is applicable to a broad spectrum of electronic systems. Additionally, the $2\pi$-flux PBCs facilitate the systematic construction of $2\pi$-flux MBFs, offering a viable alternative to the conventional flux insertion method. This approach provides a novel perspective for defining and characterizing topological order in $2\pi$-flux twisted bilayer graphene. Finally, our proposed $2\pi$-flux PBCs can be utilized to examine the impact of open edge boundary conditions on the edge states of $2\pi$-flux twisted bilayer graphene. Specifically, we demonstrate that open PBCs give rise to a new type of edge state, termed $2\pi$-flux zigzag edge states, which possess a distinct topological nature compared to open AA/BCC PBC states. These $2\pi$-flux zigzag edge states are expected to exhibit novel transport properties, including $2\pi$-flux Aharonov-Bohm oscillations. These conclusions are supported by numerical calculations. To facilitate future $2\pi$-flux theoretical investigations, we have provided a Python code that enables the direct calculation of $2\pi$-flux quasienergies and MBFs, as well as the visualization of $2\pi$-flux electronic states. This tool is available at https://github.com/zhongqiangwang/2pi_flux_TBC. Steganography involves concealing secret messages within plain text. While steganographic text is typically generated by embedding hidden data into existing documents, producing high-quality output in controlled environments remains difficult. To overcome this, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to synthesize new text specifically designed to mask secret information. Our findings indicate that this model can effectively generate readable cover text that successfully conceals secrets without compromising integrity. Furthermore, a new automatic evaluation method demonstrates that model-produced text is statistically indistinguishable from human-written text of similar semantics. This capability enables the creation of steganographic systems operating in fully controlled settings. Although fully automated steganographic systems using our model are currently susceptible to summary-based steganalysis, manual preprocessing can significantly enhance their resistance to detection. Additionally, we observe that the model's output quality is highly sensitive to the degree of secrecy employed. Finally, we release our model and corresponding Python library as open-source to facilitate future research and applications of model-based steganography. By providing a robust, versatile, and efficient solution, our work establishes a foundation for developing fully controlled steganographic systems and advancing the field of steganography. Specifically, this research addresses the limitation that steganographic text creation is often hindered by the difficulty of writing in plain text while embedding hidden messages. By enabling the direct generation of high-quality covers that seamlessly integrate secrecy, our work offers a promising pathway for future investigations into the feasibility of fully automated steganographic systems and for driving innovation and growth within the field of steganography.

Keywords: steganography, synthesis, LSTM, secret communication, information hiding, fully-controlled steganography, steganalysis, information theory, cryptography, natural language processing, text generation.

Unit commitment (UC) represents a critical resource allocation issue within power systems, demanding the selection of optimal power supply schedules while adhering to various operational constraints. Conventional approaches typically rely on learning costs to simplify the problem and accelerate solutions; however, this strategy can result in suboptimal outcomes because a static cost framework fails to capture the dynamic nature of learning. To address this, we introduce a dynamic learning cost model that quantifies operation costs based on violation levels, thereby enabling a more accurate representation of the dynamic decision-making process. This model is developed using linear programming and can be solved rapidly. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates how this model facilitates constraint checking and proposes a novel fast algorithm for handling constraint satisfaction. Numerical experiments conducted on IEEE bus systems validate the effectiveness of this new algorithm. The results indicate that, compared to traditional UC algorithms, the proposed method reduces total operation costs by up to 10% while maintaining compliance with all operational constraints. Additionally, the approach achieves a 1000-fold reduction in computational time. Consequently, this fast constraint satisfaction algorithm provides a highly efficient solution for real-time power system operations. Finally, the study discusses the potential of this fast constraint satisfaction approach for other applications, such as unit dispatching. Overall, this work is anticipated to significantly advance the field of resource allocation. Keywords: Unit Commitment, Constraint Satisfaction, Linear Programming, Decision Making, Power Systems.

Furthermore, pressure enhances the magnetic moment, with a pronounced jump observed at the dimerization transition. We propose that the antiferromagnetic order in $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ arises from the superexchange interaction between in-plane ions, a mechanism that remains stable despite pressure-induced disorder of the Kitaev sector. These findings confirm that Kitaev quantum spin liquid candidates can exhibit robust long-range magnetic order. Additionally, the coexistence of long-range magnetic order and potential topological properties in this system may facilitate the observation of pressure-induced topological phase transitions. Synthetic control (SC) methods are widely used to create a single SC unit from a normalized blend of control units, offering a compelling approximation of a treated unit. However, the existing literature lacks rigorous theoretical underpinnings for SC. This study provides such a framework, focusing on a "nearby" scenario where the post-treatment outcome of a treated unit is approximately a linear combination of those of the control units, alongside a similar near-miss condition for pre-treatment covariates. Within this scope, we demonstrate that (i) the SC unit can accurately model both pre-treatment trends and the post-treatment outcome, (ii) the SC model achieves a minimax optimal rate for estimating the treated unit, and (iii) the SC estimator for the average treatment effect is optimal when specific model components are known. Furthermore, we propose a weighted least squares estimator for the SC unit that accommodates heteroskedasticity and time-series dependencies in outcomes. Simulation results indicate that, in cases where the SC model fits the data well, this proposed estimator outperforms the unweighted least squares estimator. Additionally, we apply the method to estimate the treatment effect of the 1990 National Voter Registration Act, revealing a significant impact on voter turnout in New Hampshire. Finally, we demonstrate that our method allows for a more precise quantification of uncertainty in causal inference, particularly when the near conditions are only approximately met. To our knowledge, this work represents the first integration of theoretical guarantees for identification and inference within a synthetic control model. The data utilized in this study can be accessed at: https://github.com/ChengfengLi1991/ST-SC. This includes the code for our SC model, as well as the data for the states example and the difference-in-differences example. The latter is adapted from Abadie et al. (2010), with the original data available at: https://www.nber.org/papers/w16221. Additionally, the state-level data required for the difference-in-differences example is available here: https://github.com/ChengfengLi1991/did. Please refer to our accompanying paper for a detailed description of the data.

Identifying the most representative and distinctive characteristics of graph data is a critical challenge in topological graph analysis. To safeguard the privacy of sensitive information, researchers have developed the Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy to quantify the difference between two graphs, thereby identifying the set of graph elements that reveal the graph's fundamental structure. However, the standard Gromov-Washerstein discrepancy exposes user privacy risks by exposing specific graph components. To address this issue, this study introduces a Local Differential Privacy (LDP)-based privacy preservation framework for graph data, which modifies the traditional Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy to protect individual graph elements. We propose an algorithm to calculate the LDP-Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy, which allows users to define a privacy budget. This budget controls the information leakage level, enabling users to balance privacy and utility based on their specific requirements. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed method's privacy guarantees and empirical results that validate both its effectiveness and its potential applications. Our numerical experiments demonstrate that the LDP-Gromov-Wasser discrepancy approach effectively hides sensitive information while preserving the graph's essential structural properties. Additionally, the empirical analysis confirms that our method achieves the desired trade-off between privacy and data utility. Finally, we illustrate that the LDP-Gromov-Wasser discrepancy approach can successfully identify the community structure of a real-world social network dataset. The source code is available at: https://github.com/ChenChunwei1992/LDP-GW-Dissimilarity-Measure. A new injection mechanism for plasma-based electron injection and acceleration is introduced, designed to function with self-steepening laser pulses of any polarization. The polarization of a small, off-axis gas jet injected into the underdense medium is managed through the interaction between the laser and the jet. This technique is demonstrated using pulses of any shape and polarization, including circularly polarized pulses where relativistic induced field effects are significant. The proposed polarization management method is highly effective, achieving electron bunches with yields of several nanoCoulombs, energies in the hundreds of MeV, and temporal durations of approximately 10 femtoseconds. Furthermore, relativistic induced field effects in circularly polarized pulse-plasma interactions are examined regarding their role in charge density generation. These findings are relevant to the development of high-current, multi-GeV electron accelerators utilizing plasma wave acceleration and x-ray sources based on plasma current channels. Additionally, the study contributes to the broader understanding of laser-plasma interaction physics. Double beta decay offers a pathway to investigate fundamental particle processes beyond the Standard Model, with ongoing research focusing on nuclei containing proton numbers near 78. This study presents revised estimates for double beta decay Q-values in these nuclei, alongside novel calculations for related dark matter processes. We examine how uncertainties in nuclear mass models influence the estimated half-lives of decay and dark matter interactions. Additionally, we explore the potential of $^{190}$Pt as a target for detecting dark matter-induced phenomena. The analysis utilizes the self-consistent relativistic energy density approximation (REDA) alongside the finite-range droplet model (FRDM) to calculate double beta decay characteristics. REDA is further employed to assess the sensitivity of different dark matter scenarios within platinum nuclei. These findings are designed to inform future experimental investigations into nuclei with Z approximately equal to or less than 82. This study examines the generalized $n$-dimensional Ermakov system, characterized by an arbitrary homogeneous degree $k$ potential. The paper establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of first integrals of orders two and higher, utilizing first and second integrals to derive the full set of preservation laws. Furthermore, the analysis demonstrates the equivalence between the nonlinear generalized Ermakov system and the linear associated system. Finally, it is proven that if the generalized $n$-dimensional Ermakov system admits first integrals of order higher than two, its Lagrangian supports the Bach tensor. These findings generalize and extend previous results found in references [1] through [15]. Specifically, the existence criteria for first integrals of order greater than two align with those established by A. I. Neimark and H. A. Ivanov [4] for general nonlinear systems. In the case of order two, the derived necessary and sufficient conditions offer an alternative to the criteria set by F. Magri [2] and A. I. Neimark and H. A. Ivanov [4]. Additionally, the criteria for the existence of a first integral depend on the value of the parameter $k$: for $k \neq -2$, they correspond to those obtained by I. S. Doob [1] and H. A. Ivanov [3]; for $k = -2$, the existence of a first integral is linked to the presence of a conformal Killing vector field, a relationship also noted by H. A. Ivanov [5]. Finally, the derived preservation laws generalize the results presented by H. A. Ivanov [6]. The methodology employed involves applying the Hamilton-Jacobi theorem and employing a vector field approach. When $k = -2$, the analysis incorporates conformal transformations, whereas for $k \neq -2$, it relies on scaling transformations. These results are applicable to the study of nonlinear dynamical systems. The paper concludes with several illustrative examples. Notably, the derived preservation laws for the generalized $n$-dimensional Ermakov system differ from those previously reported in references [17] through [20]. This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 11305051). A primary obstacle in researching automated trip planning (ATP) for public transit planning is the scarcity of data that adheres to required feed specifications, particularly for trips and timetables. ATP algorithms depend on these standard specifications to create plans, yet such data is rarely released to researchers. This study addresses this challenge by employing machine learning to convert publicly accessible trip data into the necessary standard format. To achieve this, we developed a time series learning framework that captures the chronological patterns within transit data. Our approach utilizes a pre-trained recurrent neural network to forecast missing values, thereby generating the standard feed. We constructed a large-scale dataset using real-world trip data from Seoul, South Korea, to train and assess the model. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach successfully generates feed data that closely aligns with human-generated standards. Consequently, this framework enables researchers to conduct meaningful studies on automated trip planning. The proposed framework is available at \url{https://github.com/taehyung-lee97/TransitML}. Few-shot learning projects typically depend on the assumption that target classes are drawn from a predefined set of source prototypes. This study investigates whether this pool of prototypes can instead be generated dynamically from the available data. We introduce a straightforward yet effective approach to automate the creation of these prototype images. Our method is straightforward: it involves conditioning a pre-trained Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) on existing examples to conditionally generate prototypes. We evaluate this technique across various few-shot learning benchmarks and simulate domain shifts. The findings indicate that our method can enhance performance in few-shot learning tasks. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishgupta123/Conditioned-GAN-Few-shot. Future research should explore whether this methodology can be extended to few-shot semantic segmentation. Although our current approach is limited to gANs, developing an auto-encoder based variant would be highly desirable. Furthermore, our current implementation utilizes an isotropic Gaussian prior, which is inadequate for conditions requiring anisotropic features. Consequently, a non-isotropic Gaussian prior is necessary for future iterations. Additionally, the feature extractor employed in this method is relatively basic; future work could investigate more sophisticated architectures, such as those used in style transfer. Finally, the current application is restricted to natural images; extending this method to other domains, such as medical imaging, represents a promising avenue for future research.
Keywords: Few-shot learning, GANs, Prototypes.

We investigate non-invertible global symmetries, which arise as fixed points of the renormalization group flow and induce the decimation of non-condensed topological lines in condensed phase gauge theories. Drawing an analogy to COEls, we term these symmetries persistent non-invertible symmetries. We establish a Goldstone theorem for persistent non-invertible symmetries, demonstrating that their spontaneous breaking necessitates the emergence of massless modes localized on topological defects. Furthermore, within $1+1$ dimensional Abelian gauge theories, we construct examples of persistent non-invertible symmetries using topological defects and analyze the consequences of their spontaneous breaking. Additionally, we explore an extension of these examples to $2+1$ dimensions, which may be renormalization group stable, and connect this phenomenon to the emergence of higher-form symmetries in $1+1$ dimensional non-abelian gauge theories. Finally, we connect our examples to the $S_2$ symmetry found in $6d$ superconformal field theories deformed to lower dimensions. This study introduces a novel deep neural network (DNN) designed to distinguish tau decays into hadrons from background processes involving other particles. The analysis focuses on final states containing one or more charged pions, alongside neutral pions, kaons, and photons. We trained the DNN using a simulation based on a LHC scenario where 100 GeV photons interact with protons, producing final states with up to five charged particles and up to five neutral particles. The resulting discriminant achieves a significance of 4.6 sigma for identifying hadronic tau decays, surpassing the performance of the significant figure method currently employed by the CMS Collaboration in similar searches. This enhanced capability facilitates the more sensitive identification of hadronic tau decays, thereby improving sensitivity to physics processes such as dark matter production via a light mediator. Furthermore, the simulation and DNN training procedures are fully open-access, enabling the rapid replication and application of this technique in various particle physics searches. This approach is particularly relevant for searches involving light mediators that generate final states with low visible energy, low multiplicity, and low transverse momentum. The paper concludes with a discussion of the technique's applicability to other physics scenarios. These findings were presented at the 2021 CMS Global Academy. The set-union knapsack problem (SUKP) involves selecting a subset of items to maximize total value while ensuring the union of their associated elements does not exceed a specified capacity. SUKP is a generalization of the budgeted maximum coverage problem (BMCP), which focuses on maximizing coverage rather than item value. This study introduces a novel local search algorithm featuring two new operators and a new strategy for managing the number of selected items. We also examine a large neighborhood search approach. These methods are among the most efficient for BMCP, and they establish new state-of-the-art results for SUKP. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the computational complexity of these algorithms. Finally, we demonstrate that, under specific conditions, these local search algorithms possess polynomial-time complexity. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/fernandoalvarezm/SUKP. Churn prediction is a prevalent technique in business for identifying customers likely to terminate their relationships, enabling proactive retention strategies. This study focuses on predicting customer churn within online gambling in Denmark. We evaluate the predictive capabilities of various machine learning models, including random forests, gradient boosting machines, support vector machines, and neural networks, using a dataset spanning two years. Furthermore, we assess these methods' utility for early churn detection by analyzing their ability to flag customers who will churn within 1, 2, 3, 4, or 6 months. Our findings indicate that neural networks achieve the highest precision for detecting churn occurring within one to three months, whereas random forests outperform them for churns beyond that initial period. Finally, we discuss how these insights can inform the design of targeted retention campaigns. Additionally, we examine the data preprocessing pipeline, emphasizing feature engineering, and detail the construction of predictive features that incorporate both historical and temporal dimensions. Finally, we present code snippets from our Jupyter notebooks to ensure full reproducibility of our results. This work is open-source and accessible at: https://github.com/alexanderhansen1992/churn_forecasting. Our methodology is also applicable to other sectors, such as online retail. This approach enables the calculation of TMDs within TMD factorization frameworks using exclusively perturbative inputs. By employing this method, we determine the longitudinal and transverse PDFs, as well as the TMD fragmentation function $D_{q\to q}(z,\mu_{T}^{2})$, across various scales and for different hadrons. Furthermore, we derive the splitting functions required for TMD evolution up to next-to-leading order. This evolution integrates the Collins-Furmanski-Rockner (CFR) and Small (Small) formulations for the first and higher orders, respectively. Our findings demonstrate that next-to-leading order (NLO) evolution significantly impacts TMDs, particularly at large transverse momenta and for heavy quarks. Additionally, we provide explicit formulas for the splitting matrix elements that facilitate analytical investigations. Finally, we explore the connection between our Large-Momentum Practical Theory (LMPT) and Light-Cone QCD (LCQCD), showing that LMPT emerges as a specific limit of LCQCD. Finally, we show that the LMPT evolution method successfully recovers the DGLAP splitting matrix and fragmentation function in the collinear limit. Describing risk in cycling is essential for evidence-based e-bike development. This model is validated against real-world data and compared against current descriptors. The results demonstrate that this new descriptor holds significant predictive power for microtrauma, offering greater explanatory detail than existing descriptors.
