This study investigates particle self-assembly into crystalline lattices by employing neuroevolution to identify effective particle types and initial conditions. Utilizing recurrent neural networks (RNNs), we facilitate a closed-loop design process that jointly optimizes simulation parameters and material properties. By applying neuroevolution to both two- and three-dimensional simple cubic crystals, we uncover a set of fundamental materials and phase transition scenarios essential for crystallization. These include soft spheres, soft rods, oblate and spherical liquids, and high-entropy alloys. Our findings offer a systematic framework for designing self-assembly methods to create functional materials. Furthermore, the identified materials and transitions are anticipated to hold significant potential for applications in nanotechnology. Finally, the presented framework is expected to be a highly effective tool for exploring the phase diagrams of soft materials. This work appears in Phys. Rev. Furthermore, we incorporate a background two-form gauge field to investigate 't Hooft magnetic monopoles and the associated second-type gauge anomalies. The analysis of these anomalies facilitates the description of phase boundaries involving electric-magnetic transitions. This study provides a theoretical analysis of how temperature influences spin-wave magnon properties in an ideal antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model. Employing a mean-field approach, we derive the temperature-dependent bare magnon spectrum and analyze the magnon-phonon interaction, which is modeled via the Raman interaction Hamiltonian. By solving the resulting Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations, we examine the temperature-induced evolution of magnon dispersion. Furthermore, taking yttrium iron garnet as a specific case, we numerically calculate the temperature-dependent diamagnetic nonlinear shift. Our findings indicate that spin waves exhibit a strong response to temperature changes, and the proposed theoretical framework offers a foundation for future research into thermal spin-wave devices. These results are anticipated to be applicable to systems involving magnon-phonon interactions. (This work appeared in Phys. Rev. This paper introduces two modifications to Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem. The first approach is an alternative to the rank metric, while the second involves a structural change to public generators. The first method is more efficient than the second. Both techniques rely on solving multivariate quadratic systems over the base field. Although the second system is slightly larger, it is less sparse than the one in Loidreau's original scheme. We present algorithms for the first algorithm that utilize any matrix form admitting a vector with a small number of non-zero entries. Furthermore, we provide numerical results comparing these two modifications against attacks derived from lattice reduction and multivariate solving. The outcomes indicate that our proposed system offers better security than the original. Finally, we outline potential directions for future research. Minimally spanned acycles (MSAs) are novel geometric features that emerge from recent findings in algebraic topology. Given a finite point cloud $\mathcal{X}$ within a Euclidean space, we construct a simplicial complex $\mathcal{K}(\mathcal{X},\varepsilon)$ by applying the Čech or Vietoris-Rips method to a specific radius $\varepsilon$. For each simplex $\sigma$ within this complex, the minimal spanned acycle $l_\mathcal{K}(\sigma,\varepsilon)$ is defined as the weighted sum of all minimal cycles that can be formed by the convex hulls of the points constituting $\sigma$. This paper investigates the asymptotic behavior of these quantities as the point cloud size grows, specifically for random point clouds generated by Poisson processes or uniformly distributed point sets. We derive formulas for the expected value and variance of $l_\mathcal{K}(\sigma,\varepsilon)$ and demonstrate that these metrics remain independent of the radius $\varepsilon$. Furthermore, we calculate the expected value and variance for both the maximum and minimum MSAs of the constructed complexes. Finally, we present simulation results that validate these theoretical derivations. Notably, our findings indicate that while the distributions of minimal and maximal MSAs converge to Gaussians as anticipated, they do so at different rates. The theoretical results regarding the variance of maximal MSAs suggest that they may fail to converge to a Gaussian distribution, regardless of the point cloud's size. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the first and second moments for both minimal and maximal MSAs, supported by detailed proofs. This work represents the first application of Poisson point processes to the study of MSAs. Beyond their intrinsic interest in topological data analysis, these methods hold significant potential for other random geometric feature problems, such as those involving minimal spanning forests. The code used in this study is available at: https://github.com/alexei-romanov/MSA. Code for replicating the results is provided in: https://github.com/alexei-romanov/MSA/tree/main/Notebooks. The findings are detailed in the following report: https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.07005. The initial version of this research was presented at the 2022 Data Topology Conference. Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) has recently attracted significant research interest due to its ability to safeguard user data by aggregating information feature-wise across multiple parties. However, VFL often involves participants holding features from distinct dimensions, which restricts its real-world deployment. This paper introduces four novel privacy attacks targeting VFL systems, three of which represent the first of their kind. Our proposed methods are designed to be practical, leveraging pre-trained models to effectively infer sensitive data from external parties' features. Evaluations on a practical use case involving credit scoring demonstrate the efficacy of these attacks, with the best approach achieving an AUC score of 0.795 in predicting a user's credit worthiness. Furthermore, we show that common VFL privacy preservation techniques, such as Differential Privacy, offer limited protection against these novel attack vectors. To the best of our knowledge, this marks the first application of membership inference attacks within the VFL domain. Finally, we address the challenge of feature misalignment by proposing a generative adversarial network (GAN)-based solution, which significantly enhances privacy resilience while maintaining model accuracy. Our source code is available at https://github.com/ehsan-nejati/Privacy-Assaults-on-VFL. The paper can be accessed at https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03201. Building upon the QCD light-cone series rules, we investigate the exclusive production of dark antibaryons ($B \to PnD$) alongside standard nucleons. We derive the leading-twist ($\Lambda^0_D$) production amplitude by mapping the three-quark light-cone wave function of the dark nucleon $D$ to that of the standard nucleon. We further analyze how gluon contributions influence this process and estimate the branching ratio for the $B^0 \to \pi^0 nD$ channel, yielding $\mathcal{B}(B^0 \to \pi^0 nD) \simeq 1.1 \times 10^{-10} (\delta/0.01)^2$. Our findings suggest that the exclusive production of dark antibaryons is feasible and could be detected at LHCb. Consequently, this study offers a novel pathway to explore the nature of dark matter. Our work also provides a detailed examination of the $N_D$ light-cone wave function and its general implications for the exclusive production of dark antibaryons. Notably, we establish a new relation between the $NN$ and $ND$ currents that is independent of the dark baryon mass. These results may hold significant interest for understanding the structure of dark nucleons. Our work is based on the light-cone series rules derived in [arXiv:1809.01220 [hep-ph]]. This paper introduces a new real-time defense framework designed to mitigate distributed attacks targeting smart city subsystems. The system relies on an intelligent framework capable of learning from various city datasets to predict subsystem failures during attacks, thereby optimizing resource allocation for maximal attack resistance. To evaluate the framework's efficacy, we developed a next-generation defense game that integrates multiple access control systems, access points, and sensor networks. We present preliminary findings from this game, which highlight the approach's potential. Furthermore, we outline both the advantages and constraints of data-driven solutions in real-world defensive applications. This study examines the thermodynamics of phase transitions for black holes within a cavity. We demonstrate that a non-rotating, charged AdS black hole exhibits two distinct Hawking–Page phase transitions when situated inside a cavity. Furthermore, we find that the phases of black holes charged with spin charge experience a single Hawking–Page transition within the cavity. Additionally, we determine that the radius of the cavity influences both the temperature and the Hawking–Page transition conditions for black holes containing spin charge. Finally, we present numerical results regarding the free energy of these charged AdS black holes with spin charge to characterize their phase transitions. These findings indicate that our results offer valuable insights into the thermodynamic phase transitions of AdS black holes with spin charge as they evolve. Additionally, these findings may be applicable to understanding the thermodynamic phase transitions of other charged black holes within a cavity. Keywords: Black Holes; Phase Transitions; Thermodynamics. PACS numbers: 04.70.Bw; 04.20.Jb; 04.50.Kd. 1. Introduction The research into charged black holes has been a longstanding and significant area of interest in physics. This interest stems from their complex and intriguing behaviors, such as the failure of the second law of thermodynamics in certain regimes, which has been resolved by introducing surface terms into the entropy formula. Furthermore, charged black holes are closely linked to various physical phenomena, including the information paradox and holography. Consequently, they have played a crucial role in advancing our understanding of black hole physics. Over the past few decades, numerous studies have explored the entropy of charged black holes within the framework of holography [1–10]. These investigations have revealed that charged AdS black holes possess a non-trivial phase structure, which differs significantly from that of neutral AdS black holes. For instance, Hawking and Page [11] originally investigated the thermodynamics of charged AdS black holes within the holographic framework and discovered a phase transition between a black hole and a thermal gas within a cavity. This phenomenon, now known as the Hawking–Page transition, has been extensively studied in various contexts, including rotating black holes [12], charged black holes [13], and the thermodynamics of anti-de Sitter space. In this context, the radius of the cavity plays a pivotal role in determining the specific conditions under which these phase transitions occur. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the thermodynamic properties of charged AdS black holes

Since the inception of large-scale machine learning, data has frequently exhibited noise, prompting extensive research into noise-robust algorithms. While significant advancements have been made regarding noise tolerance in deep learning, the issue of noisy data in information retrieval (IR) remains underexplored. This paper introduces a novel and effective method for handling label noise in ranking that integrates bag sampling and group-level loss. Our approach first partitions training instances into bags based on their labels, then partitions each bag into groups, and finally trains a deep neural network using group-level loss across these groups. We evaluated this method on the PubMed corpus, applying both synthetic and real-world label noise. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in both scenarios. Furthermore, ablation studies reveal that the technique is computationally efficient, capable of processing millions of samples within minutes. Finally, we also show that the method can be extended to incorporate unlabeled samples. The implementation will be made available on GitHub. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have proven highly effective for node classification, yet acquiring labels for every node is often prohibitively expensive. Consequently, few-shot learning within graph contexts is a prevalent challenge. While pseudo-labeling has emerged as a key strategy to tackle this issue, current approaches frequently overlook the scarcity of high-quality initial labels and the necessity of selecting the most informative pseudo-labels. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel framework that enhances GNN performance by leveraging high-quality few-shot labels and choosing the most valuable unlabeled nodes. Specifically, our method first identifies high-quality labels through a dynamic ensemble of diverse classifiers. Subsequently, to identify the most informative unlabeled nodes, we propose a new node embedding technique that quantifies the similarity between a node and its class based on node embeddings, random walk node embeddings, and PRA scores. Finally, we employ pseudo-labeling strategies utilizing these node embeddings to iteratively refine the model. Experimental results across various real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm the significance of each component in the proposed framework. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Chenchenchenchen/ICTFLG. This study examines the emission of betatron and synchrotron radiation during the proton-electron collisionless bunch compression process under the AWAKE concept. We analyze the impact of longitudinal electron distribution and space charge forces on this radiation. Our findings indicate that while the collisionless mechanism amplifies betatron radiation, it simultaneously suppresses the radiation process. These results provide valuable insights for interpreting future radiative signals during compressionless bunch compression. Additionally, we observed that within the considered parameter range, collisionless compression fails to generate electromagnetic radiation at frequencies below 100 GHz. This limitation arises because the bunch dephasing frequency, which governs the onset of betatron radiation, remains below 100 GHz until the proton line density reaches $10^{14}$ protons/cm. Furthermore, we investigated the conditions required to achieve GW-level radiated power, identifying two such scenarios: one involving ultra-relativistic electrons and another with moderate electron energy. In both cases, the collisionless compression mechanism yields significant radiated power, making them promising candidates for future AWAKE experiments. Finally, we explored methods to enhance detected radiated power, including optimizing detection angles and adjusting the observed frequency. Ultimately, we conclude that GW-level betatron radiation can be detected at frequencies ranging from 100 GHz to 1 THz using oncoming laser-wakefield accelerators with line densities between $10^{13}$ and $10^{14}$ protons/cm. These results are highly relevant to the planned NICA CW-Linac and AWAKE-II (H) projects. To observe AWAKE Run 2 bunch compression via betatron radiation, we recommend conducting experiments at a detector positioned at a 45-degree angle relative to the collisionless compression plane, utilizing a laser-wakefield accelerator operating at 100 GHz with a proton line density of $10^{14}$ protons/cm. This configuration is expected to produce detectable electromagnetic radiation in the GHz range. Finally, we address the potential interference between synchrotron and betatron radiation caused by transverse electron oscillations during compression. Our analysis indicates that this interference is minimal, as the ratio of synchrotron to betatron radiation power is approximately $10^{-3}$, rendering the effect negligible. Consequently, further investigation into the influence of various physical parameters on the ratio of these two radiation modes is warranted. Overall, our research demonstrates that AWAKE Run 2 can detect betatron radiation through a laser-wakefield accelerator

This study addresses a critical challenge in distributed machine learning: constructing differentially private decision trees. We introduce and evaluate three private distributed decision tree algorithms: (1) a scalable, provably accurate method for binary trees; (2) a private procedure to generate the initial set of split points ensuring accuracy; and (3) a private procedure for constructing binary tree nodes that also guarantees accuracy. These approaches employ the advanced composition theorem to achieve a significant improvement in the sample complexity needed for differential privacy. Our experimental results demonstrate that, given a fixed privacy budget, our methods produce binary trees that are substantially more accurate than current state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, we observe that our binary tree algorithms scale effectively with respect to the number of distributed nodes. To the best of our knowledge, this work provides the first provably accurate differentially private algorithm for learning decision trees. This paper introduces a Bregman proximal gradient algorithm to address the regularized $\beta$-R\'enyi divergence minimization problem, where $\beta \in (0, \infty) \setminus \{1\}$. This specific divergence represents a generalized form of the Kullback-Leibler divergence. We demonstrate that employing a strictly convex, differentiable, and non-negative regularizer enables the construction of a nontrivial Bregman function. Under additional assumptions regarding the objective function, we establish the convergence of our proposed algorithm. Furthermore, when $\beta$ approaches $0$ or $1$, this Bregman function converges to the standard Bregman divergence associated with the negative entropy. Consequently, our proposed algorithm effectively recovers the recently developed Bregman proximal gradient method for $\mathrm{KL}$-divergence (applied to $\beta=0$) and the $\alpha$-divergence minimization method (applied to $\beta=\alpha-1$), which were introduced by Takahashi and Tsuboi in 2019 and Nishihara and Takahashi in 2020, respectively. Additionally, we illustrate the application of this approach to regularized Poisson maximum likelihood estimation. Numerical experiments confirm the convergence of our algorithm and demonstrate its superior performance compared to existing methods. Finally, the framework is extended to the more general scenario involving regularized f-divergence minimization. These results hold significant value, particularly for high-dimensional statistical estimation problems characterized by sparse true parameters. Specifically, when minimizing the f-divergence between two multivariate Poisson distributions with parameters $\bm{\theta}_1$ and $\bm{\theta}_2$, the f-divergence simplifies to a sum involving $f$ and the $\mathrm{KL}$-divergence between the components of $\bm{\theta}_1$ and $\bm{\theta}_2$. In this context, we demonstrate that the f-divergence-based estimator exhibits the phase transition behavior observed in the $\mathrm{KL}$-divergence-based estimator, as reported by Nishihara and Takahashi (2020). This behavior is characterized by the estimator being exactly zero with probability one below a certain threshold and exhibiting the Minimax Optimal support recovery rate above it. Chain event graph models extend the capabilities of discrete Markov chains and Markov random fields by offering a graph-theoretic framework for probabilistic modeling. While these models can be represented as ordered log-linear structures or equivalent directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), they provide more intuitive graphical representations. This paper introduces a Markov chain-based Bayesian Markov model choice procedure for chain event graph models, supporting both single and multiple scaling cuts across various graph sizes. Subsequently, a simulated annealing algorithm is developed to identify the maximum a posteriori model within this procedure. Finally, a comprehensive simulation study is conducted to evaluate the performance of the proposed algorithm. The results indicate that the method performs robustly under different prior specifications and demonstrates strong performance in selecting appropriate models for several chain event graph examples. We introduce a new dynamic framework that integrates heavy ball inertial dynamics with Tikhonov regularization on a curve space. A differential inclusion describes the asymptotic behavior of this inclusion curve space, with the parameter approaching zero at a specific rate; this inclusion features a decreasing closed convex valued function that is proper, lower semicontinuous, and Fréchet differentiable. The inclusion's solution set corresponds to the set of minimizers of the function, while the weak limit set of the dynamical solution trajectory is nonempty, compact, and weakly dense within this solution set. Assuming the function is strictly convex, we demonstrate that the trajectory converges weakly towards the least norm minimizer. Furthermore, under additional assumptions of monotonicity and differentiability, we establish the strong convergence of the trajectory to the least norm minimizer. These findings represent a generalization of previous strong-weak-strong convergence results. Finally, numerical experiments are provided to support the asymptotic results. The heavy ball method originates from Polyak's work in the 1960s and has recently been the subject of extensive research and numerical testing. This paper aims to contribute to the theoretical understanding of such dynamical systems. Additionally, we demonstrate that the heavy ball approach is a special case of our proposed framework and derive new convergence results for it. Our methodology is also applicable to first-order optimization problems, offering theoretical insights into methods like Nesterov's accelerated gradient algorithm and the proximal point method. These contributions extend and complement existing literature in the field. Our framework addresses broad classes of problems, including those defined on Hilbert spaces, Banach spaces, and metric spaces, encompassing various regularization techniques. Moreover, these results hold true for both continuous and discrete-time dynamical systems. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 provides the necessary background and preliminary definitions. Section 3 presents the main results and their corresponding proofs. Section 4 applies our framework to specific problems and derives related convergence results. This study investigates how local sensory constraints influence the global behavior of autonomous robots. Specifically, it examines a simple robot model characterized by disintegrator kinetics and nonlocal coupling. When the sensing range is integral to the coupling range, the system's dynamics can be represented on a one-dimensional circle. We demonstrate that this transition is governed by a bifurcation parameter determined by the ratio of disintegration to sensing rates. This transition is characterized by the merging of stable and unstable fixed points, resulting in the disappearance of an unstable focus. This mechanism explains the sudden shift in the area of attraction as the sensing rate increases. Furthermore, when the sensing range is slightly larger than the coupling range, the transition becomes far more complex, with bifurcation diagrams revealing a cascade of period-doubling bifurcations. This series of bifurcations, which can generate chaotic behavior, marks the most intriguing and complex transition among those observed in the model. Finally, we contend that this chaotic behavior is highly relevant to wall-following robots, as it can induce complex motion patterns in both fixed and wandering modes. These findings are based on a collaboration with an autonomous delivery company, aiming to elucidate the relationship between sensory parameters and group behavior in their robot fleet. The results offer valuable insights for the company regarding how sensory capabilities affect global dynamics, which is essential for developing effective control strategies. Additionally, we propose methods to mitigate or suppress the impact of local sensory constraints on global behavior, thereby facilitating the creation of more predictable robot groups. These approaches are supported by extensive numerical simulations. Finally, our work contributes to a growing field of research on the relationship between local sensing and global behavior in animal groups, a topic that has recently gained significant attention. To this end, we have also suggested a potential experimental setup to test the role of sensory range in collective behavior. Specifically, we outline an experiment to investigate how local sensing affects the motion patterns of fish schools. This involves comparing an individual fish's ability to sense with its actual coupling within the school, achieved by attaching a fish to a robotic agent. By adjusting the robot's movement, researchers can vary both the sensing rate and the coupling range. By analyzing the resulting behavior, one can determine the specific role of sensory range in collective dynamics. We investigate the energy-dependent conductivity of Dirac materials featuring kinetic energy-driven anisotropic superconducting gaps and extended impurities. Our analysis relies on a self-consistent solution of the Dyson equation and the kinetic equation within the dirty limit, where impurity scattering is mediated by a non-local potential. Our findings indicate that the conductivity of these anisotropic superconductors can be categorized into distinct regimes based on their dependence on the superconducting gap energy. Our results further demonstrate that extended impurities yield higher conductivity than point-like impurities, with the magnitude of the supercurrent remaining sensitive to the specific form factor of the non-local potential. Finally, we outline the experimental signatures associated with these materials. Notably, the non-local potential model enables the separation of the normal state's Drude conductivity into current-parallel and current-perpendicular components, while the normal state magnetotransport characteristics for both localized and non-local potentials align with those observed in hole-doped cuprates. Furthermore, the magnetoresistance in the normal state of anisotropic superconductors exhibits a non-monotonic behavior, a feature that persists in the superconducting state. We also explore the potential to detect the nodal supercurrent via spin-polarized tunneling spectroscopy. Ultimately, our study elucidates the low-energy properties of kinetic energy-driven conductors, including their normal state transport, and identifies key superconducting signatures that facilitate the identification of such materials in experimental settings. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for non-local potential models. Specifically, in the non-local potential model, the unitarity condition is satisfied through an effective interaction between the electron and the potential, whereas the decay of the impurity cloud is contingent upon the scattering amplitude. This mechanism offers a viable explanation for the experimentally observed gap renormalization in hole-doped cuprates. Additionally, the unitarity condition can be fulfilled by considering the self-energy of the potential. We conclude that our findings provide a comprehensive framework for understanding the energy-dependent transport properties of anisotropic superconductors and their normal state behavior. Our results underscore the necessity of developing advanced theoretical models to accurately describe the transport properties of hole-doped cuprates. In this context, the non-local potential model emerges as a promising candidate for describing hole-doped cuprates. Finally, our findings offer a theoretical basis for the recent proposal regarding the existence of a pseudogap in hole-doped cuprates. This survey examines the asymptotic behavior of crystalline plates under heat conduction and surface diffusion within the temperature field. The dynamics of these plates are represented by a nonlocal, nonlocal-in-time evolution equation for the free boundary of an open set, driven by the Laplace trace of the fundamental solution of the heat equation. We provide an overview of the short-time and long-time behaviors of this equation, demonstrating that the long-time limit occurs at a rate of $t^{-1/3}$ and results in a Wulff shape, contingent upon specific geometric and analytic conditions. Furthermore, we address the connection between the plate model and mean curvature flow, exploring the question of whether the plate model can serve as a nonlocal approximation for mean curvature flow, particularly near singularities. To investigate this, we apply the plate model to two representative examples of mean curvature flow, one smooth and one singular, to test whether the low-dimensional trace of the heat equation's fundamental solution provides an accurate description of the corresponding heat distribution. Finally, we outline several intriguing open problems in this area. Notably, the nonlocal nature of curvature, as captured by the plate model, may hold significant relevance for understanding geometric evolution equations, including their associated singularities. Additionally, we consider the impact of thermal stresses on crystalline plates, showing that they can induce a phase transition in the asymptotic behavior of flat multi-phase materials subjected to surface diffusion in the temperature field. This leads to a new model for multiphase mean curvature flow featuring nonlocal, time-dependent curvature, which itself possesses interesting asymptotic properties. We conclude by presenting a few open questions regarding this novel model. Overall, this paper presents a fresh perspective on the asymptotic behavior of multiphase mean curvature flow and offers a fresh perspective on understanding geometric singularities. These phenomena are deeply intertwined with the asymptotic analysis of multiphase heat conduction, particularly at singularities. Consequently, this work may hold value for researchers in asymptotic analysis, phase transition theory, and the theory of nonlinear partial differential equations. Furthermore, our methodology is broadly applicable to other nonlocal problems, such as fractional Laplacian evolution equations, thereby reaching a wider mathematical audience. Finally, the findings are pertinent to materials scientists studying multiphase crystalline materials, as well as to mathematical physicists analyzing solid-state diffusion and related phenomena. This survey synthesizes recent advancements and results from the first author and a broad circle of international collaborators. A primary human capability is tending to plant life, a skill that has served as a cultural cornerstone for millennia. This study explores a novel application for reinforcement learning by developing an intelligent agent capable of learning to care for plants within a simulated environment. We introduce GrowSpace, a new 3D interactive simulation where an agent, represented by a small humanoid, must cultivate foliage to fulfill user requests. We present a curriculum-based training strategy designed to guide the agent from basic movements to intricate sequences of actions. Furthermore, we examine the agent's learned behaviors, including its ability to communicate with users via a simulated tablet interface. Our findings indicate that a behavior cloning approach yields more natural-looking results than a reward-based method, and we provide a detailed analysis of the agent's movement patterns and communication strategies. Additionally, we highlight an emergent phenomenon where the agent develops a strong desire to care for plants, even when no specific task is provided. Finally, we outline potential future research avenues, such as enabling multi-agent simulations to study cooperation and conflict, as well as extending the study to indoor gardening scenarios to investigate how care requirements alter behavior. We present an explicit formula for the law of the Brownian loop established by Lawler, Morales, and Sun, deriving it through conformal welding of quantum disks and Weyl integration. Specifically, we sample the loop's length and external boundary conformally equivariantly using quantum disks, then recover the loop's law by conformally welding them together. This approach offers an alternative proof of the original formula alongside a distinct formula expressed via quantum disks. Furthermore, our methodology extends naturally to open paths with specified insertion points, yielding an alternative expression for the law of open Lyons-Sheffield paths in terms of quantum disks. Additionally, our construction provides a conformally equivariant extension of the Sheffield-Werner loop measure to the setting of quantum gravity, where the loop law is weighted by the Liouville measure and the loop law on $\mathbb{H}$ is weighted by the Liouville measure projected onto this domain. This extension aligns with recent findings by Duplantier and Miller, as well as Duplantier, Miller, and Sheffields. Finally, our framework generates a family of random quantum surfaces that conformally equivariantly couple Liouville Brownian motion, the free field, and the Gaussian free field. In the case of the loop, our construction is connected to the Liouville first passage percolation distance and its coupling with the Liouville Brownian motion, as demonstrated by Miller and Xu. We demonstrate that our construction aligns with their coupling when viewed through the lens of Liouville first passage percolation trees. The normalization of spectral biomarkers is essential for ensuring both technical reproducibility and clinical validity in imaging studies. However, current normalization techniques often lack robustness and fail to address all sources of technical variability in spectral data. This issue is particularly critical in high-dimensional datasets where missing values and noise can significantly impact multivariate analysis and spectral-based diagnosis. This study evaluates the suitability of various existing normalization methods for quantifying liquid biopsy biomarkers in oncology using Raman spectroscopy. We present a systematic investigation comparing these approaches and introduce a novel framework that integrates several techniques to enhance reproducibility in quantitative spectral biomarker measurements. Additionally, the complete R and Python code required to replicate these findings is available at https://github.com/IMBI-imni. We contend that spectral biomarker quantification in clinical imaging must prioritize rigorous normalization to ensure accurate and reproducible results. Furthermore, we contend that deep learning-based approaches to spectral normalization are unlikely to succeed until they incorporate explainable features and demonstrate substantial performance gains over conventional methods. We anticipate that this work will facilitate the development of more quantitative and reproducible liquid biopsy workflows in clinical imaging. Ultimately, we believe that spectral biomarker quantification in clinical imaging necessitates strict normalization to achieve accuracy and reproducibility. We have established a community-driven initiative, the Image Biomarker Normalization Initiative (IBNI), to foster collaboration and consensus on best practices for normalizing high-dimensional imaging data. We envision that IBNI will foster open and transparent discussions to address normalization challenges in medical imaging and provide a standardized benchmark for comparing and evaluating normalization methods. We anticipate that this effort will lead to the development of best practices and a unified standard for normalizing spectral imaging data. This initiative is especially relevant for liquid biomarkers such as blood, CSF, and tissue, where subtle changes in biochemistry can be magnified by high-dimensional imaging modalities like Raman spectroscopy, fluorescence, and mass spectrometry imaging. We believe that adopting IBNI guidelines will significantly advance the field of quantitative medical imaging. The analysis reveals that the $N\gamma\to K\Lambda$ reaction cross section is notably suppressed at low energies, with the process proceeding predominantly through the production of the $\Sigma$ hyperon. Conversely, the $N\gamma\to K\Lambda$ channel is significantly enhanced at high energies due to the contributions of the $N\gamma\to K\Delta$ and $\Delta\to\Delta K$ amplitudes. The study also examines the photoproduction of $K\bar{K}$ pairs, which occurs in conjunction with the single-strange photoproduction channels. The current experimental findings are compared against the theoretical predictions derived from this study. Additionally, the potential for detecting the $K\Lambda S_{11}(1565)$ resonance is explored, alongside an analysis of the isobaric vector $\gamma\to K\bar{K}$ decay. The results indicate that the photon flux is the primary limiting factor governing the sensitivity of the experimental setup. This study focuses on the image pre-processing of the non-symmetric sub-database drawn from the MORPH-II dataset. The data comprises 12,962 face images featuring individuals of varying skin tones and sexes, captured under diverse lighting and background conditions. The paper details the pre-processing algorithms employed to enhance image quality for the subsequent application of a deep convolutional neural network. Specifically, it addresses the challenges of low-quality inputs resulting from poor lighting and background interference. To mitigate background issues, the study utilizes a variant of the Fast Background Subtraction algorithm known as Simple Background Subtraction (SBS). To handle lighting variations, it implements a modified version of the Retinex method called DCT-Retinex, alongside traditional contrast enhancement techniques such as Histogram Equalization (HE) and Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE). The paper provides an in-depth analysis of these pre-processing procedures and their corresponding outcomes. The research concludes by highlighting the significant impact of these algorithms on subsequent facial recognition tasks. The authors suggest that this paper serves as a foundational approach for researchers aiming to utilize face databases for their own investigations. Additionally, the authors have developed a Python-based application to facilitate the implementation of these image pre-processing algorithms. This tool is made available for researchers to assist in their respective studies. Keywords: Face Database, Background Subtraction, DCT-Retinex, Histogram Equalization, CLAHE, Morphology, OpenCV.

We investigate the production of primordial black holes (PBHs) within a curvaton framework involving two fields: a standard curvaton and an additional field that generates a bump in the scalar potential, subsequently decaying into an unstable particle. This decay triggers the reheating of the universe, which, if the particle is sufficiently heavy, can induce a non-adiabatic pressure perturbation. This effect amplifies curvature perturbations on an extremely small scale, leading to the formation of supermassive PBHs in the mass range of $\sim 10^{6}-10^{23} M_{\odot}$. We outline the viable parameter space for this model and demonstrate that it can successfully reproduce the observed large-scale curvature perturbations. Furthermore, we establish that PBHs with masses around $\sim 10^{13} M_{\odot}$ could account for a dark matter component. This scenario is particularly attractive because it avoids the stringent constraints imposed on curvaton models attempting to generate ultra-large PBHs through the enhancement of curvature perturbations at the end of inflation. Additionally, this model remains robust against curvature perturbations arising from the instability of the curvaton vacuum. Finally, we discuss how this framework can be tested through the gravitational wave signals produced by the decay of the heavy particle. Our approach is broadly applicable to various scenarios where a heavy particle decays into one or more light states. In this context, the bump in the potential may originate from the stabilization of a local minimum in the scalar potential. This mechanism can be realized in a supersymmetric $\mu$-term model, where the bump is formed by a local minimum located at a relatively low energy scale. In this specific case, the stabilization of the curvaton vacuum is ensured by the superpotential, which remains independent of the potential. We also present the lightest scalar mass in this framework and analyze its implications for the curvaton problem. Finally, we show that the model can be tested via the gravitational wave spectrum resulting from the curvaton decay. We conclude that the curvaton field can be the lightest scalar in this framework, with its mass lying in the sub-GeV range. We also address the potential for detecting curvaton decay gravitational waves through the stochastic gravitational wave background. Finally, we demonstrate that the curvaton mass can be constrained by the reheating temperature, which is determined by the temperature at which the bump in the potential is filled. This study introduces a novel vehicle platoon formation control framework utilizing differential games. The proposed method is versatile, capable of managing both vehicle synchronization and spatial formation, and is highly efficient, requiring the calculation of only one additional state per vehicle. These advantages facilitate the development of intelligent, self-organizing systems. The differential game model supports two implementation approaches: a centralized, high-performance system and a fully distributed, high-security system. These strategies offer a flexible alternative to the high-bandwidth communication requirements of traditional platooning methods. The paper provides a comprehensive description of the proposed models, their advantages and limitations, and includes numerical simulations to verify the results. Furthermore, the discussion explores potential extensions of this work. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1999/Differential-Games. This work revisits the well-known limitation of logistic regression, specifically the curse of interactivity, and addresses a related issue: the presence of interaction terms despite their absence in the underlying data. Regarding the first issue, we demonstrate that the influence of interaction terms can be significantly diminished by adjusting the covariates during the estimation process. By employing a straightforward yet effective method, we achieve a substantial reduction in the bias introduced by these terms, thereby enhancing both the validity and power of inference. Furthermore, we provide suggestions for selecting the optimal reduction strategy through straightforward cross-validation. Regarding the second issue, we propose a solution utilizing a data-driven approach based on clustering. We establish theoretical guarantees regarding estimation accuracy and test power, proving that our clustering-based estimator outperforms the standard maximum likelihood estimator in scenarios with strong separability. Additionally, simulation studies were conducted to evaluate performance when strong separability does not hold. Across both theoretical analyses and simulations, we observe that while clustering methods may not always outperform maximum likelihood, they rarely result in inferior performance. Overall, the methods introduced here offer improvements over traditional approaches, particularly when at least one covariate exhibits strong separability. Finally, the paper includes a real-world application demonstrating that our procedures yield valid and potentially more powerful inferences compared to conventional techniques. Keywords: Bias reduction, clustering, high-dimensional regression, interaction terms, local orthogonalization, model selection, non-Gaussian regression, sparse regression, strong separability, theoretical analysis.

Detecting misinformation is crucial for safeguarding public discourse, and since fake news often spreads rapidly through social media, the ability to identify whether an article has been headline-generated serves as a valuable indicator of its veracity. This study addresses that challenge by formulating a lexical paraphrase task using neural models. While prior research in paraphrase modeling has primarily relied on sequence-to-sequence architectures, we demonstrate that Transformer-based self-attention models offer a more effective solution. Our findings indicate that a BERT model, fine-tuned and evaluated on the mixed-language News-Montserrat dataset, surpasses both a basic Transformer model and the previously dominant sequence-to-sequence approach. Furthermore, we present a detailed analysis of the dataset and the performance characteristics of the News-Montserrat BERT model. Finally, we explore strategies for enhancing the dataset's utility in news verification tasks. This work represents the initial application of Transformers to head-line-generated text detection on the dataset. Future research will examine the impact of pre-training on other languages to improve BERT's performance in identifying fake news. We establish the conditions for a chiral spin liquid within both amorphous and polycrystalline frustrated spin-1/2 Heisenberg systems. Leveraging a novel statistical framework, we derive a general formula for the entropy of the Heisenberg model on general graphs, expressed through the entanglement entropy of random graphs. This approach reveals that polycrystalline and amorphous structures with high entanglement are most susceptible to the emergence of chiral spin liquids. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this statistical formulation enables the calculation of the specific heat for the generic Heisenberg model via the heat capacity of the Kondo-Ising model. We analyze the thermal properties of the Kondo-Ising model, noting the presence of a first-order phase transition at low temperatures. Our findings indicate that in the late-temperature regime, the specific heat is governed by the classical limit of the Kondo-Ising model, characterized by a peak scaling with temperature. Conversely, in the early-temperature regime, the specific heat is controlled by the low-temperature phase featuring a spin gap. We propose that chiral spin liquids will be most stable in systems where the Kondo-Ising model resides in this spin-gap phase. Finally, we illustrate the stability of the chiral spin liquid in amorphous and polycrystallial systems by applying our framework to the frustrated spin-1/2 Heisenberg model on the quasicrystalline Amman-Anderson model and on a hierarchical Cayley tree. Additionally, we examine the stability of chiral spin liquids in systems exhibiting strong quantum fluctuations, such as those derived from the honeycomb and kagome lattices. Our results suggest that the chiral spin liquid phase is more stable in the Kondo-Ising model characterized by a spin gap than in the Ising model. Finally, we discuss the experimental detection of these phases through the measurement of the specific heat of the corresponding Kondo-Ising model. For an amorphous system, we show that the specific heat of the Kondo-Ising model can be fitted using a phenomenological function that incorporates the critical exponents of the second-order phase transition. This enables the accurate prediction of the specific heat in the low-temperature regime for amorphous systems. Our methodology offers a new statistical tool for Heisenberg models on general graphs and provides a means to predict the stability of chiral spin liquids in both amorphous and polycrystalline systems.

This paper introduces a suite of calibration methods designed for large-N radio interferometers, such as the Expanded Very Large Array (EVLA) and the proposed Large Multi-Element Interferometer (LMEI). These algorithms utilize a spatial FFT to leverage the specific structure of visibilities generated by baselines formed from regular grids. The approach is notably faster than the standard $O(N^2)$ visibilities-based calibration framework, instead achieving $O(N\log{N})$ complexity under the large-N approximation where $N \gg 1$. Furthermore, by employing spatial FFTs for visibilities, the method eliminates the need for explicit phase and delay calculations, which are typically the most computationally intensive tasks in calibration. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of the techniques, their underlying assumptions, and their mathematical formulations. Additionally, we introduce a hybrid calibration strategy that integrates fast imaging with traditional visibilities-based calibration, utilizing the former for imaging and the latter for calibration. This hybrid approach is demonstrated using EVLA data from the 2014 APEX Large Array (ALA) survey of the Cygnus A galaxy. The results indicate that this technique offers a viable pathway for future EVLA and LMEI calibration initiatives. Finally, the code is made available to the public. Specifically, the fast interferometric calibration method is released under the Apache 2.0 license, while the fast visibilities-based calibration method is provided as open-source under the MIT License. Both are accessible at https://github.com/evla-lmei-calibration. Furthermore, the MIT License is also applicable for EVLA data processing. This work is dedicated to the memory of Dr. David L. We have computed the polarized transition function $A_{gq}(N)$ within the Variable Flavor Number Scheme at next-to-next-to-leading order in perturbative quantum chromodynamics, corresponding to a three-loop order, for the specific case where the hard scale is twice the mass of a quark. This function is essential for establishing the scheme-independent, mass-independent evolution of polarized parton distributions. Our result is presented in a form suitable for numerical evaluation, and we have provided a corresponding analogue for the $b \leftarrow q$ transition. Additionally, we have validated our analytical findings against known results for the flavor non-singlet component of $A_{gq}(N)$ at leading order, as well as the flavor singlet component at both leading and next-to-leading orders. Finally, we illustrate how our findings influence the evolution of polarized PDFs by examining the scale dependence of the flavor singlet non-diagonal component of the anomalous dimension matrix at $O(\alpha_s^3)$. In this context, we observe that the off-diagonal terms are significantly larger than those in the flavor non-singlet scenario. This suggests that the mixing between polarized sea quark and gluon distributions could be substantial, a hypothesis supported by a comparison with the corresponding entries in the next-to-leading order matrix. These conclusions are particularly relevant for the evolution of the bottom distribution, which is expected to be substantial at high scales. Our results are also consistent with the analysis of the polarized $B$ meson distribution derived from $B_{\text{meson}}(N)$ data obtained through the operator product expansion of the electromagnetic current two-point correlation function. This consistency indicates that the evolution of the bottom distribution is likely to be a significant factor in the interpretation of the recent observation of a non-zero value for the polarized strange quark distribution at high scales, which was inferred from the non-zero value of the strange component of the anomalous dimension matrix at $O(\alpha_s^3)$. We also discuss the implications of these findings for the small-$x$ behavior of PDFs. Finally, we have made our results available through the RECIPE website. This study presents the Fermi-LAT blazar catalog (FBL), spanning the energy range of 1 GeV to 1 TeV, derived from the entire 15-year Fermi-LAT third Fermi-GAMMAPRAY catalog. Utilizing data from the Machine Learning Group at the Max Planck Institute for Physics, we employed a Bayesian neural network to classify sources into two dominant FBL sub-categories: Flat Spectrum Radio Quasars (FSRQs) and BL Lacertae objects (BL Lacs). The resulting catalog comprises 1,000 source candidates, featuring 575 FSRQs and 425 BL Lacs. This represents a threefold increase in size compared to the most recent source categorization efforts. Furthermore, the catalog's completeness is significantly enhanced, with a minimum source count achieved at flux levels as low as 1 mCrab. A comparison with the most recent source count function indicates that the two FBL categories follow distinct distributions, with FSRQs exhibiting a steeper distribution than BL Lacs. Additionally, we analyzed the spectral index distribution for both types, finding that FSRQs possess a steeper distribution than BL Lacs. Finally, we investigated the correlations between source categorization and redshift, observing that FSRQs show a stronger correlation with redshift compared to BL Lacs. The complete FBL catalog, including source properties and categorizations, is accessible via the following link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7205000. The FBL data can also be directly queried using the provided API: https://fbl-api.space. This resource allows users to retrieve and filter FBL candidates based on various criteria, such as flux, redshift, and source category. The API is hosted on the European Space Agency's data portal: https://www.esa.int/Science-Data-Context/Science-Data-Catalogues/FBL. We anticipate that the inclusion of this larger FBL catalog will significantly advance future research endeavors. Furthermore, we aim to facilitate the replication of our methodology and results, thereby enabling the development of more sophisticated machine learning models for FBL categorization. This paper details a two-year, mixed-methods research initiative focused on enhancing social media authoring interfaces to boost their accessibility. Through a literature review, we pinpointed barriers within current authoring tools and existing accessibility guidelines, subsequently designing and developing a set of novel, more accessible interfaces. An empirical study involving participants from diverse backgrounds assessed these new interfaces, revealing that while users with hearing impairments experienced significant improvements in their workflows, those without such impairments did not. We attribute this discrepancy to the absence of specific user groups in prior accessibility evaluations. Finally, the study examines challenges and limitations in adapting social media authoring tools to meet accessibility standards, highlighting key future research directions in this domain. The paper underscores the necessity of incorporating user-centered design principles into social media accessibility evaluations. Additionally, it draws a parallel between social media authoring tools and page editors, suggesting that findings from web accessibility research could inform future efforts to create more accessible social media authoring interfaces. Our work aligns with recent calls to broaden the scope of research beyond the tech industry to include a wider array of participants with varying backgrounds. Overall, this paper presents new findings and insights for advancing the accessibility of social media authoring tools. Our code is accessible via a Git repository at https://github.com/robertas-bankauskas/accessible-social-media-authoring-tool. This paper introduces a natural tensor merge operation for hypergraphs that encompasses the Cartesian, disjunction, and tensor products of graphs as specific instances. We demonstrate that this operation corresponds to the tensor product of adjacency matrices and explore its implications for the spectral properties of hypergraph constructions derived from tensor merges. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between this operation and the Cartesian fusion of hypergraph categories. The findings in the hypergraph section are extended to d-hypergraphs, with a corresponding category theoretic formulation provided for this more generalized context. Finally, the work concludes with a discussion of a proposed generalization of tensor merges to multigraphs. This generalized framework includes various notable categories as special cases, such as the categories of graphs with relations, colored hypergraphs, colored multigraphs, colored multimatroids, influence diagrams, and directed influence diagrams. Furthermore, the resulting category of directed influence diagrams possesses a particularly desirable property: it is equivalent to the category of functors mapping sets to posets. The material presented here forms the foundation for the first author's doctoral thesis. This study investigates natural cubic splines for modeling Alzheimer's disease longitudinal data within clinical trial settings. We initially address the development of effective spline basis functions to accommodate the Alzheimers' Disease Assessment Scale (ADAS-RG), a key metric in these trials. The choice of spline basis significantly influences the results of linear mixed models (LMMs), which are the standard analytical tools for evaluating Alzheimer's trial data. Consequently, we propose a model selection framework to identify the optimal LLM and corresponding spline basis. Simulation results demonstrate that our proposed spline basis outperforms the conventional equidistant grid approach regarding both bias and variance. Furthermore, we apply this basis to a real-world Alzheimer's clinical trial dataset to illustrate the practical utility of the method. Additionally, we present a sensitivity analysis to assess the impact of measurement error on the proposed spline basis. These analyses collectively provide a rigorous evaluation of the spline basis's suitability for modeling longitudinal data in clinical trials. Our findings indicate that the proposed spline basis remains a robust modeling tool even under varying conditions of measurement error. These conclusions are supported by extensive simulations and an analysis of a genuine clinical trial dataset. Ultimately, the proposed spline basis offers a flexible and effective modeling approach for longitudinal studies in clinical trials. Supplementary materials, including R code and data files, are available at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1993/Spline_basis. Keywords: Longitudinal data; Linear mixed models; Natural cubic splines; Splines basis. 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 62P10; 62F12; 62F15.

We introduce a new global optimization technique designed to identify dominant transition pathways in complex systems, such as large molecules or collective dynamics involving numerous interacting particles. By globally optimizing the "quasi-classical action," a metric quantifying the probability of a given path, our method successfully uncovers both spontaneous and driven transition routes. The driven trajectories, which correspond to the lowest action solutions, are derived using a novel continuous reparameterization of the transition process. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these driven transition routes can be converted into spontaneous ones, allowing for the determination of the activation barrier for a spontaneous transition without prior knowledge of the transition state. The efficacy of this approach is validated through two case studies: an inflectional transition in a large ring-shaped polymer and the diffusion of a helium atom within a solid. These results indicate that the proposed global optimization method serves as a highly effective tool for systematically exploring the dominant transition routes of complex systems. Additionally, the action-based probability of a transition provides a direct means to quantify the relative stability of various metastable states. The method has been implemented in a user-friendly, open-source software package that facilitates the transition to solution. This enables researchers to derive driven transition routes with a minimum of effort, potentially making it a standard procedure for the dynamic analysis of complex systems. The solution, along with input and output files for the two presented transition routes, is freely accessible at https://www.drivenpathways.com. The source code is also available on GitHub at https://github.com/DrivenPathways/DP-PathFinder. The software is titled "Driven Path Finder" and is accessible at https://www.drivenpathways.com/DP-PathFinder. Users can explore solution files for the two transition routes mentioned above using Driven Path Finder. The tool is available for free at https://www.drivenpathways.com/DP-PathFinder. Driven Path Finder offers an intuitive, user-friendly interface that allows users to easily input molecular structures and perform the global optimization to find the dominant transition route. In the framework of Bochner's abstract harmonic analysis, this allows us to represent integrable functions on $G$ as integrals of characters from $A(G)$ with respect to a complex measure. We also investigate various properties of $A(G)$ for groups that are not necessarily abelian. The approach developed here is particularly relevant for Fourier analysis, as it enables the representation of amenable groups—whether abelian or not—as structure spaces of one-dimensional groups. This resolves a specific instance of Mal'cev's problem regarding the factorization of higher-dimensional groups into one-dimensional components. We report the discovery of Andromeda XXV (M32-XV), a new ultra-faint dwarf galaxy situated approximately 770 kiloparsecs from the Milky Way. This galaxy hosts 11 member stars with a mean distance from the center of $r \sim 1.5$ parsecs and a dispersion of $\sigma \sim 1.5$ km/s. Its luminosity function peaks at an absolute magnitude of $M_V \sim -4.5$, with a total luminosity of $L_V \sim 100 L_{\odot}$. Utilizing the most recent distance estimates for M32, we derive a distance to M32-XV of $770 \pm 30$ kpc. Based on the observed kinematics of the member stars, we calculate a mass-to-light ratio of $M/L \sim 1000 M_{\odot}/L_{\odot}$, indicating that the object is gravitationally dominated by dark matter. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Andromeda XXV is likely a disrupted dwarf galaxy. We propose that M32-XV may have been stripped from the Andromeda galaxy during tidal interactions with the Milky Way. This study extends the theory of external algebras to matroid complexes, matroid superspaces, matroid schemes, and matroid stacks. Furthermore, the relationship between a matroid $M$ and its relative product $M \times_{R} M$ is examined in relation to the cohomology of associated geometric realizations. Additionally, the paper investigates the connections between external homology and cohomology for matroid schemes and stacks, demonstrating that they are duals of one another. These findings enable the formulation of comparison theorems between external homology and cohomology for matroid schemes and stacks, as well as their Cartesian products. In dialogue systems, spoken utterances are converted to text via automatic speech recognition (ASR) and subsequently parsed to identify unambiguous information for the dialogue state monitoring module. However, certain words generated by ASR remain ambiguous, as their exact form cannot be definitively determined. This paper addresses how to effectively model such ambiguous words for accurate inferences within the dialogue state monitoring module. First, we introduce the concept of Word Confusion Networks (WCNs) to capture word-level confusion. We then explore two methods for aggregating these WCNs into an information WCN (iWCN), which captures confusion at the level of information units. Finally, we integrate the iWCN into the input of a recurrent neural network (RNN) to model uncertainty during the inference process. Experimental results on the CAS-Parlance dataset demonstrate that our proposed method yields significant improvements in both entity and slot prediction tasks. Furthermore, combining our approach with attention mechanisms achieves even more substantial performance gains. To the best of our knowledge, this work represents the first application of WCNs to the field of dialogue state monitoring. Code is available at: https://github.com/zhenghaozhang1992/WCN4DSM. Continual learning (CL) involves training a model sequentially on new tasks while retaining knowledge of previous ones to prevent catastrophic forgetting. Although numerous CL techniques exist, their performance varies significantly depending on the baseline used for comparison. This paper introduces a straightforward baseline utilizing weight initialization and fine-tuning, which substantially outperforms the current state-of-the-art (SOTA) approaches that rely on pretrained models. We conduct extensive experiments across three CL scenarios to validate our findings. Our results indicate that the distinction between the baseline and SOTA methods stems from their treatment of neural layer capacities during fine-tuning. Consequently, we propose a novel capacity-aware strategy that outperforms both the baseline and SOTA by reinitializing layer weights according to their estimated capacities. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this capacity-aware approach in addressing both causes of catastrophic forgetting. Finally, we evaluate the reusability of the method across different network architectures and highlight its effectiveness in Complex Scene Text Recognition. Online multi-modal systems, including social media, email, messaging, and customer service chatbots, are increasingly being exploited for abusive language. While social media platforms typically rely on multi-modal detection using both text and images, verbal abuse in multi-agent conversation systems is often multi-modal among various users. To my knowledge, this paper presents the first research on applying multi-modal detection to abusive language in these conversation system environments. We introduce a dataset containing both textual and vocal features. Although detection is typically performed on individual modalities, we demonstrate that integrating multiple modalities can enhance detection performance. Furthermore, we emphasize the necessity of interpretability in online multi-modal systems to ensure that detected abuse is not driven by spurious correlations. Finally, we illustrate how various machine learning techniques can be employed to achieve multi-modal detection with explainable results. This work is funded by a grant from the US Department of Homeland Security. In addition to being cited in the 2022 XAI4AI Challenge, it serves as the foundation for my citation in the 2024 iC4AI Challenge. This research is also relevant to the cybersecurity domain. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/AniruddhaSarkar/Abuse-Detection. This study is also cited by the 2022 XAI4AI and 2024 iC4AI challenges. My contributions include the multi-modal abusive language detection task, a specific deep learning model, and a user-friendly interface for analyzing detection results. This work is also cored by the 2022 XAI4AI and 2024 iC4AI challenges. The 2022 XAI4AI Challenge focuses on Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) for abusive language detection, while the 2024 iC4AI Challenge addresses AI Explainability for Conversational Agents. Both challenges highlight the need for multi-modal detection capabilities. The 2024 iC4AI Challenge specifically examines verbal abuse within conversational agents, necessitating the integration of text and vocal data—a contribution realized here through a multi-modal abusive language detection task. Additionally, various machine learning techniques are utilized to achieve explainable results, a key aspect of the 2022 XAI4AI challenge which centers on XAI in abusive language detection. These contributions collectively address multi-modal abusive language detection through a dedicated task, a deep learning model, a user-friendly interface for result analysis, and methods ensuring transparency and explainability in outcomes

This study examines large-scale networks of thalamic neurons connected via excitatory and inhibitory synapses. We demonstrate that the variance in out-degrees among thalamic neurons is substantially higher than the Poisson distribution predicted by the Law of Large Numbers, a finding that aligns with empirical data. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that both the variance in in-degrees and the correlation between excitatory and inhibitory connections increase non-linearly as a function of average out-degrees, indicating a complex network architecture. To address this complexity, we developed a mathematical framework for the dynamics of large-scale thalamic networks that incorporates these observed variations in connectivity. Our model successfully captures the emergence of Up and Down states, as well as the synchronization of neuronal spiking, within both small and large networks. Additionally, we show that these models can replicate the experimentally observed power-law distribution of Up-Down event intervals. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings for large-scale neural modeling. Our work underscores the necessity of utilizing degree distributions that deviate from the Poisson law and accounting for the interdependence between degree types when analyzing large-scale neural systems. These results provide a foundation for future research aimed at enhancing the accuracy of large-scale neural models. **Keywords:** Large-scale neural networks, power-law distributions, Up-Down states, synchronization. **MSC 2010:** 92B20, 92C17, 37C45. **Authors:** Maria Antonelli, Maria Gualdi, Maria L. Automatic Program Repair (APR) has garnered significant research interest in recent years. While machine learning-based APR methods have achieved notable success, they heavily depend on the quality of the training data. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a technique for automatically generating synthetic bugs. These generated bugs are then solved by an APR system, with an adversarial generator attempting to challenge the repair process. Our approach utilizes abstract interpretation to create bugs efficiently and accurately. Evaluation on the Defects4J dataset demonstrates that our method generates bugs that are both more diverse and harder to repair than those in the original dataset. Furthermore, when confronted with these generated bugs, an APR system based on generative adversarial networks for program synthesis underperforms the original generator. This underperformance stems from the generator's failure to produce sufficiently complex bugs and its inability to incorporate adequate domain knowledge. Finally, we plan to make this method public to facilitate broader community adoption. Overall, this study highlights the critical need for high-quality training data in APR and offers a robust approach for generating challenging synthetic bugs. Any method struggling with such bugs is likely suboptimal for real-world APR applications. Additionally, the potential for generating synthetic bugs extends to other domains, such as software testing. Future work will explore applying our method to automated test generation. This study establishes the capacity region for the general interference graphically representable channel with encoder side information (GIFC). Leveraging encoder side information, the encoder generates a codebook that the decoder utilizes to decode the transmitted message. Drawing on the analogy between GIFC and graphically representable channels (CHGR), we derive the complete capacity region by integrating side-information constraints into the CHGR rate-region formulation. We demonstrate that within this region, time-sharing becomes unnecessary. Furthermore, we observe that the derived region encompasses the Shannon-Chanov capacity region as a specific subset. Finally, the results are applied to determine the capacity region for a generalized binary symmetric channel with encoder side information. Additionally, in a specialized scenario involving lossless source compression, the region reduces to the achievable rate region for a general broadcast channel with side information at the decoder, a result derived by covering all possible decoding strategies for the broadcast channel. This approach is more streamlined than the method proposed by Han and Yamamoto [1], which is limited to deterministic side information. Our findings thus offer a more efficient and generalizable alternative for characterizing the broadcast channel achievable rate region.

The geometric characteristics of small collision systems, such as those involving protons, have not been extensively investigated. This study introduces 3-dimensional flow analysis as a method to examine both the initial collision geometry and the medium resulting from nucleon-nucleon interactions. To achieve this, a two-step procedure was implemented: first, the collision system was reconstructed using event-by-event 3-dimensional initial-state Monte Carlo simulations, and subsequently, 3-dimensional flow was analyzed via principal component analysis. This research is supported by ALICE data collected in pp collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV, covering an integrated luminosity of 0.3 $\mu$b$^{-1}$, and focuses on charged particles within the rapidity range $|y|<0.5$ and transverse momentum range $p_{T}<2$ GeV/c. Results indicate that in central pp collisions, an elliptic component emerges during the early stages, with its orientation varying between events. Furthermore, the magnitude of this 3-dimensional elliptic component demonstrates a dependence on charged-particle multiplicity. These findings provide novel insights into 3-dimensional initial geometries in pp collisions and suggest that both the initial-state geometry and the Equation-of-State (EoS) of the collision system are functions of the number of produced charged particles. Consequently, 3-dimensional flow analysis offers a new and valuable probe for studying pp collisions. The event-by-event 3-dimensional Monte Carlo framework, which is essential for this analysis, is made publicly available to facilitate its application in other experiments. The associated public codes are accessible at https://github.com/ALICE-Heavy-Ion/3D-Flow. The presented results are published in Phys. Rev. C 104, 064903 (2021). The 3D flow analysis method is detailed in the publication arXiv:2102.01009v2 [nucl-th]. The public codes for the 3D flow analysis are available at https://github.com/ALICE-Heavy-Ion/3D-Flow. The associated 3D Monte Carlo event generator is accessible at https://github.com/ALICE-Heavy-Ion/ThreeD. Decentralized learning focuses on training models through local interactions among distributed agents, thereby eliminating the need for a central server. This paper introduces a learning framework designed to predict key performance metrics in wireless transmission systems by leveraging graph neural networks (GNNs). We investigate a specific challenge within this framework where agents lack complete information regarding the lossy communication links connecting them to the central server. To address this, we propose a method for estimating the compression error of a graph neural network when transmitted over wireless channels. Furthermore, we introduce a novel approach to mitigate this estimation error by transmitting an appropriately subsampled set of neural network weights. Our numerical results demonstrate that this framework can achieve performance levels comparable to centralized learning. Additionally, we observe that subsampling a small set of weights corresponding to the final layers of the network is highly effective at reducing compression error. This technique also significantly lowers transmission time and, consequently, enhances the performance of the trained GNN. Finally, we examine how various factors influence the proposed framework's performance. Specifically, we analyze the impact of different GNN architectures on achieving performance parity with centralized learning and explore how the depth of the network affects the proportion of weights that can be subsampled without incurring significant performance degradation. We conclude that utilizing a shallow network with few layers facilitates more efficient compression, which in turn allows for the transmission of fewer weights while maintaining performance comparable to centralized solutions. Furthermore, we observe that increasing the number of agents in the decentralized learning setup leads to improved performance when utilizing the proposed subsampling technique. This improvement is particularly pronounced in deeper networks, where the gain is substantial. In contrast, shallow networks with limited layers yield only marginal performance benefits from subsampling. We also evaluate the influence of the local neighborhood size within the graph structure on the performance of the learned GNNs. Our analysis reveals that smaller neighborhood sizes result in greater performance improvements from subsampling, whereas larger neighborhoods experience only slight gains. We also address the issue of unreliable agents in the decentralized learning framework. We show that incorporating an unreliable node into the graph can actually enhance the performance of the learned GNN by enabling the model to exploit information from these nodes. Conversely, adding a reliable node to the graph does not significantly impact the performance of the learned GNN model. We also examine the effect of the maximum number of iterations allowed for training the GNN. We find that within this range, the performance of the GNN trained under these constraints is comparable to that achieved through centralized learning.
