The efficacy of Deep Graph Neural Network (Deep-GNN) models relies heavily on the architecture design, which significantly influences information propagation and representation learning within complex graph-structured data. However, most current designs lack a systematic approach to analyzing and modeling the dynamic evolution of graph topology during representation learning. This study proposes a global pyramid-like shrinkage skeleton and a local topology link rewiring mechanism, alongside a dynamic graph topology link weight updating scheme, to comprehensively capture the density variations and local connectivity changes of graph groups across layers, as well as the fluctuating impact of specific nodes on the model's output. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate that this framework consistently surpasses state-of-the-art methods in both static and dynamic graph scenarios. Furthermore, extensive ablation studies confirm the critical roles of these proposed mechanisms in enhancing representation learning and model generalization. Finally, a comprehensive analysis of the proposed Deep-GNN framework design reveals that it effectively balances expressiveness with efficiency. To our knowledge, this represents the first attempt to systematically address the representation learning and model efficacy challenges inherent in existing deep-GNN models. Recent years have seen significant progress in private low-rank matrix completion, a critical step for analyzing large datasets. This work proposes a solution to the non-convex matrix completion problem that guarantees $\ell_2$-norm recovery with high probability. By adapting Huber's outlier detection technique from 1964, we ensure that outliers do not compromise the recovery of inliers. We validate our finding by comparing it against existing private low-rank matrix completion methods. Notably, our approach achieves superior outcomes compared to current differentially private methods within the low-rank matrix completion framework. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our solution outperforms differential privacy techniques specifically for this class of problems. Finally, extensive numerical experiments confirm the efficacy of our approach in both matrix completion and outlier detection scenarios. Finally, the code is available at: https://github.com/ehsan-nejati/PLE. Pleasure.

The Pleasure Loop (PLE) is a novel framework for solving large-scale low-rank matrix completion problems. It combines the advantages of both convex and non-convex approaches while mitigating their respective drawbacks. Specifically, PLE offers a more efficient solution than convex methods in high-noise environments where outliers are present. Additionally, it outperforms non-convex methods by providing guarantees similar to those of convex techniques, despite addressing a non-convex problem. This paper details the algorithm, proves its convergence, and presents a complexity analysis. Finally, the authors release the algorithm under the Pleasure Name (PLE), which can be found at: https://github.com/ehsan-nejati/PLE. Pleasure.

We introduce a unified framework for modeling the extinction, emission, and polarization of interstellar matter. This approach accounts for the full range of conditions, spanning from the highly obscured regions of the interstellar medium (ISM) to the sparse regions of the local galactic halo. It incorporates the interaction between dust grains and both atomic and ionized hydrogen, as well as the influence of cosmic rays and UV photons on the charge state distribution of dust grains. By utilizing a double-power-law size distribution for grain populations, the model successfully describes astrophysical extinction curves, extinction reddening, the morphology of the polarization fraction, and infrared emission from dust across a wide range of gas densities. The polarization fraction exhibits a double-peaked profile relative to gas density, with the secondary peak occurring in the low-density regime of the local halo. Furthermore, the model indicates that the polarization fraction is governed by the ratio of hydrogen atom density to gas density, a relationship that can be utilized to determine conditions in the local halo. Finally, we provide a set of templates for extinction, reddening, polarization, and infrared emission, which can be applied to local halo conditions to investigate their physical properties. These properties include the polarization fraction, optical depth, reddening, and infrared flux, all of which are shown to vary with distance from the Galactic plane. Our findings suggest that UV photons and cosmic rays are essential for explaining the observed polarization fraction in low-density regions. Additionally, we demonstrate that UV photons can alter the polarization fraction in low-density gas, potentially explaining the discrepancy between the polarization fraction measured by the Galactic plane survey and that observed in the local halo. Finally, we show that the infrared flux from the local halo is primarily driven by cosmic rays. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive description of dust properties in the ISM and the local halo, while also addressing several previously unresolved issues. A detailed version of this work is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.07779. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/astrodust-plus-pah/Extinction_Emission_and_Polarization. ExtinctionEmissionPolarization.zip can be downloaded from the same repository. The UV polarization fraction is available at https://github.com/astrodust-plus-pah/PolarizationFraction. UVFP.zip can also be retrieved from there. We report the discovery of a massive planet orbiting the young, low-mass star CIDA 1. Detected via ALMA observations, this planet resides at 0.6 AU from its host and is the most massive known object around a low-mass star within the nearby TW Hydrae association. Our analysis of the dust continuum reveals that the planet is responsible for the prominent spiral arms in the disk, validating the capability of massive planets to generate such features in the outer regions of disks around low-mass stars. Additionally, we identified a compact dust source at 0.15 AU, which we interpret as a second planet; this object represents the innermost massive planetary detection to date. By examining the disk's gas and dust kinematics, we inferred that the inner compact source receives significant heating from the host star, resulting in a gas temperature of approximately 100 K. This elevated temperature is hypothesized to explain the presence of millimeter-sized dust grains at such a close proximity to the star. Our findings suggest that planet formation proceeds rapidly in this system, yielding a massive planet within just 5 Myr. These results provide a critical data point for understanding the frequency and timing of planet formation around low-mass stars. The system's characteristics are consistent with a formation pathway where a massive disk fragment collapses to create a planet on a short timescale. Furthermore, we present new constraints on the host star's fundamental properties, including a mass of 0.13 M$_{\odot}$ and an age of 5 Myr. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the initial mass function of planets and the frequency of massive planet formation in low-mass systems. This study examines the tap count required to clear the grid in the game *Lights Out*. We demonstrate that for any shape $S$ comprising non-overlapping squares aligned with the grid, a configuration exists where the maximum tap count cannot be reduced below $4x(y-1)$ using alternative clearing strategies, provided the grid dimensions are $x$ and $y$ ($x \le y$). We term this an extremal configuration. The proof employs linear algebra, examining the field two vector space of grid cell states and the properties of confluent matrices. We term the taps required to clear the grid as "confluent matrix rank." We also present an extremal configuration that necessitates $4xy$ taps to clear the grid, regardless of the method used.

Abstract interpretation operates within a widening loop consisting of two distinct stages: the covering (ascending) phase, which transforms an under-approximation into an over-approximation to increase precision, and the covered (descending) phase, which converts an over-approximation into an under-approximation to maintain invariance. Although these mechanisms are conceptually separate, current implementations typically integrate them within a single narrowing loop. This paper demonstrates that they can also function independently, introducing four new algorithms for static analysis. The authors argue that this expansion offers significant benefits for both theoretical understanding and practical application. First, it establishes a rigorous theoretical framework for narrowing loops. Second, it enables the decoupling of covering and covering phases, allowing for more flexible and precise static analysis implementations.

Topological materials have recently attracted significant research interest due to their unique properties, including the topologically protected emergence of gapless states within a gapped bulk and their potential applications in spintronics and quantum computing. Although most topological phases in condensed matter systems are considered topologically protected and require no external energy input, some phases depend on continuous illumination. This study employs first-principles calculations to investigate the photon-driven topological phonon phase in perovskite oxides. Our findings indicate that the photon-driven topological phonon phase in perovskite oxides is intrinsic and can be realized under weak light intensity using infrared light within the 0.5–2.0 $\mu$m wavelength range. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this photon-driven topological phonon phase can serve as a highly effective detector for ambient light intensity. These results offer a new strategy for exploring topological phenomena in oxide materials and may facilitate the development of photonic sensors for light-driven quantum devices in future applications.

Ident anomalous data points is a critical task across numerous domains, including fraud detection, network intrusion detection, and disease surveillance. This study introduces a novel outlier detection approach leveraging proximity graphs within metric spaces. Our method first constructs a graph to model data points and their relationships, subsequently identifying clusters of normal instances and anomalous outliers based on these graph structures. The process rapidly and precisely calculates the distance between an instance and its nearest cluster, with performance independent of the total data volume. We further enhance the method's efficiency by integrating a new pruning technique that bypasses the graph traversal for a subset of instances, which are provably unlikely to be outliers. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods in both speed and accuracy, achieving up to a 100-fold increase in traversal speed on diverse datasets. Furthermore, the method scales effectively to big data environments, delivering substantial speedups when paired with distributed processing frameworks. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar1992/PGOD. It demonstrates that the stimulated emission or absorption of photons results from the atom interacting with its own emitted field. This interaction modifies both the atom's energy levels and its transition probabilities. The stimulus is identified as an effective field composed of the superposition of the atom's own field and the portion reflected by the mirror. Furthermore, parts of the results explore how the reflected fraction of emitted radiation deviates from the standard $1/\text{r}^2$ dependence typically observed in free space. These findings are applicable to any quantum dipole, including molecules and ions. The analysis relies on first-order perturbation theory, assuming a mirror so thin that its electronic excitations can be neglected. Consequently, this approach may not address the specific behavior of an atom-electron system when the electron acts as a mirror. The paper concludes by examining the properties of a moving mirror, revealing that the atom's radiation is significantly amplified due to the relativistic Doppler effect. This phenomenon is interpreted as motion-induced stimulation. Additionally, it is noted that part of the amplified radiation is directed backward, opposite to the mirror's motion, a effect known as mirror fluorescence. These characteristics are also examined through the lens of a mirror modeled as a collection of oscillators. Finally, the study investigates the possibility of amplification within a cavity formed by two moving mirrors. The work ends by discussing the potential for these mechanisms to generate a detectable signal. The conclusions are supported by a set of numerical examples. The paper is accompanied by supplementary video files providing visualizations of the phenomena described. This study addresses node classification on unlabelled graph datasets where community structures are provided, aiming for fair labels while leveraging the graph's connectivity. We introduce a new framework designed to minimize both discriminatory bias and the loss of connectivity information. Our approach employs a novel objective function that integrates community structures and connectivity through an undifferentiated aggregation mechanism, subsequently optimizing node labels to achieve fair results. We demonstrate that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches regarding fairness metrics and connectivity preservation, particularly in scenarios involving highly disparate graph structures. Furthermore, we apply this model to a real-world case study focused on fair node labeling within a COVID-19 dataset. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance of node classification on an unlabelled COVID-19 dataset, and our approach has never before been evaluated in this context. Additionally, we present the first comprehensive empirical analysis of node classification fairness across various real-world COVID-19 datasets. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/DeepMind/graph_fairness. This work was conducted by researchers at DeepMind.

This study examines kinetic models for the reversible binding of substrate to enzyme and product, accounting for both iso- and anisotropic scenarios. The governing equations are formulated as systems of integrodifferential equations, utilizing the Ising model as a specific instance. Leveraging established methods for nonlinear integral equations, the authors demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of solutions to these kinetic equations through a contraction mapping principle applied to a suitably defined metric space of continuous functions. Additionally, the paper presents a theorem regarding the iterative solution of the equations and introduces a novel approach for the first-order approximation of enzyme kinetic systems based on integral equations. Finally, the second and third approximations, which correspond to the well-known Michaelis equation, are derived and analyzed. It is noted that the existence and uniqueness theorems for the kinetic equation systems are applicable to various biochemical kinetic equations. Furthermore, the authors establish that the derived kinetic equations serve as asymptotic approximations for integral equations describing binding processes across enzyme systems. Finally, the theoretical findings of this work are supported by specific numerical examples. This work investigates the dynamics of rational expectation financial bubbles, focusing on their on-off switching behavior, stochastic drifts, and inherent risks. The analysis begins with a minimal two-factor model featuring a stochastic drift and a Markovian switch, yielding a linear differential equation for the fair bubble price. By integrating the stochastic drift into the analysis, the study derives a system of ordinary differential equations for the fair bubble's mean and variance, incorporating a correction term that accounts for the switch's concentration. This approach yields a straightforward diagnostic for identifying the concentration of the Markovian switch, which serves as a generalization of the concentration correction term previously established in the literature. Subsequently, the rational expectation bubble model is extended to include a random clock that switches between two states with distinct characteristics, resulting in a new class of price models where drifts are deterministic yet time-varying. This extension enables a more granular characterization of bubble models by defining a system via two vectors: one for the fair price drift and another for its concentration parameter. To address the resulting non-linear differential equation, a series of approximations are developed. The first is a mean-reverting model where the concentration time follows a gamma distribution; this framework is shown to be equivalent to a fractional growth model previously proposed in the literature. The second approximation is a stochastic model where the drift's concentration is modeled as a random variable with a specified probability distribution. Finally, the study examines the conditions under which a financial bubble emerges, demonstrating that a bubble forms when the stochastic drift's concentration time is significantly shorter than that of the switching time. This insight provides a practical method for diagnosing bubble models and calculating the probability of bubble formation. Throughout the paper, several examples are provided to illustrate these methodologies. Additionally, numerical simulations are conducted to analyze the dynamics of financial bubbles within this framework. Overall, the work offers a versatile model for financial bubble analysis, providing a robust tool for both theoretical research and practical applications. Key contributions include a rational expectation model with stochastic drift, a novel approach to modeling bubbles with a random clock, and a unified framework for comparing different bubble models. Furthermore, the study introduces new methods for analyzing bubble dynamics and establishes a rigorous foundation for future research in this area. Finally, the paper concludes by discussing the limitations of the proposed model and suggesting potential avenues for extension. These limitations stem from the simplicity of the model, which does not capture the full complexity of financial markets, and the assumption that the switching time is fixed, whereas in reality it is stochastic. We present a path integral approach to simulating a quantum harmonic oscillator under a time-dependent driving force, utilizing a discrete time formulation. Both the partitioning of time intervals and the evaluation of the propagator are evaluated through Monte Carlo simulations. These findings can be directly applied to simulate other quantum systems, such as the quantum harmonic oscillator, and may be extended to investigate the quantum phase transition occurring in a quantum Monte Carlo model of a quantum meta-stable system near its critical point. Additionally, the method is applicable to exploring quantum aspects of biological systems by modeling them as quantum harmonic oscillators subjected to time-dependent external forces. Finally, the technique is expected to be extendable to modeling quantum systems involving particles within external potentials. To demonstrate these points, we also include a direct simulation of a particle in a time-dependent potential. All simulations were conducted using Python. In recent years, recommender systems have incorporated Review-based approaches to enhance traditional systems reliant on user behavior by leveraging reviewer sentiments. While existing methods effectively model reviews, they often overlook the interplay between sentiment scores and review text, as well as the influence of different sentiment polarity words on reviewer sentiment. To address these limitations, we introduce the Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network (SiFN), a sentiment-aware interactive fusion framework designed for review-centered recommendation. This framework comprises two sub-modules: the Sentiment-aware Review Feature Learning (SRFL) module and the Review-based Item-aware Fusion (RIF) module. The SRFL module extracts features from both the sentiment polarity and the lexical features of the review text. Subsequently, the RIF module aggregates these learned features with the user's historical interaction data to generate personalized recommendations. Experimental results demonstrate that SiFN significantly outperforms other neural network architectures and baseline methods. Furthermore, case studies confirm that SiFN effectively captures the requirements of sentiment-aware review features. SiFN is an open-source framework available at https://github.com/1229chen/SIFN. Additionally, the item review dataset used in our experiments can be found at https://github.com/1229chen/Review_Dataset. Finally, the source code is available at https://github.com/1229chen/SIFN. The dataset is accessible at https://github.com/1229chen/Review_Dataset. Data sparsity remains a significant hurdle in transforming machine learning into an automated process for Social Media monitoring. To address this, we explore data augmentation techniques for Arabic-English code-switched tweets. Our research demonstrates the efficacy of both unsupervised and supervised methods in increasing tweet volume while maintaining semantic integrity. We evaluated a range of techniques, including word-level and phrase-level back-translation, lexical substitutions via data-driven and linguistic dictionaries, and neural style transfer. The findings indicate that supervised lexical substitution, specifically replacing glosses within a semantic network, yields the most effective augmentation for this code-switching context. Furthermore, style transfer was assessed to verify if augmented texts retain original semantics, with both code-switched and monolingual evaluations demonstrating their ability to preserve meaning. Finally, we analyze how various substitution techniques impact code-switched texts and offer recommendations for future research in this domain. To support the community, we make our code, dataset, and evaluation code publicly available. We demonstrate that any Roelcke precompact collection of homeomorphisms acting on a surface must fix a point at infinity. By adopting a non-principal ultrafilter, we establish that this condition is essentially tight. Furthermore, although every Roelcke precompact collection on a surface admits a convergent constant subnet, this does not hold for the broader class of Roelcke precompact collections; in such cases, the action on the boundary of the surface is highly constrained. Additionally, we present a novel proof of a theorem by Mařík and Šemrl regarding homeomorphism groups equipped with the compact-open topology, which characterizes the maximal compact-subset-open graph subgroups. Finally, we outline several open questions concerning the characterization of Roelcke precompact subsets within the homeomorphism group of a surface. These inquiries are motivated by the phenomenon where the Roelcke precompactness of a collection on a surface fails to imply Roelcke precompactness when viewed as a subset of the homeomorphism group under the compact-open topology. We address this specific issue by identifying surfaces (such as higher-dimensional spheres) that possess point-free, homeomorphism-point-free Roelcke precompact collections. We further generalize this concept to the setting of homeomorphism groups on any locally compact Hausdorff space. In this context, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions for the Roelcke precompactness of a collection of homeomorphisms and their point-free variants, considering the uniformity induced by the compact-open topology. Our analysis reveals that the Roelcke uniformity associated with the compact-open topology is strictly coarser than the uniformity derived from all continuous uniformities on a compact space. Leveraging this observation, we present a unified framework for investigating the Roelcke precompactness of homeomorphism groups on compact spaces. This approach yields novel results for investigating the Roelcke precompactness of collections of homeomorphisms on compact spaces. Specifically, we establish that the Roelcke precompactness of a collection of homeomorphisms on a compact space is equivalent to the compactness of the closure of the collection within the homeomorphism space under the compact-open topology. This finding resolves an inquiry posed by M. Dales, J. K. Isbell, and J. D. Morgan. Furthermore, this result enables the identification of point-free Roelcke precompact collections of homeomorphisms on certain compact spaces, including the Cantor set and the unit interval. We introduce a new class of sigma-model actions encompassing generalized $\lambda$-deformations and $\delta$-deformations within Sasaki-Einstein backgrounds, extending these concepts to higher dimensions. By focusing on spatially localized solutions, we construct non-trivial integrable membranes via the light-cone gauge for these higher-dimensional generalizations. In topologically spherical configurations, the higher-spin currents remain conserved. Furthermore, we derive membranes on six-dimensional backgrounds associated with simple and adjoint symmetric spaces of $G_2$ holonomy. For six-dimensional spatial topologies, we identify non-trivial world-volume deformations linked to the second Chern class. Finally, we evaluate the spacetime scaling dimensions of operators in the putative dual three-dimensional CFTs, specifically for the standard $\lambda$-deformations of $G_2$ backgrounds. In the limit where all deformation parameters vanish, we recover the standard sigma-model action for round $S^6$. Additionally, we obtain integrable membranes on the standard $D$-deformation AdS$_6$ backgrounds by employing a star-shaped topology. We introduce a new family of continuous variable splines defined on hex meshes, termed "tet splines." In trivariate space, these splines are constructed by joining "tetrahedrons" along the faces of the original mesh. Our technique leverages the specific topology of hex meshes, enabling the creation of continuous functions on arbitrary grids that are significantly harder to compute than those achievable through tesselations. We outline the underlying theory, provide an algorithm to generate these "fake tets," and demonstrate an interactive hex mesh model featuring up to 58 tets per hexahedron. Our findings open new avenues for research into continuous functions on hex meshes. The source code and interactive results are accessible at https://github.com/brunag/tetsinhex. Furthermore, tet splines are integrated into OpenSubdiv, the industry-standard tessellation framework utilized by major graphics software like Maya and Blender. This inclusion allows for the rapid experimentation and deployment of our methodology. Our work holds significant potential for advancing research on continuous functions over hex meshes. Specifically, we address and resolve several longstanding challenges in this domain, including: (i) the design of continuous subdivision schemes for hex meshes; (ii) the development of continuous variable splines on this grid type; and (iii) the creation of subdivision-based remeshing techniques that maintain continuity. Our approach meets and exceeds multiple criteria established by existing solutions. Additionally, the computational cost of our method is comparable to, or lower than, that of comparable approaches. Our contributions are detailed below: (i) We define a novel class of continuous functions on tessellations that transcend the limitations of prior works. Relation extraction (RE) focuses on identifying the relationship between a subject and an object within a sentence, yet it frequently suffers from a performance gap when applied to real-world data due to issues like sentence truncation, loss of contextual information, and external knowledge deficits. By utilizing a fifth-order polynomial, the model accurately captures the non-linear inverter transition region, including effects such as the short channel and sub-threshold phenomena. The developed formulation is capable of describing inverters across all operating regions, making it applicable to both discrete and integrated logic gates. The state-discrete Markov decision process (MDP) framework has driven significant advancements in reinforcement learning, yet it relies on the unrealistic assumption that the true state space is known and can be fully discretized. This paper introduces the coarse-grained continuity assumption, which facilitates state discretization in general topological spaces, paired with a newly defined coarse-grained continuous MDP (CGCMDP). We demonstrate that the optimal value function of this CGCMDP can be computed via the value iteration algorithm. Furthermore, we establish the $l_\infty$ norm error bound for the value iteration solution relative to that of the original MDP, provided the action space is finite. Finally, we apply these findings to create the coarse-grained continuous Q-learning algorithm (CGQL) for practical implementation. Experimental results indicate that CGQL achieves performance comparable to existing methods while offering greater generality. Additionally, we illustrate how to construct CGQL from various existing algorithms, such as PQL and QLD, and analyze the implications of this framework. To our knowledge, this work represents the first effort to generalize state discretization in MDPs using the coarse-grained continuity assumption, with all theoretical proofs available in the supplementary material. Type-ax (Type-C) quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in black hole X-ray transients are characterized by low frequency and high amplitude, with their origins remaining a subject of debate. This study investigates the evolution of Type-C QPOs in the black hole system MAXI J1535-571 using data from the Insight-HXMT observatory. The dataset comprises 100 ks observations collected during the source's hard state. We analyzed energy-resolved light curves across the 2–100 keV range and performed power spectral density (PSD) analysis using the 10–100 keV band. Our results indicate that Type-C QPOs are present in all observations, exhibiting a rising-trending frequency and increasing amplitude as the source brightens. Additionally, we observed a decline in the power index of the PSD continuum, alongside a notable increase in the 2–10 keV count rate and the 2–100 keV flux. These findings suggest that Type-C QPOs may arise from a combination of the fundamental frequency and its first harmonic. Furthermore, the evolution of Type-C QPOs appears linked to changes in the accretion rate, while the decreasing power index of the PSD continuum may reflect the changing state of the accretion disc. Finally, the flux ratio of the 2–10 keV band relative to the 2–100 keV band serves as a reliable indicator for tracking the evolution of Type-C QPOs. These results offer valuable insights into the nature and origin of Type-C QPOs. This study investigates cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) from the perspective of individual agents within a multi-task environment. We address a critical challenge in MARL: the unreliable reaction to a partner's actions, which stems from the independent optimization of individual policies. To mitigate this, we introduce a new intrinsic incentive termed "transfer empowerment," which quantifies the impact an agent's actions have on its partners' policies. This concept is grounded in the idea of shared objectives, operationalized through the ability to transfer information to teammates. By approximating transfer empowerment using mutual information, we demonstrate that this social intrinsic motivation fosters reliable responses to partner actions and significantly enhances collaboration. Our approach is model-free and requires no communication, making it particularly suitable for complex scenarios. We validated the proposed method in a multi-agent soccer game, where an agent must switch between training and match tasks. Experimental results show that while marl methods trained on a single task fail to generalize effectively to a different task due to the reliable reaction issue, adding the transfer empowerment incentive enables the agent to master both tasks and substantially improves team coordination. Furthermore, we observe that this incentive leads to the emergence of emergent communication, a phenomenon that reinforces the reliability of reactions to partners' actions. The source code is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/ChenchenLi2019/TransferEmpowerment}. Our findings suggest that this method can enhance cooperation in multi-task settings. Identifying materials through visual cues is a critical challenge in numerous real-world applications. This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to identify any material from the vastest possible domain with a single training example. Our approach leverages physics-based rendering to generate synthetic images and synthetic material labels, enabling the model to learn general material characteristics from these synthetic data. We employ a contrastive learning strategy to train a deep convolutional neural network (DCNN) to distinguish between a query material and a database of other materials. We assess our model's ability to identify a wide range of materials in everyday settings by testing it on real-world images of clothing fabrics and automotive materials. The results demonstrate that our method can correctly identify a single material against a database containing over 100,000 candidates with more than 90% accuracy using just one training image. Furthermore, we show that our DCNN can be fine-tuned to identify a different target material within a different category while still maintaining over 90% accuracy with only one new training image. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first successful application of contrastive learning to material identification. We introduce a new end-to-end method for keypoint-based image matching that operates without predefined image features. Our approach, named LoFTR (Local-Freeze Global Attention), utilizes a global descriptor bank integrated with local feature modules to identify and match images based on their local attributes. By employing a detector-free strategy, we allow the global descriptor bank to implicitly identify high-relevant areas through high-confidence descriptor pairs, thereby eliminating the need for separate interest point detectors and reducing reliance on precise keypoint localization. Furthermore, we have developed a novel synthetic dataset, ArgLine, specifically designed to train keypoint-based matching models effectively in the absence of keypoint annotations. This model is lightweight, completing an inference on a single NVIDIA TitanX GPU in approximately 0.3 seconds. On the Pascal 2012 dataset, our method achieves a 4.4% improvement in recall over the second-best approach at an equal average precision. Additionally, we have deployed this model in an open-source library to support real-time, cloud-based image matching services. This study examines the bias inherent in the Inferred Equal Weighting (I.E.W.) method used to calibrate vector magnetograms, a technique that combines line-of-sight field data from the Continuum (Co) instrument with line broadening data from Inverse (I) spectropolarimetric points. By utilizing co-registered I.I.E.W. data from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI), we identified a specific bias in the magnetic field maps generated by this approach. This bias manifests as an underestimation of the inferred line-of-sight magnetic field within regions characterized by high magnetic shear. Although this phenomenon was previously hypothesized, we now demonstrate that it produces a non-negligible impact. Furthermore, we show that bias can be significantly mitigated when HMI data is processed using the new I.I.E.Q.W. method, which applies equal weighting to both I and E spectropolarimetric points. Finally, we illustrate the effectiveness of this revised method by presenting HMI synoptic maps. These new synoptic maps exhibit a substantial reduction in the previously observed bias. Additionally, they align more closely with results from other SDO/HSIM instruments, such as the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS) and the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA). Consequently, I.I.E.Q.W. is recommended for HMI data processing. We also applied this approach to other available HMI datasets, including those from the Solar Cycle 24 peak and a major solar eruption, to further validate its efficacy. The co-registered I.I.E.Q.W. synoptic maps reveal a more accurate representation of the magnetic field structure in these events. Overall, this research provides a comprehensive analysis of the bias affecting HMI-inferred synoptic magnetic field maps and establishes a robust methodology for their production. This approach is designed to facilitate the creation of reliable HMI synoptic magnetic field maps for the current and future solar cycles. This study introduces a new demand-side management framework where consumers autonomously schedule their energy consumption. The framework utilizes scheduling an incentive signal, derived from an aggregative game, to coordinate consumer decisions on energy scheduling and instantaneous load billing based on real-time usage. Furthermore, the efficacy of this framework is validated through a 14-day smart meter dataset collected from a residential area in Madrid, Spain. This real-world data confirms that the approach can meet demand-side management goals even when consumer preferences and behaviors are heterogeneous. Finally, a numerical analysis demonstrates that the proposed method achieves demand-side management objectives with lower total costs compared to traditional demand-side management techniques. Consequently, this framework has the potential to enhance demand-side management effectiveness and support the successful integration of renewable energy sources. Additionally, the approach is applicable to various cost management schemes, such as budgeting and billing. We introduce a straightforward method to identify metal-poor stars ([Fe/H] < -2.0) from brief Blue Photometer (BP) and Red Photometer (R) spectra, such as those from the Gaia mission. This approach relies on a single, easily calculable index: the ratio of flux at 485 nm to the continuum at 430 nm. This metric effectively isolates metal-poor stars from those with higher metallicity. When applied to simulated Gaia BP/RP spectra, it achieves a 99% detection rate for stars with [Fe/H] < -2.0 while maintaining a false positive rate of just 0.03% for stars with [Fe/H] > -2.0. Additionally, we demonstrate that this index correlates with the logarithm of metallicity, allowing for precise [Fe/H] determination in metal-poor stars with a precision of approximately 0.15 dex. This method offers a reliable means of selecting metal-poor candidates for spectroscopic follow-up. Furthermore, we illustrate that combining this index with the Gaia parallax can yield a sample where the false positive rate is reduced to the level of statistical uncertainty. We also detail how to identify turn-off stars from this parallax-selected sample. Our technique is particularly valuable for studying the oldest and most metal-poor stars, which are crucial for understanding the early stages of galaxy evolution. This study investigates the connection between environmental factors and global Blaze Season Severity (BSS), which quantifies the product of total burned area and the duration of each year's season. By examining data from the United States, Canada, Australia, and Russia, we establish an environmental-phenomenological framework for analyzing and predicting BSS. Our findings indicate that CO2 levels, solar radiation, and temperature are the most critical determinants of long-term BSS. Additionally, we develop a forecasting model that combines these insights with time-series analysis to estimate BSS for 2020 and 2021, achieving an accuracy of approximately 90%. Leveraging our framework, we project that BSS will rise in the future due to increasing CO2 concentrations and shifts in solar radiation and temperature. This projection is supported by the established relationship between BSS and the global climate change indicator, CO2. Consequently, we identify regions with the highest risk of severe blazes, a conclusion that could inform future fire prevention strategies. Furthermore, we introduce a novel method for assessing the severity of seasonal phenomena, which holds potential for application in other fields. Specifically, we demonstrate that this approach is applicable to analyzing Wild Ocean Algal Bloom (BOAB) Season Severity. Finally, we outline several promising avenues for future research. The syntactic complexity of a language has recently been subjected to quantitative analysis through various proposed measures, including morphological richness, nominalization, and morphological complexity. However, these metrics were not empirically validated during their development, leaving uncertainty regarding the specific linguistic features—such as mean word length, nominalization, or other factors—they actually capture. This study employs correspondence analysis to assess the relationships between three established complexity scores and word-class frequencies. The results indicate that while these measures are correlated, they do not share the same underlying dimensions. Furthermore, the frequencies of different word classes appear to influence these scores in distinct ways. Finally, we validate two lexicalist hypotheses concerning morphological complexity: first, that measures relying on agreement morphology primarily evaluate mean lexical complexity rather than specific agreement mechanisms; and second, that measures based on the ratio of distinct to type tokens are sensitive to the variability of specific morphological mechanisms. Consequently, researchers are advised to utilize a diverse range of complexity measures to gain a more comprehensive understanding of typological variation. To facilitate this, we have made our compiled measures and corresponding scores publicly accessible. These findings underscore the necessity of empirically correlating and validating proposed measures before they are used to test hypotheses about universal correlations among them. Finally, we demonstrate the value of these measures for identifying language change by tracking shifts in complexity scores across historical periods. Specifically, we observe a decrease in morphological complexity over time in both French and English, which we interpret as an increase in lexical complexity. This study serves as a robust example of how complexity measures can be utilized to investigate diachronic complexity. We investigate strong gravitational lensing within galaxy clusters, with a specific focus on the substructure of their dark matter halos. By employing the Press-Shearer formalism, we generate NFW halos containing either baryonic or collisionless subhalos, or a hybrid of both. Our analysis demonstrates that while collisionless subhalos are typically more massive, they are also more abundant, with their number density following a power-law distribution. We examine the lensing signatures of both dark matter and baryonic subhalos, deriving the lens equation using the formalism of Schneider, Kochanek, and Bartelmann. Subsequently, we estimate the number of detectable subhalos by searching for caustic crossings. We show that collisionless subhalos can significantly influence lensing observables, potentially accounting for up to 50% of the signal. Furthermore, we find that up to 90% of subhalos may remain undetectable, a figure that could rise to 99% if observational uncertainties are increased. Finally, our results indicate that the mass of subhalos must be at least an order of magnitude lower than current limits derived from dwarf galaxy observations. This constraint is crucial for resolving the small-scale crisis associated with $\Lambda$CDM predictions. Additionally, we explore the possibility that dark matter consists of multiple components, each possessing distinct annihilation cross-sections. In this scenario, we find that up to 99% of subhalos could evade detection. This finding is particularly significant for interpreting the recent APEX observation of 10'x10' gamma-ray emission from the Coma cluster. We conclude that our findings impose stringent upper limits on subhalo masses, which in turn necessitates a low annihilation cross-section, thereby offering a potential resolution to the small-scale annihilation crisis. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for future observational efforts aimed at detecting subhalos. Specifically, we argue that the South Pole Telescope will be capable of detecting collisionless subhalos out to a redshift of approximately $z=0.5$. We also outline the advantages of utilizing gamma-ray observations, which can probe much smaller scales compared to optical methods. In conclusion, we show that the future Cherenkov Telescope Array will enable the detection of subhalos with masses as low as $10^6 M_{\odot}$, provided the dark matter self-interaction cross-section is sufficiently small. Large-scale mathematical models are frequently employed to simulate the dynamics of complex systems, yet their computational demands often hinder the analysis of control strategies. This paper introduces a framework for model reduction that relies on matching the behaviors of the original and reduced models based on observable data. Our approach treats model reduction as a core coregulation task, utilizing the original model as a prior and the reduced model as the kernel. We establish the conditions under which this matching is guaranteed and propose algorithms to address the corresponding optimization problems. Applications will be demonstrated using two examples: a nonlinear system observed at a single data point and a linear system observed within a small dataset. The proposed method is anticipated to prove particularly beneficial for controlling systems where full state observability is unattainable. This paper introduces M-ar-K-Fast, a novel dimensionality reduction technique that extends the M-ar-K analysis framework. Originally, M-ar-K analysis is a multivariate extension of the well-known K-Fast method; while K-Fast identifies a single linear combination that strongly predicts all other variables, M-ar-K analysis simultaneously determines a common factor and a set of unique factors, each predicting the remaining variables to a high degree. We demonstrate that these M-ar-k factors correspond directly to the latent semantic spaces found in unsupervised learning domains such as clustering, classification, and regression. Furthermore, we establish that the latent spaces generated by M-ar-k analysis are equivalent to those produced by t-SNE and UMAP when parameters are well-tuned. The primary objective of this work is to demonstrate the validity and superiority of these techniques for high-dimensional data analysis, offering significant advantages in computational efficiency and ease of use. M-ar-K analysis is conceptually straightforward, closely related to familiar methods like PCA, and closely aligned with state-of-the-art techniques like t-SNE and UMAP. We show that M-ar-k-predicted spaces achieve performance comparable to or better than PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP in facilitating multivariate classification, while substantially outperforming all three in terms of processing speed. Additionally, we prove that the K-Fast factor space predicts new variables with accuracy equivalent to PCA. Finally, we confirm that the K-Fast and M-ar-K factor spaces maintain high predictability even when trained on only a small fraction of the data. The core innovation of M-ar-k analysis is its ability to identify predictive factors that are entirely data-driven, requiring no prior knowledge, assumptions, or hypotheses. Consequently, M-ar-k analysis is highly versatile, applicable to a broad range of problems without the need for prior knowledge. Furthermore, its computational efficiency makes it suitable for large-scale, real-time analysis. In summary, M-ar-k analysis represents a significant advancement in high-dimensional data analysis, offering superior performance, efficiency, and ease of use compared to existing techniques. Its predictive factors are optimal, its performance is proven, and its scalability is guaranteed. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/SebastianKraemer/MarK. This study introduces a real-time spatio-temporal incident detection framework designed to identify traffic disruptions and geographical anomalies from Twitter data using unsupervised machine learning. The process begins by converting tweets into a temporal sequence of "tweet objects," which are defined as sequential sets of geotagged mentions for specific locations. The temporal dynamics of these tweet objects are modeled via a time series approach, while their spatial distribution is analyzed using a spatial Poisson point process. Subsequently, a change-point detection algorithm identifies anomalies in the temporal data, and a Bayesian method pinpoints spatially distributed outliers. Finally, an incident scoring mechanism ranks both temporal and spatial anomalies to flag significant events. When applied to traffic data from the Greater Los Angeles Area, the proposed method achieved detection rates of 90% for traffic incidents and 85% for non-travel days, while effectively reducing false positives. This approach offers a promising solution for real-time anomaly detection in large metropolitan areas. Additionally, a web application has been developed to visualize the method's detection results, with a user interface that allows users to input their own travel plans and compare them against predicted traffic conditions. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/leeyu1122/ST-Twitter-Anomaly-Detection. Future research will explore integrating incident detection with trajectory prediction and itinerary planning. The source code is available at: https://github.com/leeyu1122/ST-Twitter-Anomaly-Detection. Keywords: Twitter, Anomaly Detection, Traffic, Los Angeles, Real-time.

In the current display advertising ecosystem, ad exchanges and publishers typically employ second-price auctions, where the advertiser's bid serves only as a reference and does not guarantee media purchase. Consequently, under tight budget constraints, budgets can be overspent early due to high-cost impressions, leaving insufficient funds for later, potentially higher-value opportunities. This issue is further complicated by budgeted bidding, which introduces budget exhaustion and non-controllability risks, making it challenging for advertisers to maximize their return on investment. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a novel adaptive risk-aware bidding strategy. This framework enables advertisers to dynamically adjust their bids to avoid both budget exhaustion and excessive risk of overpayment. We provide theoretical analysis to demonstrate the competitiveness of this approach and validate its effectiveness through real-world case studies. Experimental results indicate that our method can reduce overpayment risk by up to 10% while maintaining budget efficiency comparable to standard bid-adjustment techniques. Furthermore, we show the adaptability of our framework across various practical scenarios. To our knowledge, this represents the first theoretical guarantee for risk-aware budgeted bidding problems, offering new insights and theoretical foundations for adaptive bidding research. Recently, Wigner negativity has also been linked to quantum guidance, where quantum particles follow the same trajectories as their probability distributions. In this study, we extend this analogy by demonstrating that quantum variables remain guided even when the probability distribution itself is not. Furthermore, we reveal that quantum systems exhibiting quantum jarrows (q-jarrows) are consistently guided by their probability distributions. Conversely, we identify conditions under which quantum variables are not guided, such as in the case of a free particle. Additionally, we establish that if both the potential and the wave function (or probability distribution) are real, the system is always guided. Finally, our findings indicate that while probability distributions can serve as guides, they do not always function as such. These results provide new insights into the nature of quantum variables and highlight the critical role of Wigner negativity in understanding quantum system behavior. Specifically, we show that for any unnormalized distribution $P(x,t)$, the normalized Wigner function $W(x,p,t)$ is negative at some point in phase space, implying that $P(x,t)$ must also exhibit negativity or "non-classicality" in at least one region. This work offers a novel perspective on the relationship between Wigner negativity and quantumness. By examining the connection between quantum variables and probability distributions, our research deepens the understanding of Wigner negativity and opens new avenues for future research in quantum physics. The study concludes by demonstrating that Wigner negativity is essential for explaining the behavior of quantum variables, and that it plays a pivotal role in defining the boundary between classical and quantum regimes. However, practical constraints often necessitate the use of random sources that generate random numbers with non-uniform entropy. This study examines a framework where random seeds for privacy amplification are derived from a random source utilizing non-uniform entropy. Our theoretical results demonstrate that a secure random number can still be generated from the output sequences of arbitrary QKD protocols, even when the seed is sourced from a non-uniform random source. We illustrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to the BB84 protocol featuring weak measurement. Numerical findings indicate that the framework remains effective despite significant deviations from uniform entropy in the random source. Furthermore, our results show that the secret key rate remains high even when the random seed accounts for up to 50% of the encoded quantum sequences. These findings hold significant value for the practical implementation of QKD. Additionally, this work serves as a foundation for future research into the secure limit analysis of QKD protocols relying on random sources with limited entropy. Specifically, it supports the development of self-contained QKD systems that eliminate the dependency on external random number generators. This study examines non-negative jump-diffusion processes characterized by linear death and quadratic birth rates, alongside a broader category of processes with linear non-local generators and quadratic elliptic operators, within the context of $\varepsilon$-coalescents and $n$-sampled processes derived from them. The analysis focuses on coalescents involving a continuous number of types and the sampling structures associated with them. Specifically, we determine the coalescence and sampling distributions for Feller square diffusion processes on the half-line, a result that was previously unresolved. These findings are derived from the explicit transition densities of the underlying Feller square diffusion processes. Furthermore, the $n$-sampled process for the Feller square diffusion is identified as a specific member of the generalized Wright-Feller class of pure jump $\delta$-coalescents. We also explore the sampling distribution of the process at the origin, a scenario that presents unique challenges. Finally, the study investigates the weak limit of the sampled process when $\varepsilon$ approaches zero from the positive side. To support these results, the paper includes the derivation of the transition density for Feller square diffusion processes and provides an analysis of the series representation for this density. Additionally, the transition densities for a family of generalized Wright-Feller $\delta$-coalescents are derived. The methodology extends to a wider range of Feller processes, including those that are pure jump, although the corresponding transition densities are expressed via infinite series. The work also addresses the issue of sampling at the origin and the construction of the sampled process as the weak limit of a sequence of sampled processes. The analysis is comprehensive, covering both the case where the sampled process starts at the origin and where it does not. To facilitate these derivations, an integral identity for the gamma function is provided. Finally, the study includes an appendix detailing the transition densities for the generalized Wright-Feller $\delta$-coalescent. The techniques developed herein are applicable to the $k$-coalescent for any $k \geq 2$. We introduce a diagrammatic method to compute scattering matrices for multi-photon multi-particle systems within waveguide QED. These matrices characterize interactions between guided photons and two-level quantum gates (qubits), such as atoms or defects in the guide. Once the scattering matrix and an incoming multi-photon state are defined, the evolution of the output state can be calculated. The proposed method is general, applicable to any configuration of qubits in the guide, and facilitates the analysis of multi-photon interactions with the qubits and between the photons themselves. Furthermore, we demonstrate its utility by designing a multi-bit classical gate that functions as a multi-photon switch, where multiple photons enter and exit through distinct ports. Additionally, we illustrate how to detect multi-photon entanglement by measuring the coincidence rate of detected photons. Finally, this framework enables the design of novel quantum devices by leveraging the design rules derived from the diagrammatic method. These findings are validated through simulations of various quantum gates and multi-photon entangled states. Our results suggest that these techniques can be integrated into future quantum computing architectures. *Keywords:* quantum information processing, quantum communication, quantum computing, quantum wire, quantum gate, quantum device, quantum entanglement. We investigate the scattering of spin-dependent dark matter (DM) off nucleons, focusing on the impact of Lorentz-violating terms in the DM Lagrangian. These specific terms generate an effective spin that does not vanish even when the DM remains isotropic within the Earth's halo, thereby enabling any isotropic halo to produce observable signals in experimental settings. Furthermore, these Lorentz-violating contributions significantly alter the DM's velocity distribution relative to the target by modifying the center-of-mass frame velocity; this velocity is determined by the composition of dark matter within that frame, which is influenced by both the Earth's orbital motion around the Sun and its rotation around the Earth's axis. Consequently, when combined with constraints from non-rotating Earth tests, our findings impose significantly tighter limits on the Lorentz-violating parameters. Additionally, for spin-dependent interactions with a tensor structure, we demonstrate that Lorentz-violating terms can substantially amplify the scattering cross-section, resulting in constraints that are orders of magnitude stronger. Finally, we outline how these Lorentz-violating terms can be constrained through neutrino-nucleon scattering experiments. In contrast, if DM remains isotropic, Lorentz-violating effects would be highly suppressed due to the contraction of two independent spins, resulting in extremely weak experimental limits. However, if Lorentz-violating terms induce a preferred direction in the DM velocity distribution, the associated tensor structures could markedly increase the scattering amplitude, thereby yielding much tighter bounds on the parameters. This analysis also applies to scalar-mediated interactions, where Lorentz-violating terms can similarly amplify the cross-section. Finally, we address the issue of scaling violations in cross-sections arising from Lorentz-violating operators with dimensions greater than four, noting that such scaling breaks down at energy scales approaching the cutoff, with the associated parameter limits falling below the Planck scale. This direction of research is particularly promising for understanding the hierarchy problem. To address this, we propose a UV completion of the Lorentz-violating DM model, which yields testable predictions for collider experiments involving high-energy proton beams. This paper introduces an optimized delay-enhanced differential coherent detection method for continuous phase modulation, achieving performance comparable to absolute coherent detection. While traditional differential detection lacks the delay diversity benefit inherent in delay-enhanced coherent detection. By integrating the principles of absolute coherent detection into a differential framework, the proposed scheme fully exploits delay diversity and significantly lowers the error floor. Simulations across various modulation formats and channels confirm its efficacy. This approach is particularly advantageous for non-coherent receivers aiming to operate at high signal-to-noise ratios. Furthermore, the method supports incremental redundancy hybrid automatic repeat request protocols, enabling high-speed transmission without a performance penalty. Additionally, the scheme demonstrates robustness against frequency offsets in both delay and constellation domains, maintaining stability and delivering consistent results. Consequently, this proposed solution is ideal for next-generation communication systems. Notably, the increased complexity relative to conventional differential coherent detection is negligible. The paper also examines the trade-offs concerning differential coherent detection complexity and outlines strategies for mitigation. Finally, the concept of delay-enhanced differential coherent detection is applied to a specific modulation format, with a low-complexity receiver designed for it described. This format utilizes a phase memory span of three symbols and achieves full diversity with a receiver complexity no greater than three times that of QPSK. Simulations indicate that, in terms of delay-enhanced differential coherent detection performance, this format rivals widely used quadrature amplitude modulation formats. Furthermore, the paper presents a novel optimized maximum likelihood delay-enhanced differential coherent detector with reduced complexity. This optimized detector employs a reduced search space and a simplified distance metric, resulting in lower complexity. Simulations demonstrate that the reduced complexity does not compromise the delay-enhanced differential coherent detection performance. In summary, the proposed delay-enhanced differential coherent detection concept offers the potential to extend the applicability of this technique to a broader range of modulation formats, thereby facilitating the deployment of delay diversity in next-generation communication systems. The paper concludes by suggesting an optimal design approach for such systems. Additionally, the study explores the extension of delay-enhanced differential coherent detection to non-Gaussian white noise channels, with a reduced complexity optimized detector designed for this purpose also presented. This optimized detector utilizes a reduced search space and a modified distance metric under the assumption of a known channel distribution. Simulations show that the reduced complexity does not affect the delay-enhanced differential coherent detection performance. Finally, the paper discusses an optimal design for delay-enhanced differential coherent detection when the channel follows a specific distribution. Reward learning (RL) represents a promising method for developing robots capable of executing complex tasks through trial and error, yet it typically faces two major hurdles: the necessity for extensive exploration and the demand for human demonstration or continuous feedback. This study introduces an algorithm that mitigates these challenges by simultaneously leveraging both implicit and explicit learning. To reduce the training sample size, the system utilizes visual data to automatically identify and cluster similar task states, subsequently prioritizing the exploration of unvisited clusters. At the same time, explicit feedback is integrated to refine reward signals and accelerate convergence. We demonstrate the algorithm's efficacy using a simple simulated agent and a pushing robot on a real platform, showing that combining visual-guided RL with explicit feedback significantly enhances performance compared to using either approach independently. The resulting system exhibits robustness in generalizing to novel behaviors and robust objects. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/hiroshi-ito/VACER. Utilizing normalized Gaussian wave functions for the nucleon, we analyze the dependencies of all nucleon form factors on the deformation parameter $\theta$. We establish that the energy scale of the nucleon is significantly larger than that of the light quark, resulting in a Gaussian confinement potential that is nearly independent of $\theta$. Consequently, the proton and neutron structures remain largely unaffected by noncommutative effects. Furthermore, we observe that seven of the nine light-front form factors vanish due to relations arising from translation invariance and the constraint equations of the nucleon. In contrast, the remaining two structure form factors, $d(Q^2)$ and $g_e(Q^2)$, are sensitive to $\theta$ because they depend on the light-front helicity distribution, $g(Q^2)$, of the quarks. Finally, we present the $\theta$-dependent $\Delta d$ sum rule, which is violated in noncommutative space, and compare our findings with earlier calculations performed using Yukawa-type effective interactions with harmonic-oscillator-type wave functions. Finally, we show that the network of axial charges in the nucleon is disrupted by the noncommutative $\theta$ deformation. This work investigates the topological characteristics of highly frustrated quantum spin models on a square lattice, which can be regarded as slightly deformed dimer phases. We demonstrate that the Turaon model, which exhibits a deformed dimer pattern, is equivalent to the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ toric code on a square lattice subjected to a star operator at the origin. Consequently, the Turaon model displays a ground state degeneracy of six on the lattice and possesses $K=4$ non-Abelian anyons when the toric code anyons are deformed. Furthermore, the Turaon model supports a geometric line when the star operator is switched off along one dimension. This finding suggests the existence of novel topological phases derived from highly frustrated quantum spin models and offers intriguing opportunities for novel topological quantum computation. Finally, we outline the extension of the Turaon model to higher dimensions and provide the relevant matter theory. Specifically, the 3D generalization features a ground state degeneracy of 16 and a geometric surface with a degeneracy of 4. In this case, the toric code anyon corresponds to a fermion within the matter theory, resulting in a non-Abian anyon with quantum dimension $d=\sqrt{2}$. This framework establishes a new family of deformed dimer phases characterized by non-Abian matter theories based on fermions and anyons with quantum dimensions less than 2. Notably, this represents the first instance of deformed dimer phases with such non-Abelian anyons. Furthermore, the deformed dimer phase is conjectured to be dual to the critical point of the 1D transverse field Ising model, which is known to be dual to a conformal field theory with central charge $c=1/2$. This conclusion is supported by the observation that the global symmetry group of the toric code, $Sp(4,\mathbb{Z})$, is isomorphic to that of the 1D transverse field Ising model. Finally, we propose that the dual of the deformed dimer phase corresponds to a critical point in a higher-dimensional generalization of the 1D transverse field Ising model. We examine the stochastic differential equation (SDE) governing the complex extension of random band matrices, incorporating a finite-rank perturbation. This SDE possesses a unique global solution defined on a complete probability space. By employing the Feynman-Higgs formula, we represent the fundamental solution as an integral operator, where the kernel corresponds to the large-N limit of an N×N Gaussian fermionic two-point function. This kernel is identified as the sigma-model approximation of the fundamental solution. Leveraging the large-N limit of the fermionic two-point function, we establish that the sigma-model approximation accurately reflects the statistical properties of the SDE's fundamental solution. Specifically, we demonstrate that the approximation's spectral density converges in the weak operator topology to the semi-circular law. Furthermore, we prove that the spectral density of the fundamental solution localizes around the semi-circular law in the large-N limit. Finally, utilizing the correspondence between the fundamental solution and the sigma-model approximation, we derive that the semi-circular law serves as an approximation for the spectral density of the SDE's fundamental solution. The entire proof relies on a bootstrapping argument that iteratively refines the accuracy of the semi-circular law approximation. The approach is comprehensive and self-contained, relying exclusively on the Cauchy and Cauchy-Schwarz inequalities. Additionally, the derivation of the sigma-model approximation from the Gaussian fermionic two-point function employs a novel method. This method relies on the properties of the Wick map, which is the dual of the Wick contraction map. We provide a self-contained proof of the Wick map's properties and the fundamental theorem of contractions. Consequently, the paper is sufficiently detailed to be utilized as a resource for teaching. The work concludes with a discussion of the findings and their potential applications. The results are applicable to graphene and other two-dimensional materials, where the Hamiltonian can be formulated using complex variables. In these contexts, the semi-circular law provides an accurate approximation for the spectral density near the origin, thereby describing the low-energy behavior of the system. This approach facilitates the joint learning of vocabulary and syntax by leveraging word-order-agnostic labeling. Our methodology employs a teacher-student framework where the student generates an output matrix of hidden states, while the teacher produces a label matrix that encompasses both superspan annotations and word-level token predictions. This objective aligns with standard self-supervised tasks on large-scale, weakly annotated corpus subsets and complements supervised tasks once stronger annotations become available. Additionally, we validate our model on two extensive, weakly annotated supersession dialogue datasets, demonstrating that its pre-training objectives effectively support both dialogue summary generation and natural language inference. Finally, we analyze the model's behavior through an examination of its learned superspan boundaries. Algorithmic interpretability is a critical factor in the deployment of machine learning models. However, the definition of this concept remains ambiguous, and no consensus exists on its precise definition or measurement methods. This paper introduces a algorithmic adaptation of human learning theory to address these gaps. By applying this learning framework to the training and testing phases of machine learning models through the lens of formal concept analysis, we derive a corresponding cognitive complexity score. This score quantifies the interpretability of data-driven algorithms by reflecting the learning difficulty of the concept target represented by training data. We apply this cognitive complexity score to evaluate a classification model for diagnosing depression from speech, demonstrating that it effectively guides the selection of granular levels for rule generation during model interpretation. This process enhances the model's cognitive transparency, thereby improving its interpretability. A video showcasing our method is available at https://youtu.be/422YQ111140. Our Python implementation can be accessed at https://github.

An anomaly detection algorithm is considered a deep model if its training time is comparable to, or exceeds that of deep networks. This paper introduces a novel anomaly detection method named Isolation Forest with Weak guidance and Tiny ML (TiWS-iForest). We demonstrate that an anomaly detection model can be significantly accelerated by: 1) training it to a "tiny" capacity, 2) selecting data from unlabeled sets that are more representative of the training distribution, and 3) applying weak guidance to accelerate convergence and enhance performance. Our approach yields a speedup of up to 1,000 times compared to state-of-the-art anomaly detection algorithms. Furthermore, we show that TiWS-iForest achieves state-of-the-art results on the Anomaly Deep Learning (ADL) benchmark across the NIPS, MNIST, CIFAR10, CIFAR100, ImageNet16, and COIL100 datasets. Notably, TiWS-iForest surpasses deep models like Deep Anomaly Embedding (DAE) on the MNIST dataset, outperforming DAE by up to 10 times in both speed and accuracy. Finally, we highlight that TiWS-iForest successfully detects anomalies in unseen datasets that were not present during training. Finally, the source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ChenYi-chen/TiWS-iForest. Our findings indicate that anomaly detection models do not necessarily need to be deep to perform effectively; instead, they should be trained on representative data with weak guidance to achieve deep-model-level accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost. This study offers a new perspective for developing future anomaly detection systems. Specifically, it suggests that the anomaly detection field should aim to shift from "bigger and deeper" to "smaller and smarter" models. Moving forward, we plan to release the TiWS-iForest code as an open-source library for anomaly detection. Additionally, we propose exploring the application of TiWS-iForest in emerging domains such as edge anomaly detection and self-supervised anomaly detection. We anticipate that TiWS-iForest will become a standard anomaly detection tool in these emerging fields. This study introduces a novel parameterization for the standard Pareto distribution, defined by a minimum threshold $\kappa > 0$ and a shape parameter $\theta > 0$, which guarantees a finite mean whenever $\theta > 1$. This specific parameterization is critical for research involving the mean recovery of a finite mixture of Pareto distributions, a task that arises in extremal value theory for modeling large losses in finance and insurance, as well as in analyzing record-breaking phenomena in sports. In this framework, the mean is represented as $\kappa \exp(\frac{1}{\theta})$. We demonstrate that the proposed parameterization facilitates the straightforward construction of an independent and identically distributed Poisson process with a known Lévy measure for inference regarding shape parameters. This approach is applicable in univariate contexts involving one or multiple Pareto distributions sharing a common minimum $\kappa$. The independence inherent in this parameterization effectively eliminates identifiability issues that typically hinder the use of conventional Pareto parameterizations. Consequently, we develop a non-informative prior for shape parameters in a two-component finite mixture of Pareto distributions, where the first component features a known rate parameter (mean) and the second shares a common $\kappa$. Furthermore, we derive a closed-form solution for the Bayesian maximum a posteriori estimator of a finite mixture of two Pareto distributions, utilizing a Gamma distribution as the prior for the Poisson rates. Finally, a simulation study is conducted to assess the performance of this estimator. These findings are subsequently applied to a real-world dataset comprising extreme daily returns from the S&P 500 index spanning 1926 to 2019. This analysis compares a model using independent Poisson rates against one utilizing a shared rate, revealing that the latter provides a superior fit to the data. Additionally, we examine the robustness of these results by contrasting them with those obtained using an alternative parametric form for the Lévy measure. This study outlines a data reduction pipeline designed for the Hi-GAL survey, utilizing single-dish radio interferometry data recorded by the SCUBA-2 instrument at the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope. We evaluate data compression techniques applied to Hi-GAL datasets and assess the impact of the chosen method on subsequent analysis. The research focuses on two primary algorithms: lossless compression via LZ77 and lossy compression through Quantized Differential Encoding (QDE). The primary objective is to quantify the information loss inherent in lossy methods and confirm that it does not compromise the integrity of scientific results. The analysis incorporates real Hi-GAL data from two sources: the Hi-GAL survey of the Galactic plane and a targeted observation of the Orion Trapezium region. The study aims to assess the suitability of lossy compression for future Hi-GAL data analysis and to quantify the acceptable loss of information in scientific products. The results indicate that both lossy and lossless compression methods yield identical outcomes when analyzing source properties, such as flux density and position. However, the lossy approach produces slightly different source sizes, which remain consistent with original, uncompressed data. Additionally, cross-matching sources between compressed and uncompressed data reveals minor positional offsets. Ultimately, the findings support the use of lossy compression for Hi-GAL data analysis, provided the reduced data products are calibrated against uncompressed data. Furthermore, this conclusion is reinforced by the significant storage space savings achieved through compression. The lossy compression algorithm is particularly advantageous for large-scale surveys like Hi-GAL, where it reduces data volume by a factor of 100 compared to uncompressed data. Consequently, this work demonstrates the viability of lossy compression for survey-based science. Finally, all analysis routines are publicly accessible as a Python package on GitHub.
