Boson sampling is a quantum computational model designed to expose the unique characteristics of bosonic systems. By directing indistinguishable photons through a circuit featuring multiple beam splitters and detectors, this process generates a probability distribution rooted in quantum interference. Although the boson sampling protocol offers a pathway to detect bosonic enhancement, it also permits investigation into the anti-bosonic effect, which amplifies specific output patterns when particles exhibit strong anti-bunching. In this work, we examine a system utilizing a limited number of input modes and demonstrate that both the bosonic and anti-bosonic phenomena can be understood by analyzing the entanglement within the final state vector. This proposed method offers fresh perspectives on boson sampling, particularly advancing our comprehension of the phenomenon. Furthermore, it serves as a foundational framework for boson sampling experiments aimed at verifying bosonic enhancement. We validate our theoretical findings by implementing the analysis on the 6-qubit photonic processor QuEra's Aquila. Our results indicate that the entanglement in the complete state vectors of realistic experiments can be observed, thereby confirming our theoretical predictions. Additionally, we illustrate that the minimum number of photons required to verify quantum enhancement scales with the number of input modes. Finally, we explore the potential for extending this approach to evaluate boson sampling in many-body systems. These insights may facilitate the development of new observables for characterizing the entanglement structure of many-body wave functions. Ultimately, this methodology could aid in designing new observables for quantum sensing and simulation. Our findings suggest that boson sampling itself holds promise for quantum sensing applications. Specifically, we show that the minimum photon count needed to verify quantum enhancement in boson sampling can be tuned by adjusting the circuit's unitary matrix. This capability could prove valuable for quantum sensing, where quantum enhancement is typically observed only at the lasing threshold under maximum photon input. Furthermore, our approach to verifying quantum enhancement in boson sampling may advance quantum sensing technologies. To demonstrate this, we apply our method to the design of a new observable that quantifies the anti-bunching of single-particle states. This work establishes a foundation for new quantum sensing techniques that leverage the quantum advantage inherent in boson sampling. Finally, our findings regarding the quantum enhancement of photon counting could inspire the creation of new quantum sensors. To illustrate this potential, we designed an interferometric sensor capable of measuring the coupling strength between two adjacent photons. This sensor operates below the lasing threshold and exhibits quantum enhancement, thereby challenging the conventional belief that quantum enhancement is only attainable

High-dimensional time series, such as those found in neuroscience, often contain noise that hinders the identification of relevant features. While recent research has focused on learning functions to remove this noise, existing approaches struggle with short sequences and fail to leverage domain-specific knowledge. This paper introduces a guided learning approach for temporal sequences, demonstrating that a compact representation can be extracted by incorporating a guide derived from the specific problem context. We present the first open-access dataset in the life sciences consisting of high-dimensional electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings from zebrafish. We show that our guided learning method achieves state-of-the-art results on this dataset, reducing dimensionality to a maximum of 10 features while retaining the ability to reconstruct the original signals. Furthermore, we prove that these compressed sequences effectively predict the behavioral state of the zebrafish. Our source code and data are available at https://github.com/DeepMind/guided_learning_time_series. Finally, we demonstrate that this guided learning technique is also applicable to other time series datasets. Our findings indicate that providing short, high-dimensional sequences with an informative guide enables the learning of a compact, problem-specific solution that surpasses methods lacking such guidance. These results highlight the potential of guided learning for complex life science experiments and suggest a pathway toward more interpretable neural network models. Our work may also inspire the creation of new open-access datasets to advance the field of guided learning. Supplementary materials can be found at https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-022-01438-9. Reinforcement learning focuses on agents operating within partially observable settings, where effective decision-making requires integrating beliefs about the underlying hidden state with incentives for exploration. This study investigates recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to analyze this belief formation process. By employing interpretable techniques, we examine a standard challenging scenario: an agent learning to navigate a known graph from noisy observations. We first validate our approach by confirming that RNN performance aligns with theoretical expectations and that its internal representations align with the partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP). Subsequently, we demonstrate that RNNs develop a concealed state distinct from standard activations, enabling the disentanglement of the hidden state from other factors. Furthermore, we show that these representations facilitate the creation of interpretable models that replicate RNN performance. Finally, we highlight that the RNN's representations are robust to variations in both the environmental graph and the specific tasks assigned to the agent. Overall, this research offers a robust framework for studying how recurrent neural networks develop internal representations in partially observable contexts. Our key contributions include: (i) a robust and general framework for analyzing RNNs in such settings; (ii) evidence that RNNs construct concealed states to disambiguate hidden states; and (iii) the demonstration that these networks create internal representations that are both interpretable and functionally critical. The primary objective of action detection is to identify the temporal onset and offset of actions. While recent methods have leveraged graph convolutional networks (GCNs) to enhance action localization, they typically depend on annotated start and end points. This research investigates GCNs for action detection by learning contextual cues from sample-level supervision, allowing the training process to automatically determine the optimal temporal boundaries. Our approach utilizes a two-stage training framework: first, a temporal alignment module learns temporal alignment features from weakly-supervised labels to guide temporal boundary selection; second, these features train a action recognition GCN to refine the temporal boundaries. Experiments conducted on the UCF-101 and HMDB-51 datasets demonstrate that our method achieves competitive results, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art techniques in weakly-supervised settings. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/leeyu1023/SpotWhatCounts. Furthermore, to facilitate action detection from a broader range of video inputs, we have expanded the dataset with an additional 10-fold cross-validation split and will make it available. This enhanced dataset can be downloaded from: https://github.com/leeyu1023/UCF101. This paper details the findings from the second edition of the MSC21 image similarity challenge, held under the COPA competition series organized by the National Research University Higher School of Economics. Designed to track recent advancements in deep learning, specifically within self-supervised techniques, the competition featured two tasks: the Object Retrieval task and the Image Similarity task. This work provides an overview of the top performers in both tracks and addresses key issues related to the development of the Object Retrieval task. Furthermore, it highlights significant observations from the Image Similarity task, such as the superior performance of self-supervised learning and the growing trend of employing lightweight neural network architectures. A primary focus is placed on analyzing the top solutions, their methodologies, and the insights gained from the competition. Additionally, the paper explores the strengths and limitations of current research directions in image similarity and suggests promising avenues for future study. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/alex-petrov-alex/2021_MSC21_IC.

This study examines diffusion processes characterized by particle loss through degradation or boundary reflection. The primary objectives are to analyze the main powers of the generator under Dirichlet boundary conditions, determine quasi-stationary states, and investigate the metastability of confined diffusion within periodic media. Initial attention is devoted to establishing the Dirichlet problem, specifically proving the existence and uniqueness of solutions within an appropriate functional framework by comparing them to the original problem. Subsequently, the problem is reformulated using integral equations, solved via a successive approximation method, and its connection to the weak formulation is established. The spectrum of the operator is then derived, followed by an analysis of metastability in a periodic setting. Finally, the scenario involving a small perturbation of the potential is explored, revealing a homogenization phenomenon. The analysis begins with a perturbation scale linked to the second eigenvalue, subsequently examining the regime where the scale is orders of magnitude smaller. In this limit, the problem is approximated by an effective equation featuring a constant coefficient determined by the unique solution to a specific auxiliary cell problem. The uniqueness of this cell problem is rigorously proven, and an iterative scheme is proposed to demonstrate the uniqueness of the resulting effective potential. Furthermore, the validity of this homogenization limit across various models is discussed. The research is conducted within $L^2$ spaces, with preliminary remarks also provided in $C^0$ spaces. These methodologies are applied to several representative models, including those with a piecewise constant diffusion coefficient representing a porous medium. Additionally, specific instances are analyzed where the perturbation of the potential is governed by a small parameter $\varepsilon$, yielding significant findings in the $\varepsilon \to 0$ limit. These results are illustrated through numerical examples. The methodologies and examples utilized in this work were previously presented in various forms at a series of seminars and conferences. This manuscript represents a comprehensive synthesis of those presentations. Specifically, it addresses topics covered in the author's contributions to the {\it Perturbations d\'es op\'erateurs de diffusion et applications aux sciences naturelles} colloquium (Orsay, 2001), the {\it Natural and artificial boundaries for diffusion processes} conference (Buenos Aires, 2003), the {\it Quasi-stationary states and metastability} conference (Orsay, 2005), and the {\it Metastability in diffusion processes} conference (Orsay, 2007). The latter topic was subsequently addressed in a separate publication

This study investigates the properties of symmetric nuclear matter at zero temperature using the lowest-order Cornwall-Vogt-Callan-Viswanath (LOCV) technique. By solving the LOCV equation for the energy gap, we derive the ground-state energy per nucleon. We then analyze these findings in strong magnetic fields, focusing on the symmetry energy and incompressibility coefficient. Finally, we compare our results with those of the Skyrme-Hartree-Fock method. Throughout the analysis, we consider two distinct sets of Skyrme forces. Our findings indicate that as the magnetic field strength increases, the LOCSV energy approaches the Skyrme energy, leading to a reduction in both symmetry energy and incompressibility coefficients. Furthermore, the magnetic field induces a collapse phenomenon in nuclear matter, causing the symmetry energy to vanish at low densities within the magnetic field regime. Additionally, we observe that the symmetry energy in magnetic fields exceeds that predicted by the Skyrme model, which aligns with previous research. These results demonstrate that the LOCSV method offers a viable alternative to the Skyrme-Hartree-Fock approach for studying nuclear matter in strong magnetic fields. Finally, we provide constraints for the LOCSV energy functional, which can be applied to study other nuclear systems. This technique proves particularly valuable for analyzing nuclear matter under extreme conditions, such as those found in neutron stars, where intense magnetic fields are present. Future work will extend these calculations to finite nuclei and other exotic nuclear systems. Privacy and security have become critical concerns in the rapidly expanding field of federated learning. This study addresses these challenges by introducing a new framework called "Difference Privacy-Revised Convergence Error," which integrates difference privacy, security, and communication efficiency into federated learning processes. This revised convergence error serves as the objective function for training the difference privacy-revised federated learning system. The proposed framework is evaluated using two methods: (i) a theoretical proof, and (ii) numerical simulations. Theoretically, we demonstrate that the error between the global model and the empirical risk of the training dataset remains bounded under our framework, thereby guaranteeing the privacy and security guarantees of federated learning. Numerically, we show that the proposed difference privacy-revised federated learning system achieves superior privacy and security while maintaining reduced communication overhead compared to existing solutions. Furthermore, we establish that this approach provides security and privacy benefits over standard federated learning systems. Finally, we prove that the difference privacy-revised federated learning system offers enhanced security and privacy, along with improved communication efficiency, relative to the federated exponential privacy-revised system. These findings are supported by evaluation results obtained through numerical simulations. Consequently, we conclude that integrating difference privacy-revised federated learning systems yields better performance than other methods in terms of privacy, security, and communication efficiency. Overall, this research demonstrates the viability of difference privacy-revised federated learning systems for practical applications. The primary contribution of this work is the development of such systems, which will facilitate the growth of federated learning applications in both industry and academia. Additionally, these systems provide stronger privacy and security assurances, including robust protection against backdoor attacks. To the best of our knowledge, this work represents the first effort to introduce difference privacy-revised federated learning systems, a field that has not previously been explored. We anticipate that these systems will play a significant role in advancing the exponential expansion of federated learning. Our results are expected to contribute to the development of difference privacy-revised federated learning systems, which will offer superior privacy and security compared to other existing federated learning approaches. We conducted far-ultraviolet (FUV) observations of the Taurus, Perseus, Aquila, and Taurus clouds using the Galaxy Evolution Explorer (GALEX) to analyze their dust emission, fluorescence, and ionized atomic hydrogen. These observations provide the first FUV data for the Taurus and Aquila clouds and a third FUV detection for Taurus. By comparing our FUV findings with existing near-UV (NUV) and optical images, we identified previously unseen emission features. Additionally, we performed low-resolution spectroscopy on Taurus, Perseus, and Aquila to map their FUV spectra. Our spectral analysis reveals that the observed FUV emission originates from both dust continuum radiation and resonance scattering of Lyman-$\alpha$ photons. We determined that the FUV continuum flux in Taurus, Perseus, and Aquila is primarily driven by nearby O and B stars, whereas the FUV flux in Taurus results from a mix of O/B stars and the nearby $\rho$ Ophiuchi cluster. Furthermore, Lyman-$\alpha$ fluorescence in Taurus, Aquila, and Taurus is driven by Ophiuchi, IC 348, and IC 2936, respectively. Finally, we detected ionized hydrogen emission in the Taurus cloud, indicating a significant presence of H$_{II}$ regions within young star clusters. Our results suggest that FUV observations can effectively probe the physical properties of young star clusters and their surrounding molecular clouds. This study is based on data from the GALEX archive.

Modern document retrieval systems are increasingly dependent on graph neural networks to model the internal structures of documents, particularly layouts, by assigning unique node representations to individual text lines. This paper introduces a layout-aware graph neural network approach that explicitly incorporates these line representations into the graph neural network representation embedding training process. By directly optimizing the neural network embedding training using extracted line semantics, the method ensures that structural information is deeply embedded within a latent space, thereby enhancing the performance of table retrieval systems. Experimental results on the ICDAR13 PDFDB dataset demonstrate that the proposed approach yields a significant performance gain, surpassing a strong baseline by 14.5% in mean average precision. Furthermore, ablation studies on the performance of various graph neural network architectures and the impact of utilizing extracted line semantics reveal that the system's performance is highly dependent on these structural details. Finally, a comparison of the method against competing graph neural network architectures underscores the necessity of employing the proposed line representation embedding strategy. To support future research, the authors have made the PDFDB dataset, annotated with tables, links, and cell-level annotations, available online. We introduce a cognitive hierarchy framework for multi-stage games characterized by incomplete information. We demonstrate that a comprehensive hierarchy exists and characterize the support of the resulting equilibrium. Furthermore, in the context of extensive form games with imperfect information, we establish an existence theorem for these equilibria. Additionally, we show how this equilibrium can be derived from a non-cooperative game played among types and cognitive hierarchy levels. Finally, we calculate the expected payoff for an agent within a first-best coverage model. This specific example illustrates that cognitive hierarchy equilibria are not necessarily equivalent to Harsanyi Bayesian Nash equilibria. Consequently, our findings suggest that standard refinements, such as sequential equilibrium, are not directly transferable to games involving insufficient information. Notably, agents within this framework are not required to assign probability zero to events that are, in fact, impossible. These insights may have significant implications for understanding the behavior of decision-makers who lack complete information. Our work extends the scope of the cognitive hierarchy model, originally developed for single-stage games with independent types, to encompass multi-stage games with insufficient information. This extension broadens the application of the model to include scenarios like multi-period signaling games and repeated games. Additionally, we outline potential directions for calculating these equilibria using machine learning techniques. Our analysis reveals that the cognitive hierarchy equilibrium represents a mixed strategy Nash equilibrium in a specific non-cooperative game involving players with varying levels of information and cognitive capacity. This connection may facilitate the development of more efficient computational methods for these equilibria. Our proposed approach involves training an agent to behave according to cognitive hierarchy equilibrium strategies by utilizing the underlying non-cooperative game as a proxy. We demonstrate that such an algorithm converges to a cognitive hierarchy equilibrium and provide a numerical illustration of this method. Finally, we present an open research question regarding the existence of a second-best model within the cognitive hierarchy framework, alongside other avenues for future investigation. By clarifying the relationship between cognitive hierarchy and non-cooperative games, our methodology may facilitate the extension of solution concepts from non-cooperative games to the cognitive hierarchy equilibrium. For instance, we may be able to define and compute a cognitive hierarchy subgame perfect equilibrium. Our approach involves approximating the non-cooperative game at each stage and applying the cognitive hierarchy equilibrium calculation procedure to it. This study demonstrates the technical viability of autonomously estimating human populations from census data using deep learning, a method that could significantly lower the costs and time required for future censuses. We introduce a new deep learning framework designed to generate high-quality population estimates for census grids. Through case studies using census data from two regions in Mozambique, we show that our model generates population counts comparable to recent census results without requiring any population labels for training. Our novel approach is highly efficient and can be easily adapted to various census systems. Additionally, we release a comprehensive technical report and a specialized deep learning model pre-trained on satellite imagery from our case study areas, which can be directly applied to other regions and countries. This research represents a significant step toward a more sustainable, long-term solution for population estimation. By reducing reliance on human labor for census design and data collection, it facilitates more frequent estimates that can inform government policies and resource allocation. Furthermore, it enables non-governmental organizations to plan their activities and assess the impact of their work. Ultimately, our work advances the goal of a more sustainable future for population estimation. While our approach does not guarantee a complete solution to every census challenge, we believe it marks a significant step forward in that direction. We have made our code and models accessible to the broader community to foster further research and development in this area. Data structures designed to trade off exactness for gains in computation, memory, or runtime efficiency are termed filters. This paper introduces the Fl集合 (FL set), a novel structure that operates with a collection of items containing no elements that should have been present. The FL set achieves constant-space storage per element, supports O(1) average time for membership queries, and provides O(n) time for insertions and deletions, where n represents the current collection size. Its core mechanism relies on a new approximation strategy known as the "bag of dots," which maps each element to a set of prime numbers such that the least common multiple of the sizes of these sets exceeds the total number of elements in the collection. This approach is demonstrated to be superior to methods previously applied to hashing. Furthermore, the paper establishes theoretical bounds for this technique regarding storage requirements and the average length of the dot bag. These storage and collision trade-offs are analyzed using probabilistic methods within the assumptions of uniform hashing and uniform hashing with independent collisions. Additionally, the study explores connections to several related mathematical fields. Finally, a fl集合 implementation is provided with benchmarking results comparing its performance against established filters, including Bloom filters and Cuckoo filters. The proposed implementation outperforms all other filters in both theoretical analysis and empirical testing. Given its efficiency, the FL set is well-suited for use in data structures that combine filters with other components. An application demonstrating this is a new approximate union data structure called the近似集合 (Approx set), which offers constant-space storage per element, O(1) average membership testing, and O(n) time complexity for insertions and deletions. The Approx set is implemented using disjoint unions of FL sets. Furthermore, the paper introduces a new algorithmic paradigm called the "dot method," which constructs filters by approximating a collection as a multiset of "dots" where each element is mapped to multiple dots, with a member test returning true if any dot indicates the element's presence. This method is shown to be applicable to various filters, including those based on hashing and probabilistic counting. Finally, the paper outlines several open problems and areas for future research. This study theoretically examines spinor atom-molecule transformation driven by laser-induced three-body recombination across different spin-components. The analysis covers both conservative and dissipative scenarios involving the absorption of weak residual laser photons. The dissipation arising from laser photon absorption is demonstrated to facilitate the coupling of two atomic states via an effective electric dipole interaction, thereby enabling the control of atom-molecule interaction strengths. The theoretical framework is applied to a $^{7}$Li spin-1 spinor system, with results indicating potential applications in simulating interacting particle-particle and particle-hole systems. Furthermore, the study explores applications within cold Fermi gases by addressing an effective two-spinor system derived from a $^{6}$Li two-component spinor. The resulting theory is anticipated to be applicable to cold three-body systems across various atomic and molecular species. Finally, the findings discuss implications for light-assisted three-body recombination, offering new perspectives on laser-induced three-body reactions. Additionally, the analysis examines the specific role of residual laser photons in generating effective two-body interactions between atoms. Finally, the study examines the relationship among three-body recombination, Feshbach resonances, and Fano resonances. Specifically, it demonstrates that the dissipative coupling constant can be adjusted to mimic the behavior of the Feshbach factor, which characterizes the strength of the Feshbach resonance. This offers a novel approach to simulating two-body interactions without the need for magnetic fields. Furthermore, the findings address the previously unexplored link between the autoionization rate of a Rydberg atom and the three-body recombination coefficient. The proposed theory is expected to find broad applications in Rydberg three-body physics. Additionally, the theory is applicable to photo-induced three-body recombination scenarios where photon absorption is the primary mechanism. Finally, the theory is applicable to the field of quantum defect chemistry, which investigates the link between three-body recombination and quantum defect levels. Finally, the findings discuss the relationship among three-body recombination, Feshbach resonances, and Fano resonances. Specifically, the dissipative coupling constant is shown to be tunable to mimic the behavior of the Feshbach factor, characterizing the strength of the Feshbach resonance. This study introduces a SPH-IBM framework designed for multiphase flows interacting with solid boundaries. We integrate the IBM approach by Sadhal and Myint [Phys. Fluids 26, 025102 (2014)] with a straightforward density reestimation technique, enabling the simulation of fluid-structure interactions between incompressible multi-component flows and solid objects. To enhance computational efficiency for large-scale scenarios, we employ R-Patch [J. Comput. Phys. 227, 8453 (2008)] to generate a multi-resolution mesh. This mesh facilitates the use of adaptive mesh refinement, permitting finer discretization in regions demanding greater accuracy while maintaining coarser grids in less critical areas to reduce overall computational costs. To further optimize performance, we implement a parallel parallel-in-time (PiT) parallel (P3T) parallel algorithm for solving the coupled system of hyperbolic and parabolic equations derived from the Riemann invariant formulation combined with the IBM method. The study concludes by demonstrating the versatility of this approach through applications to various fluid-structure problems, including two-phase flows, immiscible multiphase flows, and gravity-driven problems. These findings underscore the framework's capability to accurately and efficiently model diverse fluid-structure interaction challenges. The proposed P3T parallel algorithm is anticipated to significantly broaden the applicability of SPH-IBM methods to large-scale fluid-structure problems. This study explores quantum machine learning applied to quantum computational chemistry. We demonstrate that unsupervised learning on a quantum processor can effectively cluster molecular eigenstates to categorize symmetry-adapted molecular orbitals. This approach utilizes the superposition capabilities of an ultracold-atom simulator, enabling the analysis of hundreds of basis states within a single experimental run. We show that applying a unitary transformation to these states allows for model refinement without the overhead of additional data collection. Our research indicates that unsupervised quantum models are competitive with classical counterparts and offer a promising pathway for integrating machine learning into quantum chemical workflows. This work aligns with the objectives of the Quantum Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (QuAIL) and the emerging field of quantum-enhanced scientific workflows. Specifically, we examine how quantum-guided workflows can be implemented on current classical hardware to leverage quantum advantages in chemistry and other scientific disciplines. We outline the necessary algorithmic and hardware advancements required to transition from current classical practices to future quantum-enhanced regimes. Finally, providing access to the QuAIL open-source code repository, we demonstrate the implementation of both classical and quantum-enhanced workflows using this repository. This paper introduces a pitch correction system based on the recently developed fast neural synthesizer, FastPitch. To enhance its pitch controllability, we employed pitch augmentation, a technique that increases dataset size by generating synthetic pitches through pitch stacking and shifting. Notably, our model successfully maintains the source audio's timbre even after repeated stacking. Additionally, we implemented a timbre loss using a VQ-Vocoder to further protect the timbre during pitch shifting. Experiments conducted on speech with varied fundamental frequencies (F0) demonstrate that our system significantly improves pitch controllability compared to the original FastPitch model. Furthermore, we show that our system can effectively perform pitch augmentation, thereby boosting the F0 range of existing pitch datasets. The code and models are accessible at https://github.com/kenjiyoshimura/Improved_FastPitch. Finally, we have released a pre-trained model that achieves a broader F0 range while successfully preserving timbre. A demonstration audio clip is available here: https://github.com/kenjiyoshimura/Improved_FastPitch/tree/master/Demo. Listeners were invited to evaluate whether our model better preserves timbre compared to FastPitch via a subjective listening test. Both the controllability of the target pitch and the timbre preservation were rated as significantly better than FastPitch. The listening test code can be found at: https://github.com/kenjiyoshimura/Timbre_preserving_pitch_correction_LearningTimbre.git. Our system also exhibits a significantly lower mean square error (MSE) for timbre features, such as Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC), compared to FastPitch. Overall, our system is more than 10 times faster than DEEPSHIFT and offers superior timbre preservation, making it a timbre-preserving pitch correction tool. We have also made our timbre comparison code available at: https://github.com/kenjiyoshimura/Timbre_preserving_pitch_correction_LearningTimerc比较.git.
Keywords: Timbre-preserving pitch correction, Timbre loss, Timbre-preserving neural synthesis, Timbre-preserving pitch augmentation, VQ-Vocoder.

This paper introduces Hopper, a novel Transformer-based framework designed for multi-hop inference in spatiotemporal applications. In these contexts, the outcome of one prediction step serves as input for the subsequent stage, a process referred to as multi-hop inference. This approach is essential in scenarios like weather forecasting, where intermediate outputs are crucial for downstream tasks, such as determining suitable clothing based on current conditions. We demonstrate that the Transformer excels at multi-hop inference by enabling pre-training on complex, multi-relational graph data. To fully leverage the self-attention mechanism for long-range predictions, we developed a custom data generation method that creates synthetic spatiotemporal weather datasets. Furthermore, we propose a novel architecture, the Temporal Attention Block, which efficiently captures long-range dependencies in such data. Our results indicate that Hopper outperforms state-of-the-art models on established weather datasets, achieving speed improvements of up to 10x during inference. Additionally, we show that Hopper can predict up to 12 time steps ahead, a capability beyond the reach of current models. Finally, we apply this framework to generate synthetic weather data for a video game, successfully capturing both local and global weather patterns. We present a precision measurement of the standard model cross section for lepton-pair production in association with a $b\bar{b}$ pair, utilizing $t\bar{t}$+jets events at the LHC. This approach offers a highly precise differential observable that is exceptionally sensitive to the $W$ boson mass. By employing state-of-the-art $O(\alpha_s^3)$ QCD predictions for the inclusive cross section, we achieve a total uncertainty of 10%. We establish a world-record precision of 1.5% (68% CL) for the inclusive $\sigma(t\bar{t} + \text{jets})$ in the region where the transverse momentum of the $b\bar{b}$ system satisfies $p_T(b\bar{b}) < 100$ GeV. Additionally, we introduce a novel, precision electroweak measurement of the cross section for $t\bar{t}$+jets $Z/\gamma^*$ production, which yields a $W$ mass determination of $m_W = 80.28 \pm 0.16$ (stat) $\pm$ 0.16 (syst) GeV. This value is consistent with both the CDF and ATLAS measurements but remains in tension with the most recent result from Fermilab. Finally, we demonstrate that combining our measurement with the new Fermilab result enhances the precision of the $W$ mass determination to 0.07 GeV, thereby enabling a direct comparison with the recent Fermilab finding. Furthermore, we show that incorporating our result into the full LHC dataset improves the precision of $m_W$ measurements derived from direct $W$ production. These findings underscore the potential of $t\bar{t}$+jets observables for future high-precision electroweak studies. Our findings are accessible via JHEP. Our results can be reproduced using the publicly available MadGraph5_aMC@NLO event generator. We have also provided a comprehensive set of $O(\alpha_s^3)$ QCD predictions for $t\bar{t}$+jets production at the LHC through the newly developed Top2Jet framework, which is accessible via arXiv. This tool is also available on the public website of the authors. Furthermore, we have released a suite of $O(\alpha_s^3)$ QCD predictions for various $t\bar{t}$+jets observables

Telepresence robots (TPRs) facilitate a sense of presence and foster social connections across distant sites, making them valuable for both professional and consumer applications. To ensure these systems remain usable for a broad audience, it is essential to understand how performance influences user experience quality (QoE). This study employs an interactive approach to evaluate QoE across the entire software stack, including the camera, video transmission, and robot interface. Findings indicate that software-layer QoE is highly sensitive to hardware specifications, particularly the camera. Furthermore, hardware upgrades do not necessarily enhance software performance; instead, they often result in increased resource usage and reduced efficiency. Finally, our results demonstrate that both the frequency and duration of video freezes significantly impair user satisfaction. Given that current consumer-grade devices often lack the necessary resources to meet the demands of a full TPR system, we recommend that vendors either optimize their software or invest in higher-specification hardware. This research is based on a collaboration with Logitech, the leading manufacturer of consumer TPRs. Code and datasets are accessible at https://github.com/robertkoster/logitech-tpr-evaluation. Hierarchical linear models are linear regression frameworks that incorporate the hierarchical structure of their data. These models are essential for analyzing data points that are not independent, as independent data analysis can result in invalid inferences and misleading conclusions. Modern Bayesian computational techniques have made hierarchical linear models a staple in data analysis. This tutorial will derive the hierarchical linear model, explain the data independence issue, offer an overview of Bayesian methods, and offer hopes for future applications. This introduction is designed to be accessible to undergraduate students and individuals new to the topic. Additionally, a corresponding Python analysis will be provided in parallel.

Abstract: A hierarchical linear model serves as a specific form of linear regression designed for data collected in hierarchical structures. Ignoring this hierarchy when data independence assumptions are violated can lead to incorrect inferences and flawed conclusions. The advent of Bayesian methods has made hierarchical linear models a fundamental analytical tool. This tutorial aims to derive the hierarchical linear model and highlight the significance of Bayesian computation, targeting an audience with minimal prior knowledge. Furthermore, the tutorial will accompany a Python analysis, which can be accessed here: https://github.com/ahmedhassan123/Gentle-introduction-to-Hierarchical-Linear-Models.

Keywords: Hierarchical linear models, Bayesian analysis, Data independence, Python analysis, Undergraduate level, High school level.

The Mafia game serves as a social party experience that many find both entertaining and enigmatic. This paper establishes a mathematical framework using extensive form games to model the dynamics of Mafia. We conduct an ex-ante analysis based on uniform prior beliefs, demonstrating that symmetry within the framework leads to specific, predictable outcomes. Additionally, we perform a numerical analysis of asymmetric scenarios to illustrate how belief distributions influence player behavior. Ultimately, ex-post analyses reveal that while the mathematical model effectively captures the game's basic structure, it fails to fully explain actual player conduct. The intersection of mathematics and the Mafia game opens the door for future research exploring various perspectives. Our work serves as a foundation for such inquiries; for instance, our model assumes all players are equally skilled and possess identical belief structures, whereas subsequent studies could investigate how individual skill levels and divergent prior beliefs interact to create diverse playing styles. Furthermore, our model does not address how players' beliefs and skills evolve as the game progresses and new information emerges. These factors significantly impact decision-making and can be analyzed by examining how the game's mathematical structure influences player behavior. Finally, our model focuses on a single round of the Mafia; therefore, future research should consider how multiple rounds influence the game and how the optimal number of rounds can be determined. By analyzing the game through the lens of extensive form games, we have made the first step toward constructing a mathematical model of Mafia. We believe this model will facilitate a deeper understanding of the game and contribute to the broader field of game theory. Our work aims to inspire others to explore the fascinating world of Mafia from a mathematical perspective. We look forward to seeing how this understanding will grow and how these insights can be applied to enhance gameplay. However, the disk's response to accretion by a pair of giant planets, particularly their migration and mass gain, remains poorly understood. **Aims.** This study investigates the accretion of gas by a pair of giant planets and the resulting impacts on the disk's structure. **Methods.** We conducted a parameterized analysis of concurrent gas accretion by two planets, examining their influence on accretion rates, migration, and mass accumulation. **Results.** The presence of a second planet in a close configuration significantly alters the accretion of the first, resulting in a final mass that is 1.5 to 2 times greater than if the planets had accreted sequentially. This effect is primarily driven by the planet–planet interaction, which generates a distinctive and localized accretion flow. The flow originates at the planet–disk $L_4$ point, moves toward the planet, and subsequently feeds both the planet and the disk. This process is most pronounced for planets with a total mass between 0.5 and 1 Jupiter masses. This study presents a phenomenological model that successfully explains the temperature-dependent conductance fluctuations observed in a single (10,10) armchair carbon nanotube. The authors argue that electron-phonon coupling facilitates phonon-assisted tunneling through a barrier between two electron confinement regions, akin to a quantum dot. The model's phenomenological nature stems from the absence of detailed information regarding the specific potential profile. By utilizing a symmetric double-well potential to represent the confinement regions and a narrow central barrier to simulate the tunnel region, the researchers calculated temperature-dependent conductance. They determined the average height and width of the central barrier by fitting the calculated conductance to the experimentally measured data. The findings indicate that phonon-assisted tunneling is more probable than coherent tunneling. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that a barrier height corresponding to approximately 0.03 eV below the conduction band minimum is required for the model to accurately reproduce the experimental conductance data. Finally, the impact of varying the potential profile on the resulting conductance is also examined. These results provide significant insight into electron-phonon coupling within carbon nanotubes. The observed mechanism is anticipated to occur in other carbon nanotube geometries and is expected to play a crucial role in electronic transport across various carbon-based nanostructures. This research holds particular promise for developing high-performance carbon-based nano-electronics. Additionally, the proposed model is expected to be valuable for investigating electron-phonon coupling in other low-dimensional nanostructures. The study demonstrates that a phenomenological model can effectively explain conductance measurements in carbon nanotubes, offering a practical alternative to computationally intensive first-principles simulations. This approach enables the rapid determination of key parameters, such as barrier height, without the need for complex calculations. Consequently, the proposed model serves as a vital tool for investigating electronic transport in carbon-based nanostructures. Moreover, the model can be easily adapted to analyze the impact of structural asymmetry on conductance. Overall, this work represents a significant advancement in our understanding of electronic transport in carbon nanotubes and other low-dimensional nanostructures. It highlights the potential of carbon-based nanomaterials for next-generation electronic devices and provides a foundation for future research into their electronic properties. This study introduces a novel fuzzy clustering algorithm designed for high-dimensional data, which may contain redundant or irrelevant features. In many real-world scenarios, a dataset comprises a vast number of variables, rendering traditional clustering methods ineffective. To address this, we propose a new approach that simultaneously performs feature selection and data partitioning. We enhance the standard Feature Weighted Fuzzy k-means algorithm by integrating the concept of irrelevant features directly into the objective function. Furthermore, a novel entropy-based cost function is incorporated to effectively identify redundant features. This method has been tested on high-dimensional datasets, including both synthetic data and the well-known Wisconsin Breast Cancer dataset, to demonstrate its efficacy in real-world applications. Experimental results indicate that the proposed algorithm successfully identifies the most relevant features while simultaneously partitioning the dataset. Finally, the study confirms that the proposed fuzzy clustering scheme effectively groups samples into distinct classes based on their associated features. The source code is publicly accessible at: https://github.com/ahmed-ibrahim/Relevant-Feature-Selection-and-Clustering. Our objective is to develop a new algorithm capable of identifying the most relevant features and grouping them into separate classes without requiring prior knowledge of the number of classes. We believe this approach is applicable to various cost functions and feature selection techniques. Additionally, the method is not limited to high-dimensional data; it can be applied to any dataset where irrelevant features hinder traditional clustering algorithms. The primary challenge lies in identifying the most relevant features for partitioning the dataset. We have implemented the algorithm in Python, and the implementation is available on GitHub at: https://github.com/ahmed-ibrahim/Relevant-Feature-Selection-and-Clustering. Our focus is on creating a novel fuzzy clustering algorithm that automatically selects the most relevant features to partition the dataset. We aim to establish a new method for simultaneously selecting relevant features and clustering data using those features. This algorithm is applicable to any dataset, whether high-dimensional or not, provided that irrelevant features prevent the use of traditional clustering techniques. The main difficulty involves identifying the most relevant features to partition the dataset. We intend to implement this algorithm using Python. The implementation is available on GitHub at: https://github.com/ahmed-ibrahim/Relevant-Feature-Selection-and-Clustering. We aim to develop a new feature selection algorithm utilizing fuzzy clustering, specifically to identify the most relevant features for partitioning the dataset. The cost function is defined as follows: Cost = Entropy + Sum of distances between each data point and its respective cluster center.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a well-established model used for both function approximation and clustering. In this framework, a set of expert models, weighted by a distribution, are aggregated to form a predictive distribution. This approach has demonstrated superior performance compared to alternatives in both theoretical analysis and component efficiency. However, when the number of experts is substantial, current state-of-the-art MoE estimation methods often fail to converge, rendering them impractical for real-world applications. This paper aims to address this limitation. We present a novel, general-purpose MoE framework that allows for an arbitrary number of experts. Within this framework, we develop a new clustering technique grounded in the concept of "separable experts." Leveraging this separation property, we propose a general clustering algorithm that utilizes a general gradient estimator. This proposed algorithm is provably consistent for learning MoE models and is substantially more efficient than existing solutions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method can adapt to the intrinsic complexity of the learned MoE, thereby accelerating convergence in practical applications. Finally, extensive experiments confirm that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in terms of performance. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/ChaoZheng1997/Breaking-MoE. Additionally, we have released a new open-source Python library called \texttt{PyMoE} (Python Mixture of Experts) at https://github.com/ChaoZheng1997/Breaking-MoE, which implements the proposed methods. This library will serve as a foundation for future research. PyMoE is available on PyPI and can be installed via `pip install PyMoE`. The paper and library are accessible at https://chaoz.github.io/Breaking-MoE/. The source repository is located at https://chaoz.github.io/Breaking-MoE/. The authors are Chaohong Zheng and Yihang Li. These notes offer a combinatorial overview of the Jacobian and Prym varieties associated with covering graphs, incorporating an introduction to divisorial and Riemann-Roch theorems within that framework. These notes are based on a seminar presentation of the same title by the author at the London School of Economics. The text includes exercises and supplementary material for the reader. Specifically, I have not yet explored the explicit Riemann-Roch isomorphism on the edge space, alongside other material referenced in [6]. Similarly, I have omitted the explicit descriptions of the Riemann-Roch map and its inverse for Jacobians and Prym types, which are detailed in [10]. Finally, I have excluded the explicit characterization of the Riemann-Roch map for Jacobians using Fuchsian models, as presented in [2]. Although string theory suggests that quantum gravity can preserve all global symmetries, generic expectations indicate that quantum gravity should favor a landscape of vacua where at least some non-anomalous global symmetries exist, which are unstable when coupled to gravity. In contrast, gauged local symmetries are universally accepted as compatible with quantum gravity. Consequently, numerous phenomenological models in quantum gravity propose mechanisms to dynamically promote a global symmetry to a local one. This work introduces a novel cosmic microwave background signature of vacuum breaking for global symmetries, termed "cosmic double refraction," which arises from the breaking of degeneracy between two sets of polarized gravitational wave modes. We demonstrate that this signal offers a clean, unambiguous detection method for vacuum breaking in global symmetries, enabling experimental constraints that exceed those imposed by other observables. We apply this method to constrain a widely studied effective field theory (EFT) model of quantum gravity, the Schwinger mechanism, which predicts vacuum breaking in superplanckian magnetic fields. Our analysis shows that the double refraction signal could be detected if the graviton polarization scale $M_2$ is below $\mathcal{O}(10^8)$ GeV, assuming the graviton production amplitude is comparable to that of the cosmic microwave background. Even if the production amplitude is suppressed by an $\mathcal{O}(1)$ dimensionless parameter, the experimental bound remains at $\mathcal{O}(10^7)$ GeV. These findings indicate that the double refraction signal is crucial for experimentally verifying that quantum gravity dynamics prevent vacuum breaking in the presence of a non-abelian gauge field. Furthermore, we outline the approach required to constrain other quantum gravity models of vacuum breaking, including the confinement mechanism, which should yield limits in the $10^9$ GeV range. Finally, we discuss the potential for significantly tighter constraints if future experiments can measure the graviton production amplitude independently. Our results confirm the community's long-held belief that quantum gravity must eliminate all vacuum breaking modes through either confinement or promotion to a local symmetry. Additionally, we highlight that existing experimental limits on quantum gravity vacuum breaking are insufficient to test this consensus, and that achieving such tests necessitates a direct probe of vacuum breaking in superplanckian fields. We conclude that the only proposed experiment capable of doing so is the detection of the double refraction signal. Transferability is a vital capability for deep learning, underpinning numerous applications like transfer learning and knowledge transfer. This study re-examines two core agreements regarding transferability: (1) the transferability of task-independent skills from unsupervised source tasks to diverse downstream tasks, and (2) the consistency of downstream task performance across similar source tasks. To address the first agreement, we introduce a downstream evaluation framework that reports the average accuracy across varied tasks, rather than relying on a single task for specific scenarios. For the second agreement, we propose a performance distribution metric to quantify downstream task similarity, utilizing this metric to analyze the transferability of pre-training tasks. Through comprehensive experiments, we validate these two agreements and identify the optimal representation learning scenarios based on evidence. Additionally, we develop a general pre-training strategy that effectively transfers skills to diverse tasks by integrating multiple training samples, yielding substantial performance improvements. Finally, we conclude by outlining potential future research directions inspired by the findings of this work. Furthermore, our results can be replicated at: https://github.com/ChenYixuan2019/RepPretrain. Other replication resources are also accessible at: https://github.com/ChenYimagen/Replication. Finally, our source repository can be found at: https://github.com/ChenYixuan2019/Revisiting-Transferability.

Network structure significantly influences the propagation of information, diseases, and contagions. While numerous studies have explored how a network's topological architecture impacts the diffusion of data, knowledge, and illness, network size and community structure have received less attention. This study investigates the mechanisms governing the speed of information diffusion, specifically examining the roles of network size, total nodes, total edges, mean degree, diameter, and mean degree against order parameter. Our findings indicate that both the network size parameter and the total edge parameter are critical in regulating the rate of information spread. Furthermore, we observed that smaller network size parameters facilitate the rapid diffusion of information within a limited number of nodes, whereas edges contribute to the diffusion process across all nodes. Additionally, our results demonstrate that the total edge parameter influences the speed of diffusion by connecting nodes in both small and large communities. These insights offer a comprehensive understanding of how network size and community structures impact information dissemination, with significant implications for managing knowledge transfer in social networks. These results can guide the design of effective online advertising campaigns, online knowledge management systems, and advertising networks. Finally, our approach is applicable to other domains, including the spread of knowledge, viral marketing campaigns, and the diffusion of knowledge and diseases within community structures. This paper introduces a novel methodology for designing and implementing knowledge management systems and online advertising networks, providing a foundation for future research. We believe this work will be highly valuable to the scientific community. Our code will be made publicly available to facilitate the replication of this study. This paper presents discrete-time precision analysis for the time-domain regular perturbation model of an unamplified radio link, modeling the perturbed oscillator as a discrete-time random process. By treating perturbation samples as both spatially and temporally correlated, we derive closed-form expressions for the conditional autocorrelation of the perturbed process and calculate the perturbation's entropy rate. Additionally, we develop precision metrics for phase, group delay, and frequency, demonstrating that analysis accuracy improves when using a larger number of samples. The study concludes with precision performance results for a 2 GHz satellite downlink scenario. This model offers precision analysis for radio functions occurring at a rate significantly higher than the perturbation's entropy rate, effectively addressing cases where perturbation samples are temporally independent. Such independent samples are typically obtained from phase detectors in software-defined radio systems, which measure phase deviations at every software sample instant. Furthermore, this discrete-time approach is applicable to other radio links where perturbation entropy rates are insufficient to justify stochastic process modeling for precision analysis. The proposed methodology and derived formulas are implemented in an open-source tool available on GitHub. All source code, including the implementation, is provided in the supplementary material. Finally, the paper begins by reviewing the time-domain regular perturbation model and its discrete-time approximation, followed by the derivation of closed-form expressions for conditional autocorrelation and entropy rate. Precision metrics for radio signals and observables are then developed, with all derivations utilizing z-transforms in the discrete-time domain. Precision performance is evaluated for various oscillators, and the impact of using different numbers of z-transform samples on the accuracy of precision metrics is examined. The paper concludes by summarizing its key contributions. The emergence of deep learning-driven mobile application security analysis has heightened the susceptibility of app stores to tampering attacks, which typically involve either directly modifying application code or subtly altering input features to deceive classifiers. This paper offers a comprehensive review of the input feature tampering technique, introducing a novel concept known as "issue-space evasion attack." This attack aims to bypass classifier scrutiny by modifying feature spaces while preserving the functional integrity of the application. We provide detailed attack procedures, theoretical foundations, and examples demonstrating the feasibility of this new attack vector. Furthermore, we examine the challenges inherent in detecting issue-space evasions and explore potential countermeasures to mitigate this threat. The study concludes with a discussion on future research directions regarding the input feature modification domain, specifically addressing whether local or global modifications are more effective for evasion, and the impact of multi-classifier systems on detection capabilities. Ultimately, this work serves as a foundational survey that deepens the understanding of these attacks and establishes a basis for subsequent research. Additionally, it presents a survey on multi-classifier-based detection, which remains an under-explored area. We demonstrate that the Thakurta metric, which models a cosmological black hole, fails to accurately represent such objects. Its form is derived by substituting the Schwarzschild radius into the Friedmann equation, a procedure that lacks physical justification. Consequently, this approach is only applicable to primordial black holes, as it incorporates their dynamics while neglecting their spacetime geometry. By employing a more rigorous cosmological model, we establish an upper limit for PBHs across various eras, yielding the same results as Thakurta's original proposal. Furthermore, we examine a scenario where cosmological constant density, rather than black hole density, dominates the universe, revealing that this also describes a cosmological black hole, albeit with a different metric. Ultimately, we conclude that primordial black holes can be modeled as cosmological entities, whereas established cosmological bodies like stars and galaxies are not. We acknowledge that this work may encourage researchers to pursue the mathematical consistency of their proposals. Additionally, we note that cosmological constants should be treated as independent parameters rather than being derived from black hole densities. Finally, we observe that defining PBHs in this manner could influence the interpretation of gravitational wave data from LIGO-Virgo. Specifically, we find that cosmological bodies would possess a minimum mass of approximately $10^{10}kg$, a constraint that does not affect LIGO-Virgo observations. Therefore, we recommend that the minimum mass limit for cosmological PBHs remain at $10^{16}g$, consistent with LIGO-Virgo bounds. We also note that other studies have reached similar conclusions, and we have examined some of these works in our analysis. In summary, we have shown that cosmological black holes cannot be described by their own Schwarzschild radius, and we have provided more accurate models for these bodies. We believe this research will significantly advance the field of cosmology. Accretion of small particles onto a growing planet core is a critical mechanism in forming super-Earths and the gas giants Jupiter and Saturn. This process, known as pebble accretion, is influenced by gas density fluctuations caused by pressure disturbances from pressure bumps and spiral arms. We conducted 2D hydrodynamical simulations to track the growth of a 0.5 M_E core under this accretion mode, incorporating gas density fluctuations and their impact on pebble accretion rates. Our findings indicate that gas density fluctuations can either accelerate or inhibit planet formation, contingent upon the statistical characteristics of these fluctuations. Specifically, gas density enhancements facilitate planet formation when (1) the Gaussian coefficient is negative and (2) the standard deviation of gas density fluctuations is high. Conversely, gas density suppressions slow down planet formation under these same statistical conditions. These results suggest that the formation timescale of super-Earths and Jupiter is highly sensitive to gas density fluctuations. Furthermore, the significant influence of gas density fluctuations on pebble accretion implies that the migration of super-Earths and Jupiter, which depends on their formation timescale, is also strongly affected by gas density fluctuations. Consequently, the present-day locations of super-Earths and Jupiter serve as constraints on gas density fluctuations during the protoplanetary disk phase. These constraints can be applied to observations of gas density fluctuations in T Tauri stars and exoplanetary disks. Additionally, the effects of gas density fluctuations on planet formation may be applicable to scenarios involving planet formation without pressure bumps. Finally, the present study provides a fundamental understanding of planet formation via pebble accretion, offering a benchmark for future research. It is widely recognized that the success of numerous learning algorithms hinges on having a hypothesis space small enough to be well-generalizable. In contrast, the phenomenon of benefitting from a hypothesis space large enough to be under-generalizable has received less attention. This paper examines the origins of this under-generalization, specifically focusing on computational constraints. We demonstrate, through both theoretical analysis and experimental validation, that the practical utility of a large hypothesis space stems from the fact that not all of its elements are computable within a reasonable timeframe. Furthermore, we reveal that the benefits arising from these computational limits can be recaptured by employing a smaller, computable hypothesis space, such as one regularized via gradient descent's implicit bias. Our findings are backed by tests on synthetic data as well as image data featuring representations that are either public or proprietary. Ultimately, our results indicate that explicitly leveraging uncomputable components of a large hypothesis space offers no advantage over utilizing a smaller, computable one. Consequently, the path to building more capable learning algorithms likely involves making representations and algorithms that capture these "hidden" capabilities more accessible. This study examines a dial-a-ride problem tailored for an urban dial-a-bus scenario, featuring ridepooling and transfer capabilities. The objective is to construct feasible routes that minimize delays at pickup and destination locations. We introduce a Branch-and-Cut framework supported by various branching and valid inequality techniques. To demonstrate the method's efficacy, we solve instances derived from real data collected in Turin, Italy. Our experimental results indicate that this approach effectively handles small- to medium-sized problems. Furthermore, we show that several inequalities traditionally associated with the classical dial-a-ride problem offer limited enhancement in an urban context due to specific problem characteristics. Finally, we explore how specific problem parameters influence the difficulty level. Future research will focus on extending the framework to include time-window violations and developing a heuristic to generate high-quality initial solutions. This paper introduces the new Deep InfoMax method for predicting the progression to Alzheimer's disease (AD). Maximization of mutual information (MI) between current and future data is utilized to forecast AD progression. The study addresses three key questions: (1) Is this approach effective for predicting AD progression? (2) How does it compare to other methods? This mechanism allows the model to circumvent tachyon instabilities that typically plague conformal scalar sectors. We examine the spectrum of a metastable vacuum, which arises from a de Sitter minimum created by the addition of an explicit symmetry-breaking term. This de Sitter minimum sits at a large field value, adjacent to the conformal minimum that exists at zero for the explicit breaking term. We calculate the decay rate of the false vacuum and estimate its lifetime, demonstrating that it far exceeds the age of the universe. Furthermore, we show that the mass of the conformal field is numerous orders of magnitude smaller than the mass of the de Sitter minimum within our proposed framework. We discuss how this scenario offers a novel approach to understanding the dark sector. Specifically, we propose that the conformal field could account for a portion of dark matter, with its density established during the decay of the false vacuum. Additionally, we outline a method to derive the correct radiation temperature following this transition. This framework provides a new perspective on the standard cosmological evolution, including reheating and the generation of the light element abundances observed today. We also address the issue of domain walls, which form along the flat direction of the potential; however, we demonstrate that these walls become unstable and decay before they could significantly alter the evolution of the universe. Enhanced sampling of nucleic acid conformations is difficult due to their inherent rigidity, which results in a narrow range of thermal fluctuations. We introduce the Rigid Substrate Biasing (RSB) method, which improves the sampling of nucleic acid conformations by artificially anchoring the molecule to a fixed substrate to suppress thermal fluctuations, thereby accessing regions of conformational space that are inaccessible through standard thermal fluctuations alone. RSB achieves this by applying a restoring force to a molecule's center of mass, proportional to its displacement from the substrate. We demonstrate that RSB enhances the sampling of DNA sliding-helix conformations, which are critical for biological processes such as protein binding and transcription. RSB achieves this by introducing an entropic bias that drives the molecule away from the substrate, with a specific restoring force constant identified that effectively explores the sliding-helix conformational space. Furthermore, we show that the free energy landscape of the enhanced sampler accurately reflects the underlying thermal-hydrodynamic landscape of the system. RSB is applicable to any nucleic acid conformation that resides on a free energy minimum separated from the B-form helix by a low free energy barrier. RSB is fully compatible with all standard molecular dynamics enhanced sampling techniques, including metadynamics, umbrella sampling, and metadynamics-based thermalization. This approach enables the study of nucleic acid conformations that are otherwise inaccessible through conventional thermal fluctuations. The Ansitz-Uhler-Norbert-Schneier method (ANS) is a multiplicative encoding technique designed to achieve adaptive entropy pooling, a capability that sets it apart from most other universal codes. This adaptive behavior allows ANS to function as a self-synchronizing code for entropy pooling and to maintain optimal performance even when subjected to localized errors. In this work, we first provide a theoretical analysis of the ansification process for sequences with finite alphabets and finite support. Subsequently, we empirically evaluate the encoding and decoding speeds of ANS across various scenarios. The dielectric properties of cement-based construction materials have garnered significant interest due to their potential for condition monitoring. However, the dielectric response of cement paste and the connection between its polarizable components remain poorly understood. This study investigates the frequency- and temperature-dependent dielectric behavior of cement-based materials through dielectric spectroscopy, X-ray computed tomography, and molecular dynamics simulations. We provide the first experimental measurements of dielectric constants for individual cement minerals and pore solution. Our findings indicate that the dielectric constant of bulk cement paste is governed by the dielectric properties of both the solid matrix and the pore solution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the dielectric response of cement-based construction materials is primarily dictated by the pore solution. These insights offer valuable guidance for developing non-destructive techniques to assess the integrity of cement-based structures. Additionally, the research enhances the understanding of the complex interactions between mineral surfaces and electrolyte solutions. This review examines contemporary experimental and theoretical progress regarding possible massive-heavy hadronic molecules. We begin by outlining the basic principles of two-body recombination and the characteristics of such molecules, while also addressing experimental constraints derived from both collider and fixed-target studies. Furthermore, we analyze theoretical predictions for compact exotic states featuring at least one heavy quark. Finally, we provide an overview of these predicted states, including an evaluation of their binding energies, sizes, and decay modes. The review also explores the relationship between massive-heavy hadronic molecules and compact exotica, as well as the concept of a molecular graph designed to map predicted two-body recombosons based on theoretical and experimental data. This graph is intended to guide future experimental efforts in identifying and studying these predicted states. In conclusion, we outline the future prospects for researching and confirming these exotic hadrons. Keywords: Hadronic molecules, Exotic hadrons, QCD sum rules. The Lyman-$\alpha$ forest serves as a valuable tool for investigating cosmological models, yet its analysis is complicated by the difficulty of accounting for the underlying mean absorption from undetected associated galaxies alongside absorbers unrelated to the epoch's mean density. This study demonstrates that the statistical correlation between Lyman-$\alpha$ absorbers can be utilized to mitigate these challenges. Specifically, we show that the true correlation function of neutral density, $\xi_{\rm H}(r)$, can be derived from the observed correlation of absorption cross-sections, $\xi_{\sigma}(r)$, by applying a deconvolution of the window function. Furthermore, we establish that the large-scale behavior of $\xi_{\rm H}(r)$ is primarily determined by the cosmological model, whereas small-scale behavior is heavily influenced by the spatial distribution of associated galaxies. By combining this deduced $\xi_{\rm H}(r)$ with the predicted correlation function $\xi_{\rm th}(r)$ based on a standard cosmological model, we can derive the model's parameters. This methodology is applied to simulated quasar samples from the SDSS-BOSS and QSOES surveys, yielding constraints on the Hubble constant, matter density, and the amplitude of density fluctuations. Additionally, we show that the predicted $\xi_{\rm th}(r)$ is largely shaped by the assumed radial density profile of associated galaxies, which can be constrained through cross-correlation analyses between absorbers and galaxies. Ultimately, we find that the combination of $\xi_{\rm H}(r)$, $\xi_{\rm th}(r)$, and $\xi_{\rm mag}(r)$ enables the tight constraints of fundamental cosmological parameters. This represents a novel approach for analyzing the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest, with future high-resolution spectroscopic surveys expected to significantly enhance the precision of these cosmological parameter constraints. This work is based on simulated data, designed to establish a new analytical framework for future observations. We provide a python package to facilitate the deduction of cosmological parameters from these analyses. We demonstrate the successful transfer of both transverse and longitudinal emittances from a source oscillator to an oscillator with a larger mass using undamped normal mode oscillations in a ion trap. Initially, non-linearities in the trap potential were utilized to compress the transverse and longitudinal emittances of $^{40}$Ca$^+$ ions to a factor of a few above the quantum limit. Following this compression, the ion cloud was confined with a heavier non-invasive background gas, argon. By precisely controlling the damped oscillation frequency, the full transverse and longitudinal emittances were transferred to this second mode over a timescale significantly longer than the transverse damping period. This technique enables the decoupling of emittance reduction from the final observation of the ion cloud, allowing for the achievement of record-breaking low emittances that are unattainable through adiabatic invariant control alone. Furthermore, this approach facilitates further longitudinal compression via adiabatic invariant control and opens avenues for studying quantum dissipative dynamics. The entire experiment, including emittance measurement, was conducted using radio-frequency Paul traps. Additionally, we discuss the potential for extending these results to larger particle numbers and more complex systems. This study introduces a novel analysis of hidden complexity within stochastic neural networks. We evaluate three distinct metrics designed to quantify the discrepancy between a network's actual joint output distribution and its independent approximation. These metrics are the total variation distance, the $\mathbb{L}_p$ distance, and the KL-divergence. To establish a comparative framework, we investigate a simple Boltzmann machine featuring symmetric couplings and site-independent probabilities. Our primary finding is that, under these specific conditions, the KL-divergence and $\mathbb{L}_p$ distances are fundamentally equivalent, differing only by a constant scaling factor. We also extend these results to more complex Boltzmann machines and discuss the broader implications for other spin glasses and phase transition phenomena. Finally, we highlight the relevance of these insights to learning algorithms, specifically examining how gradient descent behaves when $\mathbb{L}_p$ distance and KL-divergence are used as objective functions. Additionally, we explore an alternative approach that utilizes information-theoretic measures to define a learning protocol, which may offer superior convergence properties.
