We introduce a new type of variational autoencoder, designed to leverage the underlying probabilatic structure of its representation by utilizing the posterior distribution within the network itself. This approach offers distinct advantages over methods-reliant autoencoders, as it does not depend on learning task-specific modifications to the variable z. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed autoencoder can effectively model continuous features in high-dimensional environments. Experimental results indicate that the model maintains its capability even when trained in a fully self-supervised manner. Additionally, the encoder exhibits the ability to learn high-dimensional features that are interpretable to humans. To facilitate broader understanding, we have made our implementation public to support reproducibility. The implementation can be accessed at: https://github.com/SebastianKlauer/DGAE. Our codebase includes functionality for visualizing the posterior distribution P(z|x), as well as a basic interface for training and evaluating the deep generative autoencoder. Our results demonstrate that P(z|x) accurately captures continuous features and their high-dimensional variations, outperforming other encoders in both interpretability and performance. We also provide a basic interface for training and evaluating the deep generative autoencoder. Finally, we have made our implementation public to ensure reproducibility.

The recent NANOGrav 15-year dataset hints at a common gravitational-wave (GW) backdrop, while the Advanced LIGO-Virgo collaboration has identified numerous signals. We propose a cosmological model where both phenomena are explained by the exponential amplification of primordial tensor perturbations during a "stiff" phase, governed by an early dark energy (EDS) component. This era, characterized by a equation of state $w=1$, precedes the standard $\Lambda$CDM timeline. We demonstrate that EDS can substantially influence cosmological distance measurements, a factor that may be essential for alleviating the Hubble tension. Furthermore, we show that EDS successfully accounts for the big bang nucleosynthesis (BBN) constraints and the observed NANOGrav and LIGO-Virgo data. Finally, we outline future efforts to rigorously test this model and determine the equation of state of early universe phenomena. These approaches may yield new insights into the nature of dark energy and energy. Additionally, we illustrate that the EDS model can be constrained using BBN and large-scale structure data, with future radio and GW observations expected to provide tighter limits. We conclude by emphasizing the critical role of future GW data in advancing our understanding of early universe physics. The Atacama Compact Array (ACA) functions as an interferometer with an effective aperture of just 16 meters, specifically designed to observe molecular line emission from extended sources. This instrument has proven valuable for characterizing large-scale molecular outflows from stellar objects and identifying extended emission associated with circumstellar disks. In this study, we utilized the ACA to conduct a survey of cometary emission within the cometary nucleus of C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS). Our observations targeted $^{13}$CO, $^{12}$CO, CS, and H$_2$CO, revealing that CS exhibits a distinct extended emission component beyond the nuclear source. We propose that this phenomenon results from the destruction of CS within the comet's atmosphere. By analyzing the extent of the emission, we determined the distance from the nucleus and the production rate of CS. Furthermore, we compared these findings with H$_2$CO observations to assess the viability of the photodissociation model. Additionally, we present observations of $^{13}$CO and H$_2$CO, which appear to originate from the comet's coma. These results align with production rates derived from H$_2$CO emission, supporting the conclusion that CS is produced via neutral-neutral reactions in the coma. This study represents the inaugural ACA survey of a cometary nucleus, demonstrating the ACA's utility for cometary research and offering insights into outgassing processes within the nucleus. Our findings indicate that CS is not produced within the nucleus but rather in the outermost layers of the atmosphere. Consequently, we suggest that the ACA serves as a valuable tool for studying cometary atmospheres. This work was conducted using data from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), a partnership of the ESO, International Science Council, and National Radio Astronomy Observatory (NRAO). Unsupervised speech synthesis (USS) has recently gained significant attention for its ability to generate speech from transcriptions without requiring speaker-specific audio data. While prior methods typically infer speaker identity by clustering extracted acoustic features, they often struggle with isolated speakers lacking a strong match to a centroid, resulting in a generic, speech-like quality. To address this, we introduce UniForm Speech (UNIFORMS), a straightforward unsupervised approach that directly models the speaker distribution using a conditional diffusion process. This technique enables the generation of more natural and diverse audio by simultaneously producing pitch and spectral features. Experimental results demonstrate that UNIFORMS achieves superior performance compared to previous approaches and even surpasses supervised systems in many instances. This paper examines the Tsallis holographic dark energy (THDE) model, treating the universe as a single fluid composed of matter and dark energy. We introduce a complex form of the Essence model, which is constructed as a superposition of the universe's total density and pressure within the THDE framework. This theoretical approach offers a comprehensive framework for understanding dark energy, dark matter, and their interactions. We demonstrate that this complex Essence model can account for the matter-dark energy transition, the matter-dominated era, and the current accelerated expansion of the universe. Furthermore, we show that oscillatory behavior can be observed in both the state parameter and the deceleration parameter. Finally, we analyze the stability of the THDE model using the complex form of the Essence model. Our findings indicate that THDE, when described by the complex Essence model, is stable under certain conditions. Multi-Objective Mixed-Integer Non-Linear Programming (MO-MINLP) problems are prevalent in numerous real-world scenarios, yet their combination of non-linear constraints and discrete decision variables renders them computationally challenging. Although global optimality can be guaranteed for single-objective INLPs using methods like Branch and Bound, achieving this for multiple objectives remains difficult. This paper introduces a Branch and Bound (B&B) algorithm utilizing convex relaxations to address the non-linear nature of the problems. To enhance efficiency, the proposed approach integrates a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm to identify high-quality initial feasible points, which significantly accelerates the B&B search. Furthermore, to mitigate the computational cost of checking a vast number of convex relaxations, a dynamic constraint updating strategy is employed. This technique initially solves the B&B using a limited subset of constraints and strategically adds the most impactful ones to eliminate regions containing non-feasible optima. Numerical experiments demonstrate that this novel B&B framework outperforms existing approaches in the literature. Additionally, a computational study reveals that while the non-linearity of test problems contributes to high solution times, the primary source of complexity arises from the need to solve numerous linear Branch and Bound subproblems. Finally, the study confirms that employing a large number of cuts effectively reduces complexity by rapidly locating high-quality feasible points. The proposed B&B method supports both weak and strong Pareto optimality; however, the weak multi-objective B&B variant is computationally more efficient, as it avoids solving a mixed-integer linear programming problem at each node. Instead, it utilizes a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm to derive a set of high-quality initial feasible points for the B&B process. This approach facilitates the identification of the weak Pareto set and ensures weak Pareto optimality. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that this variant can efficiently solve large-scale problems within a reasonable timeframe. To illustrate its performance, the paper applies the proposed weak Pareto B&B method to various instances of the "Energy Hub" problem, which is widely utilized in the energy management sector. These numerical results confirm the method's capability to handle large-scale applications efficiently. The study concludes that the proposed weak Pareto Branch and Bound approach offers a highly effective solution for addressing multi-objective mixed integer non-linear programming problems. **Keywords:** Multi Objective Optimization Problems; Non-Linear Programming; Mixed Integer Non-Linear Programming; Energy Hub Problem; Energy Management. **AMS Classification:** 90C29; 90C39; 90C26; 9

The growing availability of high-performance computing (HPC) and extensive data repositories has allowed life-sciences researchers to generate substantial datasets, including genomic and proteomic sequences, images, and spectra. However, sharing these data often introduces significant security risks due to sensitive personal information and intellectual property, while the computational resources required for analysis are frequently inaccessible to collaboration partners. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a novel approach to secure biomedical data sharing via a "plug-and-play" model. This model utilizes a gateway service that enables authenticated users to access resources and data without requiring direct connections between partners. We have developed a proof-of-concept implementation leveraging the Open Data Gateway (ODG) and Cyberinfrastructure Gateways (CIG) frameworks. This solution allows users to analyze data within an HPC environment from any location and integrates specialized tools that were previously unavailable to them. Additionally, we outline key enhancements needed for production deployment, including refined authentication and authorization protocols, the use of trusted execution environments, and a specialized web interface. Finally, we demonstrate the service's utility through a real-world case study in a biomedical data sharing context. (This work was supported by NSF grants CNS-1422993 and CNS-1544917.) Aspect-based sentiment analysis enables the evaluation of product attributes in fine-grained sentences, allowing us to identify the specific aspects expressing emotions and their corresponding sentiment polarities. Nevertheless, the inaccuracy of identifying aspects remains a significant challenge in current research, primarily because the interplay between aspects and emotions is complex and context-dependent. To address this issue, we introduce a pre-training model designed to learn the context-dependent implicit emotion representation of aspects. This model utilizes a new pre-training dataset featuring sentences with annotated aspects and sentiment polarities, generated using a novel rule-driven approach. During pre-training, a new module named the Supervised Contrastive pre-training (SCoPe) module is employed to reconstruct sentiment polarities and recover the count of aspects with positive sentiment polarity. Subsequently, the SCoPe module reconstructs aspect labels to recover aspect indices. Finally, the SCoPe module is integrated into the end-task training to fine-tune the pre-trained model, thereby enhancing the model's ability to recover context-dependent implicit emotions in aspect-based sentiment analysis. Extensive experiments on the latest benchmark datasets confirm the model's effectiveness. The source code is available at: https://github.com/zhongyuan1997/Supervised-Contrastive-Pre-training. This study explores the identification and estimation of mediation effects within case-control designs featuring a binary outcome and a binary mediator. We demonstrate that, under the standard assumptions of no unmeasured confounding for treatment-mediator and mediator-outcome relationships and no direct effect confounding, the natural direct effect is generally unidentifiable without additional data. However, if the probability of the mediator equals either 0 or 1 at minimum treatment values, the effect becomes identifiable. The identification of the natural indirect effect requires supplementary data or a specific functional connection between treatment and the mediator. Furthermore, we present a parametric mediation model that accommodates both binary outcomes and mediators. This model relaxes the strict extreme minimum assumptions, thereby enabling an efficient and consistent estimation approach for all three causal effects. Through a Monte Carlo simulation, we demonstrate the performance of the proposed estimator. Additionally, we apply our method to a case-control study investigating the mediation role of body mass index in the link between childhood obesity and adult obesity. In this specific context, the natural indirect effect could not be identified without extra data; consequently, we employed a mediation model that imposes a linear treatment- mediator relationship to achieve point estimates and confidence intervals for all three effects. Our findings indicate that, in this case-control study, mediation effects are statistically significant. To facilitate application, we have provided an R package that implements our mediation effects estimator. This package allows researchers to easily adjust the treatment- mediator model to suit their specific study design and assumptions. Our analysis reveals that the proposed estimator performs well in terms of bias, coverage, and power. The R package is available at: https://github.com/ChenLiyuan1990/MediationCaseControl. Keywords: Case-control study design; Identification; Estimation; Mediation effect.

This study examines a secure, multi-user wireless system enhanced by a Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS). The RIS is positioned to intercept and redirect signals from a power-amplified RIS-assisted (PA-RIS) source to a set of passive RIS (PA-RIS) users, aiming to maximize the generalized secrecy sum rate (GSSR) under a total transmit power constraint. The PA-RIS source transmits an amplified analog beamforming signal toward a random user distribution, utilizing the RIS to adjust the analog beamforming vector and phase shifting matrix. The system is analyzed considering both ideal and non-ideal hardware conditions. Under non-ideal hardware assumptions, the impact of double-sided amplitude truncation and in-phase quadrature (I/Q) imbalance on the system's performance is evaluated. To address the optimization challenge posed by the non-convex nature of the problem, the authors introduce two distinct algorithms: one based on the Generalized Eigenvalue Problem (GEVP) and another utilizing the Successive Convex Approximation (SCA) method. Finally, numerical simulations are conducted to verify the effectiveness of the proposed schemes. Keywords: Phase shifting matrix, Phase reconfigurable intelligent surface, Analog beamforming vector, Double-sided amplitude truncation, I/Q imbalance, Generalized secrecy sum rate. (C) 2022 IEEE. Executive function encompasses a wide array of skills, from managing emotions to controlling impulses. This paper aims to introduce a new conceptual framework for defining, modeling, and simulating such capabilities. Specifically, we propose a novel contrastive value approach for planning and policy learning that utilizes hindsight summarization to reframe past experiences. Within this process, retrospective goals are generated to recontextualize and re-label a simulation agent's historical perceptions. Furthermore, we present a strategy to model and replicate the mechanisms of metacognition and theory of mind through the development of meta-agents. These meta-agents represent higher-order functions dedicated to learning to learn, simulating the cognitive capacity of introspection. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework by applying it to a simple learning task.

The Unruh effect predicts that uniform acceleration generates a perceived difference between the vacuum and an excited state by establishing a horizon that separates future and past light cones. In this study, we demonstrate that the entanglement between these light cones, along with the associated mixing of vacuum and excited modes, manifests through a Berry phase acquired by a qubit undergoing accelerated motion. Consequently, we propose a theoretical experiment utilizing a cryogenic atom-cavity system to detect this timelike Unruh phenomenon. Our analysis indicates that, within the cavity, an excited atomic state can evolve into the Unruh vacuum within a feasible duration, offering a promising pathway for experimental verification. This Berry phase could serve as a novel method for observing physics linked to accelerated observers, including the Unruh effect and Unruh radiation. Furthermore, our proposal establishes a theoretical framework for investigating quantum effects involving time and acceleration, a domain that has received relatively less attention compared to spatial considerations. Finally, the proposed scheme may offer a means to explore quantum gravity phenomena, such as time dilation, in regimes that are otherwise difficult to access. These anticipated experimental results could provide valuable insights for understanding the intersection of quantum mechanics and gravity. Additionally, the scheme is compatible with the observation of Unruh-deWitt correlation functions, which describe entanglement between the accelerated observer's past and future. This correlation has been suggested as a means to probe quantum gravity effects, including entanglement entropy, at a fundamental level. Thus, our proposal may advance our understanding of the relationship between quantum mechanics and gravity. Finally, the discussed effects could be observable in various experimental contexts, such as those involving ultracold atoms, superconducting circuits, and even quantum emitters within solid-state materials. In these scenarios, spatial curvature or the motion of the quantum emitter could be manipulated via external electric fields, thereby opening new avenues for investigating physics involving accelerated observers. These phenomena may also contribute to our understanding of black hole physics, including the information paradox. Specifically, the entanglement between an accelerated observer's past and future, as well as the associated correlation functions, may offer new insights into the information loss problem in black holes. Moreover, our theoretical analysis suggests that the entanglement between an accelerated observer's past and future, along with the resulting correlation functions, could be observable in these experimental setups, potentially shedding light on the fundamental nature of spacetime and information. In conclusion, the proposed scheme may contribute to our understanding of the relationship between quantum mechanics and gravity, while also opening up new avenues for future research in this field.

When interpreted as a temperature-dependent modifier to the gauge coupling, the theory emerges as an effective framework for quantum chromodynamics (QYCD) at intermediate energy scales. This repulsive gravitational phenomenon serves as the fundamental mechanism to explain the origin of bipolar outflows from young stellar objects and protostars. By applying Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation to Astrophysics (AS2A), we establish a novel framework for understanding bipolar outflow dynamics. This approach offers a distinct alternative to the longstanding hypothesis that jet formation relies on the helical magnetic field. The gravitational force magnitude is calculated using the azimuthally averaged linear mass density, radial distance, rotational speed, and the linear growth rate of bipolar lobes. Furthermore, the repellent phenomenon is demonstrated through two illustrative examples involving the bipolar outflows of CS22348 and IRAS17250-2406. The paper concludes by discussing the limitations of this theory. These findings suggest that the repellent gravitational phenomenon is a viable explanation for the origins of bipolar outflows, and the proposed gravitational force law provides a new perspective for future research in this field. Additionally, the methodology for calculating the repellent force is applicable to other bipolar systems. Ultimately, the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (AS2A) is presented as a new approach for analyzing bipolar outflows in young stellar objects and protostars. This study reports the results of an optical follow-up campaign for 11 well-observed fast radio bursts (FRBs) that exhibited multiple, bright millisecond bursts. The investigation utilized two telescopes: the 4-meter Siding Spring Snider Telescope (S$^4$) and the 2-meter University of Washington telescope (UWTelescope). We conducted optical observations between 30 seconds and 1.5 hours prior to the radio emission, as well as simultaneously within $\pm$1.5 seconds. No optical emission was detected from any FRB at either wavelength. Consequently, 3$\sigma$ upper limits on the simultaneous optical flux were established for all targets, ranging from $1.1 \times 10^{-12}$ to $1.1 \times 10^{-9}$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$. Furthermore, we analyzed the non-detection of any delayed optical emission from FRB 20190520. Our findings indicate that the optical luminosity of this burst was less than $1.1 \times 10^{39}$ erg s$^{-1}$ at a redshift of $z < 0.0002$. These results suggest that the optical emission from FRBs is likely significantly weaker than their radio output, with a radio-to-optical power ratio exceeding $10^6$ at a confidence level of 99.9%. Additionally, the observed non-detection of optical emission from FRB 20190520 occurred approximately 1.5 seconds after the radio burst, implying that the radio emission is not delayed by more than 1.5 seconds relative to other components. These constraints offer valuable insights for future multi-messenger research involving FRBs. The data used in this analysis are publicly accessible at https://frb-obs.uw.edu/. The brightness of charged particle beams is defined as the product of beam current density and charge per particle. This study presents a new method for measuring beam current density via brightness scanning. The process involves determining the charge density across a plane by recording the total charge density within that plane as it passes through an aperture of varying sizes. The described algorithm is straightforward to implement and can be readily adapted for real-time acquisition and post-processing. It is applicable to all non-relativistic charged particle beams, including electron beams in accelerators and particle beams generated by gas discharges. The technique's accuracy is governed by random and systematic errors, with the former depending on count statistics and the latter on assumptions made during current density distribution analysis. While systematic errors can be significantly reduced by appropriately selecting the distribution function, systematic uncertainties inherent in choosing specific function types cannot be eliminated. Consequently, the precision of current density analysis is ultimately limited by the accuracy of current density distribution function theory. We demonstrate that existing theoretical models are sufficiently precise for many applications, though further development is necessary for other uses. This development work is currently underway. Additionally, we outline a novel method for measuring current density distribution functions using brightness scanning. We have successfully applied brightness scanning to measure the current density distribution function of a gas discharge beam. Furthermore, we have developed a diagnostic system for electron beam current density distribution using brightness scanning. We report on the design and operation of this system and present its measurement results. Finally, we discuss a technique for detecting beam position using brightness scanning. This approach offers a new method for position detection that utilizes the entire beam cross-section, thereby eliminating systematic errors related to the beam offset from the beamline center. This detection method could enable the development of a new beam position monitor design. We have designed and built a prototype of this new BPM and have conducted tests to evaluate its performance. The paper details the design and operation of this prototype. In conclusion, brightness scanning is a versatile and robust diagnostic tool capable of effectively measuring current and position. Its advantages include simplicity, cost-effectiveness, and robustness. Consequently, brightness scanning is widely employed in various fields, such as electron beam lithography and gas discharge particle beam fusion. We anticipate that this technique will continue to be utilized in diverse applications. This paper aims to offer a comprehensive overview of current research on brightness scanning and to stimulate further exploration and development in this field. Consequently, there is a strong demand for accurate control methods grounded in precise models. This article serves as a comprehensive survey of modeling and control techniques for soft robots. It begins by categorizing these robots into three primary families based on their deformation mechanisms: pneumatic soft robots, fiber-reinforced soft robots, and soft robots utilizing soft actuators. Table-based fact verification focuses on determining the truthfulness of a given claim by analyzing a supporting evidence table. A significant challenge in this domain is extracting premise hypotheses from the table that directly align with the components of the claim being verified. This article examines the challenges of extracting such premises for Chinese and English data and proposes a novel disassembly strategy to address this. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods on the CHINESE-TF and TABFAC (English) datasets. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are capable of producing high-quality images, yet current techniques for controlling GAN image generation are insufficient for complex scenarios. We present HSCC (Hidden Space Conditioning on GANs), a novel approach that enables complex image generation by adapting the latent space of conditional GANs. Our method is straightforward: it involves conditioning the encoder of a trained conditional GAN with an auxiliary generator to create an auxiliary network. This auxiliary system is trained to map an input image to a complex hidden space, thereby facilitating the generation of complex images. We evaluated HSCC across various datasets and compared it against other conditioning methods. The results demonstrate that HSCC can generate complex images and surpass both other conditioning methods and other conditional GANs. Furthermore, our approach is versatile, as it can be applied to diverse types of conditional GANs to achieve complex image generation. Additionally, the training of the auxiliary network is independent of the specific GAN architecture, making the method highly generalizable. Finally, our approach is more efficient than other conditioning strategies because it avoids the need for an expensive search process. Experimental validation confirms the efficacy of the proposed method. Code and models are available at https://github.com/taehyung-lee97/hidden-space-conditioning. Video demonstrations can be viewed here: https://youtu.be/4241422222s. Supplementary materials are located at: https://github.com/taehyung-lee97/hidden-space-conditioning. Keywords: Generative adversarial networks, Image generation.

The objective of distance labeling in graphs is to assign label sets $S(u)$ to every vertex $u$ such that the shortest distance between any pair of vertices matches the length of their label set intersection, i.e., $|(S(u) \cap S(v))| = dist(u,v)$. This concept is particularly valuable for graph algorithms that depend on vertex proximity, enabling them to function correctly even with constant label errors. While most research focuses on labeling general graphs, this study advances the field by demonstrating that planar graphs admit distance labeling schemes resilient to $O(1)$ label faults, specifically requiring $O(\log^* n)$ colors. Furthermore, for outerplanar graphs, a more practical scheme is proposed that needs $O(\log n)$ colors. Finally, the paper introduces a general distance labeling scheme for graphs with treewidth $w$, which can be precomputed in $O(mw \log w)$ time and applied to planar graphs and graph families with bounded treewidth. Although this general approach is less efficient than existing methods for planar graphs, it holds significant potential for graph classes that are not currently known to support distance labeling schemes. Notably, it is the first such scheme for chordal graphs and minor-free graphs. Additionally, the study confirms that every chordal graph can be labeled with $O(1)$ colors, thereby resolving a longstanding conjecture. Finally, the paper addresses the problem of maintaining distance labeling schemes under dynamic graph updates, demonstrating that updates to a planar graph's distance labeling scheme result in a label set modification of $O(\log^* n)$. The proposed method is straightforward and effective for updates involving a single vertex. Finally, the paper examines the problem of maintaining distance labeling schemes when the graph structure itself changes. Specifically, it demonstrates that for a planar graph $G$, a labeling scheme exists that allows the graph to be transformed into a tree $T$ with $O(\log^* n)$ colors, ensuring that the distance between any two vertices $u$ and $v$ in $G$ matches that of an arbitrary embedding of $T$. We introduce a statistical time-domain analysis technique designed to characterize the stability of optical clocks that operate without periodic modulation. This approach enables the simultaneous time-series analysis of both primary clock signals and their systematic perturbations. By integrating this method with Bayesian statistics, we can robustly separate true stochastic clock instabilities from measurement noise, while also quantifying external factors that impact short-term performance. We validate this analysis using a high-precision continuous strontium optical clock, demonstrating that it effectively handles non-periodic data collection, addresses long-term systematic variations, and accurately estimates stochastic short-term stability. These capabilities significantly expand the experimental window for conducting comprehensive clock performance analyses. Furthermore, we outline the extension of this methodology to periodic optical clocks, showing that it can recover and generalize existing time-domain analysis techniques used in that domain. This broader methodology facilitates the direct comparison of performance across both periodic and non-periodic clocks, thereby streamlining the pursuit of the ultimate precision oscillator. This study introduces a fog-assisted Software Defined Network (SDN) architecture integrated with Fog Computing (FC) to address challenges in Service Function Chain (SFC) flow restoration following link and node failures, as well as to curb fault rates. The primary objective is to minimize the frequency of link and node failures. To achieve this, the proposal incorporates fault prevention mechanisms alongside efficient restoration strategies for SFC flows, alongside an energy-efficient resource management system. This approach leverages FC to execute functions locally within nearby fog nodes, thereby reducing latency and enhancing resource efficiency. Furthermore, to prevent faults, the system continuously monitors network resources and adjusts them dynamically to mitigate failure risks. For restoration, the method utilizes local processing capabilities at the nearest fog node to facilitate swift recovery. These two FC-driven features significantly benefit SFC restoration, while the fault prevention aspect further reduces failure occurrence frequencies. The proposed solution is evaluated through simulations that represent various failure scenarios. Results indicate that, compared to existing proposals, this method reduces link failure frequency by 17% and node failure frequency by 20%. Additionally, it demonstrates improvements of 10% in SFC restoration latency, 11% in resource utilization, and 14% in energy efficiency relative to current solutions. Finally, the proposed approach offers substantial benefits for real-time applications utilizing SFC and FC within a fog-assisted SDN environment. To support this, the paper introduces the FC-First module for fault prevention and the FC-Relay module for restoration, both of which incorporate local fog processing to enhance SFC performance. The work concludes by discussing the advantages and limitations of the proposed solution. The paper is structured into eight sections, with the first three providing an overview, related work analysis, and problem formulation. The remaining five sections detail the proposed solutions for SFC restoration and fault prevention in fog-assisted SDNs. Section four focuses on fault prevention, while Section five addresses SFC restoration. Section six explores energy-efficient resource management, and Section seven concludes the paper with future research directions. The final section concludes the work. In multi-objective reinforcement learning (RL), a prevalent approach involves optimizing a weighted combination of multiple loss functions to train a policy. However, this technique often yields unstable training results and inconsistent performance across varying weight configurations. This paper investigates the impacts of the L2, L1, and weighted sum loss functions on policy evaluation and gradient computation. We offer a unified gradient framework that reveals the fundamental distinctions between these loss types and their respective influences when applied to the policy gradient theorem. Our analysis demonstrates that the L2 loss function induces greater gradient variance compared to the L1 and local weighted sum variants. Furthermore, we show that the gradient behavior of the global weighted sum loss function shifts dynamically depending on which weights are non-zero. Based on these findings, we propose a local weighted sum loss function designed to mitigate the gradient issues associated with the L2 loss, thereby enhancing policy evaluation stability. Empirical results confirm that our proposed loss function outperforms existing alternatives. Additionally, we release a new Python package supporting various loss functions for RL, which can be accessed at https://github.com/Chenchen998877/LossFunctionsRL. This repository will be continuously updated to incorporate further developments. Finally, we acknowledge that loss function selection remains a significant challenge in practical applications, and we hope this research inspires future investigations into developing more robust and effective loss functions. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first systematic examination of loss function effects specifically within policy gradient methods. Given that policy gradients are a cornerstone of RL, we anticipate these insights will hold relevance for a broad spectrum of policy gradient algorithms. This study investigates the distribution of interfilamentary spacings within the Galactic Center to evaluate whether these structures arise from a Poisson process. The analysis employs two distinct spacing metrics: the distance from a randomly selected point to its nearest neighbor and an arc-length-based measure. Results indicate that both metrics, when calculated using an arc-length definition, fail to align with Poisson statistics. Furthermore, the arc-length-based measure proves to be the more reliable of the two. This discrepancy suggests that the filaments are not randomly oriented and hints at the presence of a specific pattern or an interaction mechanism between them. These conclusions are supported by a simulation that randomly distributes lines on a sphere, demonstrating that such lines are expected to exhibit non-random orientations. Consequently, the observed non-randomness points toward either a magnetic field configuration or another physical process linked to the filaments. Finally, the paper examines the relationship between these findings and the distribution of spacings regarding the Hubble Law. Additionally, the study explores how the choice of spacing definition influences the detection of Poisson characteristics in other physical phenomena. To facilitate this, a Python script is provided that computes the probability distribution of generalized spacing variables for any given set of objects. This tool is particularly useful for researchers studying filamentary systems, such as those in the early universe. This study investigates the optimal conservation voltage reduction (OCVR) problem within integrated primary-secondary distribution systems featuring distributed generation (DG). Since voltage regulation in distribution networks is critical for enhancing power system reliability, OCVR has emerged as a widely adopted technique for voltage control. The objective is to determine the optimal magnitude of active power reduction for each distributed generator, minimizing total power losses while avoiding voltage sags. A sufficient condition is derived to guarantee that the reduced active power yields optimal OCVR. This study introduces a delay-dependent advisor benchmark, inspired by the nonstochastic delay-tolerant tight advice framework established by Sanchis and Pál. In this model, an advisor observes arm pulls and subsequent rewards with potential arm-dependent delays. An advisor is deemed delay-tolerant tight if its benchmark regret grows sublinearly with the maximum delay. We present a linear programming-based algorithm, ALP, with delay-dependent guarantees. When applied to a specific advisor benchmark where every pull incurs a delay of at least $D$, ALP achieves a tight delay-dependent benchmark regret of $\tilde{O}(K\sqrt{DT})$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ALP effectively addresses the classical nonstochastic tight advice problem with unknown arm-dependent success probabilities, yielding an optimal regret of $\tilde{O}(K\sqrt{DT})$. Text-based web chat applications are becoming increasingly common, and users typically prefer interacting with an agent that writes like a human rather than one that merely understands human language. To address this, we introduce a framework called LEARning to produce EHTerosexual responses (LEATHER), which learns to generate charming, human-like dialogue specifically tailored to the conversational contexts of these web chat systems. Within this framework, we explore several training strategies, data augmentation methods, and objective functions. Our empirical results demonstrate that this approach outperforms baseline methods in producing text that is more charming, emotionally intelligent, and stylistically similar to human users. Additionally, we provide an analysis of the LEATHER outputs to investigate sexual preference bias and evaluate their overall quality. **Background:** Accurately predicting stress time histories for structural components is vital for the structural integrity and reliability of offshore wind systems. Current state-of-the-art methods typically rely on probabilistic structural dynamics simulations to model various failure modes, requiring extensive computational resources. **Aims:** This study introduces a novel surrogate model for offshore wind-turbine stresses, designed to maintain high-fidelity stress time histories while significantly lowering computational costs. **Results:** The proposed chained Gaussian process (GpC) outperforms the traditional surrogate approach (GpS) in capturing the statistical characteristics of stochastic stress time histories. Specifically, GpC reduces the root mean square error by 20% compared to GpS. **Conclusions:** Chained Gaussian processes effectively model stress time histories by representing the nonlinear, hierarchical relationship between environmental parameters and structural stresses. This efficiency is achieved without sacrificing model fidelity. The method is validated using data from a 5 MW semi-submersible wind turbine. Furthermore, GpC is highly adaptable to other stochastic responses in offshore wind systems, such as fatigue loads, and can be extended to other offshore structures. **New Contribution:** The study proposes Chained Gaussian Processes (GpC) as a new method to model stochastic responses in offshore wind systems, capable of accurately predicting stress time histories for specific environmental conditions. This model is also applicable for analyzing the sensitivity of stochastic responses to environmental parameters. Additionally, it can be used to predict the fatigue performance of specific offshore structures. **New Contribution:** The paper introduces Chained Gaussian Processes (GpC) as a new approach for modeling stochastic responses in offshore wind systems, enabling the accurate prediction of stress time histories under specific environmental conditions. Social media platforms have emerged as essential tools for information dissemination, a capability demonstrated by the 2020 Izmir Earthquake in Turkey. This study examines Twitter activity surrounding the event to analyze user demographics, discussion topics, and information-sharing behaviors. Data were gathered via the Twitter API, exhibiting a strong temporal pattern with a 16-day lifespan. Demographic findings reveal that younger individuals, particularly males, drove the discussion, showing a decline in interest over time. The activity was segmented into six distinct periods using topic modeling, covering diverse subjects from the epicenter to rescue operations. Furthermore, highly active users were identified as the primary drivers of this discussion. These insights into user behavior and interest patterns can inform future social media strategies. This study introduces a new framework for reconstructing complex, time-dependent structures, such as quantum states and quench dynamics. We develop a generalized Bayesian inference method that integrates forward-optimization with a data basis representation to ensure robustness against the specific features of time-resolved experimental data. This approach facilitates the robust reconstruction of structures defined by time-domain kernels, including Fourier, anti-Fourier, coherent Gaussian wavepacket, and Wigner distributions. Additionally, the forward-optimization step accelerates reconstruction for time-dependent potentials and structures characterized by vast configuration spaces. The efficacy of this methodology is demonstrated through several test cases, including a benchmark Gaussian wavepacket subjected to a time-dependent harmonic oscillator potential, as well as the reconstruction of quench dynamics in a many-body Fock state and a Wigner distribution. The methodology is implemented via the open-source PyQMC library. This method is applicable to a wide range of systems, encompassing molecules, materials, and other quantum structures. The PyQMC library is available at https://pyqmc.org. Supplementary information is provided at https://doi.org/10.1088/2053-1583/ac9228. Supplementary materials include many-body wavepacket dynamics, benchmark of reconstruction accuracy, reconstruction of quench dynamics in the He atom, and reconstruction of quench dynamics in hydrogen molecules. Finally, videos demonstrating the reconstruction of quantum wavepackets and Wigner distributions are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7308000. These videos were created using PyQMC version 2.0.1. However, version 2.0.1 contains a bug; users are advised to employ version 1.1.1 instead, accessible at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7308000. To facilitate the analysis of time-resolved data, we present a method for reconstructing time-dependent structures from experimental data. Our methodology is grounded in Bayesian inference, utilizing Bayesian evidence to determine optimal reconstruction structures, assess their uncertainty, and prevent overfitting. The reconstruction structures are represented using time-domain kernels based on basis sets generated by forward evolution. The algorithm is accelerated through the implementation of forward-optimization, a technique for optimizing variational quantum Monte Carlo wavefunctions. This work examines the stability of $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons within nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ geometries, specifically focusing on the case of nearly parallel $\mathrm{G}_2$-structures. We demonstrate that no non-trivial $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons exist over manifolds admitting such a structure under the assumption of constant curvature. Utilizing a suitable Fourier expansion for the instanton deformation equation, we establish that the deformed potential of an instanton becomes stable precisely when it aligns with specific pure forms. Applying these findings to the $\mathrm{G}_2$-instanton $\sigma$ identified by Lotay and Wang on their family of deformed $G_2$-tori, we determine that $\sigma$ exhibits stability exclusively on a singular subset of the manifold of nearly parallel $\mathrm{G}_2$-manifolds. Furthermore, we derive explicit deformed instanton equations for deformations parameterized by pure 3- and 4-forms, enabling the construction of a continuous family of instantons based on a prescribed one, thereby generalizing our previous work to arbitrary $\mathrm{G}_2$-geometries. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the deformed potential's properties, revealing that it remains real and positive for any chosen 7-form. Finally, by integrating our results with near-plectic $\mathrm{G}_2$-geometries, we offer a complete characterization of the deformed potential's behavior in terms of pure 2- and 6-forms. These contributions significantly expand the family of $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons, including those recently discovered by Lotay and Wang, and substantially enhance our understanding of their moduli space. Our methodology is also applicable to analyzing $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons on nearly parallel $G_2$-manifolds, though this aspect is not addressed here. Our findings are also relevant to the study of spinors on nearly parallel $\mathrm{G}_2$-manifolds, a topic we will explore in a future publication. Finally, our results contribute to the investigation of holonomy groups within nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$-manifolds, with implications for understanding the moduli space of instantons. In the context of the global fight against the COVID-19 pandemic, digital technologies have emerged as vital instruments for controlling the epidemic. Among these, contact tracing applications utilize specific mechanisms to identify and alert individuals who may have been exposed to the virus. This study conducts a privacy assessment of the Coronavirus-SUS mobile application, which employs an automated, location-based proximity detection system to facilitate digital contact tracing. By integrating the Sensitive Data Protection (SDP) framework with the Information Flow Analysis (IFA) method, the research demonstrates that the app's design allows for the leakage of both personal and sensitive information through the application logic. The paper concludes by offering recommendations to enhance the privacy of the application. Findings indicate that the application is not privacy-preserving, as it generates privacy risks for both users and third parties. To improve privacy, the study suggests implementing data minimization, enhancing user control over data usage, and adopting differential privacy techniques. These enhancements could be realized through user education regarding the application's data collection practices and by restricting data access to authorized users only. Ultimately, the analysis underscores the necessity of a multidisciplinary approach to ensure the privacy and security of such mobile technologies. A privacy-enhancing mobile application design would significantly bolster public trust in the initiative. Additionally, the research proposes that future studies should explore the application of differential privacy techniques to the Coronavirus-SUS mobile application. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/fernandolima12345/Coronavirus-SUS. The methodology employed in this work can also be applied to evaluate the privacy of other COVID-19 mobile applications. To facilitate this, the researchers have made their analysis code available at: https://github.com/fernandolima12345/Coronavirus-SUS-Privacy-Assessment. This repository includes code for the Sensitive Data Protection (SDP) framework, Information Flow Analysis (IFA) method, and a Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) tool, all of which are open-source and accessible for replication. Additionally, the repository contains a Privacy Assessment Form (PAF) that documents the analysis process and findings. The PAF is available in both English and Portuguese, allowing researchers to reproduce the assessment in their respective languages. The authors express gratitude to all contributors who assisted in this evaluation. For further details, visit: https://digital-privacy.com.br. Quantum data refers to information encoded within the state of a quantum system, which is fundamentally inaccessible through classical observation. This study introduces a quantum-enhanced neural system designed to store, process, and retrieve such data via specific quantum measurements. Representing a quantum-enhanced system-of-systems, our approach integrates an artificial neural network with a quantum system, where the former is depicted as a recurrent Hopfield network and the latter as a multi-qubit system prepared in a specific entangled state. We investigate the storage and retrieval of quantum data within this hybrid framework, demonstrating that this design effectively mitigates the readout errors typically encountered when extracting information from quantum systems. Furthermore, the proposed method establishes a viable pathway for the reliable storage and retrieval of quantum information. These findings have significant implications for the advancement of quantum-enhanced neural systems, quantum-enhanced systems-of-systems, and the broader fields of quantum and quantum-inspired computing. Additionally, the study offers a unique model for investigating the intersection between the quantum and classical domains. This paper introduces a code creator for plain ACL2 that is based on a shallow embedding of C. Unlike a semantic model where expressions and statements operate on abstract domains, this approach deep embeds C by defining its syntax and semantics directly within ACL2. The tool generates proofs confirming that generated ACL2 code accurately represents the corresponding C program. We demonstrate that this generator facilitates abstractions essential for functional programming, utilizing certifiable code generation to produce verified ACL2 code. Additionally, we present a C to ACL2 translator that leverages the code creator to generate verifiable ACL2 code, and we describe a verification condition generator that extends Dijkstra's weakest precondition calculus to support C's shallow embedding. This enables the reverse process—generating C code from ACL2, complete with verification that the C compiles to the specified ACL2 program. We illustrate the tool's practical utility through several C programs, including a bubble sort, a selection sort, a merge sort, and a function to compute the sum of the first $n$ natural numbers. For each example, we provide a C file and its corresponding verified ACL2 translation. Furthermore, we show that these code creators and translators assist in constructing a proof for Hoare's two invariants involving two sorted arrays merging into one. Overall, this work represents a significant step toward fully verified compilation, demonstrating that all phases of the C compiler chain can be formally verified within ACL2. Compiling C to a verified executable would involve two stages: first, generating verified ACL2 code from C, and second, generating verified machine code from the verified ACL2. To achieve this, all compiler passes must be formally verified, ensuring that the compiled program correctly implements the original C source code. Our approach to C to ACL2 verification constitutes a critical advancement in this domain. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions. Specifically, we aim to develop code creators for additional languages, such as Coq, and to refine code generation strategies to produce verified binaries directly, rather than verified source files. Additionally, we intend to investigate strategies for generating verified machine code from verified ACL2. Finally, we plan to extend the verification process to confirm that the generated machine code correctly implements the high-level language program. This work forms a vital step toward fully verified compilation. To accomplish this, all compiler passes must be formally verified, ensuring that the final compiled program faithfully implements the source code. Consequently, our work on C to ACL2 verification serves as an essential foundation for achieving fully verified compilation.

This study analyzes the proper elements of 31 asteroids from the (39991) Iochroma family, utilizing Tisserand parameters and S-type asteroid proper inclinations to isolate the family from neighboring asteroids. The research identifies the presence of a 2:1 mean motion resonance with Jupiter and investigates how the family's dispersion in proper elements influences its dynamical evolution. The observed angle dispersion is primarily attributed to the (39991) Iochroma itself, which is perturbed by the 2:1 mean motion resonance with Jupiter. Additionally, the study examines the persistence of the 2:1 resonance gap and the impact of asteroid self-perturbations on this resonance. The findings indicate that the 2:1 mean motion resonance gap persists for approximately 100 Myr, while the effect of self-perturbations on the resonance gap lasts for about 10 Myr. This study investigates the connections between Hurwitz zeta functions and Ramanujan's renowned series for zeta values. By employing the derivative of the Hurwitz zeta function at zero as a bridge between zeta values and Bernoulli numbers, we derive a specific relation linking the two. This approach enables us to generalize Ramanujan's formula for zeta values and characterize the arithmetic properties of the Hurwitz zeta function. Furthermore, we establish an infinite family of integral identities involving zeta values, which arise from an integral connection between the Hurwitz zeta function and the gamma function. In particular, our findings offer an elementary proof of Ramanujan's identity for odd zeta values. Finally, we explore the implications of these results for the arithmetic properties of L-series. To facilitate future research, we have compiled a comprehensive table of integrals that include both integer powers of natural numbers and zeta values. Additionally, we extend these results to more general integrals incorporating gamma functions. This work serves as a foundation for our subsequent paper, which demonstrates that the arithmetic properties of L-values can be derived from those of the Hurwitz zeta function. Our results thus provide a unified framework for understanding the arithmetic nature of both zeta and L-values. This article is based on a thesis written in the Romanian language. Machine learning has emerged as a highly effective machine-accessible language for modeling the dynamics of physical systems. Nevertheless, current methods often overlook the underlying structure of these systems, such as the conservation laws that emerge from symmetries. This manuscript demonstrates that conservation laws can be derived from the topological structure of data via algebraic topological methods. We introduce a framework for representing data through simplicial sets and define a procedure to identify conservation laws within this representation. Our approach is validated through a standard machine learning regression task involving both synthetic and experimental data. Furthermore, we outline strategies for extending this methodology to broader contexts, suggesting that algebraic topology can serve as a foundational language for machine learning applications in physics. Our research is available at github.com/beyerscher/algebraic-topology-ml. ArXiv link: 2105.04604v1.

The rapid advancement of solar power generation necessitates a highly precise modeling approach to effectively analyze and mitigate its significant impacts on power system operations and stability. This paper introduces a solar-driven, computationally efficient model that captures the discrete nature of solar generation, solar-driven loads, and solar farm characteristics—specifically their spatial and temporal distribution—as well as their coupled interactions. These factors are critical in explaining the unique dynamics of power systems with high solar penetration. The proposed model is formulated as a Gaussian quadrature problem on the projective line, weighted by solar irradiance data. Leveraging recent advancements in high-order Gaussian quadrature on the projective line, we develop the Solar-Weighted Gaussian (SWG) quadrature rule, which delivers exceptional accuracy. The weights in the SWG rule are explicitly defined in terms of evaluated solar irradiance and its $k$ derivatives at $k+1$ quadrature nodes, with the nodes determined as the roots of orthogonal polynomials. We provide an efficient algorithm for calculating the nodes and weights of this solar-driven quadrature. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the SWG rule maintains stability under perturbations in solar irradiance, ensuring that node perturbations remain bounded. This is achieved by proving that the condition number of the associated Vandermonde matrix is polynomially bounded with respect to the number of nodes and the derivative order. Finally, the efficacy of the SWG quadrature is validated by its application in high-order modeling of solar irradiance and power systems with deep solar penetration. This approach yields high-order accurate models for power systems, including the solar-weighted high-order swing equation, solar-weighted high-order voltage dynamics, and solar-weighted high-order small-signal dynamics. These models accurately reflect the physical properties of power systems with substantial solar integration. Notably, the solar-weighted swing equation reveals a non-Newtonian dynamical system driven by solar irradiance, while the solar-weighted voltage dynamics equations indicate that voltage dynamics are influenced by both real and reactive power injections from solar farms. Additionally, the solar-weighted small-signal dynamics equations show that frequency response functions are dependent on solar irradiance. The computational efficiency of the SWG quadrature is highlighted by its ability to deliver high-order accuracy with a minimal number of nodes, resulting in minimal computational cost. This efficiency is particularly evident in the low computational expense required to achieve the system identification task. The curvature information of optimization landscapes is vital for training deep neural networks (DNNs), as understanding the local geometry provides deep insights into the training process. This paper introduces a novel curvature estimation framework based on the generalized Gauss-Newton (gGN) matrix, which serves as an approximation of the Hessian. Our approach leverages the low-rank characteristics of the gGN matrix to define a low-rank representation of this matrix. We further develop a curvature measure using the latter half of this low-rank form, which is computationally efficient, particularly for deep networks. Our results demonstrate that this curvature metric captures fine-grained insights into the local geometry of deep learning tasks, revealing how the generalization gap between source and target tasks can be significantly reduced through curvature-aware transfer learning. Additionally, we show that the proposed curvature analysis can be integrated with the popular curvature-adaptive optimizer, Yogi. Code is available at: https://github.com/ashwinbhatia/ViViT. This study examines how grammatical gender influences word representations in neural language models using English, which is predominantly a gender-transparent language. By employing a cross-conditional conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) to enforce gender consistency across a dictionary while allowing semantic variability, we observe that the model induces significant shifts in the majority of lexical items. The exceptions are nouns that are either inherently gendered or denote male or female animals. We attribute this finding to human annotators utilizing gendered language as a heuristic to enhance the efficiency of lexical acquisition. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this heuristic is sufficiently effective to enable a transformer model trained on English to learn gender-marked morphologies for a German-like language. This research offers new insights into psycholinguistic theories regarding how humans acquire gender assignment and reveals a functional advantage of grammatical gender in language learning. Additionally, this work holds significant implications for the field of multilingual neural machine translation, which often struggles to accurately transfer gender features. Finally, we provide a Python implementation of the proposed cGAN model. The source code and pre-trained models are accessible at: https://github.com/ashwinbhat/ConditionalGAN. The first author's primary focus is on multilingual neural machine translation, while the second author is primarily interested in natural language generation. Both authors utilize grammar as a lens to explore how computational language models can elucidate the cognitive processes of human language acquisition. We aim to explore these and related questions through a collaboration between a psycholinguist and a computational linguist. This paper serves as a foundational step toward that partnership. Consider a connected semisimple algebraic group $G$ defined over a field of characteristic zero, where $G(\mathbb{R})$ is compact. The purpose of this note is to demonstrate that the group $G(\mathbb{R}) \cap G(\mathbb{Q})$ exhibits a linear bound on its charmability within any finite Galois extension of $\mathbb{Q}$. This result follows from a more fundamental theorem: for any semisimple algebraic group $H$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ and a finite Galois extension $L/\mathbb{Q}$, there exists a constant $C$ dependent solely on $H$ such that every element in $H(L)$ with a trivial $S$-orbit satisfies $|\mathrm{char}_L(H)| \leq C$. In the specific scenario where $H$ possesses a nontrivial split $\mathbb{R}$-torus and $L=\mathbb{R}$, this inequality yields a quadratic bound. Furthermore, the proof technique provides additional insights into the structure of semisimple algebraic groups. Specifically, for a semisimple algebraic group $J$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ and a field extension $K \supseteq \mathbb{Q}$, we establish the existence of a constant $C$ based exclusively on the isomorphism classes of $J$'s connected components such that the dimension of the space of $S$-invariant elements in $\mathrm{char}_K(J)$ does not exceed $C$. This finding has potential applications in Arakelov theory, particularly for addressing problems concerning the finiteness of Minkowski's charm across all number fields. Additionally, we explore the relationship between the charmability of $\Gamma$ and the "stiffness" of its associated building, where $\Gamma$ is a uniform lattice within a semisimple algebraic group $G$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. Our approach involves analyzing the building $\mathcal{B}$ associated with $G(\mathbb{R})$ through the lens of hyperbolic geometry. We show that $\Gamma$ acts as a quasi-crystal on $\mathcal{B}$ with thinness $O(\log[\Gamma:\Gamma_0])$, where $\Gamma_0$ represents the stabilizer of a fundamental domain within $\Gamma$. Position estimation is a critical task that facilitates numerous downstream applications, including detection, tracking, and pose estimation. While most existing methods are trained and evaluated on specific datasets, focusing on well-defined categories like cars or pedestrians in fixed environments, there is a lack of research on estimating the global pose of category-level objects for open-world classes where no training data exists. This work addresses that gap by estimating the 3D scale, orientation, and 6D position of category-level objects from a single image without any task-specific training. Our approach leverages a pre-trained diffusion model to synthesize 3D object instances and utilizes a novel regression framework based on 3D Gaussian Splatting to estimate the object's final pose. We introduce the first benchmark for this problem and demonstrate state-of-the-art results on several new benchmarks. Furthermore, we show that our framework effectively enhances 3D diffusion generation and supports cross-attention mechanisms. This study introduces a new deep learning framework designed for short-term traffic forecasting on large-scale, high-dimensional road networks with sparse data. The proposed method addresses two primary challenges: the need to generate features from high-dimensional input nodes to enhance model performance, and the necessity to leverage data from similar nodes to mitigate the effects of data sparsity. To achieve this, the research proposes two core components: (1) a dynamic similarity matrix generation technique that utilizes both static and dynamic information to produce a similarity matrix, and (2) a graph attention-based attribute extraction approach that uses this matrix to integrate similarities and isolate the most relevant nodes for feature extraction. Experimental results using real-world data demonstrate that the proposed approach delivers competitive performance compared to existing methods. Furthermore, an ablation study confirms the effectiveness of the two key strategies within the proposed model. Finally, the performance of the proposed method is evaluated against two baseline models to verify its effectiveness in improving both generalization and convergence. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1998/Similarity-based-Attribute-Extraction. Future research will explore the application of this framework in other domains, such as supply chain management. Given the current challenges in global trade, there is a significant demand for efficient forecasting methods capable of handling high-dimensional, sparse, and highly nonlinear data. Additionally, the similarity-based attribute extraction mechanism holds potential for use in other graph-based models, including graph neural networks (GNNs). However, current deep learning methods for traffic forecasting often rely on predefined similarity matrices, which limits their ability to learn from the complex relationships between traffic nodes. By integrating a similarity-based attribute extraction mechanism with existing deep learning models, it may be possible to achieve superior forecasting results on large-scale road networks. This could pave the way for more efficient decision-making in urban planning and traffic management. Furthermore, the proposed framework could serve as a foundation for developing more interpretable and explainable traffic forecasting models, which is crucial for gaining stakeholder trust and facilitating better decision-making. Finally, the similarity-based attribute extraction mechanism could be applied to other GNNs to extract relevant attributes and improve their performance on large-scale road networks. However, further research is needed to evaluate the generalizability of this mechanism across different GNN architectures. Additionally, the framework could be extended to incorporate additional data sources, such as weather and events, to enhance forecasting accuracy. This would require developing new mechanisms to extract attributes from these diverse inputs and adapt the framework to handle the resulting increases in data dimensionality and complexity

In electrical power systems, maintaining voltage within acceptable limits is essential for the stable operation of devices and the overall network. This challenge is intensified by rising nonlinear electrical loads, such as power electronics. This paper examines the impact of an alternative frequency control strategy on stabilizing voltage dynamics. By utilizing passive matrices to model the coupling between frequency and voltage at electrical loads, this control approach allows frequency to regulate power consumption in power systems characterized by significant voltage-exponential loads. Consequently, the frequency-control model within an energy management system is decoupled from voltage-related issues involving voltage-exponential loads. The study demonstrates that this alternative control enhances stabilization in both steady-state and dynamic conditions. Specifically, it facilitates the stabilization of complex, nonlinear differential equations governing network voltage through feedback control of voltage magnitudes at boundary buses. Additionally, the method enables stabilization of dynamic systems governed by nonlinear difference equations through local frequency control. The proposed solutions rely on the analysis of differential and difference Lyapunov functions, respectively. The benefits of these strategies are illustrated through a case study of the Brazilian power system. Furthermore, the study addresses stabilization via optimal control, utilizing an infinite-horizon quadratic cost function alongside boundary conditions for boundary buses. Numerical simulations confirm the efficacy of these proposed approaches. Finally, the paper explores extensions regarding nonlinear difference equations with time delays and nonlinear difference-inclusion problems. Over recent decades, diverse disciplines have embraced the concept of "intelligent systems," with a shared objective of embedding a specific collection of components with varying degrees of autonomy into a unified entity capable of autonomous operation. This study examines such a composed system within the context of power grids, specifically analyzing the impact of introducing intelligence into the grid itself, rather than solely within its consuming loads. By leveraging a control-theoretic framework, we demonstrate that the system can be decomposed into multiple smaller, loosely coupled intelligent subsystems. Furthermore, we establish that the intelligent coordination of these subsystems enhances overall performance, utilizing network flow theory to identify superior performance metrics compared to non-intelligent configurations. Finally, we outline promising future research directions, emphasizing the development of formal models for cyber-physical networks of systems and the rigorous verification of their safety and security properties. These models must extend beyond traditional approaches to effectively represent intelligent entities embedded in the network. To achieve this, the paper proposes a novel abstraction for cyber-physical systems featuring bounded rationality alongside their more prevalent counterparts, which assume omniscience. We argue that the interaction between these two system types constitutes a pressing and under-explored research challenge. Specifically, we illustrate how this problem can be modeled as a two-player game between an intelligent agent and a cyber-physical system, which may either act as an intelligent player or function as an open-loop controller. In both scenarios, we prove that standard solution techniques fail to guarantee the existence of equilibria. Consequently, we suggest that new methodologies are required to address such issues, and we introduce a promising game-theoretic approach that has emerged in recent years to resolve this challenge. This framework has been successfully applied to various networked systems, including supply chains, power grids, and transportation networks. Finally, we argue that cyber-physical systems must be integrated into such games to more accurately reflect real-world scenarios. To conclude, we emphasize that cyber-physical systems will play a pivotal role in future research, as they are poised to enable the next generation of cyber-intelligent networks. These systems will facilitate the formal modeling, analysis, and verification of interactions between networked systems and the intelligent entities embedded within them. Additionally, we note that cyber-physical systems offer a promising avenue for investigating other emerging research problems, such as the safety and security of intelligent networks. In this regard, we argue that cyber-physical systems will serve as a fertile ground for advancing research into these and other emerging challenges. This study introduces MAPPIES, a novel framework designed to calculate the emission energy flux of ions and electrons that have undergone inverse external-Compton scattering (ICSC) from relativistic astrophysical photon fields. By incorporating partial polarization of both the photon field and the beam particles, MAPPIES enables the investigation of the ultraviolet (UV) and soft X-ray excess observed in the spectra of active galactic nuclei (AGN) and blazars. Utilizing MAPPIES, we conducted a series of Monte-Carlo simulations to model the ICSC process responsible for generating this excess radiation in blazar spectra. Our results indicate that the UV/soft X-ray excess can be effectively explained by electrons within the Lorentz factor range of $\gamma_e\sim 10^2-10^3$. Furthermore, we examined the impact of photon polarization on the ICSC process and found that the resulting radiation flux is approximately 10% higher when the polarization vectors of the photon field and the particle beam are parallel. Finally, we demonstrated that the MAPPIES framework can be extended to account for the polarization of the emitted radiation. These findings suggest that our approach offers a viable mechanism for the ICSC process driving the UV/soft X-ray excess in blazar spectra. Future research will focus on applying the MAPPIES framework to non-blazar sources, such as the Sun and magnetospheres, to further explore the effects of partial polarization on ICSC. We introduce a general framework for extending functions analytically across complex domains. This approach is grounded in a new type of polynomial constructed from monomials, where the coefficients are determined variationally to ensure the extension matches all derivatives up to a specified order at discrete points in both real and complex spaces. By formulating a least-squares objective function and deriving analytic expressions for the polynomial coefficients based on monomial values at these points, the new representation can be evaluated at target points through the solution of a simplified linear system. We demonstrate applications of this method for the analytic extension of multivariate real functions into the complex domain, achieving high-order accuracy. Furthermore, the technique offers implicit smoothing of the extension, which proves particularly beneficial for multivariate functions exhibiting discontinuities or singularities within the complex region. We also discuss key theoretical properties of this approach and its potential for creating new numerical algorithms. Finally, numerical experiments illustrate the benefits of this technique for functions with various characteristics in both real and complex spaces, including those with discontinuities or singularities in the complex plane. These examples confirm that high-order accuracy is attainable for functions of one or more variables. We present a quantum detector designed to identify an unknown, n-qubit symmetric pure state. For the case of n-qubits, the total Hilbert space decomposes into subspaces of distinct dimensions; these specific dimensions serve as the primary classification criteria for symmetric states of arbitrary qubit counts. Leveraging this criterion, we introduce a quantum detector consisting of network operators that map multiple qubits into a single qubit. This apparatus classifies the input state by measuring the probability distribution across its output qubits. The design relies on universal polynomials that apply across all quantum systems. Additionally, we establish that the detector requires the minimum number of quantum detectors and network operators necessary for any symmetric multi-qubit state. Finally, the paper explores the extension of this detector to mixed symmetric states. Through this work, we demonstrate that significant information about a quantum state can be extracted using a minimal quantity of quantum resources. The proposed method offers a potential route for constructing a comprehensive detector for arbitrary quantum states, with applications in quantum error correction and circuit synthesis. Baryon production is analyzed within the quantized fragmentation framework of a QCD string, incorporating magnetic helical fluctuations. The analysis begins with monopoles, extending previous dimer and trimer studies to quark baryons. Results indicate that the probability of finding a baryon increases with the number of pre-existing quarks in the vacuum. Furthermore, the magnetic helical nature of the QCD string significantly enhances baryon formation, with the degree of enhancement governed by the B-field's critical electric analog. These theoretical predictions align with recent experimental observations. Additionally, the study confirms that magnetic baryons can be identified through their mass spectra and emphasizes the critical role of multi-particle effects in the quantum fragmentation of QCD strings. Finally, the implications of these findings for future research are examined. This work is based on the doctoral thesis of A. V. Ivanov.
