Centralized exchanges have a history of significant user fund losses due to exploits, fraud, and mismanagement. While blockchain-based distributed exchanges offer a solution by leveraging trustless, transparent, and permissionless features, they remain in the early adoption stage, necessitating a thorough analysis of their technical, operational, and user-centric challenges. This study employs a systematic mapping review to identify these challenges, assess their significance, and explore proposed solutions. Ultimately, this review aims to guide future research and development for blockchain-based distributed exchanges. Additionally, the paper introduces a new exchange design utilizing a novel "conditional swap" mechanism, which enhances usability, scalability, and trustworthiness. This mechanism facilitates faster and more efficient trades, particularly for large orders, without compromising security. We have implemented a prototype of this approach, demonstrating that it outperforms existing solutions in various scenarios. A comprehensive performance evaluation is provided to validate these claims. Finally, to ensure the practicality of this new design, we conducted an extensive cost analysis, examining both the financial expenses and computational overhead required for deployment. The results indicate that blockchain-based distributed exchanges can achieve deep order books and high throughput, comparable to traditional centralized exchanges, thereby offering a viable solution for crypto-trading. Furthermore, we have identified and analyzed the challenges associated with this new architecture. Given its advantages in terms of speed, efficiency, and trustlessness, we believe this approach will significantly contribute to the widespread adoption of blockchain-based distributed exchanges. Our code and detailed documentation are available at https://github.com/ashish-agarwal-1994/conditional-swap. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion on the limitations of this work and outlines several directions for future research. Specifically, we are currently investigating the trade-offs between different fulfillment strategies and their impacts on user experience, order book depth, and system performance. Additionally, we are exploring the viability of utilizing zero-knowledge proofs to maintain privacy regarding user addresses and transaction amounts. Lastly, we aim to further evaluate the system's performance under various network conditions and to analyze the associated development and deployment costs. These efforts will aid in better managing expectations regarding the adoption of blockchain-based distributed exchanges. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first work to comprehensively address the challenges of blockchain-based distributed exchanges through a systematic mapping review and to propose a new technical approach for enhancing their performance. We hope this work will inspire further research into these exchanges. In summary, this research demonstrates that blockchain-based distributed exchanges can now effectively address the trade-offs of efficiency, usability, and trust

The E-value, a metric for sensitivity analysis in missing data contexts, quantifies the maximum factor by which the original E-stimator's estimation can deviate due to adversarial missingness patterns. We demonstrate that incorporating the E-value into Bayesian model comparison facilitates sensitivity analysis. Furthermore, we illustrate an application of this methodology to missing data sensitivity analysis within a retrospective cohort study. Additionally, we provide E-value calculation code for R and Stan to support sensitivity analysis in models employing adversarial estimation. This approach is particularly advantageous when likelihood-based methods are impractical, as it allows for sensitivity analysis even when the analysis model is specified in more complex programming languages like Python or PyStan. The methodology is detailed in the paper accompanying this software release, where Python implementation code is also described. Additionally, sensitivity analysis considerations are addressed in an upcoming paper that details a C++ implementation of the Python code. We have also released a Python package that implements the Python code, although this package does not include the sensitivity analysis considerations. New versions of the software are available on the BayesEE GitHub repository. This work investigates the Laurent extension of a finite-type quantum surface by analyzing its symmetries. We demonstrate that its $q$-Riemann surface is of genus zero and incorporate a comprehensive collection of explicit generators for the algebra, drawn from recent research. Furthermore, we examine the subset of symmetries possessing finite trace and present a complete classification of all $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-module quantum surfaces within this category. The study concludes with an exploration of extensions involving higher-rank quantum groups. As applications, we detail the quantum torus and its Lie algebra as symmetries of specific quantum surfaces, noting that these structures were previously unexamined in existing literature. Additionally, we provide the first complete classification of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_3)$-module quantum surfaces. Finally, we address the issue of equivalence relations in quantum surface theory, a topic that has recently become a focal point of attention. This analysis includes a discussion of free quantum surfaces, which are conjectured to be the most fundamental building blocks of the theory. We also examine equivalence relations in the context of quantum tori and their Lie algebras, as well as those of quantum groups associated with higher-rank Lie algebras. Finally, we present an explicit example of a free quantum surface. Our methodology relies on examining the action of Lie algebra elements on quantum surfaces, a technique that has recently become a key focus of the field. We anticipate that the methods developed here will facilitate the construction of free quantum surfaces and free quantum groups. The convergence of the Internet of Vehicles (IoV) and Machine Learning (ML) holds immense promise for enhancing traffic management, enabling intelligent driving, and optimizing road conditions. However, IoV's inherent resource constraints and the risk of data leakage in centralized environments hinder ML's potential. Federated Learning (FL) addresses these challenges by enabling ML training on local devices without sharing raw data, while Blockchain (BCN) offers an immutable ledger for secure, transparent operations. This study presents a comprehensive systematic literature review of recent research on BCN-enhanced FL frameworks within the IoV context. The review covers four primary aspects: (1) the benefits of BCN and FL for IoV, (2) FL framework architectures supported by BCN, (3) FL implementation strategies utilizing BCN, and (4) FL challenges and future research directions involving BCN. By analyzing existing literature, the paper identifies key research gaps and proposes a future roadmap for this emerging field. Ultimately, this work serves as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners, offering insights and a clear roadmap to guide further investigation and innovation in BCN and FL-enabled IoV. To determine the contributions of long-lived and short-lived beauty hadrons to non-prompt mesons, an analysis was performed on the flavor composition of these particles. The results indicate that non-prompt mesons arise from both beauty and charm production. The study reports differential cross sections for both non-prompt and prompt mesons relative to transverse momentum and rapidity, as well as the relative beauty fraction ($f_b$) within the kinematic range of $2<p_{\rm T}<7$ GeV/$c$ and $2.0<y<2.5$. Ratios of non-prompt to prompt mesons were also calculated for $p_{\rm T}>15$ GeV/$c$ across the three rapidity regions: $-2<y<-1$, $-1<y<2$, and $2<y<3$. The Roadmap for Superconducting Quantum Technologies at the National Science Foundation's National Science and Technology Council identifies a critical need for a superconducting quantum computer system capable of cooling 200+ qubits below 20 mK. To address this, Fermilab, in collaboration with the Pennsylvania State University and the University of Maryland, is developing a specialized dilution refrigerator designed for quantum computing. This system aims to support a quantum processor with 200+ qubits, achieving an efficiency exceeding 200 mK/W at 4 K and reaching temperatures below 20 mK. This paper outlines the design and engineering specifications of the cryogenic infrastructure required to achieve these objectives. The proposed appliance will facilitate large-scale superconducting quantum computing research at the Quantum Science Center. A prototype, intended to support up to 64 qubits, is scheduled for installation at the University of Maryland in 2022. The full system, supporting 200 qubits, is planned for deployment in 2024. We anticipate delivering a functional quantum processor cooling system that meets the QSC's requirements for large-scale superconducting quantum computing within three years. This study examines the application of Python cryptography in the wild, specifically within projects on GitHub, PyPI, and Gitee. Due to Python's well-known vulnerabilities, our analysis aims to identify common misuses and offer guidance on avoiding them. By leveraging extensive experience with Python, we detected 1,000 projects exhibiting at least one of five distinct configurations across three categories: elliptic curve misuses, salting errors, and hash function misuses. To assist developers in writing more secure code, we also provide a set of security checklists. Finally, we outline several potential directions for future research. This work serves as a valuable resource for developers seeking to understand Python crypto security more deeply and for researchers exploring related topics. To our knowledge, this represents the first research effort dedicated to analyzing Python cryptographic implementations on these platforms. The datasets used in this study can be accessed at: https://drive.google.

This paper introduces a robust, automatic tagging system for vast collections of images depicting urban settings. Our approach relies on a voting-based taxonomy that aggregates detections from multiple image encoders, ranging from small to large models. While individual encoders may struggle with significant errors when operating in isolation, a consensus formed by combining their voting vectors allows for robust and accurate tagging. The framework is straightforward to implement and can be integrated with any tagging architecture. To validate our method, we employed a detector ensemble featuring a pre-trained, state-of-the-art model alongside two larger detectors trained from scratch on a substantial dataset. Our results demonstrate that this configuration effectively tags 100 classes within the i2b2-urban dataset (comprising 100,000 images) and 200 classes in the MSRC dataset (comprising 2,000 images). Furthermore, we achieved an average accuracy of 85.7% on the Flickr-FacesDB dataset, which contains 5,179 images across 170 celebrity classes. Finally, we show that our method enables the training of larger detectors with superior performance by requiring only a fraction of the labeled data. This study addresses sparse signal recovery, a critical challenge in numerous applications. The most prevalent method for achieving this involves minimizing the $\ell_1$-norm of the signal. However, we contend that this approach enforces uniform sparsity, as it applies identical penalties to all signal components. To address this limitation, we propose an alternative framework for nonuniform sparse recovery. This framework integrates multiple individual sparsity constraints, each tailored to a specific subset of coefficients, by employing a proximal average operator to combine them. We demonstrate the theoretical equivalence between minimizing the proximal average of sparsity constraints and minimizing a carefully constructed nonconvex penalty function. Leveraging this equivalence, we develop a novel neural network architecture named NuSPAN, designed to learn the optimal sparsity groups for reconstructing signals via deep learning. Numerical experiments confirm that NuSPAN significantly surpasses existing learning-based recovery algorithms. Furthermore, we apply NuSPAN to seismic reflectivity inversion, a method that enhances the quality of synthetic seismic data. Finally, we demonstrate how NuSPAN can be integrated with a deep learning network to perform joint seismic data inversion and classification. All source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1994/NuSPAN. Additionally, a video showcasing our application to seismic data inversion is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1122222222. Future research will focus on extending NuSPAN to handle coupled sparsity constraints. Our work is available under a Creative Commons Zero (CC0) license. This paper presents non-continuous integrability theory originally developed by the second author. It introduces a broad class of non-continuous integrals designed to address the specific needs of non-autonomous differential equations and to integrate functions defined on the extended real line $\overline{\mathbb{R}} := (-\infty, \infty]$. Among other achievements, this approach enables the construction of solutions to non-autonomous differential equations via maximal integrals and facilitates the calculation of the limit semigroup associated with a non-autonomous vector field through the calculation semigroup. Additionally, we have initiated an investigation into non-continuous Riemann-Stieltjes integrability, a topic reserved for future research. This study relies on two theorems: the first asserts that a function is non-continuous integrable with respect to a continuous function if and only if it is Lebesgue integrable with respect to the square of that continuous function; the second applies to continuous functions on $[0, \infty)$ taking values in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$, stating that they are non-continuous integrable with respect to a continuous function on $[0, \infty)$ taking values in $[0, \infty)$ if and only if they are Lebesgue integrable with respect to that function and their integrals converge. These findings form the foundation for the theory of non-autonomous differential equations, which we will explore in our upcoming research. The paper includes several examples illustrating the application of non-continuous integrability. Furthermore, the work incorporates historical notes on the evolution of the concept of a Riemann integral and its extensions.

Surface error correction is a crucial method for achieving fault-tolerant quantum computing by actively reducing errors in multi-qubit operations, yet it demands substantial hardware resources, including numerous ancilla qubits and extensive control circuitry. This study introduces a novel surface error correction approach that significantly lowers hardware demands by utilizing hidden inverse gates to eliminate errors following two-qubit operations. The proposed protocol employs the framework of "hidden inverse" theory to design an efficient method for error reduction and mitigation in superconducting quantum devices. By integrating these hidden inverse protocols with quantum circuits, an effective error-correcting mechanism is achieved that avoids the need for additional hardware. Using numerical density matrix simulations, the performance of various error-correcting schemes was evaluated, with results indicating that the hidden inverse protocol can substantially lower error rates in superconducting devices. Furthermore, the protocol is compatible with existing error correction techniques, such as the Shor code, to achieve low overall error rates. These findings demonstrate that implementing surface error correction via hidden inverse protocols offers a viable strategy for error mitigation in superconducting quantum hardware. Additionally, the research code is accessible at https://github.com/Chenchen-chenchen/QEC-by-hidden-inverse. Finally, the code is being integrated into educational curricula to facilitate the training of a new generation of quantum scientists. The study investigates spatial extremes in marine environments, which frequently exhibit multivariate natures. A key challenge involves predicting the joint occurrence of multiple significant events, known as conditional extremes. To address this, we propose a multivariate spatial conditional extremes (Multivariate SpCE) model. This framework combines a multivariate Gaussian copula with a Vine copula and incorporates a multivariate latent process to capture dependencies and spatial-temporal correlations. The multivariate latent process is further enhanced by an autoregressive latent factor model designed for multivariate spatial data. To facilitate efficient simulation, the latent process is reparameterized into a multi-layered structure, alongside the development of a new algorithm for drawing samples from the multivariate latent process. Validation is demonstrated through case studies of extreme sea surface wind speeds in the North Sea. The results show that the proposed model outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. Additionally, the model displays strong performance in forecasting extreme conditions within the North Sea and the Pacific Ocean. Finally, the framework is versatile and can be readily adapted for other regions or variables. These outcomes underscore the model's potential for a wide range of applications in marine environments. The source code is publicly accessible at: https://github.com/ChenchenLi1993/Multivariate-SpCE. Current text encoders in vision-language models rely on large-scale image-text pairs, resulting in descriptions that lack visual specificity and fail to capture the full range of object attributes. To address this gap, we introduce VT-Texts, a novel dataset comprising visual-directed descriptions generated by fine-tuning pre-trained large language models (GPT-3.5) on image captioning data. These texts are specifically oriented toward the visual domain to enhance fine-grained attribute representation. Our findings indicate that VT-Texts effectively boosts the performance of existing open-set vision-language models on standard benchmark classification tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that integrating VT-Texts with various pre-trained LLMs yields superior VT-CLIP models compared to using either component independently. Finally, we explore the application of VT-CLIP in image retrieval, highlighting its potential to deliver more precise and relevant results. Additionally, we release an open-source implementation to foster future research and development in this area. Our code and data can be accessed at https://github.com/ChenYi-1999/VT-CLIP. This paper introduces a novel operator transition approach designed to address the transition problem in the presence of noise. The transition problem seeks the most probable path connecting two quantum operators, a concept that extends the single-path optimization framework originally formulated by Mandelstam and 't Hooft. We introduce the generalized noisy transition problem, which integrates both Mandelstam--'t Hooft transitions and the constraints imposed by noise. To solve this, we develop the generalized noisy transition (GNT) equation, a first-order differential transition equation applicable to arbitrary quantum operators. This equation generates the "thickened" operator path that represents the most probable transition route. Furthermore, we examine the optical parametric oscillator as a case study to demonstrate the application of the GNT equation. Our findings indicate that noise significantly impacts the operator path, causing the transition to occur over a broader range of spacetime. We anticipate that the methods presented here will facilitate the investigation of operator paths in diverse quantum systems. Additionally, the transition of Heisenberg algebra generators derived from this method holds specific utility in quantum field theory. Future research will focus on advancing these applications. Image annotations represent essential data in the fields of radiology and pathology, encompassing both expert-generated outputs, such as segmentation masks and bounding boxes, and those produced by machine intelligence algorithms. These data facilitate critical downstream applications, including the evaluation of new models and the integration of AI into clinical workflows. However, the lack of standardization in data formats and exchange protocols has led to fragmented tooling and incompatible software. To address this, we present highdicom, a Python library that offers a standard format and API for creating and manipulating image annotations. Powered by the DICOM PS3.10 standard, highdicom enables the direct generation of DICOM instances and abstract layer representations for annotated images. It also supports the conversion of annotations from other common formats like TIFF and QCIF and provides validation tools to ensure annotation integrity. Currently, pathologists and radiologists utilize disparate tools that hinder collaboration and impede the development of AI in these domains. By offering a unified solution for the creation, manipulation, and standardization of image annotations, highdicom facilitates interoperability and collaboration across the field. The library is freely accessible at https://pypi.org/project/highdicom/. Its source code and documentation are hosted at https://github.com/medical-imaging-decision-support/highdicom. Further details regarding its usage can be found in our tutorial at https://medicinal-imaging-decision-support.github.io/highdicom/. We demonstrate its application by developing annotation visualization plugins for popular visualization libraries. Additionally, we illustrate how to streamline the development of machine learning models for annotated images using highdicom in conjunction with the pydicom and monai libraries. The source code for these examples is available at https://github.com/medicinal-imaging-decision-support/highdicom/tree/master/examples. The documentation for these examples can be accessed at https://medicinal-imaging-decision-support.github.io/highdicom/. Furthermore, the gravitational Noether charge adheres to the first law of thermodynamics at the horizon, yielding the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy for non-extremal Kerr and Kerr-Newman black holes. These outcomes validate this approach as a viable alternative to holographic methods for calculating black hole entropy. While this result is not unique, it represents the sole boundary term consistent with the first law. Consequently, it fails to contribute to the non-conserving part of the Smarr formula for Kerr and Kerr-Newman black holes, distinguishing it from the area term. Current deep learning approaches that model DNA sequences typically rely on features derived from established biological knowledge. This study employs an unsupervised embedding technique to automatically capture DNA sequence features, demonstrating its effectiveness across multiple applications. First, we construct a DNA language model using these unsupervised embeddings and contrast the findings with a one-hot encoding baseline. Second, we apply the embeddings to a gene promoter region analysis task, showing that they facilitate the discovery of new regulatory elements. Our results indicate that the proposed unsupervised method yields superior performance compared to the baseline in all evaluated scenarios. The implementation can be accessed at https://github.com/taehyung-lee/Unsupervised-DNA-Embedding. Furthermore, the identified regulatory elements are expected to offer valuable insights for future investigations into gene regulation mechanisms. Finally, we provide a user-friendly interface accessible at https://dna-embedding.netlify.app/ to demonstrate the system's capabilities. The metal-insulator transition (MIT) in V$_2$O$_3$ has been extensively studied due to its significant electronic and magnetic shifts, as well as its utility in developing ultrafast memory devices and neuromorphic computing. In this study, we synthesized V$_2$O$_3$ films via molecular beam epitaxy on c-plane Al$_2$O$_3$ and examined their electronic and magnetic characteristics as a function of thickness. Our findings indicate that the surface-modified MIT state in these thin films differs from the bulk material, exhibiting a more pronounced insulating phase. Furthermore, we observed that surface oxygenation can effectively reverse this MIT. These results offer valuable insights into the mechanisms driving the MIT in vanadates and may inform the design of novel materials for next-generation technologies. Finally, our observations regarding the MIT in thin films are consistent with first-principles calculations. To support reproducibility, we have made our data accessible through a public repository. This paper presents a systematic method for transforming Poisson structures into a canonical form introduced by F. R. Tang and B. Zhang. Such canonical transformations facilitate the computation of quadratic Casimir invariants and allow for the visualization of the local geometry of the dual space. The approach is particularly applicable to finite-dimensional Lie algebras, particularly those defined by Frobenius Lie triples. As a demonstration, the paper derives the canonical forms for specific co-adjoint orbit Lie algebras, including $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ and $\mathfrak{so}(5)$. Additionally, the method is extended to infinite-dimensional algebras, with a specific focus on the rigid body motion of an ellipsoid within a fluid. This canonical form is demonstrated to be highly effective for a variational principle involving the Euler-Arnold equations alongside Euler-Lagrange equations. The paper concludes by deriving the canonical equations from the Clebsch variational principle, which yields a system of first-order ordinary differential equations. Finally, the application of these canonical equations to specific co-adjoint orbit Lie algebras is illustrated. Notably, the canonical equations on these Lie algebras are shown to correspond to the Euler-Lagrange equations on an associated fiber bundle. Furthermore, the canonical form enables the explicit construction of a maximal integral of motion, which is utilized to derive finite-type solutions for the rigid body's motion in the fluid. This approach offers a new perspective on the finite-time exact integrability issue regarding the rigid body's motion in a fluid. The work begins by reviewing the classical Lie-Poisson structure on a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ and its associated quadratic Casimir invariants. It then details the derivation of the canonical form and applies these findings to the $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ and $\mathfrak{so}(5)$ algebras. Subsequently, the Frobenius Lie algebra is examined, followed by an analysis of an infinite-dimensional Lie algebra. Finally, the paper investigates the Lie-Poisson structure on a direct sum of Lie algebras $\mathfrak{g} \oplus \mathfrak{h}$, where $\mathfrak{g}$ represents the Lie algebra of the symmetry group acting on a Riemannian manifold $M$, and $\mathfrak{h}$ represents the Lie algebra of a fluid. This section details the derivation of canonical forms for rigid body motion equations using both classical and fluid Lie-Poisson structures.

We present the final results of a search for planetary anomalies in 2018 sub-subfields from the KMTNet Planet Survey. This study covers four sub-subfields: N10, N11, N12, and N13, which were the only ones not previously analyzed. We identified 11 new planetary candidates, including six transiting systems and five single-transiting planets. Two of these are likely single planets, while the remaining five probably represent long-period members of multi-planet systems. Additionally, we report on four previously detected anomalies: two likely planets and two possibly planetary. We also discuss a candidate anomaly that is likely an eclipsing binary rather than planetary in nature. The eight anomalies confirmed as likely planets have radii ranging from $R_p = 1.04 - 1.94 R_\oplus$ and periods between $P = 1.8 - 11.4$ days. Among the six transiting candidates, five are consistent with existing radius-period relations, while one, with a radius of $R_p = 1.94 R_\oplus$ and period of $P = 1.8$ days, appears to be an inflated planet. The six multi-period candidates exhibit periods spanning $P = 1.8 - 11.4$ days and semi-major axes from $a = 0.02 - 0.06$ au. We compare our findings with prior KMTNet sub-subfield anomaly searches and discuss the implications of these results for exoplanet statistics. These findings support the development of a new fully-implicit scheme featuring a linearly-implicit treatment of the non-linear terms. Specifically, a novel time-step controller is introduced to dynamically adapt the time-step during simulations, thereby enhancing the efficiency of existing fully-implicit algorithms. The proposed scheme is rigorously analyzed regarding its consistency, stability, and convergence, with numerical experiments provided to validate these theoretical results. Furthermore, the potential of this linearly-implicit approach for other parameter-dependent conservation laws is explored, and an outline of an optimal fully-implicit scheme is presented as a direction for future research. Finally, preliminary discussions outline a pathway to a more comprehensive and rigorous analysis of the proposed linearly-implicit scheme. This study examines machine learning models for predicting the default status of a loan portfolio, utilizing 242 features derived from the NPL dataset. Various models, including logistic regression, random forest, and gradient boosting, were evaluated to determine their optimal fit. Feature importance analysis was conducted to identify the most influential variables and those contributing minimally to the target variable. Ultimately, a XGBoost classifier achieved the highest accuracy, reaching 99.15%. During Step 2, we split the dataset into training and testing sets, with optional stratification. Step 3 involved data visualization, including correlation analysis and the impact of missing values. Step 4 addressed missing values by imputing them using mean and median methods. Finally, in Step 5, we developed a logistic regression model, while also exploring random forest and gradient boosting approaches. A comprehensive evaluation followed, comparing multiple algorithms such as logistic regression, random forest, KNN, SVM, and XGBoost. Additionally, we conducted random forest feature importance analysis and performed model selection based on feature importance using KNN and XGBoost classifiers. In the final step, we applied KNN and XGBoost classifiers, selected the best model, and analyzed feature importance for both classifiers. Finally, we compared the KNN and XGBoost models, selected the final model, and presented the final results.

Dyck trails connect two specific corners within a Young diagram of shape $\lambda$, where $\lambda_1 \leq n-1$. A Dyck sphere $D(\lambda)$ is formed by the union of all such trails; the resulting object is a graph-manifold, a type of combinatorial manifold. The chromatic symmetric function $CS(t_\lambda)$ for a Dyck sphere is defined as the sum of the chromatic weights of all valid colorings. This paper establishes that $CS(t_\lambda)(q)$ acts as the generating function for counting $k$-tuples of cells within a specific region of the diagram $\lambda$, subject to constraints where cells in a designated subset $\Omega$ cannot share a chromatic neighbor. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for any partition $\lambda$, the generating function for $k \times 1$ sub-configurations in the diagram—where the final column is excluded and cells in a specific subset $\Omega$ are excluded—is a multiple of $CS(t_\lambda)(q)$. These findings extend the principles of $q$-rook theory to the realm of combinatorial manifolds. Additional results include the $t$-positivity of $CS(t_\lambda)$, the unimodality of $CS(t_\lambda)(q)$, and the determination of the location of its first peak. Additional theorems involve an inverse basis analogous to the fundamental symmetric function basis for elementary symmetric functions, an expansion utilizing new invariants derived from the Poincaré polynomial of the boundary of the Dyck sphere, and an interpretation of $CS(t_\lambda)$ through the cohomology of the space of all colorings. Finally, the boundary of the Dyck sphere is interpreted as a $q$-manifold, and its Poincaré polynomial is shown to correspond to the coefficient of $q$ within the chromatic symmetric function of the Dyck sphere. The escalating global threat of the COVID-19 pandemic has created an urgent need for rapid, accurate, and cost-effective diagnostic tools to mitigate its severe health and socioeconomic impacts. While Computed Tomography (CT) scans offer a reliable method for detecting the virus, the high volume of data generated necessitates advanced computational techniques for analysis. This study introduces a two-stage Time-Distributed Capsule Network (TD-CDU) designed for human-level COVID-19 detection using Low-Dose (LD) CT scans. In this framework, a primary TD-CDU network extracts and classifies features from individual CT slices, while a secondary TD-CDU network aggregates these features to make a final diagnosis. The proposed model was evaluated against three established baselines: ResNet50, a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), and a Random Forest (RF) model. Experimental results demonstrate that the two-stage network significantly surpasses all baseline approaches, achieving an accuracy of 98.50%. Furthermore, the robustness of the network is confirmed by its superior performance on a test dataset containing mixed patient data. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1998/Two-stage-TD-CDU. This study examines the distribution of active and inactive active satellites in low-Earth orbit across specific altitude and inclination ranges. It introduces a spherical shell-based spatial distribution model, which represents low-Earth orbit as stacked spherical shells corresponding to altitude and inclination. The research validates this model using a catalog of 1,030 active satellites from 2018 and compares the results of a simulation involving 106,000 satellites against both the 2018 data and existing literature. The findings indicate that the size of spherical shells and inter-satellite distances are critical factors in accurately predicting satellite distribution. The outcomes demonstrate that the proposed model can effectively estimate satellite distributions and support space situational awareness and traffic management. Furthermore, the study offers insights into potential future distribution patterns, aiding in the planning of satellite constellations and the design of ground-based observation systems. Finally, the paper addresses the challenges and opportunities for achieving sustainable low-Earth orbit operations. This paper introduces an algorithm designed to derive exact analytic formulas for the expected value, variance, and the fourth central moment of the sample correlation coefficient ($r$) across all possible arrangements of data within a rectangular grid. Since $r$ is frequently employed to quantify the linear dependence between two random variables, its distribution is critical for hypothesis testing and confidence interval estimation. However, because the distribution of $r$ lacks a simple closed-form expression, calculating these theoretical moments has historically been hindered. While approximations exist for continuous domains, this work focuses on the discrete domain of integer pairs $(x,y)$. Our approach generates the analytic expressions for these moments by systematically enumerating all possible data arrangements and determining the corresponding values of $r$ through a recursive, bottom-up search algorithm implemented in C++. These formulas are then validated using Monte Carlo simulations, which demonstrate convergence to the same results via the simulated average, variance, and fourth central moment of the generated data. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first derivation of exact analytic formulas for the first four moments of the sample correlation distribution over a discrete domain. The resulting formulas are provided in the supplementary material, where they are also implemented in Python for accessibility. We illustrate their utility with two examples: first, recovering the known analytic formula for $r$ when data is uniformly distributed over the grid; and second, showing convergence to the expected moments by applying the formulas to a dataset where $(x,y)$ pairs follow a Gaussian distribution. These outcomes serve as a proof of concept for analyzing $r$ under a Gaussian distribution of the pairs. Furthermore, the Python code utilized in this study is released as open-source under a permissive license. We conclude that these formulas provide a valuable theoretical foundation for comprehending the properties of the sample correlation distribution over a discrete domain. Future research will aim to extend this framework to other distributions, such as the uniform distribution, and to multivariate settings involving more than two variables. Additionally, we plan to investigate the extension of these formulas to the continuous domain, where they would yield analytic expressions for moments over the interval $[a,b]$. This would enable the calculation of theoretical moments for the sample correlation of two independent random variables drawn from the uniform distribution over $[a,b]$. Finally, we anticipate that these formulas will find applications in various fields, including image processing, econometrics, and machine learning. This text outlines the S-matrix approach's potential to generalise gravity and beyond, drawing from a talk at the 50th Solvay Conference on Physics. The S-matrix framework offers a profound physical perspective on quantum field theory (QFT), positing that the fundamental framework of QFT emerges from an even more elementary level grounded in relativistic causality and unitarity. The S-matrix method demonstrates how the complex structure of QFT can be derived from these basic principles. In this narrative, space and time are not fundamental concepts but instead arise from a more primitive domain where only physical observables—specifically future scattering amplitudes—exist. Consequently, the primary objective is to identify constraints on these observables by enforcing relativistic causality and unitarity. The discussion will examine how this perspective can be extended to include generalised gravity and higher-spin fields. Furthermore, it will outline an ongoing effort to formulate a non-perturbative gravity theory using the S-matrix framework, with the talk addressing both its promising achievements and its significant challenges. The fundamental objects of this proposed theory are on-shell states representing two-graviton bound states, which are conjectured to be massless; their properties are believed to be captured by a single function known as the "worldsheet amplitude." This amplitude is proposed to be equivalent to a string theory amplitude on a curved background, where strings propagate on a two-dimensional sheet defined by null-separated points in spacetime. The talk will outline the arguments supporting this proposal and the difficulties encountered in the process. Finally, it will suggest a possible future direction for the S-matrix approach, specifically the construction of a two-dimensional conformal field theory on the complex plane. While this may seem unrelated, it is deeply connected to the earlier discussion through the correspondence between bound states and strings. Ultimately, the S-matrix framework is viewed as a new path toward quantum gravity. However, it is crucial to acknowledge that we are still in the early stages of this journey, and many aspects remain unclear. Therefore, the talk aims to provide a broad overview of current progress and to inspire further contributions to this endeavor. **Keywords:** String Theory, Quantum Field Theory, Quantum Gravity. **MSC Codes:** 81T15, 81T18, 81T10, 81T13, 81T25, 81T20, 81T25, 81T30, 81T37,

This study addresses a smooth, linear control system representing the Navier-Stokes equations, defined by low Reynolds number, within a bounded domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ where $n=2,3$. The domain features a smooth boundary and employs Dirichlet boundary conditions. We introduce a finite-dimensional feedback control mechanism localized within a critical sub-domain $\omega \subset \Omega$, excluding the boundary. This mechanism utilizes measurements of the Navier-Stokes velocity field taken inside $\omega$. Our primary finding is that this feedback control can uniform stabilize the Navier-Stokes system, subject to appropriate initial conditions, against any square-integrable external force. This stabilization is achieved without imposing restrictions on the feedback gain or the control dimension, and it avoids the need for a stabilization zone extending to the boundary. Furthermore, our approach utilizes a control region that is disjoint from the measurement region. These results hold for $L^q$-based Sobolev and Besov spaces. Specifically, for the 2D case, we establish uniform stabilization in $L^q(\Omega)$ for any $q \in [1, \infty)$; in 3D, we provide results for $L^q(\Omega)$ where $q \in [1, \infty)$ regarding energy norms and for $L^q(\nabla) \subset L^2$ regarding kinetic energy norms. Additionally, we extend these findings to scenarios involving non-homogeneous boundary conditions. Finally, we demonstrate the uniform stabilizability of a finite-dimensional open-loop system that is 0-differential with respect to space. These contributions are derived from a novel technique for regularizing the Navier-Stokes equations. This technique is also applicable to other Navier-type equations, such as the heat equation. Our methodology is constructive and enables the design of the feedback control. We also examine the robustness of these results by analyzing the uniform stabilization of a perturbed system. The perturbation includes errors from velocity measurements and potential errors in the domain where both measurement and control are located. We demonstrate that, provided the measurement error is sufficiently small, robust feedback stabilization remains achievable. This is accomplished through an adaptive, extended, and generalized feedback control region that encompasses both the measurement and control areas. Consequently, robustness is ensured even when either the control or measurement region lies on the boundary. Our results are also valid for unbounded domains, including $\mathbb{R}^n$ and half-spaces. In these settings

Although the Open Source English Wikipedia represents one of the largest open-source encyclopedias, it remains inaccessible to users who do not speak English. To address this limitation, we present the LitMind Lexicon Dictionary, an innovative real-time translation system that enables non-English speakers to access English dictionary definitions in their native languages. As a natural language processing tool, the Lexicon integrates three core components: (1) a definition text generator, (2) a multilingual word embedding model, and (3) a sentence-level cross-lingual semantic matching algorithm. This architecture facilitates precise mapping between a source word in the target language and a English query word, followed by accurate matching of the corresponding definition. We assess the Lexicon's performance using Definition Exact Match (DEM) and Definition Semantic Similarity (DSS) metrics, comparing it against established baselines. Experimental results demonstrate that the Lexicon achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, with DEM scores of 82.2% and 76.0% for single-word and phrase queries, respectively, and DSS scores of 70.5% and 68.0% for single-word and phrase queries. The system's source code and interface are publicly available at https://github.com/litmind/lexicon. By leveraging advanced NLP techniques, the LitMind Lexicon supports educational and information dissemination activities, thereby fostering greater social inclusion. This work was partially funded by the Singapore Ministry of Education under the LitMind Research Partner grant. This paper appears in the proceedings of the 12th International Conference on Educational Data Mining. The full paper can be found here: https://github.com/litmind/lexicon. Recent efforts have sought to enhance the interpretability of black-box recommenders using local explainers, such as LIME-RS. However, the absence of evaluation metrics hinders our understanding of these methods' performance. This study introduces adherence and consistency as two key metrics for assessing the quality of generated explanations. We apply consistency to compare the quality of various LIME-RS variants, identifying an "early out" variant that delivers superior results with minimal effort. Additionally, we demonstrate the utility of the adherence metric in evaluating the impact of different feature selection strategies within the LIME-RS framework. Finally, to promote future research in explanation quality, we provide open access to a new benchmark designed for this purpose. This repository, which includes datasets, black-box recommenders, and our proposed evaluation metrics, is available at https://github.com/fernandocosta1996/explanation-quality-benchmark. The benchmark is hosted within the RecSys community. We invite the research community to explore this resource and contribute to the continued advancement of explainable recommendation. This work was developed in collaboration with the Explanable RecSys Research Group at the University of Surrey. Specifically, Francesco Montagnani and Nando Luis Silva, the group's principal investigators, provided valuable insights and guidance on this research. The group's broader objective is to advance the study of Explanable RecSys through both fundamental and applied research. For further information, visit www.explanablerecsys.net. We welcome collaboration; please contact us at info@explanablerecsys.net. The Fermi level in doped InAs, situated just above the conduction band edge, creates an electrostatic challenge when fabricating near-surface quantum wells. This issue causes significant band bending that pushes the band minimum away from the surface, thereby misaligning the quantum well. We demonstrate that applying an external gate voltage can counteract this pinning effect, restoring the band minimum to its proper position at the quantum well's intended depth. Furthermore, we analyze how this gate-induced band bending affects the quantum well's electronic structure. These findings are essential for the precise fabrication of near-surface quantum wells in high-mobility InAs heterostructures. Additionally, they hold relevance for designing new topological insulators and developing high-performance, low-temperature superconducting devices based on InAs. To achieve this, we utilize a combined approach of photoemission spectroscopy and first-principles calculations. Photoemission provides experimental data on the position of the band minimum, while theoretical calculations model the impact of gate voltage on electronic band structure. Our results indicate that a gate voltage of approximately 10^12 cm^-2 is sufficient to shift the band minimum back to the target quantum well location. These outcomes advance our understanding of the electronic properties essential for fabricating state-of-the-art low-temperature superconducting devices in doped InAs quantum wells. Additionally, we investigate the potential of InAs quantum wells to become topological superconductors when in contact with superconducting materials. To achieve this goal, we propose a strategy to raise the Fermi level toward the valence band. Our findings suggest that a heavy mass implantation technique could be an effective method to induce this shift. Our work provides a pathway for fabricating high-quality, low-temperature superconducting devices from doped InAs quantum wells and enhances our understanding of the electronic properties necessary for realizing topological superconductivity in these systems. Ultimately, these results pave the way for the next generation of quantum devices. This paper is based on the work of J. Krawczyk, M. Krawczyk, and A. L. Barker. This paper investigates how access to local inquiries enhances robustness in tabular data. Building on the work by Yang et al. (2021), we demonstrate that for any dataset with support size $n$, their local inquiry method can be adapted to necessitate only $\tilde{O}(n)$ samples, representing a substantial reduction from the original $\tilde{O}(n^2)$ requirement. Furthermore, we present an algorithm with access to local inquiries that achieves a sample complexity of $\tilde{\Omega}(n)$, proving that local inquiries can significantly boost robust learning efficiency in tabular settings. Finally, we extend the primary result of Yang et al. (2021) to high-dimensional data by introducing a novel local inquiry algorithm. Our approach achieves a sample complexity of $\tilde{O}(d^2)$, improving upon the previous $\tilde{O}(d^3)$ bound. We also establish a matching lower complexity of $\tilde{\Omega}(d^2)$ through a new application of the adversary method. Collectively, these findings indicate that local inquiries can enhance robust learning sample complexity from $\tilde{O}(d^3)$ to $\tilde{O}(d^2)$ for high-dimensional data. To our knowledge, this marks the first application of local inquiries to robust learning. Additionally, we explore a conceptually new variant of local inquiries designed for high-dimensional contexts, which supports our findings and may hold independent significance. Empirical results confirm that our methods are more sample-efficient than existing approaches. Finally, we examine how local inquiries can be leveraged to improve robust generalization in deep learning. By querying perturbations that maximize loss on unseen examples, we demonstrate that this approach can substantially improve the performance of large neural networks. This work paves the way for utilizing local inquiries in learning theory and machine learning engineering. Code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYang2021/LocalQuery. The source code for the high-dimensional extension can be found at https://github.com/ChenYang2021/LocalQuery/tree/high_dimension_extension. The corresponding implementation is available at https://github.com/ChenYang2021/LocalQuery/tree/explicit_adversary. Furthermore, our explicit adversary implementation is available at https://github.com/ChenYang2021/LocalQuery/tree/explicit_adversary. The examples supporting our claims can be accessed at https://github.com/ChenYang2021

This study introduces Fast Sinkhorn II, an approach that achieves both precision and efficiency by utilizing a collinear transport plan matrix. The algorithm operates at linear time complexity, parallelizes effectively, and delivers precise results without the need for arbitrary cutoff thresholds typical of approximate methods. By reformulating the classical iterative Sinkhorn algorithm into a vector form, we develop a novel matrix formulation for the OT problem that decomposes the transport cost matrix into five distinct components, allowing for optimized computation. This decomposition facilitates linear time complexity for data sets exhibiting specific geometric structures, such as spherical, toroidal, or graph surfaces. Furthermore, the proposed vector formulation is inherently parallel, making it well-suited for execution on GPU hardware. We validate the method's precision, efficiency, and hardware adaptability across various examples. Notably, we demonstrate how to calculate the precise optimal transport distance between two 32,768-point 3D point clouds in under a second. Additionally, the paper provides a comprehensive mathematical analysis of OT problems under linear time complexity. This analysis reveals that certain problems can be resolved with machine precision in linear time while maintaining polynomial space complexity, as the collinear matrix can be represented using $O(N)$ memory. This represents a significant advancement over current state-of-the-art techniques, which often trade off precision for time complexity or memory usage. Overall, this work establishes a new foundation for the efficient and precise computation of Optimal Transport. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/chenyixing2000/fast-sinkhorn-2.0. Keywords: Optimal Transport, Precise, Linear Time, Collinear Matrix, Fast Computation, Fast Sinkhorn. The young, active M dwarf AU Microscopii (AU Mic) hosts two confirmed planets, b and c. This study examines observations of AU Mic conducted during two X-ray flares to understand the star's extreme ultraviolet (EUV) and far-ultraviolet (FUV) variability, as these high-energy photons are critical for the atmospheric evolution of its planets. By analyzing EUV and FUV spectra taken during the flares and comparing them with archival X-ray data, we determined that FUV emission scales linearly with X-ray flux. Additionally, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of six years of FUV data to characterize the star's overall variability. We observed that FUV flux fluctuates by factors of 2 to 3 over timescales ranging from hours to years, with a mean variation of 1.5 times over six years. Furthermore, we identified a notable decline in FUV flux over this period, a finding supported by the 6-year X-ray light curve. Finally, we modeled the effects of these EUV and FUV variations on the atmospheres of planets b and c, concluding that both planets experience extreme fluctuations in high-energy irradiation. These results suggest that the atmospheres of AU Mic b and c are likely undergoing significant erosion. Future observations of AU Mic and its planets should prioritize monitoring high-energy fluxes, particularly when using the Hubble Space Telescope's Cosmic Origins Spectrograph. This study examines the dynamics of charged particles and beams interacting with both the vacuum and a resistive material medium, incorporating radiation reaction effects. The analysis demonstrates that the critical field for runaway electron motion is substantially lower in a medium than in a vacuum. Additionally, the paper explores the application of this theoretical framework to various practical scenarios, including radiation pumps, free electron lasers, and charged particle beams. These investigations reveal that charged particle dynamics within a material medium are inherently complex, necessitating numerical solutions to the governing equations. Consequently, the present work introduces a new, self-consistent analytical formalism, alongside a set of routines capable of solving the complex differential equations that describe particle motion in a medium under radiation reaction forces. This newly developed material-based radiation reaction code is applicable to any charged particle or beam, irrespective of its energy. The findings and code routines can be utilized to study particle behavior in diverse materials, such as those found in free-electron lasers, laser-plasma wakefield accelerators, and high-intensity laser-solid interactions. Furthermore, the study identifies a novel phenomenon where particles or beams entering a medium from a vacuum undergo abrupt deceleration and are "plugged" into the medium. This effect is driven by the charged particles' propensity for "runaway" motion when transitioning from the vacuum into the medium. The magnitude of this plug-in effect is contingent upon the specific material properties and the initial conditions of the particle or beam. Finally, this work establishes a foundation for future investigations into the complex interactions between charged particles, particle beams, and material media, all governed by radiation reaction forces. Such a foundation is essential for the proper interpretation of intricate experimental data and for the accurate modeling of material properties within the context of particle-radiation-matter interactions. Ultimately, this provides a comprehensive understanding of particle behavior in the presence of complex interactions with both vacuum and matter. These results are derived from a rigorous and comprehensive theoretical framework that accounts for radiation reaction forces, offering a unified understanding of particle behavior across all intensities, velocities, and energies. This framework is particularly significant for high-energy physics, astrophysics, and high-intensity laser-matter interactions. In classification tasks involving imbalanced datasets, the distribution of instances across different categories is highly uneven, often resulting in significant disparities between the most and least frequent classes. This imbalance can introduce bias into classification results. To address this, we introduce a novel classification approach that integrates the k-Nearest Neighbor (kNN) algorithm with resampling techniques, specifically upsampling and downsampling. The proposed method constructs multiple classifiers based on kNN by applying various resampling strategies to the original dataset. It subsequently identifies the best classifier by evaluating its performance on a hold-out set, a validation set, or by synthesizing performance metrics from both. Experimental results demonstrate that this method outperforms standard kNN classifiers and other existing techniques when dealing with imbalanced data. The source code is publicly accessible at: https://github.com/ChenchenLi1993/Closest-Neighbor-Classification. Future research will explore applying this method to real-world classification problems and investigating the optimal value of k. Additionally, the method's application in clustering will be considered. We present the second paper in a series, which reports on the discovery of 11 new quasars and 10 previously known bright quasars from the skyMapper DR3 quasar catalog. These objects were identified through photometric data, with their identities confirmed via spectroscopy. By integrating our findings with the first paper in this series, we have compiled a sample of 32 quasars with $i$-band magnitudes $i \leq 14.5$ and $i-z \leq 3.5$ within the skyMapper DR3 catalog. The average redshift for this sample is $\langle z \rangle = 2.6$, with a notably bright tail extending to $z \approx 6.5$. We have determined the redshift distribution for this group of 32 quasars and compared it against predictions from the Madau2019 and Choudhury2011 models. Additionally, we calculated the quasar luminosity function across the $i$-band magnitude range of 12 to 15.5, finding that the number density of the most luminous quasars ($M_i \leq -26.5$) is $1.1 \pm 0.2 \times 10^{-4} h^3 Mpc^{-3}$. This value aligns with results from other studies. We also present the $i$-band light curves for these 32 objects, with the most luminous quasar exhibiting a brightening rate of 0.004 mag/day. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the evolution of the bright end of the quasar luminosity function. Our sample of 32 quasars is now available for the community to utilize. The skyMapper DR3 catalog is renowned for its exceptional depth and completeness in identifying bright quasars, and we have demonstrated that it contains a sample of high-quality quasars surpassing those found in other surveys. This collection is particularly valuable for investigating the bright end of the quasar luminosity function and the early evolution of supermassive black holes. We have made the spectra of these 32 quasars publicly accessible. This research was conducted using the SkyMapper DR3 quasar catalog. We present an experimental investigation into charge tunneling between a quantum dot and a superconducting island using radio-frequency gate-sensing techniques. This approach allows for the real-time monitoring of both the island's capacitance and impedance. Our results reveal a strong coupling between the dot and the superconducting mode, characterized by a resonant enhancement in coupling strength that persists up to tens of millikelvins. This resonant increase in capacitance indicates that screening charges shift from the dot to the superconducting island, facilitating tunneling via a Cooper pair charge-transfer mechanism. Furthermore, we quantify the coupling strength using radio-frequency gate-sensing and compare it against a quantum chemical model that accounts for Cooper pair tunneling. This methodology is applicable to various systems, enabling the study of quantum interactions between disparate materials. Additionally, this approach establishes a foundation for developing high-fidelity gates between a semiconductor quantum dot and a superconducting island.

This research investigates contraction properties for entropy-admissible discontinuities in hyperbolic systems of conservation laws, aiming to establish a universal criterion for system contraction. We demonstrate that for arbitrary convex entropies, contraction holds if and only if the contractions among all entropy variables remain non-strict. Furthermore, within the class of strictly convex quadratic entropies, contraction is equivalent to the non-strict contraction of entropy variables associated with any single entropy. These findings enable the development of a systematic framework for analyzing contraction in nonlinear conservation law systems. To illustrate our methodology, we provide contraction criteria for a selection of prominent nonlinear models, including gas dynamics, water waves, traffic flow, and gas elasticity. Additionally, we examine contraction for nonstrictly hyperbolic systems by focusing on the shallow water system, which exhibits a transition from a strictly convex to a nonstrictly convex regime. Our analysis reveals that contraction for entropy-admissible entropy solutions of the nonstrictly convex shallow water system occurs precisely when the Mach number does not approach zero. Finally, we present a comprehensive and detailed verification of our contraction criteria using the computational software SUNDIALS. We have constructed a comprehensive database of well-tested contraction tests for numerous nonlinear conservation law systems, which is available for download. This resource facilitates the verification of our contraction analysis and may support researchers in validating their own contraction hypotheses. We anticipate that this methodology will serve as a valuable tool for contraction analysis in numerical methods for conservation law systems. Our findings are also intended to aid researchers in identifying contraction properties for the systems they model. We provide a general procedure to determine whether a given conservation law system satisfies the contraction criteria for either nonstrictly convex or arbitrary strictly convex cases. Finally, we outline an approach for constructing a contraction-preserving numerical scheme, specifically a finite volume method, applicable to both nonstrictly convex and arbitrary strictly convex contraction property cases. We conclude by presenting numerical examples of both the direct and inverse problems to illustrate the contraction behavior of our proposed numerical scheme. These examples encompass various two-dimensional systems, such as the Euler system, the entropy-driven Burgers system, and the Euler system adapted for nonstrictly convex cases. Our conclusions indicate that the proposed contraction-preserving numerical scheme is well-suited for shock-capturing simulations of conservation law systems. We believe this contribution will assist researchers in designing their own contraction-preserving numerical schemes. Additionally, we have made our code available for download to assist researchers in verifying their own contraction-preserving numerical methods. Our conclusion suggests that this code will be a valuable resource

Single-view 3D rendering aims to create a 3D scene from a solitary input image. Perpetual view generation focuses on producing novel views from unlimited angles based on these unconstrained single-view 3D representations. We introduce DiffDreamer, a new framework that leverages conditional diffusion models to achieve reliable single-view 3D perpetual generation. This approach integrates two key strategies: first, it employs a two-step generation process to enhance reliability, and second, it utilizes a two-stage training regimen to boost performance. Specifically, we first train a conditional diffusion model to produce high-quality 3D scenes, which subsequently guides a second model to generate 3D scenes conditioned on the initial generation. This two-step mechanism effectively mitigates the mode collapse frequently observed in diffusion-based 3D generators. To further improve results, the first stage is trained to generate 3D scenes with high-quality textures, whereas the second stage uses the latent code from the first stage as a conditional input to produce novel views. By combining these methods, DiffDreamer surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches on standard benchmarks, including the single-view 3D NeRF generation task on the COLOR360 dataset and the zero-shot 3D shape completion task on the ShapeNet dataset. The project can be accessed at https://github.com/1000x1000/DiffDreamer. Our code, pre-trained models, and tutorials are available at https://github.com/1000x1000/DiffDreamer. Networks are fundamental to the structure of our physical world, serving as the backbone for numerous physical and biological systems. While significant research has focused on controlling networked systems to achieve specific targets, networked process control remains an emerging field. This study introduces a straightforward, purely data-driven framework for predicting, optimizing, and controlling networked processes that relies solely on local observations. By utilizing a parsimonious Gaussian process model, the approach effectively captures the complex, nonlinear dynamics of the process. Furthermore, it employs a scalable strategy that requires only local information to derive system-wide control actions, thereby eliminating the need for full system dynamics or global network topology knowledge. The framework's efficacy is demonstrated through the control of a networked SIS epidemic model, where simulations reveal its ability to robustly suppress outbreaks in each community while significantly reducing both computational and communication costs. Additionally, the network's inherent structure is leveraged to further optimize control efforts. The example also highlights how local observation quality and communication costs influence network control performance. The framework's utility is further validated by successfully controlling a real-world network of 1,000 neurons in the visual cortex. The methods are implemented in Python and accessible via an open-source library. The proposed framework is anticipated to benefit various other networked processes, such as those found in power grids and water distribution networks. The method is detailed in our recent publication in arXiv (2105.05000). This work is led by Dr. Seyedeh Mahsa Ghafourian, who can be reached at s.ghafourian@tudelft.nl. Her upcoming dissertation will be titled "Data-driven control of networked processes." Her research focuses on developing data-driven techniques for the control, optimization, and design of networked systems, with a specific emphasis on neural networks. This study numerically examines the Rayleigh-Plateau instability affecting a liquid film on a solid cylinder, where surface tension drives the formation of droplets. The initial state involves a thin, uniform film with a small amplitude relative to the cylinder's circumference. Surface shear is modeled via a slip boundary condition, where the tangential stress within the liquid is proportional to the slip velocity across a thin shear layer at the interface with the outer cylinder. This setup simulates a thin liquid film on a wettable cylinder coated with a thin, slippery substance that itself slips against the parent cylinder. The analysis focuses on the initial growth rate of the most unstable mode and the slip-enhanced amplification of amplitude growth. Results indicate that the tangential stress in the outer cylinder significantly accelerates the growth rate when compared to the no-slip scenario. The slip enhancement factor for growth rate increases with both the slip (Knudsen) length and the shear viscosity ratio between the film and the parent cylinder. Furthermore, the slip-enhancement factor for amplitude growth over the initial perturbation period is governed by the slip length, the viscosity ratio, and the thickness ratio of the initial film. These findings suggest that the slip-enhanced growth rate can be over an order of magnitude greater than the no-slip case. These outcomes are interpreted as the combined effects of the shear-driven instability identified by Buggin et al. (2018) and the slip-induced growth mechanism described by Strittmatter et al. (2019). Finally, the influence of slip on the formation of droplets along a wettable cylinder is highlighted. These insights may be applicable to various thin liquid films on wettable cylindrical surfaces, such as liquid bridges on fibers or coating streams on rollers. Additionally, the numerical approach employed is versatile and can be adapted to other relevant scenarios. Finally, potential applications in microfluidic devices and fiber coating processes are explored. This work extends the research presented in Buggin, Strittmatter, and Thorne (2019). This study investigates the initial-boundary value problem for the Hunter-Saxton model within suitable Sobolev spaces. We establish local Lipschitz stability for this model in these same spaces. This result serves as a strong analogue to Cauchy problem Lipschitz stability in the homogeneous periodic setting on the circle, which was previously demonstrated by Bourgain and Nakanishi. Our approach relies on several key elements: a novel characterization of the Hunter-Saxton equation as a geodesic equation in Sobolev spaces, the property that the equation is completely integrable, the development of novel compactness methods within low-regularity Sobolev spaces, and the use of the trace theorem. These findings collectively enable us to prove the Lipschitz stability of the Hunter-Saxton model. Additionally, our proof provides an alternative derivation of the strong periodic result by Bourgain and Nakanishi. This achievement is made possible by a new characterization of the Hunter-Saxton equation utilizing a family of operators that preserve Sobolev norms. Finally, we demonstrate the uniqueness of the solution to the Hunter-Saxton model in low-regularity Sobolev spaces by employing a compactness argument grounded in the equation's complete integrability. This facilitates an extension of the Hunter-Saxton equation to a context involving measures rather than functions. Through a novel compactness method, we establish the well-posedness of this new model in $L^{\infty}$, thereby providing a complete picture of the Hunter-Saxton model across all low-regularity spaces. Furthermore, this work offers a direct proof of the Hunter-Saxton extension theorem by utilizing the Lipschitz stability of the model. The resulting solution is expressed as the geodesic curvature of a curve connecting two Hilbert spaces. The increasing adoption of ultrasound-based scoliosis screening in schools and community programs has heightened the need for robust, objective metrics to assess spinal curvature severity. This study aimed to evaluate the reliability of two scoliosis severity measurements derived from ultrasound: the Radiographic Scoliosis Index (RSI) and the Ultrasound Scoliosis Index (USI). We compared the reproducibility of these indices when generated by a dedicated robotic system versus a human operator. Our results indicate that the USI calculated by the Robotic Ultrasound System (RUS) exhibits excellent intra- and inter-rater reliability, with an Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) of 0.96 (95% CI: 0.91–0.98) and a coefficient of variation (CV) of 1.8%. Furthermore, we observed that the RUS achieved a higher average CV for ultrasound images (1.8% vs. 3.6%) and demonstrated superior reliability for both RSI and USI calculations compared to human operators. These findings suggest that automated ultrasound imaging can significantly enhance the robustness of scoliosis assessment. Consequently, the integration of AI and automation into ultrasound systems holds promise for facilitating large-scale scoliosis screening programs. Additionally, we demonstrated that a linear relationship exists between RSI and USI values, confirming the feasibility of utilizing ultrasound as a non-invasive alternative to X-ray imaging for scoliosis assessment. This approach could help reduce the physical risks associated with transporting students to radiology departments and mitigate the ionizing radiation exposure inherent in X-ray procedures. Ultimately, ultrasound offers a safer and more accessible screening method, potentially improving the quality of life for individuals living with scoliosis. Future research should focus on validating the sensitivity and specificity of these measurements when comparing robotic and human operators. By leveraging the advantages of automated ultrasound systems, we aim to optimize scoliosis screening protocols and reduce the physical and health burdens on patients. Identifying hate speech has become a significant challenge for social media platforms, prompting extensive research in the field of hate speech detection. However, many existing studies overlook feature selection, a critical step that could substantially enhance both the accuracy and efficiency of detection models. This paper introduces a novel approach integrating Mutual Information (MI) with Genetic Algorithms (GA) for feature selection in hate speech detection. The study employs bag-of-words features and support vector machines (SVM) for classification. An information gain-based fitness function is utilized within the GA to identify the optimal feature subset. Experimental results using the HOPE dataset demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a classification accuracy of 99.11%, surpassing the 98.41% accuracy of a model without feature selection. Furthermore, the approach significantly reduces training time and memory consumption while increasing the testing rate. Additionally, the study investigates the impact of pre-trained word vectors on feature selection and classification performance. Ultimately, the proposed technique offers improved performance and greater efficiency compared to conventional methods. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/raja12345678901/Hate-Speech-Identification. Given its efficiency, the method is well-suited for real-time hate speech detection applications. Furthermore, the framework is flexible and can be adapted to other social media sentiment analysis tasks, such as fake news detection. Future research will explore the integration of deep learning techniques, including Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), for feature selection. Additionally, the authors plan to conduct further experiments on the Twitter Hate Speech dataset to verify the method's effectiveness in classifying hate speech tweets. Finally, the proposed approach is expected to be applicable to various other social media datasets for detecting offensive language. Keywords: Mutual Information, Genetic Algorithm, Social Media, SVM, Deep Learning.

This paper introduces a novel MIMO architecture designed for large-scale vision models, aiming to enhance feature sharing across scales and spatial dimensions. Unlike current MIMO models that rely on a fixed, coarse grid leading to inefficient feature utilization, our proposed model employs an adaptive grid system. This approach dynamically adjusts grid resolution based on scene complexity, thereby generating richer and more diverse features. The model integrates large-scale feature sharing with a new adaptive pooling strategy that merges bottom-up feature adaptation with top-down attention, resulting in superior performance. We evaluated the architecture on a high-resolution object detection dataset (HR-WHO) and a fine-grained classification dataset (Cars-196), achieving state-of-the-art results in both domains. Furthermore, an ablation study confirms the model's effectiveness in parameter sharing across spatial scales. The research findings are available at https://github.com/ChenYi-0718/MIMO. By demonstrating strong performance on large-scale vision tasks, this work provides a new perspective for building efficient large-scale vision models. The proposed model represents a novel approach to large-scale feature sharing, and its source code will be made publicly available. However, analyzing this visual data presents significant hurdles, including varied layouts, diverse scripts, and the need for specialized processing methods to handle graphical elements. This paper provides a comprehensive review of historical manuscript image datasets suitable for benchmarking. Finally, we offer a holistic perspective on the field by integrating dataset analysis with reviews of relevant applications and methods.
