This study addresses the flatness-based regulation of a DC motor driving an industrial robot joint without modifying the mechanical drive structure. Typically, DC motors in such systems connect directly to the drive, lacking position sensors like rotary encoders; position data is often inferred from current levels or cost-prohibitive rotary sensors. To achieve precise trajectory tracking, the dynamics linearization approach utilizes position feedback linearization, while optimal control techniques employ flatness-based open-loop trajectory planning. The core challenge lies in designing position controllers capable of leveraging these advancements without access to direct position feedback. The paper demonstrates that secondary encoders, which measure the output shaft (load side) position, enable the closed-loop regulation of DC motors representing the drive's last joint section. The proposed flatness-based controller is implemented in MATLAB/Simulink and validated on a real-world secondary encoder from a robotic arm joint. Results indicate that, contrary to expectations, secondary encoders provide sufficient feedback for effective closed-loop regulation. Furthermore, the study confirms that flatness-based algorithms yield superior trajectory tracking performance compared to classical control methods. This work paves the way for applying flatness-based strategies in industrial robotics to develop high-performance, cost-effective motion controllers. The case study focuses on the final joint of the drive system, where nonholonomic constraints are most significant, though the findings are equally applicable to other system dynamics. Finally, both the plant model and the secondary encoder are identified using the flatness-based framework. The paper concludes with a discussion on future research applications. Keywords: DC motors, flatness-based algorithms, identification, industrial robots, nonholonomic constraints, optimal control, precision control, secondary encoder, trajectory planning. We illustrate its utility by analyzing multiple time-to-event data from patients who have experienced myocardial infarction. **Summary:** A new multidimensional method for multiple time-to-event data is introduced and applied to time-dependent covariates and competing risks. This facilitates the study of how early-life exposures influence the risk of multiple diseases later in life. The molecular continuum is an emerging interdisciplinary field that synthesizes molecular biology and chemistry to construct a spatial and functional framework for cellular and organismal biology. By integrating high-quality molecular data into a unified spatial framework, researchers can derive novel spatial insights and achieve spatial registration. We present a spatial biology technology designed to facilitate molecular data integration through multi-channel imaging. This method employs image registration to merge multi-center imaging systems, utilizing fluorescence imaging of tissue sections alongside organ-level imaging to align molecular data across different centers. We demonstrate the application of this multi-center integration approach in creating a comprehensive spatial atlas of the human colon. Furthermore, we show how this atlas can be utilized for spatial insight generation and tissue segmentation tasks. Our work establishes a new framework for integrating molecular datasets, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of human tissue architecture and cellular organization. The colon atlas is accessible at https://atlas.cancerimagingarchive.net. Additionally, our code and container image are available on GitHub (https://github.com/DeepMindLab/image-fusion) and Docker Hub (https://hub.docker.com/r/evgeniyd/nnunet/). We have released a pre-trained 3D U-Net model trained on our synthetic data, which performs well on real data for nucleus segmentation and cell classification. Our code supports both single-center and multi-center integration techniques. We anticipate that this work will facilitate significant advancements in molecular data integration, high-fidelity spatial representation, and multi-organ atlas construction. Specifically, our approach offers a more accurate and comprehensive solution for multi-organ atlas creation compared to current state-of-the-art methods. We demonstrate this by generating a high-fidelity multi-center lung atlas and performing precise segmentation of major pulmonary structures. We believe this work will substantially enhance the field of molecular atlas creation. Source code is available at https://github.com/DeepMindLab/image-fusion. Docker Hub: evgeniyd/nnunet. The colon atlas can be accessed at https://atlas.cancerimagingarchive.net. We provide pre-trained 3D U-Net models trained on synthetic data that achieve performance comparable to current state-of-the-art results in nucleus segmentation, cell classification, and tumor segmentation.

Atmospheric circulation in simulated hothouse climates on Earth is characterized by a boundary layer jet, intense surface winds, and a significant reduction in the number of episodic downpours. While the first two characteristics have been previously explained, the cause of the reduced downpour frequency remains unclear. This study demonstrates that the decline in downpours is a direct consequence of the jet's formation. Specifically, when a simulated hothouse climate features a thermal-tide-induced jet, the phase lock between thermal tides and the solar day leads to a lower total eddy kinetic energy. Since the thermal-tide jet forms under these conditions, it implies that eddy activity is suppressed by the jet. Consequently, the lower total water vapor flux associated with the jet results in a decrease in the total number of episodic downpours. These findings indicate that the unique atmospheric dynamics of simulated hothouse climates are intrinsically linked to the thermal-tide-induced jet. Furthermore, this conclusion is supported by a simple model that captures the essential characteristics of the atmosphere in these hothouse scenarios. This model suggests that the formation of the thermal-tide jet is driven by the interaction between thermal tides and the topography of mountain ranges. Therefore, the presence of mountain ranges is essential for the development of a jet, which in turn suppresses episodic downpours. These results provide a theoretical basis for understanding the dynamics of simulated hothouse climates. Additionally, the dynamics of simulated hothouse climates may offer insights into the atmospheric behavior of actual hothouse climates, such as those found on simulated super-Earths or on actual hothouse planets like the current or future Earth. Finally, the mechanisms driving simulated hothouse climates could help clarify the atmospheric dynamics of real hothouse planets. For instance, the dynamics of simulated hothouse climates may shed light on the atmospheric behavior of actual hothouse worlds, such as Venus and early Earth. Furthermore, the formation of a thermal-tide-induced jet could serve as a viable mechanism for jet formation in hothouse climates, including those on simulated super-Earths. This hypothesis is backed by numerical experiments showing that jets form in simulated hothouse climates when jet formation is triggered by super-rotation. Furthermore, the formation of jets in simulated hothouse climates may provide a viable pathway for jet formation in hothouse climates on simulated super-Earths. This hypothesis is supported by numerical experiments demonstrating that jets form in simulated hothouse climates when jet formation is initiated

We introduce the natural generalization of the twistor action describing self-dual Yang-Mills fields to arbitrary higher-spins and colors. This extension follows the pattern seen in single-self-dual massive scalar fields. When combined with a single-self-dual massive scalar field, the twistor action yields a higher-spin extension of the 4D Yang-Mills field content by incorporating spin-0 particles, a phenomenon previously observed in lower-spin cases. Furthermore, this twistor action accounts for a higher-spin generalization of Yang-Mills theory, where the non-abelian gauge symmetry corresponds to a higher-spin version of holomorphic bundles. Finally, we examine the action's behavior under deformations away from self-duality. In the massless limit, this produces a higher-spin extension of Yang-Mills theory, characterized by spin-0 particles and color charge, alongside a higher-spin gauge symmetry. Additionally, the action exhibits a global $U(1)$ symmetry that relates to a higher-spin generalization of Kähler geometry. In the presence of mass, this symmetry is broken, resulting in a higher-spin generalization of Yang-Mills matter. These theoretical constructions may contribute to understanding quantum gravity, specifically through an extended self-dual formulation of Yang-Mills theory. In this context, the action serves as a self-dual extension of Yang-Mills theory, where the non-self-dual component consists of a holomorphic bundle of higher-spin fields. This perspective may offer insights into how spin-0 particles emerge from pure gravity. Finally, we explore connections to a self-dual higher-spin extension of General Relativity recently proposed by one of the authors. In this scenario, the field content comprises both holomorphic and anti-holomorphic higher-spin fields, with color charge emerging as a consequence of field interactions. We also address the issue of color charge in higher-spin extensions of Yang-Mills theory. While this charge is conserved in our action, we demonstrate that it ceases to be conserved in certain deformations of the action. Consequently, we argue that color is not universally conserved in higher-spin Yang-Mills theory, although it remains conserved in specific instances. We conclude by discussing how these findings connect to recent research on color charge in spin-0 particles and higher-spin color. In this context, we identify the origin of color charge as a higher-spin generalization of the center of mass, alongside a corresponding charge current. We also elucidate the relationship between this charge and the Kähler symmetry, showing that the charge arises from the center

Addressing this challenge, we introduce a straightforward and computationally efficient approach that mitigates the impact of noisy labels during training. Our method utilizes Bayesian statistics to calculate the probability distribution of each class and subsequently applies a rule-based label rejuvenation mechanism to correct noisy labels. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method effectively reduces the impact of label noise and achieves superior accuracy compared to current state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, ablation studies reveal that the label rejuvenation mechanism is highly effective at restoring noisy labels to their original values. This paper examines several estimates regarding the norm of a projection operator onto the space of $n$-point interpolating polynomials of degree at most $m$, denoted as $\mathcal{P}_m(t)$. Initially, an upper bound for this norm is derived under specific conditions concerning the operator's matrix representation and certain geometric characteristics of a compact set $K$. Furthermore, the study addresses the inverse problem: determining the set of all possible matrices associated with a given projector for any fixed $m$. Finally, the first author's earlier work on this topic is briefly reviewed. The discussion begins with an analysis of the relationship between the norm of a linear projector and that of its adjoint.

Timed definitions offer an alternative to standard hol_defer and hol_promote, balancing the promptness of defer with the delayed evaluation of promote, with the duration of the delay determined by EBNF syntax. In extended definitions, timing information is shown alongside each clause, while in mini-definitions, it is displayed only for specific clauses. The hol-defer and hol-promote commands function as special cases within the framework of timed definitions. The syntax for timed definitions was introduced in 2012 and has since been refined through various iterations. This paper examines the syntax and semantics of both extended and mini-definitions, analyzes the rationale behind the implementation decisions, and details the various semantic options available for each style. Additionally, the work presents a formal specification of both semantics in HOL4 and describes the mechanisms used to handle conflicts between overlapping definitions. Finally, several examples illustrate the advantages of using timed definitions. All code related to this study is available in the h4ex repository. The suggested syntax for timed definitions has been adopted by the HOL community and is now supported by HOL Light, HOL 4, and EDTB. Furthermore, the EDTB system includes a command to enable or disable timed definitions. EDTB also features an option to choose between the two semantics for extended definitions. The authors thank the HOL community for their feedback, which led to improvements in the syntax. Specifically, clause timing is now indicated using brackets rather than square brackets, and the definition body is referred to as the "clause set" instead of the "specification." The authors also acknowledge the contributions of the HOL community for the terminology used to describe conflicts. Finally, the term "conflict" is preferred over "error" as it more accurately reflects the nature of the situation. The authors also wish to thank the reviewers for their comments and suggestions.

We introduce a data-driven strategy to enhance models based on coherent structures, which are vital for capturing the instantaneous dynamics of wall-bounded flows. By leveraging high-resolution direct numerical simulation (DNS) data from turbulent channel and boundary layer scenarios, we refine both Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) and large-eddy simulation (LES) frameworks. Central to this approach is the coherent structure identification (CSI) method, which utilizes proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) of time-series data derived from wall shear stress and velocity. This process isolates the primary modes governing the dynamics of wall-bounded turbulent flows. Subsequently, the Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) and large-eddy simulation (LES) models are calibrated using these identified primary structures. The resulting models effectively replicate the primary mechanisms of wall turbulence, thereby yielding improved predictive capabilities. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed data-driven framework can be applied to external aerodynamic flows involving complex geometries and unsteady incoming conditions. Our findings indicate that these data-driven models can significantly boost the performance of data-assimilation techniques, such as the Kalman filter, for identifying flow structures and correcting state variables in future flow simulations. Consequently, this represents a promising pathway for developing the next generation of data-driven flow models. This paper serves as a foundational step toward that objective. To facilitate replication and extension of our work, we have made the corresponding code publicly available. We investigate self-dual vortex/quantum flux solitons within the framework of the Born-Infeld variant of the infant Skyrme model. Initially, we establish the existence of these self-dual solitons by analyzing a third-order non-linear ordinary differential equation. Subsequently, employing the shooting method, we numerically generate a vast array of self-dual vortex solitons characterized by high winding numbers and large coupling constants. Our findings indicate that this model supports the presence of self-dual solitons across the entire parameter space. We further conduct an analysis of the mass spectrum for these solitons, demonstrating that the infant Skyrme model's action is capable of yielding bound states. Finally, we present detailed observations regarding the characteristics of these self-dual solitons. Our results suggest that the birth of black holes could be modeled by a modified version of the infant Skyrme model. Additionally, we explore the potential of this theoretical structure to describe both stable and metastable self-dual solitons. Notably, our analysis reveals that these solitons can be interpreted as extended objects possessing both electric and magnetic charges. Through numerical methods, we have successfully constructed self-dual vortex solitons with winding numbers up to 100 and coupling constants reaching 1000. Our results also highlight that the birth of (anti-)black holes can be simulated using either a modified or the original infant Skyrme model. This work significantly advances our understanding of self-dual solitons in a modified infant Skyrme model and holds significant implications for theoretical physics. This study examines a three-dimensional Hofstadter model featuring out-of-plane magnetic fields and on-site exchange interactions, resulting in a Weyl Hofstadter insulator that displays Hofstadter fractal spectra. This system can be transformed into a Weyl Hofstadter metal by introducing carrier doping. Notably, the Weyl Hofstadter insulator/metal exhibits an exceptionally large number of Weyl points and Hofstadter fractal bands, arising from the interplay between the rational flux phase, time-reversal symmetry breaking induced by exchange interactions, and Landau fan resonances. Furthermore, these Hofstadter fractal bands are anticipated to generate numerous chiral and anomalous Hall states, which hold significant promise for topological quantum metrology. In addition to Hofstadter fractal states, the rational flux phase is expected to give rise to a unique Hofstadter spectral pattern, comprising flat bands at rational momenta and dispersive bands at irrational momenta. This distinct spectral configuration is fundamentally different from the conventional Hofstadter butterfly observed in two-dimensional lattices subjected to a strong perpendicular magnetic field. Additionally, we demonstrate that these Hofstadter fractal bands can be effectively tuned by adjusting exchange interactions and carrier doping. This adjustability is crucial for advancing quantum metrology and exploring the Hofstadter molecular spectrum. Finally, our findings offer a viable pathway for experimentally observing Hofstadter fractal states in three-dimensional molecular conductors. Specifically, we propose a feasible experimental scheme to realize this Weyl Hofstadter metal by depositing a single layer of a three-dimensional molecular conductor, such as Cl$_{16}$TMTSF$_{16}$, onto a graphene sheet subjected to a strong in-plane magnetic field. This approach is highly promising for investigating topological quantum metrology. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first proposal for a Hofstadter fractal that is independent of external magnetic fields. Consequently, our proposed Hofstadter fractal model could significantly expand the existing research landscape. Furthermore, our proposed Hofstadter metal could serve as a new platform for investigating various Hofstadter-related phenomena, including fractional quantum Hall states, quantum anomalous Hall states, and topological quantum metrology. Our proposed Hofstadter metal is expected to attract considerable experimental attention. We anticipate that our findings will stimulate further research into the Hofstadter effect within molecular conductors. We present a hybrid dielectric-plasmonic nanoantenna system designed to convert non-luminous excitation photons into a highly efficient, unidirectional plasmonically enhanced luminous photon source. This system comprises a dielectric rod with an integrated subwavelength aperture, positioned above a noble metal film featuring a complementary periodic grating. Upon absorbing light at a specific frequency, the dielectric rod emits a single photon at a distinct frequency through a sub-diffraction aperture. This plasmonic emission couples with the complementary grating to generate in-phase plasmons, resulting in strong field enhancement at the dielectric rod's base and a unidirectional, luminous source operating at a different frequency than the input. The proposed device is modeled using a combination of finite-difference time-domain and boundary element methods. We introduce the concept of plasmonic enhancement factors, defined as the ratios of emission efficiency, luminosity, and directionality to their respective single-rod values. Our design achieves plasmonic enhancement factors of 1000, 100, and 90 for plasmonic nanolaminates composed of silicon and gold, silver, or copper, respectively. This novel source holds significant potential for applications including nanoscale imaging, spectroscopy, sensing, and the study of light-plasmon interactions at the single-photon level. Additionally, it can function as an on-chip optical modulator or as a single-mode, sub-diffraction laser. Anomalous screening describes the unusual behavior of charged grains in dry granular systems, where charge correlations induce a screening exponent of $\kappa=1/2$, diverging from the standard $\kappa=1$ seen in both liquid and solid electrolytes. In the presence of a point charge, this results in a $1/\sqrt{r}$ Coulombic potential that decays more slowly than in conventional media. While these phenomena have previously been validated through simulations, this study offers the first experimental confirmation. We generated a dusty plasma within a granular system and analyzed the plasma of interstitial gas ions surrounding the grains. Our findings demonstrate that the characteristic screening length of the anomalous screening mechanism in the granular system is approximately $10$ times shorter than that of a reference system composed of free electrolytes. Additionally, the spatial distribution of trapped charges around the grains aligns with anomalous screening theory. These results provide robust evidence supporting the hypothesis of anomalous screening in dry charged granular materials. Furthermore, we conducted a numerical analysis to corroborate these findings, revealing a strong correspondence between the experimental data and theoretical predictions. This work represents a significant advancement in the study of granular matter, offering a robust framework for the field. The implications of anomalous screening extend beyond dusty plasmas, potentially influencing the study of granular materials in geophysics, civil engineering, and other disciplines. Ultimately, this research enhances our understanding of granular matter and its role in the broader scientific community. By advancing our knowledge of this complex system, we pave the way for future innovations and discoveries. Silicene, a two-dimensional allotrope of silicon, has recently attracted significant attention due to its promising electronic attributes and potential applications in spintronic devices. In this study, we employ density functional theory to investigate the electronic properties of silicene supported on a hexagonal boron nitride substrate and the impact of surface decoration with various magnetic elements. Our findings indicate that while the undisturbed system exhibits band-gap opening, the introduction of magnetic atoms such as Mn restores the Dirac cones and induces a finite magnetic moment on the Mn atoms. Furthermore, we observe that Mn atoms preferentially occupy the hollow sites above the lattice. Additionally, we demonstrate that magnetic anisotropy energy can be tuned by substituting surface Mn atoms with other magnetic species. These results suggest that surface engineering offers a viable method for manipulating the physical characteristics of supported silicene. Consequently, these materials may hold promise for developing novel spintronic components. This investigation paves the way for exploring other supported two-dimensional materials for future spintronic applications. Finally, we highlight the critical role of substrates in two-dimensional materials and propose a novel approach to designing and fabricating magnetic two-dimensional systems. This design strategy involves selecting a substrate that band-gap matches that of the target material to facilitate the growth of a thin, epitaxial magnetic layer. We anticipate this approach will significantly advance the development of two-dimensional materials for spintronics. We have made our code available to the community. Sgr A East, situated near the Galactic center, is a remnant believed to be the result of a supernova that disrupted the Galactic center molecular ring. We have modeled this event as a Type Ia supernova exploding within the ring and developed hydrodynamic simulations using the ENZO code. Our findings indicate that the supernova's explosion ejected approximately 140 solar masses of ring material into the Galactic halo. By integrating these results with current observational data, we estimated the supernova's distance from the Galactic center to be roughly 0.35 parsecs. Furthermore, the shock wave generated by the explosion is predicted to trigger star formation in specific regions of the ring, potentially explaining the presence of young stars in that area. This research underscores the significant role that Galactic center star clusters play in shaping the Galaxy's structure. The simulations are accessible via our GitHub repository. The challenge of classifying text has garnered significant attention from both the machine learning and natural language processing communities. To address this, various approaches utilizing deep learning techniques have been proposed. However, a persistent issue in text classification remains class imbalance, where certain categories are vastly more numerous than others. This imbalance can hinder model performance, leading to degraded accuracy in classifying minority classes. To mitigate this, researchers have developed data resampling methods that generate additional samples for minority classes. This paper examines four such techniques—SMOTE, SMOTEC, the proposed OverK, and bootstrapping—by applying them to a multi-class text classification task and comparing their efficacy. To ensure a rigorous evaluation, the study employs multiple dataset variations alongside a consistent classifier. The findings indicate that OverK is the most effective method, yielding an average F1-score improvement of 0.0259 compared to SMOTE and 0.0185 compared to SMOTEC. Furthermore, the research investigates the impact of different sampling strategies on a specific classifier, with detailed results and code available at [1]. Finally, the paper discusses the implications of these results and outlines potential directions for future research. This study examines the relationship between COVID-19 reporting volume (measured by AP News Association content), regional disease severity (cases and deaths), and demographic factors within the United States. We develop a non-linear, multi-variable model utilizing linear regression, which demonstrates that higher COVID coverage is linked to larger, older, and more diverse populations, as well as lower infection and mortality rates. We also analyze the correlation between news consumption and the virus, finding that, contrary to expectation, greater audience engagement correlates with higher COVID rates. Finally, we explore the connection between news production and local audience engagement, revealing a counterintuitive result: areas with higher infection rates tend to show increased media engagement. These findings collectively suggest a paradoxical pattern where communities with the highest COVID coverage and infection rates exhibit the most local audience engagement. We conclude by discussing the potential implications of this phenomenon. Our research relies on a unique dataset comprising nearly a decade of newspaper audience and content metrics from the AP News Association, combined with local demographic and state-level COVID data from the Johns Hopkins University Center for Systems Science and Engineering. We conclude that our findings have significant policy and practical relevance, particularly regarding the need to carefully evaluate the quality of news consumed by highly engaged communities during the pandemic. Furthermore, we examine the broader implications of our results for the newspaper industry. We anticipate that our research will assist news organizations in understanding the connections between their audiences, content production, and local demographics and health outcomes. Additionally, we believe these insights can guide editorial and management decisions concerning content production and distribution throughout various stages of the pandemic. Finally, we outline potential avenues for future research. We anticipate that our findings will inspire further inquiry into the relationship between news consumption and public health, as well as the nature of the audience engaging with news during the pandemic. Additionally, we propose that future research could examine the long-term impacts of news coverage and audience engagement on community health and well-being. Ultimately, we believe our findings hold significant value for the news industry and our society as we continue to navigate the challenges posed by the pandemic. By understanding the connections between news coverage, community demographics, and health outcomes, we can work towards a future where news serves as a vital tool for promoting public health and social equity. We look forward to contributing to this ongoing conversation and supporting efforts to build a more informed and healthy society.

The Fast Multipole Method (FMM) is a widely used algorithm for accelerating the computation of long-range interactions in multipole expansions. However, despite its computational efficiency, standard FMM formulations often suffer from significant numerical errors due to aggressive error tolerances. This study presents a novel variant of the FMM designed for vector quantities that enforces strict error control, thereby ensuring the high precision required for conservation laws. The method's accuracy is demonstrated through two test cases: a collection of particles in free fall within a uniform gravitational field and a set of particles orbiting a rotating Jupiter. Both benchmarks confirm that the proposed algorithm maintains long-term conservation of energy and angular momentum with the same order of accuracy as direct time integration. Additionally, the approach exhibits superior computational performance compared to other precise fast methods, such as the Hierarchical Multipole Automatic Method (HAMM). This efficiency stems from the fact that the proposed fmm operator represents a new formulation specifically tailored to preserve conservation properties. Overall, the work demonstrates that high precision in fmm operators can be achieved without compromising computational speed. Consequently, this novel approach is particularly well-suited for applications in astrophysics and cosmology where conservation laws are critical. The corresponding Python source code is publicly available. This study presents the one- and two-dimensional polarization transfer coefficients for elastic scattering, incorporating spin-dependent corrections up to order $m_e/m_p$. Additionally, the spin asymmetry in the final proton is calculated as a function of the final proton angle in the laboratory frame, or equivalently, as a function of either the scattered electron energy or angle. These findings facilitate experimental tests of the symmetry between vector and tensor analyzing powers and enable the determination of nuclear form factors with a systematic error arising from unknown higher-order spin-dependent terms. The results are applicable to the JLab experiment employing a polarized proton target, specifically the EpSide experiment. Furthermore, the necessary code is provided for generating one- and two-dimensional polarization transfer coefficients and spin-dependent cross sections, facilitating the fitting of experimental data to extract proton form factors. This tool is also valuable for analyzing data from other facilities, such as the MAMI $H2$ experiment, which measures double-polarization asymmetries. Additionally, the computed spin-dependent terms can be utilized by groups conducting single-polarization experiments, exemplified by the $G2$ experiment at JLab, which measures elastic scattering using a polarized electron beam on an unpolarized proton target. Finally, the influence of radiative corrections on the symmetry between vector and tensor analyzing powers is examined. Based on these calculations, the expected precision for testing this symmetry is estimated at the level of a few tenths of a percent. This test is feasible using the EpSide experiment with a polarized proton target, the MACIE detector, or the MAMI $H2$ experiment. Furthermore, the anticipated precision for determining the proton magnetic dipole and quadrupole moments is also around a few tenths of a percent. These outcomes can be achieved with a statistical error of a few percent, which is readily attainable given the high luminosity of the anticipated experiments. Finally, the predicted precision for measuring the proton electric and magnetic form factor ratios is estimated to be a few percent. These conclusions are supported by the high beam energies available at the Electron Accelerators of Mainz (MAMI) and Jefferson Lab (JLab), the high beam currents, and the high target densities of the relevant experiments. Additionally, the use of double-polarization techniques eliminates the need for the extensive polarization flip corrections required in single-polarization experiments. Consequently, the precision in measuring the proton form factor ratio is expected to be significantly improved. We validate this technique in two key domains: multi-slice medical image segmentation for brain and abdominal structures, and multi-modal image-to-image translation involving skull-stripped and non-skull-stripped head MRI and pathological whole slide images. In our medical image segmentation application, the technique enables an expert learning paradigm that reduces the average per-slice memory footprint by 60% while delivering superior segmentation outcomes. Additionally, we observe a 10% enhancement in the overall sample efficiency of our image translation application. Comprehensive experiments across these domains underscore the versatility of our method. Furthermore, we extend our approach to handle imbalanced data distributions for expert models, achieving a 5% gain in mean Intersection over Union (IoU) for slice-wise evaluation in multi-slice segmentation. This study investigates Higgs boson pair production occurring in association with a vector boson ($W$ or $Z$) during proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The analysis utilizes data from the ATLAS detector collected by the LHC at a luminosity of 36 fb$^{-1}$, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 36.1 fb$^{-1}$. The search targets the diphoton signal mode combined with either a $W$ boson decaying leptonically or a $Z$ boson decaying hadronically or leptonically. No significant excess above the expected background was observed. Consequently, upper limits on the production cross-section were established relative to the Standard Model predictions for both $VH$ and HH$\to bb\gamma\gamma$ processes. These limits, determined at 95% confidence level and normalized to Standard Model expectations, range from 10% to 60% across various vector boson and Higgs boson mass combinations. The most stringent constraint was achieved for $m_W = 80$ GeV and $m_H = 125$ GeV in the $bb\gamma\gamma$ channel, yielding a limit of 0.11 (0.25) times the Standard Model prediction. This result surpasses the sensitivity of the previous search conducted at $\sqrt{s}=$ 8 TeV by a factor of 1.6. The analysis was also applied to the combined datasets from 13 and 8 TeV collisions, resulting in an average limit of 0.22 times the Standard Model expectation for $VH$ across all masses. These findings are consistent with Standard Model predictions and align with the sensitivities of current and upcoming searches for Higgs boson pair production. Furthermore, the results align with prior searches for Higgs boson pair production in association with a top quark. This investigation represents the first search for Higgs boson pair production in association with a $W$ boson and the second for associated $Z$ boson production, following a 2016 study using 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of 13 TeV data. A digital spin laser operating on $^{13}\text{Rb}$ atoms has been demonstrated. The "pump" mechanism relies on resonant light scattering that restricts the spin relaxation of the alkali atoms to a single magnetic sublevel within the $F=2$ manifold of the $5\text{P}_{3/2}$ state. The laser emission originates from the $F=2\rightarrow F'=2$ transition, where the narrow linewidth is determined by the linewidth of the scattering light. Both features are critical for achieving lasing. Due to the linear dependence of spin relaxation on incident light intensity, a saturated light intensity is identified, beyond which further pumping becomes impossible. Additionally, extending the scattering duration extends the scattering lifetime, enabling lasing at lower laser power. Leveraging these advantages, a detector operating at room temperature with high sensitivity and a large field of view was constructed. By adjusting the scattering time, the detector's sensitivity can be calibrated. With an optimal scattering duration of 10 ms, a sensitivity of $10^{-11}\text{W}/\text{mm}^2$ is realized. Furthermore, the operating principle suggests that this "spin-laser" can function without an external magnetic field. Removing the external field causes the laser's emission frequency to evolve due to the quadratic Zeeman effect. This frequency shift can be suppressed by selecting a scattering light wavelength that is detuned from the laser transition, allowing the spin-laser to operate without an external magnetic field. This capability enhances the detector's field of view to $2.5^\circ$. The principle of utilizing a "spin-laser" offers a promising avenue for developing new types of quantum light sources. Additionally, the operating principle suggests that this spin-laser could serve as a candidate for a quantum coherent detector. The high sensitivity of this detector establishes a new benchmark for quantum coherent detection using alkali vapor. Consequently, the detection limit of $10^{-11}\text{W}/\text{mm}^2$ sets a new record for room-temperature microwave radiation detection. This achievement is achieved without requiring an ultra-high vacuum or any external magnetic field. The primary challenge in dark matter research involves identifying the specific particle responsible for the non-baryonic, neutral component of dark substance. In the Standard Model, no particle possesses the necessary dual characteristics: being non-baryonic and neutral while also acting as a viable dark matter candidate. Consequently, researchers must rely on indirect evidence, such as the gamma-ray spectrum, to validate hypotheses regarding the nature of dark matter. This study examines a scenario in which the dark substance component is fully or partially composed of a stable neutralino. Particles that could have annihilated into neutralinos during the early universe include WIMPs, lightest supersymmetric particles (LSPs), and supersymmetric electroweak gauginos. Furthermore, significant contributions to the neutralino population may stem from oscillations of right-handed neutrinos, which could explain the matter-antimatter asymmetry. This analysis specifically investigates whether the gamma-ray background can be attributed to the late-time decay of neutralinos, which subsequently decay into gravitinos. The gravitino, being the lightest supersymmetric particle, is considered a strong dark matter candidate. Utilizing the Monte Carlo code FLUKA, we calculated the gamma-ray spectrum in the early universe resulting from neutralino decays. Our findings indicate that this decay process could account for a notable portion of the observed gamma-ray background. Additionally, we explored the potential for distinguishing this signal from other sources, such as decaying super-Heavy particles, through their gamma-ray spectra. Finally, our results suggest that future space-based gamma-ray observatories could provide critical evidence supporting the neutralino hypothesis. This could significantly advance our understanding of the early universe and offer compelling indirect support for supersymmetry. Ultimately, this research aims to investigate the possibility of detecting gamma rays originating from neutralino decays in the early universe. Such detection would constitute significant evidence for the existence of supersymmetry and potentially validate the theory of leptogenesis. Consequently, this study could offer valuable insights into the fundamental nature of dark matter. Our findings underscore the critical role of gamma-ray astronomy in the ongoing quest to understand the nature of dark matter. By providing indirect evidence for the existence of neutralinos, our results could help guide future theoretical and experimental efforts in the field of particle astrophysics. In conclusion, this research highlights the potential for gamma-ray spectroscopy to provide valuable insights into the nature of dark matter and its potential connection to the fundamental laws of physics. Our findings could pave the way for new avenues of investigation in the ongoing quest to unravel the mysteries

We demonstrate the existence of a effective polynomial-time approximation scheme (EPSAS) for genuspoly, a collection of polynomials where each term's coefficient corresponds to the genus of graphs with a specific number of vertices and edges. This enables an exact polynomial-time computation of the genus for any dense graph. Our approach is grounded in Nica and Sch\"{o}nenheim's expansion formula, which expresses mixed graphs as a linear combination of graphs featuring cyclic symmetries, a subset we term the symmetry set. We establish that the genus of a highly symmetric graph can be determined in polynomial time, contingent upon the genus of a corresponding "unfolding" with fewer vertices and edges. Leveraging this result, we develop an EPSAS for symmetry set polynomials, which subsequently yields an EPSAS for genuspoly. Furthermore, we refine an earlier EPSAS for genuspoly to ensure it operates within a polynomial time frame. Finally, we apply our results to establish an EPSAS for the cross ratio polynomial, a tool utilized in our prior research. This advancement facilitates the first polynomial-time calculation of the crossing number for all fully symmetric graphs. Additionally, we enhance an existing crossing number algorithm for symmetric graphs, originally proposed by the second author, by reducing its exponential complexity to polynomial time. This improvement facilitates the first comprehensive enumeration of minimally crossing fully symmetric graphs. Our findings also allow for the determination of the crossing number for the complete graph $K_{12}$, revealing it to be 18, and provide an upper bound of 19 for $K_{11}$. These results bolster the evidence supporting the conjecture that the crossing number of $K_{11}$ is precisely 18. Finally, we offer an alternative derivation of the crossing number for the Petersen graph, confirming it to be 6, and propose an associated conjecture. This conjecture is validated by the polynomial-time enumeration of minimally crossing fully symmetric representations of the Petersen graph, which total exactly six. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the crossing number of the utility graph $K_{3,3}$ cannot be established via symmetry alone, necessitating the application of existing algorithms to achieve a polynomial-time determination. We also identify the unique minimal crossing representations of $K_{3,3}$ as planar embeddings of the Petersen graph minus a single edge. This study addresses distributed convex optimization involving one master and multiple agents, where each agent possesses private data and can communicate solely with the master. We introduce a stochastic Newton approach enabling agents to collaborate with the master in estimating a global Hessian derived from individual local Hessens, thereby facilitating the computation of a descent direction for the master to minimize the objective function. We investigate two communication frameworks: asynchronous and synchronous modes, analyzing the impact of communication delays on convergence. Our primary contributions are as follows: (i) In an asynchronous setting, we demonstrate that with a suitable step size, the proposed method achieves a convergence rate of O(log T/T) in expectation for the expected projection error, matching the performance of synchronous stochastic gradient descent (SGSD); (ii) In a synchronous setting, we prove that the method attains the optimal convergence rate of O(1/t) for the projection error, equivalent to that of synchronous full Newton method (FNM). These findings are supported by a numerical example on image denoising. Notably, despite relying on the master to guide descent, our results indicate that this master-guided stochastic Newton (MSN) method surpasses synchronous SGD (SSGD) and SGSD in terms of convergence speed. Furthermore, we show that MSGD outperforms SGSD by an order of magnitude regarding convergence speed and improvement in objective function value. Finally, we discuss how to adapt these methods to settings with intermittent communication.

Keywords: Distributed optimization, asynchronous, synchronous, stochastic Newton method, convergence rate.

This study investigates the effectiveness of transfer learning for detecting hate speech in Hindi and Bengali by building upon a large English dataset. A comprehensive comparison was conducted among various Transformer-based models, including BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT, to identify the most effective approach for each of the three languages: English, Hindi, Bengali (using English weights), and Hindi (using English weights). The research demonstrates that transfer learning yields the best performance across all three languages, with Bengali (using English weights) achieving scores of 92.5% accuracy, 92.5% precision, and 92.5% recall through fine-tuning RoBERTa. Additionally, the study explores the possibility of developing a universal multilingual model for hate speech detection.

We introduce a technique to isolate a specific scintillation photon from a photomultiplier tube by analyzing its waveform. This approach enables a three-hit hitless hit-detection system suitable for gas Time Projection Chambers. The identified hit can be reconstructed with high precision using a dedicated readout channel, which determines the event's local time of arrival. This creates a compact, self-contained hit-detection module ideal for identifying particle scattering events. When events are detected simultaneously across multiple TPCs, this method facilitates cross-reconstruction, allowing for the determination of the complete 3D position of the ionization region. Furthermore, the system's high scintillation photon detection efficiency allows for the measurement of total light yield. Finally, this technology opens new avenues for scintillation-based recoil detection in dark matter experiments. Specifically, it allows for the independent measurement of electron and nuclear recoil signals, providing a robust discrimination method for nuclear recoil identification. Additionally, it supports the measurement of total light yield from particle interactions within gas detectors. This approach is currently being tested in a 100 mL TPC filled with 90% Xe and 10% O2, which operates in a dual-mode configuration: one mode functions as a conventional TPC, while the other utilizes the two-hit, hitless hit-detection system. We will present initial performance results from this prototype. Additionally, we will discuss future applications of this technique for triple-coincidence detection in liquid argon TPCs for dark matter searches and for enabling high-efficiency light yield measurements in gas TPCs for collider physics. These future systems will rely on a scalable and cost-effective readout solution capable of identifying and processing a high rate of scintillation photon hits. This capability is crucial for achieving the necessary sensitivity for dark matter research. To address this, we are developing a new scintillation photon detector featuring a large-area, high-sensitivity, and cost-effective readout, which we will also present. This development is a key step toward a large-scale liquid argon TPC designed for both particle physics and dark matter research. Such a detector would offer superior particle identification capabilities compared to current technologies. A primary example of this proposed large-scale detector is the Dual-Phase Xenon (DPX) experiment, a next-generation neutrino and dark matter observatory. DPX aims to simultaneously measure neutrino oscillation parameters, conduct neutrinoless double beta decay searches, and investigate other fundamental physics questions. This study examines the introduction of computer vision-based commercial driving tests, utilizing video and sensor data from roadways in Sweden, Norway, and Canada. Drawing on an extensive literature review, we analyze the strengths and limitations of these tests through the lens of algorithmic governance. Furthermore, we demonstrate the risks of indiscriminely adopting technological solutions by examining a specific case: an expert-driven approach to evaluating commercial driver performance. Finally, we suggest broader guidelines for moderating commercial driving tests to ensure they effectively balance safety, security, and efficiency. These recommendations aim to inform both the development of computer vision systems and their future adoption within commercial driving assessment programs. By integrating these solutions into a comprehensive algorithmic governance framework, we seek to prevent the narrow focus on efficiency that often characterizes such systems. Instead, this framework promotes a balanced, intelligent, and contextual use of technology that serves the public interest. Additionally, we highlight that moderating algorithmic decisions via expert analysis can significantly enhance the fairness of automated, computer vision-based driving evaluations. Ultimately, our findings provide a foundation for creating more fair algorithmic systems and offer a pathway to mitigate the risks associated with their adoption in commercial driving tests. This paper details the outcomes of the Out-of-Categories challenge, in which models were evaluated on a test set featuring categories and entities never encountered during training. The top three competing approaches were: (1) an ensemble of GPT-J trained on the Cohere dataset with prompt engineering to elicit correct NFC; (2) a fine-tuned T5 model utilizing an auxiliary NFC classification task to guide the model toward categories absent during pre-training; and (3) a fine-tuned BERT model employing an auxiliary NDE classification task to identify entities missing from the vocabulary during pre-training. All three methods successfully demonstrated the ability to handle out-of-category and out-of-domain issues to varying degrees. The results indicate that while predicting categories for previously unseen entities is straightforward for most models, predicting novel entities remains a significantly more difficult task. Furthermore, it was observed that certain models generate hallucinated NFCs that do not align with the labels provided by the dataset creators. Finally, the limitations of the challenge and directions for future research are discussed. Given that real-world scenarios frequently involve the prediction of novel entities and NFCs, this challenge holds significant relevance for practical applications. Consequently, we hope it will inspire further research in this area. The code and datasets can be accessed at: https://github.com/DeepMind/out_of_category. In recent years, data-driven neuroscience has increasingly focused on analyzing data within non-Euclidean frameworks. This study demonstrates that geodesic paths offer a principled approach for computing distances and similarities between data points situated on random field manifolds. By employing information geometry, we establish a metric tensor defined by the data points and their associated uncertainty structures. Geodesic distances are then derived using the exponential map defined by this metric tensor. We illustrate the application of these distances across three distinct data sets: two synthetic examples and one involving empirical analysis of resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) time series. To mitigate the computational complexity of evaluating geodesic paths on these manifolds, we implement two specific algorithms: one based on Newton's method and the other on gradient descent using geodesic distances as the objective function. Finally, we compare our proposed algorithms against alternative manifold distance metrics, including principal geodesic distances, spherical distances, and the Euclidean distance of Euclideanized data. These comparisons demonstrate that geodesic distances provide a robust and effective tool for analyzing data on random field manifolds. Our findings suggest that this approach is particularly advantageous for data sets containing few samples relative to their dimensionality. Additionally, the methodology is broadly applicable to any Gaussian data set residing on a random field manifold. We examine the problem of determining the length of a periodic solution to a second-order differential equation driven by a function $f(x)$, which arises in various geometric contexts, notably within geometric variational calculus. Specifically, we seek to identify the minimal length $M_f$ associated with such a solution. By employing a novel framework of "periodically" short $n$-periodic solutions to the Euler-Lagrange equation, we demonstrate that $M_f$ equals the infimum of the lengths of these solutions. This approach is applicable to specific classes of general second-order differential equations. Furthermore, leveraging geometric variational calculus, we establish that this infimum is attained by a short $n$-periodic solution, thereby proving that a periodic solution yielding the minimal length always exists. We also outline applications for this result in nearly geodesic length problems, the Lagrange problem, the Bertrand problem, the Euler problem, the nonholonomic problem, and the Chaplygin problem. Additionally, we provide an algorithm for constructing the minimizing periodic solution, which finds application in the aforementioned problems. Finally, we illustrate our methodology with a concrete example. Notably, the length-counts algorithm is not only effective for solving periodic length problems but also for minimizing the integral of any function $f(x,v)$ over its domain. This work builds upon the authors' prior research published in *Results in Physics*, Volume 12, 2018, Pages 403–410. For further details, visit: http://www.math.uh.edu/~ramos/length.html. The denominators of distinctive values at distinctive points for $L$-functions associated with modular forms are bounded. This result extends to the case where the discriminant's absolute value approaches infinity. The proof is presented in two distinct styles. Furthermore, we have re-examined the related topic of the boundedness of the distinctive values themselves (with respect to distinctive complex variables), yielding an improved result. Specifically, we demonstrate that the growth rate of $Q(\tau)$ can be reduced from $e^{4\pi s |\tau|}$ to $e^{4\pi s \Im(\tau)}$, where $s$ denotes the weight of the modular form $Q(\tau)$. Consequently, the degree of boundedness for distinctive values improves from $s-1$ to $\lfloor s-\frac12\rfloor$. Additionally, we establish a corresponding bound for the denominators of distinctive values as the magnitude of the discriminant grows, showing that the growth rate of $P(\tau)$ can be lowered from $e^{4\pi(s-1) |\tau|}$ to $e^{4\pi(s-1) \Im(\tau)}$. Therefore, the degree of boundedness for these denominators transitions from $s$ to $\lfloor s-\frac12\rfloor$. Notably, the second proof provides the tighter bound $\lfloor s-\frac12\rfloor$ for both scenarios concerning distinctive values and their denominators. Finally, we explore the relationship between our refined bounds and the Riemann Hypothesis.

**Keywords:** Modular forms, L-functions, Boundedness.

This study investigates spin-dependent transport within armchair graphene nanoribbon setups featuring spin-orbit coupling, magnetic fields, and gate voltages. By applying these technologies, one can adjust the occupation numbers of quantum dots, induce the Rashba effect, and manipulate electron spin via the Zeeman effect. Our findings reveal that electron transport exhibits significant sensitivity to the number of occupied states, total spin, and Rashba spin-orbit coupling strength. Specifically, at low temperatures, we observe that both the conductance peak width and the position of the zero conductance peak shift in response to variations in the Rashba coupling. These results highlight the potential for developing efficient spin-sensitive devices. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that this model offers a versatile and controllable approach for investigating complex many-body phenomena in nanoribbon systems. Finally, we outline a feasible experimental protocol to test our predictions using existing experimental capabilities. These conclusions suggest that our proposed model holds promise for both fundamental research and technological applications. Additionally, the ability to regulate the Rashba coupling strength opens new avenues for exploring diverse quantum phenomena in nanoribbons. Consequently, our findings may contribute to the advancement of future spin-orbitronics devices. This study establishes analogues of Korovkin's theorem for weakly nonlinear and monotone operators acting on the space $C(K)$ of continuous real-valued functions defined on a compact Hausdorff space $K$. These findings extend the classical Korovking theorem, which specifically addresses linear positive operators with composition laws. The proof leverages the unique representation of the set $T(K)$ consisting of weakly nonlinear, monotone operators that closely resemble linear positive operators. We subsequently present multiple examples of operators that fit this description, demonstrating that the derived analogue of the Korovkin theorem represents a significant generalization. Additionally, several implications of this research for approximation theory are explored. Finally, we outline a direction for future work regarding the extension of these results to $C(K)$ spaces of higher dimensions. Notably, the authors have already established the result for 2-dimensional spaces, and they intend to publish this proof alongside the current paper. This subsequent publication will feature a revised title, updated abstract, and modified content to accurately reflect that extension. Specifically, the relevant section will be retitled and rewritten to state that the result holds for any finite dimension, rather than being limited to cases where the dimension exceeds one. This adjustment will involve minor textual changes and the inclusion of an extra sentence. We invite readers to access this related paper, which will release with a different title, updated abstract, and modified content to ensure accurate representation of the extension. Access information: https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.01111. The new title is: "Generalization of the Korovkin theorem to the case of a finite dimension." The new abstract reads: "The primary objective of this work is to generalize the classical Korovkin theorem, which was originally formulated for linear and positive operators, to apply to weakly nonlinear and monotone operators. Specifically, this paper provides a detailed exposition of the result, which was subsequently published under a different title and with a revised abstract." A well-established theorem by Paul Erd\H{o}s demonstrates that the minimum $\delta$ such that every $n$-vertex graph $G$ with independence number $\alpha(G) \le n/(r+1)$ and minimum degree $\delta(G) > r\alpha(G)$ is Hamiltonian is $\lfloor (2r^2+2r-1)/(r^3+r^2+1) \rfloor$. This paper investigates the threshold $n\alpha$ required for $G$ to be pancyclic under Erd\H{o}s' conditions, demonstrating that $\beta$ cannot be arbitrarily small when $n=\beta\alpha$ and $\delta > r\alpha$. Furthermore, we extend these findings to conditions based on edge count, total degree, and total independence. We also examine related problems concerning the existence of large cycles and long induced paths. The proofs employ various techniques, including the use of the closure concept to derive sufficient conditions for pancyclicity. Additionally, we explore the connectedness of graphs with Hamiltonian closures and establish a sufficient condition for a graph to be pancyclic using our minimum degree result. We also address the problem of determining the minimum degree guaranteeing an $s$-walk of length at least $k$. Finally, we provide several examples of graphs that are Hamiltonian but not pancyclic. These examples illustrate that the minimum value of $\beta$ is asymptotically $r^2/(r^3+r^2+1)$, which exceeds $2r^2/(r^3+r^2+1)$. However, the authors conjecture that this lower bound is not sharp. The remainder of the paper is structured as follows: Section~\ref{pancyc} presents the primary theorems and their extensions, while Section~\ref{pancycproof} details the proofs. Section~\ref{cl} covers the closure-based sufficient conditions for pancyclicity, Section~\ref{longcyc} addresses the existence of large cycles and long induced paths, and Section~\ref{rel} presents related problems and their extensions. Finally, Section~\ref{ex} presents the examples of non-pancyclic Hamiltonian graphs. Our research was partially funded by the National Science Foundation (Grant No.~1639885). The production of charged particles at both low and high transverse momentum exhibits a directed flow that increases with collision centrality. In low centrality collisions, the direction of this flow aligns with the spectator plane, whereas in high centrality collisions, it follows the reaction plane, consistent with predictions from full three-dimensional Glauber and IP-Glasma models. By comparing isobar collisions, we observe that the magnitude of directed flow remains nearly identical across all centrality classes, while the slope varies by approximately 10% between $^{132}$Cs and $^{132}$Ba. These observations reinforce the conclusion that the directed flow of high-transparency charged particles serves as a sensitive probe of the chiral magnetic effect. Additionally, the study reports the directed flow of forward and backward $D$ mesons, which is positive and shares the same sign as the forward $D$-meson non-plane dependent component. Furthermore, the directed flow of forward $D$ mesons is roughly twice that of backward $D$ mesons, and the ratio of these values is independent of centrality. The forward and backward $D$ meson results demonstrate that the directed flow of heavy flavor particles shares similar characteristics with that of hadrons. Finally, the analysis also covers the production of all-electric charge and all-magnetic moment hadrons. This study introduces a new algorithm that integrates sparse grid spectral methods with the sparse grid variational approach to significantly accelerate the Adaptive Spectral Koopman Method originally proposed by Niu et al. These two techniques are computational tools designed to address large-scale nonlinear dynamical systems by approximating high-dimensional eigenfunctions. The suggested improvements achieve substantial gains in computational efficiency, reducing runtimes by up to 50% while maintaining the same approximation accuracy. Furthermore, numerical experiments demonstrate that these techniques can even enhance approximation error without increasing computational cost. This paper introduces the development of the outer complex scaling (OCS) method within Dirac's relativistic framework for strong dc fields. For finite systems represented by OCS wave functions, the OCS approach yields the correct infinite-range exchange correlation (EC) potential at large distances, thereby resolving the significant issue of spurious particle reflection off this artificial barrier. Furthermore, the OCS method enables the calculation of autoionization resonance parameters for relativistic relativistic dc-bound states. Additionally, this approach facilitates the study of relativistic dc autoionizing states in atoms and molecules using the relativistic configuration interaction method. The efficacy of the OCS method is demonstrated through OCS calculations for the relativistic dc-bound 1s state of the hydrogen atom. These computations employ a single-component OCS wave function to determine the energy shift and width (ionization energy) of the 1s state, as well as a two-component OCS wave function to calculate the autoionization width of the relativistic dc-autoionizing 2p state. The OCS results for the 1s state show excellent agreement with nonrelativistic OCS findings as well as with non-OCS relativistic results derived via the Dirac-Coulomb method. Additionally, the OCS calculation accurately predicts the autoionization width for the relativistic dc-autoionizing 2p state, matching the result obtained using the Dirac-Coulomb method. Finally, the OCS calculation accurately reproduces the autoionization energy for the relativistic dc-autoionizing 2p state using a single-component OCS wave function. These findings confirm the effectiveness of the OCS approach for relativistic dc autoionizing states. Finally, the paper provides detailed mathematical derivations of the Dirac-Coulomb and OCS Hamiltonians along with a step-by-step derivation of the OCS energy shift and width (autoionization energy) for the 1s state. This detailed exposition is intended to assist future researchers in applying the OCS method to their own calculations. Overall, the introduction and development of the OCS method for relativistic dc-bound states constitute a significant advancement in relativistic quantum theory. The successful implementation of OCS for both single- and two-electron systems marks a crucial step toward extending this methodology to many-electron systems. The Sinkhorn algorithm is a standard approach for addressing the Schrödinger problem; this study examines its convergence behavior when a solution to that problem does not exist. Specifically, we demonstrate the following: (i) For a finite dataset, we establish convergence to Sinkhorn convergence sets at an exponential rate under an identifiability condition regarding the joint power law weights, and we illustrate these findings through simulations. (ii) In the asymptotic regime involving a growing number of data points, we prove convergence to the same sets provided the sample covariances converge to their population counterparts. However, for both finite and asymptotic scenarios, the reverse implication does not hold. (iii) We also establish convergence to Sinkhorn orthogonal sets, which correspond to power law joint weights with exponents tending to $-1$. These results are supported by simulations drawn from a mixture of two Gaussians. Furthermore, in the asymptotic case, we establish convergence to the set of Schrödinger problems whose solution spaces have a trivial closure within the space of square-integrable functions. Finally, numerical experiments highlight the impact of a specific sampling bias present in our data.

This study presents a measurement of the top-quark pair ($t\bar{t}$) production cross-section in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV, utilizing the ATLAS detector at the LHC. The analysis incorporates 23.9 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity from data collected in 2017. To ensure a comprehensive coverage of the phase space for $t\bar{t}$ events, we employ a new top-tagging approach that unifies jet quarkonium and W-boson decay methods. The cross-section is determined to be $\sigma_{t\bar{t}} = 800.2 \pm 1.4 \text{(stat.)} \pm 4.8 \text{(syst.)} \pm 1.5 \text{(lumi.)}$ pb. This thesis aims to investigate the geometric properties of the Janowski class $\mathcal{P}[\alpha,\beta]$, which comprises functions $p$ satisfying the inequality $\alpha \prec \frac{1+\beta z}{1-\beta z}$ for $\beta \in (0,1)$ and $\alpha \in (-1,1)$, where the symbol $\prec$ denotes the subordination concept. Specifically, the focus is on newly introduced functions $p$ featuring generalized Bessel functions within their power series expansions. The study addresses multiple pertinent issues, beginning with the determination of sharp sufficient conditions for Janowski subordination involving these newly defined generalized Bessel functions. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that these sufficient conditions extend to other significant geometric characteristics of Janowski class functions. Additionally, the inverse functions of elements in $\mathcal{P}[\alpha,\beta]$ are defined, followed by an analysis of their relevant properties. Finally, the order, distortion, and radii of starlikeness and convexity for analytic functions of the form $Q(p)$, where $p \in \mathcal{P}[\alpha,\beta]$, are examined. Through this comprehensive analysis, the generalized Bessel functions are shown to hold significant importance in the theory of univalent functions. All results are supported by computer-generated plots. Finally, the thesis includes an appendix presenting the first ten coefficients of the generalized Bessel functions under consideration. This work is a component of the candidate's dissertation titled "Geometric Aspects of Generalized Bessel Functions," supervised by Prof. Miroslav Kirikae and Prof. Miroslav Srivastava, and defended at the University of Calgary, Canada. This study employed machine learning to analyze nearly 100 million GPS points from over 1.5 million New York City residents, examining how behavioral changes during the pandemic influenced the income diversity of urban interactions. The research found that during the pandemic, individuals were less likely to engage with a diverse range of income groups, a trend that was more pronounced in late-night hours and in neighborhoods with higher income inequality. These findings highlight the underlying mechanisms of income diversity in urban encounters, offering critical insights for future urban planning and policy-making. Specifically, the data suggests a need for policies that promote greater income diversity in urban encounters to foster a resilient society and economy. Furthermore, these results can inform the design of effective public health interventions, such as targeted vaccination campaigns and health education programs. Finally, these insights can guide the creation of effective urban policies aimed at enhancing social and economic resilience. Additionally, cities should promote greater social diversity in urban encounters to build a resilient society, potentially through policies that support mixed-income neighborhoods and community programs that bring people from different backgrounds together. Ultimately, these findings offer a roadmap for creating more resilient and equitable cities, ensuring that urban environments continue to thrive and provide a wide array of opportunities for all residents. To this end, cities should implement policies that support a diverse range of industries and professions, as well as initiatives that foster social connections across different groups. We present a comparative evaluation of field-split implicit field-splitting (FS), multiphase implicit cross-scale decomposition (MCD), and the sequential implicit pressure- saturation splitting (PSS) methods within a heterogeneous porous medium framework. In this framework, nonlinear upscaled permeability and relative permeability functions are represented by a neural network and a Gaussian process, respectively. We demonstrate that the FS and MCD approaches are equally efficient, showing that the nonlinear upscaled permeability function is the primary driver of challenges in two-phase flow simulations. Additionally, we offer a practical guide for implementing these methods in large-scale simulations. Our findings indicate that the techniques utilized to address nonlinear residual upscaled equations for permeability in single-phase flow effectively extend to the two-phase context. Finally, we highlight that the PSS method is highly effective for this purpose, provided that appropriate corrections are applied to the saturation update step. These algorithmic enhancements can be readily incorporated into existing reservoir simulators. Furthermore, we establish that linearly convergent schemes are available for implicitly solving FS and MCD systems, ensuring that these methods retain their efficiency even under conditions of strong nonlinearity. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive and unified perspective on solving nonlinear two-phase flow problems in porous media. We show that the shift in the cavity mode's frequency results in a corresponding angular momentum transfer to the resonator's walls. Additionally, we present a novel method for directly measuring the magnitude of molecular chirality. This approach leverages the mechanical torque exerted on the resonator's mirror by the angular momentum of the light, thereby establishing a direct link between the chirality of chiral molecules and mechanical torque. This discovery opens new avenues for studying chiral molecules and paves the way for new applications in chiral sensing. Finally, we explore the potential for energy harvesting from this phenomenon, which could be utilized in chiral solar cells. We investigate the relationship between 2D JT gravity and 2D coherent string theory (Liouville CWT) within the low-curvature, low-string-coupling regime. In this limit, both the path integral measure and individual path integrands align perfectly with those of the 2D Laplace matrix model, confirming a conjecture by Maldaena, Strominger, and Yang. Additionally, we demonstrate that the path integral measure of the 2D LP matrix model also reproduces the Liouville CWT results in this specific limit. These findings suggest that matrix models are particularly effective for coherent string theory, whether it refers to 2D Liouville CWT or 3D X$_{3}$ coherent string theory. Furthermore, we explore a potential connection between 2D coherent string theory and self-adjoint matrix models. Finally, we derive exact expressions for free energy and entropy in both the Liouville CWT and LP matrix model frameworks. This latter result is based on an approximation where the large-N expansion of the matrix model is extended to finite-N by incorporating corrections from the discrete spectrum of eigenvalues. While this approximation likely overestimates the free energy, it successfully captures the correct entropy. Consequently, we observe that the coherent string description of 2D gravity primarily accounts for the entropy of the 2D black hole solution rather than its free energy. Finally, we briefly examine the connection between the 2D Laplace matrix model and the recently proposed two-dimensional Yang-Mills theory. The warping of spacetime to generate an ideal fluid drive has been revised by incorporating the influence of the cosmological constant. For the Alcubierre metric, the total energy of the ideal fluid is calculated, and a convergence criterion for energy reduction is established. Additionally, a novel "turning on" method for the Morris-Metzer metric is proposed, along with a derivation of the total energy for a duae-domain configuration using the Vantuff modification of the Misner-Sharp energy, which utilizes the domain's boundary. This new energy formulation includes a correction term in the energy density; analysis reveals that the energy required for the duae-configuration is lower than that of the single-configuration. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that a total energy of zero can be achieved through the duae-configuration. The text concludes with a summary of the paper's limitations and potential future research directions. These limitations include the necessity of refining the concept of a global time coordinate, developing a self-consistent theory of space and time to address the second problem, and conducting research on the local time coordinate. Additionally, future work should explore the relationship between the speed of light and the cosmological constant, investigate the properties of a two-dimensional string model, and examine the effects of a two-dimensional string on spacetime curvature. Finally, the possibility of a two-dimensional string driving a warp bubble should be considered.
