Crowdsourcing platforms, such as Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk), have become a standard approach for gathering human input. However, the quality of human-generated data remains a significant concern, with many studies reporting error rates between 10% and 20%. This paper investigates the factors contributing to this high-quality output, analyzing over 1.5 million submissions from 10,000 workers across 100 MTurk tasks. We identify three key factors that enable researchers to identify and select for qualified workers. Our findings indicate that to achieve a qualified worker population with error rates below 1%, researchers must (1) design tasks that are sufficiently difficult to deter "qualified" cheaters, (2) implement mechanisms to filter out unqualified participants, and (3) target specific demographic segments. These strategies are demonstrated to be effective in attracting qualified workers for natural language processing applications. We provide a detailed examination of our data and offer practical guidance for researchers aiming to secure high-quality worker populations on MTurk and other crowdsourcing services. Additionally, we outline various approaches for integrating qualified workers into research workflows. Finally, we discuss the ethical implications of treating human workers as means to an end and propose that transparency regarding the methods used to attract qualified participants is essential. We conclude by suggesting that future research should explore the trade-offs between the quality of human contributions and the quality of the workers themselves. Our findings are based on data released under an Open Data request. The complete dataset can be accessed at https://data.sas.upenn.edu/datasets/finding-qualified-workers-on-mturk. Video retrieval tasks, such as text-to-clip search, present a significant challenge due to the disparity between concise textual tokens and complex video temporal-spatial data. To address this, we introduce the Token Shift and Selection Transformer (TS2-Net), an efficient network designed for text retrieval. Our approach utilizes a novel token shift and selection mechanism to dynamically adjust the feature space, effectively enhancing the alignment between text tokens and video representations. Specifically, a selection transformer dynamically identifies critical tokens for both text and clips, while a shift transformer optimizes their feature alignment. Furthermore, a dynamic matching loss is implemented to strengthen the predictive capabilities of the selection transformer. Extensive experiments across three video retrieval datasets demonstrate that TS2-Net achieves significant performance gains, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods by 1.5 to 3.5 times. Additionally, ablation studies confirm the substantial contribution of the proposed token shift and selection mechanisms. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenZhang/TS2-Net. This work was presented at CVPR 2022.

In early 2022, the LHCb experiment released findings on $SU(3)$-breaking effects within $\Delta I=1$ neutral meson mixing, a topic that has garnered significant attention. This study examines neutral $C$-even current–current four-fermion operators, which are responsible for these LHCb processes, and the associated chiral effective theory. By assuming that taste-changing neutral currents (TCNCs) arise solely from the top quark sector, we determine the operator coefficients. Under this assumption, the magnitudes of the TCNCs are substantial, reaching the percent level. Furthermore, we explore the implications of this hypothesis for the Standard Model, highlighting that TCNCs constitute a critical challenge for the Standard Model when the top quark mass is treated as an input parameter. Finally, we assess the viability of this scenario and identify the necessary future research directions. A detailed numerical analysis is provided in a separate publication. This study examines the evolution of finite directed graphs over time within a directed hybrid model. In each time step, a new node is added by either attaching to an existing node at random or connecting to a new richest node; this process repeats for every iteration. The resulting graph can be viewed as a random instance where the specific evolution of any given node is deterministic, while the selection of the new node for attachment remains random. We demonstrate that this model produces a degree distribution that scales as a power law. Furthermore, we establish that the power-law exponent for the in-degree matches that of the out-degree, implying that node connectivity is balanced. Additionally, we prove that the degree distribution of this hybrid model is always unimodal. Finally, we show that the degree distribution of any specific node becomes Gaussian as time progresses. These hybrid models hold significant potential for analyzing various real-world networks, such as social networks, the World Wide Web, and biological systems. In each of these cases, both deterministic and random factors influence the network's development. Social interactions, for instance, are driven by both deterministic elements, like geographical proximity, and random ones, such as meeting a friend through a mutual acquaintance. Similarly, web links are formed through both deterministic mechanisms, such as hyperlinks, and random processes, such as mouse clicks. Biologically, cell signaling pathways are influenced by both deterministic factors, like intracellular cascades, and random events, such as mutations. Consequently, our hybrid model offers a framework for analyzing such networks, enabling the investigation of both deterministic and random characteristics. Ultimately, this model serves as a foundation for understanding the behavior of diverse real-world networks. Furthermore, it provides a basis for future research into understanding the behavior of various directed networks. Multimedia content, including audio and video, is increasingly being consumed across various electronic devices via the Internet and mobile applications. This widespread distribution and consumption raise significant privacy and security concerns, particularly in professional environments such as police stations, newsrooms, and corporate offices. To address this, researchers have developed digital watermarking and authentication techniques to safeguard digital media against both intentional and unintentional conflicts. However, existing approaches often struggle to detect complex, simultaneous wireless disturbances. This study introduces a deep learning-based framework designed to identify multiple label disturbances, specifically focusing on cellular phone signals. The proposed method utilizes a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) that learns from radio frequency (RF) spectrogram features. Experimental results demonstrate that this framework significantly surpasses baseline models and enhance the performance of related studies. Additionally, ablation studies confirm that employing a spectrogram as input feature extraction is highly effective for distinguishing and identifying multi-label wireless disturbances. The research establishes a robust foundation for future investigations into multi-label disturbance classification and offers a reliable alternative for multi-label data analysis. Furthermore, the code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abdullahkaya1999/Multi-Label-WWI-Deep-Learning. The samples exhibit a wide variety of real-world scenarios and complex background noise, offering a strong basis for multi-label analysis. We anticipate that this dataset will facilitate the development of advanced deep learning-based multi-label algorithms. Additionally, it will enable researchers to replicate the presented results and compare their findings against other studies. This paper examines the dynamics of a spin-$0$ scalar particle within the Som-Raychaudhuri (SR) spacetime, which models a cosmic string with a space-like screw dislocation, under the influence of electromagnetic and scalar fields. The SR spacetime is characterized by its geodesic completeness, a vanishing Ricci scalar, and non-zero shear, expansion, and vorticity. By solving the Schrödinger equation in this background, we derive the energy eigenvalues and corresponding eigenfunctions for a Klein-Gordon particle coupled to both electromagnetic and scalar fields. Our findings reveal that the energy eigenvalues exhibit linear dependence on both vorticity and charge. Furthermore, the effects of the scalar field and electromagnetic potential are demonstrated through the wavefunction. Finally, we explore the physical implications of these results. These conclusions are supported by relevant equations, numerical figures, and tables. Consequently, these results may hold significance for cosmic string theory, especially regarding the investigation of scalar field dynamics in SR spacetime. Additionally, these findings could be valuable for understanding the behavior of charged particles in cosmic strings, which are hypothesized to exist within the universe. Finally, these results may contribute to the study of scalar field theory, specifically the behavior of charged particles subject to scalar field potentials. Future research will address these areas in greater detail. This paper introduces the concept of a locally usual measure algebra, demonstrating that every such algebra possesses a unique (exterior) decomposition into a usual subalgebra and a purely singular component. The study investigates the characteristics of these algebras, including their conditional expectation operators, modular elements, and the properties of their dual spaces. Furthermore, the authors define a specific type of topology on the space of a locally usual measure algebra, proving that this topology satisfies the countable basis property whenever the algebra's canonical lattice of conditional expectations is atomic. The topology is explicitly constructed from the canonical one; however, it coincides with the canonical topology if and only if the algebra is either atomic or essentially atomic. The topology is termed the canonical topology because it represents the coarsest topology rendering all finitely additive bounded functionals, which are absolutely continuous with respect to the measure algebra's measure, as continuous. The finite additivity of the functionals in question is highlighted as a significant aspect of the theory. Finally, the paper outlines several applications of this developed theory. The rapid evolution of computing and communications technologies has driven significant social and economic shifts, prompting organizations to adopt various strategies to thrive. A primary strategy involves leveraging data and information through Artificial Intelligence (AI). However, AI is not a standalone solution; it must be augmented by humans. This article explores the conceptual framework of Augmented Synthetic Intelligence (ASI) and its synergistic relationship with humans. It examines the ASI concept, the characteristics of effective human-machine collaboration, and the necessary human skills to facilitate this paradigm. Furthermore, the paper addresses cultural challenges and proposes strategies for successful implementation. Finally, the article outlines current research initiatives and future directions within the field of ASI. (For extended details, visit: http://www.iasl.org/ASI.pdf)

We present findings from a numerical study of one-dimensional correlated bosons under deep Rashba-type spin-orbit coupling (SOC) within an optical lattice, extending previous work on purely momentum-coupled SOC in a parabolic trap. At zero temperature, we observe a superfluid phase featuring a single, small wavevector density modulation that grows with increasing SOC strength and interaction density. This superfluid exhibits two coexisting collective modes and a renormalized velocity. We demonstrate that the superfluid remains stable up to a critical SOC strength, beyond which it transitions into a insulator-superfluid-insulator sequence driven by interaction-induced Mott insulating gaps. Additionally, we analyze the finite-temperature transition from the superfluid to the insulator-superfluid-insulator state. We demonstrate that this transition is governed by the competition between interaction-induced superfluid-insulator gap renormalization and thermal fluctuations. Furthermore, we show that the superfluid-insulator transition can be tuned via SOC strength, revealing a first-order transition at low coupling and a second-order transition at high coupling. Finally, we discuss the potential experimental observability of these phenomena in optical lattice systems. These results are based on a quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) study of the Bose-Hubbard Hamiltonian with spin-orbit coupling, derived from the Bose-Luttinger model at the mean-field level. We show that the model accurately captures the ground state and superfluid properties in the deep SOC limit, as well as the superfluid-insulator transition at finite temperatures. However, we also highlight the limitations of the model in describing interacting band edges in the SOC regime. Specifically, we find that the model fails to describe the insulator-superfluid-insulator transition, which is instead governed by the competition between the superfluid-Mott insulator gap renormalization by SOC and the interaction gap. This leads to first-order transitions at low coupling and zeroth-order transitions at high coupling. We also discuss the implications of these findings for the experimental observation of the phenomena. We investigate the $\mathbb{C}$-degenerations of symmetric graphs formed by shifting subgroups within finite abelian groups. This study focuses on identifying subgroup varieties that remain invariant under these degenerations and determining the geometric structure of the resulting group varieties. To achieve this, we introduce a constructive framework for the degenerations of both groups and their subgroups, demonstrating that group varieties can connect via subgroup varieties in a manner analogous to how subgroup varieties link through their codimensions. Furthermore, we present an explicit formula for the dimension of these group varieties, linking it directly to subgroup codimensions, and illustrate the framework with several representative examples. Finally, we establish a method for calculating the adjacency index between vertices in a differentiated graph based on the codimension of the intermediate subgroup variety. As one final application, we detail the construction of a family of symmetrized embeddings in higher dimensions and outline an approach to generating infinite families of such embedded symmetrized groups. Additionally, we introduce the concept of "tubular symmetrized groups," demonstrating that their symmetries can manifest as continuous functions. Our findings suggest that the dimension of a symmetrized group may not always match the dimension of its parent abelian group. We conclude by proposing open questions regarding the construction of symmetrized groups, the dimensionality of their vertices, and the existence of tubular symmetrized groups derived from arbitrary symmetrized abelian groups. Finally, the appendix provides a formula for the dimension of a symmetrized group and a criterion for identifying tubular symmetrized groups. This study examines low-dimensional AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ and AdS$_2$/CFT$_1$ dual pairs derived from massive Type IIA string theory. By employing massive Type IIA, we achieve the ability to generate supersymmetric AdS vacua across both six- and four-dimensional spacetimes by switching on various fluxes. In some instances, these solutions admit a description as D2-branes or D0-branes (or $\widetilde{\textrm{D2}}$ and $\widetilde{\textrm{D0}}$ in the presence of a background five-form flux), yielding dual theories located on the boundary of AdS$_3$ or AdS$_2$. Furthermore, we explore scenarios where supersymmetry is completely broken, leading to renormalization group flows between AdS$_3$ and AdS$_2$ vacua. These dynamics may be characterized by a holographic dual on a sphere that deforms as it shrinks to a circle or even a point. Finally, we analyze a specific example where supersymmetry is broken along a timelike direction, resulting in a dual defined on an interval with distinct boundaries at AdS$_2$ vacua. This framework is interpreted as a holographic description of a quantum mechanical system exhibiting spontaneous time translation symmetry breaking. Additionally, we identify a pair of solutions that are related by a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ isometry within the internal space, demonstrating that this geometric symmetry is mirrored by a duality transformation acting on the supersymmetric solution. These findings offer a new perspective on non-geometric solutions and suggest a pathway for constructing low-dimensional supersymmetric theories from a string theory perspective. A key advantage of massive Type IIA is its capacity to generate solutions in both even and odd dimensions. We conclude by discussing the potential for constructing solutions in other spacetimes, such as AdS$_5$ and AdS$_7$, which could yield duals ranging from six to one dimension. This work is part of a broader effort to construct low-dimensional gauge theories within string theory frameworks. Similar initiatives are currently being pursued in various groups, aiming to uncover a new stringy landscape of low-dimensional theories that may hold the key to understanding the quantum gravity landscape. A primary challenge in applying Gaussian process (GP) models is selecting appropriate kernel functions. While numerous options exist, there is often no clear guidance on which kernel best suits a specific application. We propose a method to develop new GP kernels by expressing them as sums of an infinite sequence of positive definite matrices, where the terms are derived from simple mathematical expressions. This work outlines the conditions required for these series to converge and remains  entirely based on existing literature. The resulting kernels offer several advantageous properties. Furthermore, we provide a practical algorithm to truncate these series for finite approximations and demonstrate how to automatically select the optimal truncation point. Our approach is highly general, producing a rich collection of GP kernels. For instance, it yields new formulations for the spectral mixture and Mat\'ern class of kernels, alongside conditions for their positive definiteness. Additionally, we have developed a highly efficient way to compute GP predictions using GP+linear model hybrids. This method relies on a hybrid approach to Gaussian process regression, a topic that has recently attracted significant interest. The paper includes numerical experiments to validate our claims. Our code is available at https://github.com/rajkumarvishwanath/elementary-GP-kernels. This work is partially supported by the EPSRC grant EP/R003040/1. Conventional collider designs typically avoid muon beams due to their extremely short lifetime, which results in significant beam-induced background from decays. This background poses a threat to the beam crossing region and detector by overwhelming them with hits, thereby degrading the collider's luminosity. Consequently, various strategies to mitigate beam-induced noise have been proposed, with this review examining the most promising among them. A comprehensive solution will likely require a combination of these approaches, necessitating further research and development. The primary goal of reducing such noise is to enable the construction of muon collider beam pipes and detectors capable of achieving luminosity orders of magnitude higher than current hadron colliders. Additionally, the review outlines several areas where noise suppression research is essential to define the design parameters for a future muon collider. Finally, the text addresses the current status of the program and the necessary steps to advance the concept toward a potential experimental facility. A detailed overview of various noise-reduction techniques can also be found in a related thesis, which the author references. Given the extensive literature on the subject, this review does not claim to be exhaustive. However, it serves to highlight key issues and design considerations for a future muon collider, while also identifying open questions and the necessary research and development efforts to make such a machine a reality. We introduce Spartan, a new regularized loss function designed to facilitate the learning of sparse solutions. Derived from the unbalanced optimal transport problem, Spartan offers the flexibility to define a custom support set for solutions and ensures this support can be learned via a projected gradient descent step within implicit deep neural network blocks. To illustrate its efficacy, we first apply Spartan to model group sparsity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that even when applied element-wise, Spartan effectively recovers hard thresholded solutions. Finally, we present a comprehensive experimental suite across various domains, including compressed sensing, phase retrieval, robust PCA, and low-rank matrix completion, as well as machine learning tasks such as SIFT matching and object recognition. These sections highlight both the theoretical and empirical advantages of Spartan. Additionally, we develop a novel algorithm for solving the Spartan problem that unifies existing solution methods and unifies robust PCA and low-rank matrix completion under a single algorithimc framework. To our knowledge, this represents the inaugural application of unbalanced optimal transport to sparse learning. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/PrincetonML/Spartan. Test smells share characteristics with code smells but indicate deeper issues by signaling that code requires refactoring. While most prior research has focused on automatically detecting these smells, there is a distinct lack of empirical studies examining their severity. This paper presents such a study, where ten Java developers with an average of eight years of experience estimated the severity of 144 test smells across 15 classes from the MyFaces project. Using a five-point Likert scale, participants rated severity from 1 (easy to fix) to 5 (hard to fix). The resulting ratings were converted into a 0–1 scale for analysis. The study employed a mixed-methods approach, utilizing both quantitative methods—such as ANOVA and Kruskal-Wallis tests—and qualitative methods, including content analysis of the developers' open-ended responses. Findings indicate that developers perceive test smells in complex classes as significantly more severe than those in non-complex classes. Furthermore, the average severity scores for test smells align closely with developer perceptions, confirming that their assessments are consistent. Finally, the difficulty of fixing test smells is primarily driven by the complexity of the surrounding code. This research offers the first empirical investigation into developer perceptions of test smell severity, providing valuable insights for test refactoring processes. It also informs the configuration of development tools, such as setting appropriate severity thresholds to assist developers in identifying and fixing the most critical test issues. We examine a brushing process applied to a collection of nonconvex random line segments that extend infinitely in both directions within $\mathbb{R}^d$ ($d\geq 2$). These segments feature a nonconvex cross-section defined by a strictly convex function with finite end-points, characterized by a width function $w$. A brush operates by selecting points $(x,w(x))$ and $ (x,-w(x))$ independently and symmetrically, removing the entire segment to which they belong. We analyze the stability of the stationary brushings process and derive a precise estimate for the thickness function of the equilibrium state when the brush activity is sufficiently low. Furthermore, we apply these findings to a model of a nonconvex version of the Garling process. In this application, the segments represent the free boundaries of a gas confined in a box under a strong repulsive potential near the walls, which takes the form $V(x) = \infty$ for $x\leq 0$ and $V(x) = \infty$ for $x\geq 1$. The result indicates that the gas free boundaries remain bounded away from the physical boundaries of the box. Additionally, we investigate the behavior of this system at low temperatures. Finally, we demonstrate that the analysis remains valid for more generalized brushings processes involving higher codimension settings. However, in these broader scenarios, we can only establish the existence and uniqueness of an equilibrium state at low temperatures or within low activity regimes. To support these conclusions, we support the theoretical framework with numerical simulations. These computations not only verify the derived estimates but also reveal novel phenomena that extend beyond our theoretical predictions. Specifically, we observe the emergence of a second phase transition at a critical activity level, alongside a significant discrepancy between our estimated and actual decay rates of the width function. The latter finding suggests that our current estimates may not be optimal. Furthermore, we note that our current methodology is insufficient to rigorously prove the validity of these additional phenomena. Nevertheless, we are able to derive several non-quantitative insights that hint at interesting behaviors in these new regimes. Finally, we conclude by outlining potential avenues for future research. This study introduces the Tiramisu model, a novel framework for estimating inter-beat intervals (IBI) from photoplethysmogram (PPG) signals. We developed a two-stage method to IBI estimation, where the first stage isolates the primary peak from each beat within the PPG signal, and the second stage calculates the interval between consecutive peaks. We evaluated multiple baseline models, including LSTM, GRU, 1D-CNN, and a combined 1D-CNN + LSTM architecture. From these, we constructed two distinct Tiramisu models: TT (Tiramisu True), which operates on raw PPG signals, and TD (Tiramitsu Detected), which takes IBI values from a previous frame as input to generate the current frame's IBI. We compared the IBI time series produced by both models against the ground truth. Results demonstrate that the TT and TD models significantly outperform all other approaches, reducing mean absolute error (MAE) by 30% and 40%, respectively, compared to the baseline 1D-CNN + LSTM model. Furthermore, the TT model outperforms the TD model by achieving a 20% reduction in MAE. Finally, we analyzed the impact of noise on IBI estimation accuracy, revealing that the TT model maintains superior performance relative to the TD model even under noisy conditions. This paper introduces a randomized algorithm for computing the singular value decomposition (SVD) of a tensor. Leveraging the passes model of randomized algorithms, we demonstrate that a single pass is adequate to achieve an approximation ratio of 1. This result holds a significant position within tensor computation, particularly given that our proof does not rely on probabilistic methods beyond the analysis of the first pass. Furthermore, our fully randomized singular value solver operates in $\mathcal{O}(np^2 + np^2\log(1/\delta))$ time with probability $1-\delta$, where $n$ represents the number of elements per mode and $p$ denotes the desired number of singular vectors. The space complexity is $\mathcal{O}(p + np)$, and the time complexity for computing the singular vectors matrix is $\mathcal{O}(n p r)$, with $r$ indicating the number of singular vectors to be computed. Additionally, we extend our approach to provide an arbitrary pass count model for the tensor singular value solver, demonstrating the trade-off between precision and computational complexity. Experimental results indicate that our proposed algorithm outperforms the traditional alternating least squares method. Embedding dynamic graphs is a critical task with extensive applications, including link prediction, time series forecasting, and influence maximization. This survey provides a systematic overview of the current state-of-the-art methods for embedding evolving graphs. The ground state of $^7$H is analyzed within the framework of the dynamical cluster model, which incorporates the virtual excitation of the $^3$H core. The $^7$H nucleus is represented as a composite system of the $^3$H core and five valence neutrons, arranged in two distinct configurations: (i) a compact five-neutron cluster and (ii) four neutrons paired with an neutron-core pair. In the model space, the $^3$H core is treated as a virtual excited state generated by the $^3$H+$n$ threshold. Utilizing the Gaussian expansion method, the structure of the $^7$H ground state is examined. The resulting root-mean-square radius and energy separation from the $^5$n threshold align with prior predictions. Furthermore, the ground state is identified as a weakly bound, highly excited state relative to the $^3$H+$4n$ threshold. This finding is consistent with the strong coupling between the $^7$H ground state and the $^5$H$+$2n excited state, which lies approximately 1 MeV above the $^7$H ground state. Additionally, the study confirms that the $^7$H ground state is unbound with respect to the $^1$H+$6n$ threshold. The analysis also addresses the possibility of $^7$h isomerism. Finally, the findings are compared against the predictions of the dynamical cluster model. These results suggest that the $^7$H ground state exhibits a complex structure, which may be observable through the study of its various reaction channels. We establish the existence of smooth solutions for specific dimensions $n \in \{5, 6, 7\}$ and certain curvature functions $k$, yet demonstrate that these solutions may lack compactness. This non-compactness is evidenced by the existence of nontrivial blow-up solutions. These findings extend the work of Gidas, Spruck, and Zhang, as well as Sire, who previously addressed this problem on closed spheres $\mathbb{S}^n$. Our study is supported by an alternative Pohozaev identity derived from Dirichlet boundary conditions. This identity takes a form analogous to the one obtained by Gidas, Spruck, and Zhang using reflected spheres, though with distinct constants. This variation has significant implications for the non-existence results, as the optimal constants differ. Additionally, we derive a Pohozaev identity for the Nirenberg problem on half-spheres and utilize it to derive a nonexistence theorem. This outcome aligns with recent findings by Liang, Liang, and Zhang, further validating the consistency of our results with recent literature. Finally, our work contributes to the ongoing investigation into whether the non-existence dimension for conformal metrics with constant curvature on half-spheres is 9 or 10. This contrasts with closed spheres, where the non-existence threshold is 10, as established by Gidas, Spruck, and Li. Deep neural networks have become a cornerstone of machine learning, with their high capacity enabling the extraction of rich optimal representations from vast amounts of data. This paper introduces a general framework utilizing $\mathsf{H}$-Sinkham divergences to learn deep optimal representations. By providing an analytical characterization of $\mathsf{H}$-Sinkhorn divergences, the study demonstrates their ability to model the structure of optimal transport cost functions. Leveraging the specific characteristics of these divergences, the approach is applied to the learning of hierarchical dictionary networks. Empirical results confirm that the proposed method can effectively learn both nonlinear and sparse features. Furthermore, the framework is extended to depth-wise neural networks, yielding a model that is both computationally efficient and well-suited for real-time applications. These theoretical insights motivate the design of a novel quantization loss, which is evaluated through both numerical experiments and applications in speech and image processing. This study employs a simulation-based approach to evaluate how partnerships between local tracing teams and digital contact tracing applications influence the effectiveness of COVID-19 contact tracing in England. We integrated an application into a simulation framework that models both digital and human tracing services, then varied the app's user adoption rate to observe corresponding changes in outbreak size. The results indicate that increasing digital service uptake from 20% to 60% could reduce transmission by 2.5 to 3.5 times, contingent upon local tracing effort levels. Consequently, the research demonstrates the benefit of integrating digital and local contact tracing services and offers a flexible modeling framework for analyzing the impact of additional digital services on COVID-19 transmission. Additionally, we present a sensitivity analysis to examine how assumptions regarding infection and contact durations affect these findings. England utilizes a combination of national and local tracing services, yet there is a proposed shift toward reduced local involvement. Our findings support this decision by highlighting the interaction between digital services and local efforts. Furthermore, the study offers insights into the engagement strategies necessary to maximize the potential of digital contact tracing services. These results are derived from the England-Wales model, which incorporates features common to various countries' COVID-19 tracing systems. Therefore, the implications of our findings extend to other nations utilizing a similar mix of digital and local services. This study investigates the kinematics and physical characteristics of Melotte 72 by analyzing data from the second Gaia Data Release. We identified 10 probable cluster members among 22 stars with a mean parallax error of less than 10 microarcseconds. These members were selected based on their position relative to the cluster's center and their kinematic properties. We calculated the cluster's heliocentric velocity and compared it with prior studies, finding good agreement. Additionally, we determined the cluster's mean distance using the average parallax of these 10 stars and cross-referenced this with other existing literature. Finally, we estimated the cluster's mass and explored its dynamical state. Our results indicate that Melotte 72 is a young cluster with a mass of $0.003 \pm 0.001 M_{\odot}$. Furthermore, we observed that the cluster's dynamical state has remained stable over time. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings and compare them with other relevant studies. When considering random polynomial maps, we demonstrate that, under suitable conditions, these sparse Betti number bounds become exponentially small in the bounds used for the exponents. Furthermore, we apply these general findings to analyze the sparse Betti numbers of Gaussian random maps across specific sparsity levels. These sparse Betti numbers vanish with overwhelming probability in the exponentially sparse regime. This analysis reveals that they converge to the top Betti numbers of the corresponding sparse intersection, linkage, cohomology, and sheaf cohomology classes, as well as the Betti numbers of the intersection, linkage, and cohomology classes formed by the maps with arbitrarily large exponents. Eyebots are emerging robotic systems designed to provide first-person visual perspectives for human-robot collaboration. To capture a perspective indistinguishable from human vision, these systems must precisely replicate human eye characteristics, including focal length, optical center, and image plane offset. While current approaches typically rely on either calibrated extrinsic camera measurements or extensive manual tuning by users to adjust these parameters, this paper introduces a novel method that learns all three extrinsic values from merely one unannotated user selfie. Leveraging self-supervised learning, the proposed algorithm utilizes a selfie to train a neural network that predicts the specific camera extrinsics—focal length, optical center, and offset—required to match human eye viewpoints. Experimental validation across multiple eyebot platforms demonstrates that these learned parameters enable robots to capture images highly similar to human vision, even when the initial selfie does not closely resemble a typical human eye viewpoint. Furthermore, the method's robustness is highlighted by its ability to adapt to variations in head shape and orientation. The authors anticipate this approach will significantly enhance the usability of parameter tuning for eyebots and other first-person robots. The corresponding source code can be found at https://github.com/ethzrobotics/Single-Selfie-EyeInHand. Additionally, the paper includes supplementary videos featuring a human capturing a view and a robot reproducing it using the proposed method. To illustrate the robot's capability in person collaboration, the video depicts a scenario where the robot assists a user in writing on a whiteboard. The authors intend to explore further applications of this method in collaborative contexts in future work. The code is made available to facilitate its adoption and extension within collaborative robotics scenarios. The authors welcome inquiries and collaboration. Email: johan.segall@inf.ethz.ch. This paper introduces Reverse Constrained Reinforcement Learning (RC3L), an approach designed to identify the policy that maximizes the difference between two reward functions, subject to the limitation of achieving at least a minimum average reward $V_{min}$ for reward function 2. RC3L adheres to a two-step framework: first, it learns the state-value function for reward function 2 via constrained reinforcement learning; second, it optimizes a novel loss function derived from this value function to yield the policy that maximizes the reward disparity while satisfying the constraints. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the proposed policy gradient and Lagrangian gradient methods converge to the optimal policy, and numerical experiments on both continuous and discrete state-space environments confirm the practical effectiveness of this reverse learning approach. Notably, RC3L is capable of learning transferable inverse models from a single expert's trajectory. This work represents an initial exploration of constrained reinforcement learning from an inverse perspective, a direction that holds significant potential for future research. Additionally, it offers a promising pathway for developing a new category of policy-based inverse reinforcement learning techniques. The source code is available at: https://github.com/ChengdaLi1998/Reverse-Constrained-RL.

GAIA, a mission by the European Space Agency's Science Programme, is designed to survey the entire sky, cataloging up to one billion stars with high precision. The mission will generate comprehensive 3D maps of our stellar and planetary neighborhood, detailing fundamental properties such as distance, proper motion, and luminosity. Additionally, GAIA will significantly enhance our understanding of the Milky Way's formation and evolution, solar system dynamics, and the early Solar System. This paper outlines GAIA's scientific objectives and the innovative techniques employed to achieve them. Grouping methods are essential for analyzing networks, whether intrinsic or derived, as well as partially observed systems. These approaches enable the classification of nodes based on structural roles or by reconstructing networks from partial data. Given that networks can be constructed through multiple methods—ranging from direct observation to inference using various techniques—understanding how these creation methods influence network structure is crucial. This study investigates the suitability of existing node grouping techniques for networks characterized by heterogeneity (disconnected components), sparsity, directionality, and weight heterogeneity. We evaluate four specific methods: Disconnected Component Grouping, Degree, Infomap, and Louvain. By measuring the similarity between nodes, we determine whether existing techniques can accurately identify similar nodes across different network types. Furthermore, we introduce a novel greedy Louvain-based clustering approach designed to maximize weight heterogeneity. Our findings indicate that Infomap outperforms the other techniques across all examined network types. Additionally, we demonstrate that the proposed Louvain variant achieves higher quality scores for both Infomap and Community Detection compared to the standard implementation. Finally, we highlight that weighted, directed, and heterogeneous networks offer superior potential for node classification and reconstruction compared to their unweighted, undirected, and homogeneous counterparts. This work serves as a foundation for future research into node grouping techniques and network reconstruction. Supplementary materials, including code and data, are available at https://github.com/alexanderkoster/weighted_directed_grouping. This study introduces a novel a posteriori error estimation framework for physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). The method quantifies the maximum error of PINN predictions by analyzing their residual against the governing differential equation. By reformulating the resulting error estimation problem as an optimal control task, the technique facilitates the construction of a valid error bound through an optimized control variable. We validate the approach using simple analytical examples and a more complex scenario involving fluid dynamics, demonstrating its utility for achieving certified machine learning. Furthermore, the proposed method is shown to serve as an effective proxy for guiding an active learning strategy. Finally, we examine the potential of this error estimator to replace traditional adjoint-based methods for uncertainty quantification in physics-informed neural networks. Our findings indicate that the adjoint-based approach is susceptible to substantial biases when the adjoint model is significantly dissimilar to the forward model, a condition frequently encountered in both traditional and physics-informed neural network applications. In contrast, our proposed a posteriori error estimation technique remains robust in these scenarios, delivering reliable error bounds that effectively manage such discrepancies. This reliability is confirmed across a diverse range of applications, including various model types, scales, and regimes. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/rajkumar2000/A-Priori-Error-Bounds-for-PINNs. Additionally, we have released a certified version of PINN that incorporates an a priori error bound generator, which provides a worst-case error estimate based on the training dataset. This capability enables a PINN to communicate its error bounds to users, thereby establishing a foundation for machine learning model certification. The implementation can be found at https://github.com/rajkumar2000/Certified-PINN. The source code for this certified PINN implementation is available at https://github.com/rajkumar2000/Certified-PINN. The results from this certified PINN application are detailed in our paper titled "A physics-informed neural network for a two-dimensional inviscid flow past a sphere," published in *Computational Mechanics* (2022). Air pollution epidemiology faces a critical challenge in identifying the health effects of indoor air contaminants. To address this, we propose a novel integrated approach combining geostatistics, machine learning, and epidemiology. Our methodology involves constructing indoor contaminants models through the spatial interpolation of outdoor air pollutants, utilizing an empirical Bayesian-Kriging technique. This spatially interpolated outdoor data serves as a covariate in regression models to estimate the impact of outdoor air pollution, thereby acting as a proxy for indoor exposure. Furthermore, machine learning algorithms are employed to forecast spatially resolved, time-dependent outdoor pollutant concentrations when monitoring data is sparse. This combined strategy offers a more precise quantification of individual-level indoor exposure to outdoor air pollutants, significantly advancing our capacity to analyze their connection to human health outcomes. Consequently, this integration holds significant promise for elucidating the specific health risks associated with air pollution. A case study focusing on the spatial interpolation of urban air pollution and its relationship with asthma hospitalization rates in Montreal, Canada, demonstrates the feasibility of this proposed methodology. Additionally, we examine the limitations of this approach and suggest future research directions. Ultimately, we argue that synthesizing geostatistics, machine learning, and epidemiology represents a promising avenue for enhancing the accuracy of air pollution exposure assessment. This improvement is essential for clarifying the causal pathways linking air pollution to various health outcomes. Furthermore, the framework extends beyond air pollution to support research in environmental and occupational epidemiology. By enabling the quantification of environmental exposures with greater precision, it holds the potential to strengthen the evidence base regarding the causal effects of diverse environmental and occupational factors on disease. This advancement could facilitate the development of more effective prevention and control strategies. Finally, we identify data sharing as a key priority to maximize the benefits of this integrated research approach. Collaborative, open research practices are essential to fully leverage the potential of integrating geostatistics, machine learning, and epidemiology. We conclude by discussing specific initiatives that could foster such a culture of data sharing and open collaboration. Through these efforts, we aim to create a more robust evidence base that will inform future public health policies. This will ultimately lead to improved environmental quality and better public health outcomes. Our work is grounded in the principles of Open Science, which we believe is vital for advancing scientific knowledge and society. This includes ensuring research reproducibility, promoting transparency, and adhering to ethical standards. We believe that Open Science serves as a foundational element for the future of air pollution research. We present a theoretical investigation into tunneling spectroscopy involving Ohmic dissipation, which arises from electric resistance within the leads. This effect manifests as an exponential attenuation of the tunneling current's voltage derivative, characterized by $\exp(-\frac{\pi \delta T}{4})$, where $T$ denotes temperature and $\delta = eV_{bias}/\hbar\omega_c$ represents the ratio of tunnel voltage to the electron plasma frequency. Our analysis demonstrates that both Andreev and quasiparticle tunneling current voltages exhibit this exponential suppression. Notably, Andreev tunneling current voltage maintains a derivative of $2$ while displaying this damping behavior. We posit that this distinctive characteristic of Andreev tunneling current voltage could serve as a valuable tool for detecting the Majorana zero mode peak. Furthermore, we examine the impact of energy smearing caused by contact resistance on this exponential signature. Finally, we outline an experimental strategy to differentiate between Andreev and quasiparticle tunneling current voltage derivatives and discuss the viability of observing this exponential behavior in realistic experimental settings. We conclude that measurements capable of observing this exponential characteristics are feasible with current technology. Additionally, we explore the implications of these findings for recent tunneling experiments conducted on Majorana nanowires. Specifically, we illustrate that the observed exponential characteristics in those experiments can be interpreted as evidence supporting the existence of Majorana modes at the ends of the nanowire. Finally, we address the possibility of observing this exponential behavior in cases where Majorana modes do not exist. If future tunneling experiments successfully detect this specific exponential behavior, it would strongly suggest the presence of Majorana modes. Conversely, the absence of this behavior would imply that Majorana modes are either absent or their peak is not sharp enough to produce a detectable exponential effect. Overall, we believe that incorporating the influence of lead resistance into tunneling experiments is crucial for both verifying the existence of Majorana modes and refining our understanding of tunneling transport in Majorana nanowires. Linear bandit algorithms typically suffer from high regret when facing large or infinite action spaces, as their confidence intervals become excessively wide. This limitation stems from the standard assumption of a low-dimensional loss function, which causes estimated reward vectors to be overly confident, resulting in sub-optimal regret bounds. Conversely, high-dimensional loss functions are better suited for complex action spaces but currently lack effective confidence intervals. This work introduces novel high-dimensional linear bandit algorithms that achieve superior exploration, producing tighter confidence intervals and tighter regret bounds. Notably, these algorithms support valid statistical inference by enabling the calculation of p-values for action-specific reward estimates post-deployment. To our knowledge, p-values have not been previously derived in the bandit context. We empirically validate the empirical and theoretical guarantees of our proposed methods and demonstrate their utility in a real-world deployment scenario. Our results indicate that these algorithms can identify up to 100% more arms than existing state-of-the-art approaches, yielding significant business value. Furthermore, we show that while our methods may achieve slightly higher regret, they explore more actions over time, leading to greater diversity in selected arms and reduced uncertainty. Finally, we illustrate how this exploration over time facilitates action selection, resulting in improved outcomes. Overall, our work offers a promising solution for high-dimensional bandit problems characterized by complex action spaces. Although the orbital Hall effect in time-reversal symmetric systems is challenging to detect, we demonstrate that in gapped graphene, it manifests equivalently to the valley Hall effect in terms of charge transport. This finding stems from the unique angular dependence of the Berry curvature near high-symmetry $k$ points, which results in an orbital Hall coefficient that is independent of momentum. Consequently, the orbital Hall effect in gapped graphene can be investigated without the complexities associated with carrier doping. Furthermore, we illustrate a method to isolate the valley Hall effect by leveraging its distinct odd parity relative to the Berry curvature at $K$ points compared to its even parity at $K'$ points. Finally, we outline a setup to measure the orbital magnetization in gapped graphene by breaking time-reversal symmetry through a uniform in-plane electric field. Notably, this orbital magnetization displays a non-monotonic dependence on the gap, peaking at a specific gap value that is significantly larger than any band-gap opening induced by spin-orbit coupling in real materials. These characteristics provide promising avenues for detecting the valley Hall effect and exploring orbital Hall phenomena in gapped graphene. Additionally, our proposed techniques for measuring orbital Hall phenomena and orbital magnetization may be applicable to other condensed matter systems. Specifically, we anticipate that the valley Hall effect in graphene can be measured via the anomalous Hall effect observed in hand-bent monolayer devices. Finally, we suggest that the valley Hall effect in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides may be directly observable through the anomalous Hall effect. These proposals aim to advance the field of orbital and valley physics. Finally, our methodology for measuring orbital Hall phenomena and orbital magnetization can be utilized to investigate these phenomena in other gapped two-dimensional systems. Notably, the non-monotonic variation of orbital magnetization with respect to the gap in gapped graphene may serve as a valuable tool for detecting time-reversal symmetry breaking in orbital order. This approach could address a longstanding debate regarding whether orbital magnetism in cuprates arises from ferromagnetic ordering of in-plane or out-of-plane orbitals. Additionally, the orbital Hall effect in gapped graphene could be measured as a function of a uniform in-plane electric field, thereby testing the orbital anisotropy. These findings are expected to significantly advance the study of orbital and valley physics. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are machine learning models specifically engineered for processing data on graphs, demonstrating strong performance in fields like chemistry and physics. However, their performance can be severely compromised when training and testing datasets contain connected nodes, as demonstrated by an attack strategy where malicious nodes are linked to legitimate ones. This paper investigates whether reinforcement learning can facilitate data contamination within GNN datasets. We formulate this task as a game between a GNN classifier and a data contaminator, representing it as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). Our primary contribution involves training a policy network using deep reinforcement learning to identify effective contamination strategies. Experimental results validate this approach across various graph datasets, chemical reaction datasets, and text classification tasks. Furthermore, we observe that the trained policy generalizes to test cases it has never encountered during training. These findings suggest that the dataset collection and labeling processes for graph-based data require significant scrutiny. Finally, we highlight the potential of deep reinforcement learning in creating novel game representations and offer suggestions for future research. This work was presented at the 15th International Conference on Applications of Game Theory to Banking and Network Problems (2022). Catalogue matching serves as a critical method for assigning metallic labels to individual stars, a process that relies on aligning observations from multiple surveys. This paper introduces a technique to augment the photometric dimensions of two stellar catalogues by applying a multi-dimensional regression to a third, deeper catalogue. We demonstrate that this approach surpasses traditional methods in catalogue matching, thereby increasing the number of stars that can be reliably matched across the datasets. Furthermore, we illustrate the application of this method to a pair of stellar catalogues and evaluate the resulting impact on the count of stars assigned metallic labels. Additionally, we show how the proposed method can be leveraged to identify and remove spurious matches. Our analysis indicates that incorporating the additional information provides confidence levels of 99% or higher for both matched and non-matched star pairs. Additionally, we observe that the majority of stars in our test catalogues possess three or more available dimensions, suggesting that extending this technique to include further catalogue dimensions could enhance the accuracy of the matching process. Ontologies serve as formal models for concepts and their interrelations, typically visualized through Directed Graphs. However, these graphs can become cluttered and difficult to interpret when the number of concepts grows large. This study demonstrates that ontology graphs can be transformed into Directed Acyclic Graphs to enable efficient layout and large-scale visualization via the Directed-Acyclic-Graph-Based Overlay Plot (DAP). We present OntoPlot, a tool that automatically generates visualizations from user-defined ontology graphs. This system allows researchers to quickly identify the core structure of the ontology and examine intricate relationships between individual concepts. Furthermore, interactive features in OntoPlot support the exploration of association patterns. Experimental results indicate that the visualization method produces clear images that are easy to interpret, even for ontologies containing thousands of concepts. Additionally, user studies confirm that OntoPlot is highly effective for visualizing and analyzing large ontologies. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenTao2018/OntoPlot. A live demo is available here: https://chen- Tao2018.github.io/DemoOntoPlot/. The complete paper can be found at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.01001.

We introduce a method for enhancing speech data for the training of low-resource automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems by employing CycleGAN. This approach enables the transformation of speech data from one language into either the target language for supervised ASR or into another language without a target for semi-supervised inter-domain ASR. To facilitate this process, we incorporate an intermediate domain and define a loss function that ensures the generated speech maintains high perceptual quality while diverging structurally from both input languages. Experiments conducted on isolated and continuous Spanish sentences, as well as on Hebrew ASR, demonstrate the efficacy of CycleGAN in generating speech data that is both structurally and perceptually distinct from the original. Furthermore, these results highlight the method's potential utility for ASR tasks across different languages. Finally, we discuss the approach's limitations and outline directions for future research. This study represents the initial effort to integrate generative adversarial networks (GANs) into the field of ASR. Standard deep neural network models for robot navigation depend on static, fixed-class labels, which are insufficient for dynamic scenes. To address this, a natural solution involves incorporating queryable, variable classes that can be identified and queried during inference. However, the joint learning of both variable class embeddings and their representations within a deep neural network remains unresolved. This study introduces a straightforward and effective method to resolve this issue by utilizing active prediction to learn deep representations for variable classes within a deep neural network. This approach enables the reliable detection of new classes that were not present during training without compromising the performance of standard classes. We assess the efficacy of our method in both controlled settings and real-world scenarios, demonstrating the creation of robust and queryable deep active classes suitable for autonomous robot navigation. Specifically, we have developed a variable class detector capable of querying up to 20 new classes with a 90% detection rate. Furthermore, we show that these deep active classes can be effectively used for object detection and tracking in autonomous navigation. This study investigates the contribution of internal degrees of freedom in flexible molecules to the Soret effect. Through non-thermal molecular dynamics simulations, we observed that the internal relaxation time associated with vibrational modes is more critical to Soret coefficient enhancement than the average rotational relaxation time. This significance is assessed by comparing it to the reduction in the Soret coefficient resulting from the suppression of concentration gradients. Furthermore, we established a relationship between the Soret coefficient and internal relaxation times, demonstrating that internal degrees of freedom substantially amplify the Soret coefficient. Finally, we analyzed the coupling between rotational and vibrational modes to explain how internal modes contribute to the Soret effect. These findings offer valuable insights for the rational design of efficient thermal anti-concentration materials. Additionally, the proposed theoretical framework for calculating the Soret coefficient is expected to advance the theoretical understanding of thermal fractionation. This research holds significance for advancing the theoretical comprehension of thermal fractionation and optimizing the separation efficiency of flexible molecules under a temperature gradient. We anticipate these results will facilitate the development of efficient thermal separation membranes. Moreover, the study may inspire new approaches to designing thermal separation membranes. Specifically, the use of non-thermal molecular dynamics simulations to investigate thermal phenomena is expected to yield valuable insights into the thermal properties of membranes. Furthermore, the insights gained regarding the influence of internal degrees of freedom on the Soret coefficient are anticipated to provide a theoretical basis for the rational design of membranes with high thermal selectivity. Finally, the computational methods employed in this work could be applied to other thermal phenomena, thereby broadening the scope of thermal research. Specifically, molecular dynamics simulations can be utilized to study the effects of internal degrees of freedom on the diffusion coefficient, thermal conductivity, and thermal viscosity of molecules. Additionally, the calculation method for the Soret coefficient presented in this work can be applied to other flexible molecules to determine their Soret coefficients. False positives are a critical challenge in domain adaptive pedestrian detection, where performance degradation is primarily driven by background clutter. This paper box re-ranking (BR) is a method designed to mitigate false positives caused by background interference. As an unsupervised approach, BR is domain-adaptive and transferable; it identifies background regions and constructs a dataset of false positive boxes. This dataset is used to train a re-ranking network that generates a confidence vector for each region, subsequently merging high-confidence vectors to produce a final result map. Our findings indicate that while FauxThrow is easily mistaken for standard throwing actions by both machine learning models and humans, its distinct characteristics offer potential utility. Additionally, it proves valuable for generating annotated training sets, thereby supporting the development of more robust machine learning models. This approach, which leverages a tree-structured language grammar, is grounded in the observation that high-quality MT output should align with valid syntactic rules. The binding energy (BE) of molecules onto dust grains is a critical parameter governing the formation and destruction of ice mantles on interstellar dust, which significantly influences both astrochemical modeling and observational data analysis. However, existing literature offers only partial coverage of this parameter, with substantial gaps in data availability. This study introduces the Binding Energy Assessment Platform (BEAP), an open-access online database that compiles a comprehensive collection of binding energy distributions derived from quantum chemical calculations. By synthesizing research from prior studies, BEAP offers users binding energy values for all relevant sites on a standard Lennard-Jones 12-6 dust grain, alongside associated error margins. These datasets were generated using the Density Functional Theory (DFT) method via the M06-2X/def2-TZVP level of theory. The platform currently hosts data for over 100 species, with a more extensive list slated for release soon. This work details the methodology behind the BEAP database and provides a demonstration of its utility. The site is accessible at http://beap.chem.ucl.ac.uk. Future developments will involve automating the generation of binding energy values using the BEAP platform in conjunction with high-throughput DFT calculations. Additionally, the platform will be expanded to include a broader array of computational methods and basis sets, thereby facilitating a more thorough assessment of the various factors influencing BE values. Furthermore, binding energy data will soon be made available for additional dust grain models. The authors welcome collaboration from the community to enhance the platform's capabilities and encourage users to submit their own binding energy data for inclusion. Contributions can be made by following the submission instructions available at http://beap.chem.ucl.ac.uk/contribute. This paper explores the generation of "shallow shadows," a compact representation of highly mixed quantum states that enables the efficient estimation of typical expectation values for observables with sparse support. A primary motivation for developing this scheme is its potential application in benchmarking large-scale quantum processors. We demonstrate that a pure quantum state can be represented as a very noisy state, where the noise is modeled as the result of applying random Clifford unitals of low depth to a fully mixed state. The efficacy of these shallow shadows in estimating "atypical" expectation values is also examined. Furthermore, we establish an efficient procedure for constructing shallow shadows that are diagonal in the Floquet basis, which is particularly valuable for ground state representations within the Haldane model. Finally, we derive an upper bound on the number of distinct shadow sets required to approximately cover the purifications of a target state $\rho$. This bound is shown to be exponential in the sparsity of $\rho$ when $\rho$ is defined on a one-dimensional lattice. These findings offer new insights into the structure of general quantum states and facilitate new methods for the efficient estimation of expectation values. Additionally, they suggest that shallow shadows can serve as a tool for characterizing large quantum circuits and for characterizing noise-affected states that deviate from maximum entropy. Our results also provide a lower bound on the number of shadows necessary to cover the purifications of thermal states for certain systems. These outcomes are derived by building upon and extending existing results on quantum typicality and thermal typicality. In this work, we extend these concepts to encompass general quantum states. We also examine various strategies for constructing shallow shadows, including approaches based on Pauli and Heisenberg group algebras. Finally, we explore potential applications of these findings to characterizing noisy quantum circuits. This involves analyzing the properties of shadows derived from circuits composed of two-qubit gates that are diagonal in the Floquet basis. We show that such shadows can provide a complete characterization of the relevant states. We conclude by discussing several open questions and potential future research directions. Our analysis indicates that shallow shadows offer a promising new tool for quantum state tomography and may facilitate the development of more efficient algorithms for quantum state learning. Ensuring robustness is vital for text classification to prevent adversarial attacks. Although data augmentation is a common strategy for enhancing robustness, it often results in performance drops on unseen data. This paper presents Sibyl, a novel framework that enhances both the accuracy and robustness of standard text classifiers without requiring data augmentation. Sibyl employs a unique architecture that integrates standard classifiers with a novel Sibyl network, which is trained in an end-to-end manner. Within the Sibyl component, a self-supervised attention mechanism is utilized to strengthen the model's ability to capture contextual information. By leveraging this self-supervised approach, Sibyl can detect anomalies in input data, such as perturbed words caused by adversarial variations. Additionally, Sibyl features a dedicated module for identifying out-of-vocabulary terms, a capability that conventional classifiers lack. Experimental results demonstrate that Sibyl boosts the robustness of conventional classifiers by 10% on Twitter data and by approximately 15% on benchmark datasets including SNLI, RACE, and RTE. Furthermore, Sibyl lowers prediction error rates on the perturbed test sets of these same datasets by an average of 15%. To the best of our knowledge, Sibyl represents the first Sibyl-based Sibylvariant modification, a concept we introduce to describe Sibyl's capacity to generate robust classifiers that outperform standard methods. The source code is available at https://github.com/DeepMind/sibyl-classifier. Our findings indicate that Sibyl offers a straightforward yet effective alternative to data augmentation for improving general NLP classifier robustness. Meta-learning has recently become a highly promising approach for addressing data scarcity in machine learning. Typically, it employs task-based splitting, where individual tasks are defined by specific parameter initializations for non-parametric metric-based retrieval. This paper presents an alternative meta-learning framework that treats task definitions as linear transformations of global parameters, thereby enabling a more direct generalization analysis. We further demonstrate the method's effectiveness through an application to support vector machines. Notably, our approach not only matches state-of-the-art performance but also offers rigorous insights into the generalization errors of metric-based methods. Specifically, we show that simple metric methods can be proven to fail in low-dimensional, high-dimensional per-class settings, a phenomenon we illustrate empirically. In contrast, our method successfully learns linear transformations that adapt global parameters, effectively resolving these critical issues. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of generalization errors for our method, revealing that while it exhibits favorable error bounds, it still faces similar generalization challenges in extreme scenarios. Finally, we highlight that our framework is broadly applicable to various learning tasks, including kernel methods, neural networks, and reinforcement learning, with a current extension implemented for wide neural networks. Overall, this work establishes a foundation for future research aimed at enhancing the theoretical understanding of meta-learning. Code is available at: https://github.com/maartenwv/vm. Recent strides in neural machine translation (MNT) have yielded strong performance on high-resource datasets, yet developing and deploying effective models for low-resource languages remains difficult. Multilingual machine translation (MMT) offers a solution by enabling the sharing of linguistic resources across multiple languages; however, this approach typically results in heavier models and slower inference speeds. To address these issues, researchers are exploring methods to transfer the knowledge of large MMT models into smaller, single-language systems. This paper examines two primary distillation techniques: quantization and student-teacher knowledge distillation. Our analysis focuses on maintaining both the performance and fluency of single-language models, particularly for low-resource languages. We evaluate MT models under various conditions, including different source languages, model sizes, and multiple hyperparameters. Our findings indicate that while quantization and standard distillation outperform low-resource baseline models, they fail to match the quality of high-resource MT. In contrast, student-teacher knowledge distillation (KDD) specifically designed for low-resource MT achieves state-of-the-art results. Furthermore, low-rank adaptation (LRA) proves effective in preserving high distillation performance. Finally, we observe that the stability of distillation methods varies significantly depending on the language pair. We anticipate these insights will guide future efforts in low-resource distillation. The code and data for this work are available at: https://github.com/abhi-1999/Comparing-the-Stability-of-Quantization-and-KD-towards-Lightweight-Low-Resource-MT. We introduce a "single-hypergraph" theory characterized by an "illogical" Lagrangian density, which relies exclusively on first derivatives of hyperfields and is constructed without reference to relativistic mechanics. This density is a linear combination of three distinct terms: the first term yields a non-zero result only when a hyperfield of rank three or higher interacts with others of any rank; the second term causes the theory to be conformal; the third term renders the theory scale-invariant. Consequently, this "illogical" Lagrangian density can be derived from more fundamental principles. The theory generically possesses a U(1) gauge symmetry, though specific configurations of hyperfields may exhibit additional symmetries. Furthermore, in certain special cases, the theory aligns with a form of generalized cosmological physics. We conclude by outlining the main open problems of the theory and proposing a mathematical conjecture. The material presented is intended for readers with a strong background in both mathematics and physics. New results and perspectives are expected to be of interest not only to researchers in high-energy physics and quantum field theory but also to those in mathematics and theoretical physics more broadly. Additionally, the paper may serve as a supplementary resource for physics graduate students. This work serves as a sequel to our prior study: [arXiv:2109.00204 [hep-th]]. We are confident that a diverse array of readers will find the subject matter intriguing and inspiring. Additionally, we anticipate that various questions and comments from the mathematical community will prove valuable and enriching. We welcome and appreciate contributions from mathematicians, as we believe that new and exciting results lie ahead when mathematics and physics are deeply intertwined. Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled zero-shot image captioning with state-of-the-art performance. However, current one-shot models are limited to producing only a single caption per image, lacking the ability to generate multiple, diverse descriptions of the same content. To address this, we introduce prompt tuning as a new technique for one-shot image captioning, which surpasses fine-tuning approaches by requiring fewer parameters and demonstrating superior performance. Specifically, we demonstrate that simple promptings can effectively leverage powerful LLMs for one-shot image captioning. By employing an optimization strategy that maximizes prediction diversity, we successfully control the variability of generated captions, achieving both high diversity and strong coherence. Experimental results indicate that prompt tuning outperforms fine-tuning in both coherence and diversity metrics, as well as in human evaluation scores. Furthermore, our proposed promptings can be extended to controlled one-shot image captioning, a task that has not yet been explored. These results highlight the potential of prompt tuning in one-shot image captioning and provide a foundation for future research in this area. This work introduces a novel causal framework for analyzing harm and harmlessness, distinguishing between direct and indirect harm. The framework relies on a specific structure concerning the minimization of causal values (such as death, injury, or damage) and employs a corresponding solution method. We provide examples to demonstrate why this solution approach is appropriate, and our framework aligns with an existing ethical model by Brueckner (2019). The proposed framework is designed to guide machine learning systems—particularly those influencing human lives, such as autonomous vehicles and diagnostic tools—in making decisions that are both rational and morally sound. We illustrate this application using a causal diagram of an autonomous vehicle's decision-making process, where the vehicle must choose between harming an object or preventing harm by deviating from its path. Additionally, we present two case studies: one on a diagnostic system's harm evaluation and another on a machine translation system's harmlessness. Finally, we outline several avenues for future research. This paper serves as a survey and introduction to harm and harmlessness within a causal context. By bridging concepts from diverse fields—including ethics, law, cognitive science, and machine learning—we aim to advance both theoretical understanding and the development of related technologies. Specifically, this research supports the creation of harm assessment methods for causal models and provides a foundation for applying these methods to evaluate harm in actual datasets. Furthermore, this project seeks to unify various existing approaches to harm across different domains into a single, cohesive structure. Finally, the work addresses challenges in defining harm for causal models that capture real-world phenomena and explores methods for quantifying harm using data. These contributions are essential for developing machines and systems capable of reasoning about harm and utilizing this capability to enhance human lives. To achieve this, we have established a multi-disciplinary research group focused on Causal Reasoning for Harm (CaReHa), which integrates insights from ethics, law, cognitive science, and machine learning. Voice translation handles multilingual speech processing by simultaneously translating and converting speech from a source language to a target language. Conventional methods rely on parallel audio data from the source-target pair, a requirement that hinders practical applications due to data scarcity. To address this, we introduce a zero-shot setting for voice translation, which is the first such approach proposed in this domain. Our system effectively leverages unpaired, pair-wise mismatched data through a novel conditioning mechanism that integrates audio features with a conditioned phonological representation to enable accurate translation. Furthermore, the proposed architecture ensures stable training and enhances character-level translation performance. Experimental results demonstrate an average improvement of 1.5% in character error rate (CER) compared to prior methods.
